title: Allegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrative | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Duchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claims
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Duchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claims
Content: The future King Charles walked Meghan down the aisle at her wedding in 2018, after Thomas Markle Sr withdrew for health reasons. She became estranged from her father in the months afterwards.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenThe future King Charles walked Meghan down the aisle at her wedding in 2018, after Thomas Markle Sr withdrew for health reasons. She became estranged from her father in the months afterwards.Photograph: APMeghan, the Duchess of SussexAnalysisAllegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrativeCaroline DaviesDuchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claimsMeghan ‘deeply distressed’ by allegations against fatherFri 23 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.11 EDTShareThe depiction of the Duchess of Sussex by certain sections of the media has often been one of a fame-hungry daughter casting off an elderly father in his declining years and keeping him from his grandchildren as she embraces the international celebrity stage.Their estrangement has been the subject of countless headlines since her marriage to Prince Harry. But her statement today, released afterchild sexual abuse image allegations made against Thomas Markle Sr, 82, suggests deeper, darker fears as the cause.“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said.It has been speculated that the source of the estrangement between Meghan and Markle Sr, an award-winning TV lighting director, was over his decision to collude with a photographer and be paid for setting up shots of him preparing to attend the Sussexes’ wedding at Windsor Castle where he was due to walk her down the aisle.Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against fatherRead moreIn the end, Markle Sr pulled out of the wedding due to health issues, and it was Harry’s father, now King Charles, who lent the bride his arm on her final steps to the altar of St George’s chapel after she walked the first part of the aisle alone.Since that day in May 2018, the relationship between daughter and father has never recovered. Now it appears the reasons why are contained in a letter from the same year, sent to the Metropolitan police and containing “troubling and disturbing allegations” against Markle Sr and shared with Meghan in the summer after her wedding.View image in fullscreenThomas Markle Sr on ITV’s Good Morning Britain in June 2018.Photograph: ReutersThe precise nature of those allegations has not been clarified, though they were enough for Meghan to want to keep her own family at a distance from him, her statement makes clear.The fact she says that “the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine”, suggests the 2018 letter did not go as far as what has now been alleged.Markle Sr has vigorously denied the latest allegations, which are made by his son Thomas Markle Jr, 60. First published by the Sun newspaper, they claim Markle Sr downloaded child sexual abuse images to computers and mobile phones found at his former home in the Philippines.He has called the accusations “sick lies” from a son with whom he has a troubled relationship, and claims to have had no access to the computers and phones in question in the two years since he left Mexico, where he was previously living, for the Philippines, according to the Daily Mail.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Mail on Sunday’s 2025 story about Meghan’s father making a plea for her to visit him.Photograph: The Mail on SundayMeghan clearly hopes to reframe the narrative of her estrangement from her father, which has often been shaped by his loquacious tendencies in many media interviews.When speaking to journalists, Markle Sr has frequently lamented the breakdown of his relationship with his youngest daughter (he has two other children, Samantha Markle and Thomas Jr, from an earlier marriage). He has spoken of how he has been unable to reach Meghan, and of how he has never been allowed to meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.The media depiction has often leaned towards that of an uncaring daughter, whose father paid for her education, helped her to cultivate her interest in acting through his television work,and found himself abandoned in his time of need.For the most part, Meghan has not publicly acknowledged his many health woes – he has suffered a series of strokes and recently had a leg amputated due to complications with a blood clot – and she clearly believes this has been weaponised against her.However, in 2025, Meghan’s spokesperson confirmed that the duchess had “reached out” privately to her father when he was hospitalised and very unwell. He is now understood to be in a rehabilitation centre in Florida undergoing physiotherapy after the amputation of his leg.Whatever the outcome of this latest development, it adds a new dimension to the complicated, fractured relationship between Meghan and her family.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchyThe SunNational newspapersNewspapers & magazinesPrivacy & the mediaPress intrusionanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet | John Crace | The Guardian
description: PM and the Liverpool mayor prove to be naturals at watching TV, with a genuine connection and sense of fun
Author: John Crace
Headline: PM and the Liverpool mayor prove to be naturals at watching TV, with a genuine connection and sense of fun
Content: The Liverpool mayor, Steve Rotheram, and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on the No 10 sofa.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetView image in fullscreenThe Liverpool mayor, Steve Rotheram, and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on the No 10 sofa.Photograph: Simon Dawson/No 10 Downing StreetThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamAndy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bulletJohn CracePM and the Liverpool mayor prove to be naturals at watching TV, with a genuine connection and sense of funFri 23 Oct 2026 19.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.17 EDTShareOn nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about whattheyare watching on TV.Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer.Andy Burnhamhas requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money.Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.”You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme.The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her onGoggleboxthe only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US.‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV showRead moreMind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood.If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect.“The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People.Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception.“I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs.But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination.For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence.Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor.We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room.“You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove.Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom.Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchGoggleboxcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tinned mackerel, hand-crank radios and bags for poo: crisis-prepping guides around the world | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: UK allies have long urged people to stockpile supplies for a crisis. How are people from France to Australia being advised to prepare?
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: UK allies have long urged people to stockpile supplies for a crisis. How are people from France to Australia being advised to prepare?
Content: Staples recommended for emergency larders around the world include pasta and grains.Photograph: pundapanda/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStaples recommended for emergency larders around the world include pasta and grains.Photograph: pundapanda/Getty ImagesEmergency planningTinned mackerel, hand-crank radios and bags for poo: crisis-prepping guides around the worldUK allies have long urged people to stockpile supplies for a crisis. How are people from France to Australia being advised to prepare?Ajit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has told people tofill their pantries with food for three daysin case of catastrophe, joining a host of countries urging citizens to ready themselves for core systems failing.Such advice, once dismissed as the preserve ofpreppers, has become more common in government circles as climate breakdown worsens weather extremes and geopolitical tensions turn cyber-attacks and sabotage into a regular occurrence.Oats, sardines and crisps: emergency foods to stockpile – and why you should share themRead moreEven in countries with national strategic food stockpiles – a bufferthe UK lacks– authorities have asked individuals to play their part in societal resilience.What actions do Britain’s allies – from the US andEuropeto India and Australia – recommend people take before disaster strikes?FranceFrance calls the first 72 hours a “decisive period” in which people should monitor TV and radio news for official updates, and keep an emergency kit close by in case they have to get out fast.In addition to the essentials, such as food, water, medicine and cash, theguidelinesrecommend filling the go-bag with photocopies of documents, spare sets of house and car keys, and even games to pass the time.The strategy emphasises the need for solidarity and calls on people to be in close communication with loved ones, resist rumours and disinformation, and consider volunteering as a reservist or with civil protection organisations. Experts have warned thatmaintaining societal cohesionis crucial during crises.View image in fullscreenPeople around the world are being advised to have enough water to last several days.Photograph: Inna Dodor/AlamyGermanyAs far back as the 1960s, households in WestGermanywere encouraged to stockpile 14 days of canned food – a target that few seem to have reached despite cold war tensions.About a decade ago, the recommendation fell to 10 days, andguidanceissued last October said households should do this “where possible”, describing even three days’ worth of supplies as “a big help”. Almost half of Germans fail to meet this threshold, a YouGov poll for the German Press Agency found in January.Guidelines from the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance recommend stockpiling durable foods that are ready to eat, in case cookers stop working, and foods that have short cooking times, allowing fuel for a camping stove to last for more days in a blackout.The checklist of items also features a hand-crank or solar-powered radio, a paper list of important phone numbers, and a well-stocked medicine cabinet.USThe US emergency readiness campaign, launched in 2003, recommends people “make a plan today”, noting that members of a family may not be together when disaster strikes.Itstoolkitforesees people storing enough water for each person to have one US gallon (3.8 litres) a day, both for drinking and sanitation, as well as items such as a whistle to call for help, a dust mask to filter contaminated air and plastic sheeting for shelter.Food supply advice varies between states, ranging from a few days in California to more than two weeks in Hawaii.The guidance suggests families rethink the contents of the kit each year as their needs change. It also calls for storing supplies at home, at work and in the car.View image in fullscreenA display on emergency preparedness in Oregon.Photograph: Gina Kelly/AlamyThe NordicsNordic countries haveramped up emergency preparationssince Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.TheFinnish advicedescribes home emergency supplies, including backup power and hygiene articles, as an “excellent basis” for many situations, while warning against hoarding.It recommends people have enough for at least three days and says these supplies can help even when mundane obstacles such as illness keep one from going to the shops.Secure silos of grain that make up Finland’s ample strategic reserve provide an extra layer of security, designed to feed the population for nine months if supply chains collapse or domestic production fails.View image in fullscreenTinned fish in a Coles supermarket in Melbourne.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianTheSwedish advice, which is framed around conflict but also covers pandemics and extreme weather, says people can “contribute to collective preparedness” if they can manage on their own for at least one week.It includes specific tips such as growing berries on windowsills, freezing bottles of water, which can function as ice packs if freezers break and then be drunk once the ice melts, and, if the toilet will not flush, disposing of excrement in plastic bags covered by sawdust.Finland is ready for the next crisis, with stockpiled food and 72-hour kits – Europe should be too | Miika IlomäkiRead moreTheNorwegian guidelines, which are offered in 30 languages, also encourage people to be able to “fend for themselves” for at least a week when systems such as the internet, mobile phone networks and bank payments are down.The country is particularly reliant on electricity for home heating, and recommends people store warm clothes, sleeping bags and candles, and keep fireplaces and chimneys clean.“In a crisis or war, people must be prepared for the fact that not everything will work as normal,” it warns. “The help will first go to those who need it most.”TheDanish advicegives a sample three-day meal plan, which includes 500g of crispbread, 300g of canned mackerel in tomato sauce, 300g of chickpeas and kidney beans, 500g each of pasta and groats, and 1.5kg of tinned vegetables, as well as 100g of nuts and some vegetable oil.AustraliaThe Australian government can declare a national emergency but individual states and territories are mainly responsible for management.Most authorities recommend storing supplies to last three to seven days, though the New South Wales health service recommends planning for two weeks. Its “pantry list” recommends giving special consideration to family members with special needs, such as babies, pregnant women and those who are old or ill.Its fire services also have detailed guidance on preparing for bushfires, ranging from trimming vegetation to wearing a wide-brimmed hat to protect the head from falling embers and respirator masks to avoid the worst of the smoke.View image in fullscreenHave a battery-operated torch to hand.Photograph: Tassya/AlamyIndiaIndia’s disaster preparednesschecklist, prepared by the National Centre for Disease Control, recommends finding out which hazards threaten your home and finding safe spots for each type of disaster.It calls for storing at least a three-day supply of water and food, prioritising products that require little cooking or refrigeration, while avoiding very salty or spicy ones.The recommended emergency bag includes a battery-operated torch, chlorine tablets to purify water, a first aid book, and thick ropes. It recommends practising evacuation drills with all family members twice a year. The checklist also explicitly warns that the climate crisis is likely to lead to more frequent and severe disasters.UK checklistExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningClimate crisisEuropeFranceGermanyCybercrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final audition | James Bond | The Guardian
description: Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?
Content: Conjuring chemistry … Turner, Callum Turner at the 82nd Venice film festival, 2025.Photograph: Gisela Schober/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConjuring chemistry … Turner, Callum Turner at the 82nd Venice film festival, 2025.Photograph: Gisela Schober/Getty ImagesJames BondI expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final auditionJack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?Stuart HeritageFri 23 Oct 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis weekend, the identity of the nextJames Bondis finally expected to be known – to the insiders, at least. According to reports, a number of youngish British actors – definitely three, possibly five – will have their final screen tests.To say it has been a long time coming is an understatement. It is five years since Daniel Craig was killed in a hail of missiles at the end of No Time to Die, and in that time – even long before it – a swarm of actors have been tipped to replace him, only to age out of the role due to a combination of indecisiveness and cutthroat backstage corporate shenanigans. Whoever is declared to be 007 will be joining the franchise after what is likely to be the longest fallow period in the franchise’s 64-year history.10:14Who will be the next James Bond? - The LatestAs such, this is kind of a big weekend. Let’s run through what we know so far.The candidatesIf three actors are to screen test for Bond this weekend, then they are Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. If there are more – some outlets state that one other actor might be participating, others two – then they won’t include Jack O’Connell orJacob Elordi, who are both out of the race for one reason or another.The identity of the other actors are not yet known. Let’s take an uneducated guess and assume thatone of them is a Beatle(the best fit is Harris Dickinson) and another one is more famous but less suitable (like Tom Cruise).View image in fullscreenI spy … Jack Lowden at the Golden Globe awards, 2025.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/REX/ShutterstockThe screen testOutlets are reporting that the screen test will encompass three main elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. These are all equally important for a modern Bond. Remove stunts from the equation and your film will be boring. Remove camera presence and you’re likely to end up with a George Lazenby type, who has the potential to fluff what would otherwise be an all-timer. Remove dialogue and you’re left with Quantum of Solace, and God knows we don’t need another one of those.The chancesYou could argue that Jack Lowden is the frontrunner, if only because the first scene of the first episode ofSlow Horseswas a pretty good Bond audition in itself. It was, you’ll remember, a race against time sprint through an airport and train station, on foot and in a car, complete with hand-to-hand combat and gun play. And it was very good indeed. Working against him is the sense that he’s a bit too much of a teddy bear for a sociopath like Bond. Plus the fact that he has spent every subsequent scene of Slow Horses doing a pretty good Simon Pegg impression.Callum Turner would seem to make a sexier Bond, partly because he was able to conjure chemistry from the very sillysex purge movie One Night Only, and partly because he’s married to Dua Lipa, who would almost certainly get the role of Bond Girl Who Dies First if he were cast.View image in fullscreenLooks good … Josh O’Connor at the premiere of Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, Los Angeles, 2025.Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/ShutterstockI still think Josh O’Connor would be the best fit, though. He looks good in a tux, as anyone who has seen The Crown will testify. He is very good at convincingly delivering absolute nonsense, as anyone who has seenDisclosure Daywill testify. However, his best-known stunt work must be the long scene inThe Mastermindin which he slowly climbs up and down a ladder several times in a row.What’s missing?Now, this is all well and good for a traditional Bond film. But we’re talking about an Amazon Bond film, directed byDenis Villeneuve. This means that more will be asked of whoever gets the role, and the screen tests are the perfect way to see if they can pull it off.For example, which of the finalists will best be able to carry their voice in such a way that it isn’t drowned out by all the seat-rumbling full-volume honking noises that Villeneuve will almost certainly use instead of a traditional soundtrack? Which of the actors will most convincingly be able to interact with a side character created with the express purpose of carrying their own spin-off series, to better sustain cross-media IP synergy? Which of them will least overtly die on the inside during the scene in which an Amazon drone delivers them a gun? That is the stuff that will really make or break James Bond going forward.Explore more on these topicsJames BondJacob ElordiJack O'ConnellJosh O'ConnorJack LowdenDenis VilleneuveSlow HorsesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Swoon! London City Ballet are positively glowing in a night of dreams – and ghosts from dance history | Dance | The Guardian
description: Alina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherish
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Alina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherish
Content: Very fine … Ellie Young and Joseph Taylor in Firebird.Photograph: ASHView image in fullscreenVery fine … Ellie Young and Joseph Taylor in Firebird.Photograph: ASHDanceReviewSwoon! London City Ballet are positively glowing in a night of dreams – and ghosts from dance historySadler’s Wells, LondonAlina Cojocaru astonishes in John Neumeier’s Ghost Light, an ethereal meditation on time, while Glen Tetley’s Firebird has much to cherishLyndsey WinshipFri 23 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAghost light is the name for a single lamp left on stage when a theatre is dark, and one glows throughout John Neumeier’s ballet Ghost Light. Also never not glowing isAlina Cojocaru, superlative ballerina and guest dancer with London City Ballet, who has a longtime working relationship with Neumeier and his Hamburg Ballet – with whom this work was originally created in 2020.When Cojocaru materialises onstage in silence, so ethereal it’s almost mystical, she is like a ghost of Swan Lake’s Odette, wings fluttering, eyes half closed, lost in a memory. Cojocaru’s divine delicacy embodies all of the romance of ballet, until suddenly her steps glitch, she stumbles over a chair and comes to. The stage is a place of dreams, for all the dancers who have crossed its boards and will continue to do so (superstition says that ghost lamps also allow spirits of former dancers to return to the stage). Neumeier evokes some of these dances in this piece, from a stray sylph upstage, to earnest solos, sparky allegro and two young men in a tender duet, passing each other sometimes in parallel worlds, sometimes in moments of connection.View image in fullscreenTime and its circularity … Joseph Taylor and Alina Cojocaru in Ghost Light.Photograph: ASHThe parts of this ballet were created separately during Covid with bubbles of dancers, a practical measure. But the result is actually a beautiful rendering of the passage of time and its circularity – of dance’s, and dancers’, evolution. Neumeier, at 87, has seen his fair share of stages – likewise Cojocaru, now 45, who always brings real poignancy.This mighty cry for a goddess to help Earth proves Dickson Mbi is a bold force in danceRead moreIt’s only three years since this new version ofLondon City Balletformed and the company is looking very fine. A major strand of its USP is piecing back together forgotten ballets and tonight that’s the late Glen Tetley’s Firebird (1981), celebrating Tetley’s centenary. An impressive Ellie Young dances the Firebird character, in this case a young woman ostracised from her austere family, who finds a partner in Joseph Taylor – and what a great partner he is: strong, lyrical and so attentive.Tetley was a bridge between ballet and modern dance and the company pays exacting attention to form, in swift, clean steps and emotive expression. The narrative may be fuzzy, and the final scene – with its glorious Stravinsky score – nowhere near as majestic as in Michel Fokine’s (and designer Natalia Goncharova’s) version, but there is much to cherish here.AtSadler’s Wells, London, until 24 October.Touringuntil 6 DecemberExplore more on these topicsDanceBalletSadler's WellsAlina CojocarureviewsShareReuse this content

title: We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?  | Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow | The Guardian
description: No one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minors, say students Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: No one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minors, say students Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionChild protectionWe’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?Rose, Mae, Aylin and WillowNo one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minorsFri 23 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTShareIn the Little Feminist Book Club, we don’t read a lot of books. The group, set up by former students at our school, is more about reading poems and articles, analysing song lyrics, discussing the issues that matter to us and, most importantly, campaigning.Ourcurrent campaign– the one you might have heard of – is to ban school uniform from pornographic content. Simply put, we want to end the depiction of school uniform in pornography to ensure that minors are not viewed as anything other than what they are: children. We were shocked when we realised that this content is currently legal – most of the adults we’ve spoken to agree that it is wrong. But apparently it falls to us – students aged 14 and 15 – to take action.Anew law, due to come into force on 6 November, will ban pornography that shows sexual activity involving anyone pretending to be under 16. But it won’t outlaw the depiction of adults dressed as older schoolchildren. We want to remove this grey area in order to stop normalising the sexualisation of school uniforms. We believe children and children’s clothing should not be associated with sexual acts. Therefore, we believe that school uniform should not be shown as something “sexy”, regardless of the actual age of the person wearing it.Previous members of the Little Feminist Book Club, working withTools for Change, successfully campaigned for better access to period products in our school. We then heard about another school feminist groupwho had campaignedto get school uniforms banned from sex shops. We were appalled that they were being sold in that context, yet somehow not surprised. From an early age, some of us had noticed that school uniforms are depicted in ways that sexualise women wearing them. Mae recalls: “For me it started when I was 12, watching TV with my mother. A female character put on a school uniform to turn on a man and I thought, ‘I’m going to have to wear a uniform like that tomorrow.’”No 12-year-old should feel uncomfortable about going to school in a uniform that is designed to promote unity and community and safety. Yet we did. It made us question how we would be perceived when we left the house in our uniforms. These were women dressing up in school uniform specifically to turn on a man. The only people who should be wearing school uniform are children.This issue has affected us personally. Members of our group feel too uncomfortable to wear their uniform out of school. One no longer wears skirts at all. When we were asked to speak at a Tools for Change event in parliament in July we unanimously agreed not to wear our uniform. In a world of AI, we were well aware of the dangers of being photographed in uniform while being associated with this campaign. Before we sent our first letters to MPs and charities, we discussed what it might mean if anyone actually paid attention to what we were saying. Would we be prepared to take this on, given all that it might mean? We were, and so we did.Since starting this campaign, we have been flooded with support. Sadly, this has included other women and girls sharing their experiences of the same issue – dating back generations. Surveys show thatone in three girlshas been sexually harassed while wearing school uniform, and we have seen comments from many of them. Older women said that they have never been catcalled more than when they wore school uniform as children; others have shared with us their feelings of disgust and horror. One recalled being assaulted by a group of men in the 2000s “explicitly because of my school uniform”. A teenager said that the number of older men who sexually harass her almost every day is “uncountable”.Getting to hear people’s own personal experiences fuels our passion and drives us forward. The overwhelmingly positive response truly gives us hope that we can make a difference. We want to protect children now and in the future.As the campaign continues to gain attention, we have received support from important figures including our local MP and an MSP. One has agreed to directly passour handwritten letterto the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and to table an early day motion. We now also have a meeting scheduled with Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims, and another with Jess Asato MP and the peer Gabby Bertin, who was instrumental in the amendments to the crime and policing bill. Our MP is helping us turn our campaign into a law. He suggested that, instead of creating an entirely new law banning school uniform in pornography, it would be quicker and easier to amend existing legislation – meaning that it would take less time for children to be taken out of this harmful and dangerous position that perverted people have placed us in. But these are not decisions we can make. Everyone has a responsibility to end this cycle of sexualisation and objectification of children. We can’t do that as a few kids in the middle of our GCSEs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe have made a start by launching this petition. Now, we need the adults who vowed to protect us to get behind it. We need the politicians whopledged to halve violence against women and girlsto change the law. It’s all well and good to read this article by a group of kids explaining how we’re trying to keep ourselves safe and think this is a fantastic campaign. But that’s not enough. Things will only change when adults take responsibility for ending the disgusting practice of sexualising clothes made for children. Then perhaps one day young people can go to school knowing the only thing our uniforms signify is that it’s time to learn.Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow are students aged 14 and 15Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
