title: Online safety laws have failed to protect children in UK, Ofcom admits | Children | The Guardian
description: Campaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regime
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Campaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regime
Content: Under the Online Safety Act, tech giants had to protect children from harmful content with a series of duties introduced in summer 2025.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenUnder the Online Safety Act, tech giants had to protect children from harmful content with a series of duties introduced in summer 2025.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianChildrenOnline safety laws have failed to protect children in UK, Ofcom admitsCampaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regimeRobert BoothUK technology editorFri 23 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLandmark online safety measures have failed to limit the proportion of children suffering harm from social media, the UK’s online regulator has admitted, in an assessment branded “staggering” by campaigners.The proportion of children being fed unsafe content that often left them frightened, confused and upset, was almost unchanged, according to anOfcomreview of the first nine months of supposedly strict requirements on social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram.Under the Online Safety Act, the tech giants had to protect children from harmful content including pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny and bullying, with a series of specific duties introduced in summer 2025.But Ofcomfoundthat “at a total level there was no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content over the first nine months after the children’s safety duties came into force in July 2025”.It called the finding “concerning” and said there was no evidence indicating a change in the severity of harm since the flagship regulations, under the Online Safety Act, took effect.Examples of harms included children being shown the murder of Charlie Kirk, graphic pornography and weapon-related content making them feel unsafe in their schools and neighbourhoods. Personalised recommendation feeds powered by “for you” algorithms were repeatedly found by Ofcom to be at the root of the continuing tide of harmful material.The findings come a week after a coroner concluded that access to the suicide-related material on TikTok may have played a significant part in the decision of Adriana Retyte, a 14-year-old pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, to take her own life in May.They come a day after Clavicular, 20, a popular social media influencer who promotes surgery and drugs as part of extreme male beauty regimes and has appeared with Andrew Tate, pleaded not guilty to rape in a US court, raising fresh concerns about the influence of “manosphere” content creators.Ofcom’s research included tracking the exposure of UK children aged eight to 17 to harmful content on user-to-user services, its impact and their use of safety tools and an analysis of children’s wellbeing after exposure to harmful content. The assessment has been shared with Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport.NSPCC, a child protection charity, said the findings showed that children were being exposed to harmful content at an “alarming rate”, which it said was echoed in the flow of calls for help to Childline, its online and telephone support service. Rani Govender, the head of child safety online, said “progress is not happening nearly fast enough”.“Tech companies have had months to act, yet too many platforms are still built to keep children hooked with their algorithms continuing to push harmful content to their young users,” she said. “We urgently need stronger action from tech companies to rein in features that drive harm to children and stop putting business interests over their safety obligations.”Dame Melanie Dawes, the watchdog’s chief executive, this week told MPs: “We do not see a safety culture from these large social media companies.” The regulator is already facing a wave of legal actions from tech companies challenging its powers including the Instagram operator Meta, as well as TikTok and X, owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX group. It haswarnedit risks being “absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms”.Children most commonly reported encountering pornographic content via personalised feeds, and girls, in particular, reported feeling confused or upset after seeing such content, Ofcom found. Suicide and eating disorder content was also driven mostly through personal feeds, with girls most likely to encounter both types of harmful material. The Ofcom review also found that “young men and boys consuming motivational and self-improvement content can rapidly become exposed to more extreme content which includes the promotion of misogyny and racism”. Misspelled hashtags and coded language are often used to bypass content moderation systems that would otherwise block harmful misogynistic content.Ian Russell, the father of Molly Russell, who took her life aged 14 in 2017 after viewing suicide material on social media, told the Guardian the lack of progress was “staggering but sadly not surprising”. He blamed “timidity and lack of action” from the regulator and said: “It is time that Ofcom stood up for children and investigated the major flaws in TikTok and Instagram’s design features, not just small technicalities that have been their focus so far.”An Ofcom spokesperson said: “This is an industry that’s been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years. And so while significant progress is being made – including the introduction of widespread age checks, stronger protections against grooming, and tougher safeguards against child sexual exploitation and abuse – we’re under no illusion that there is much for the industry still to do. We’ve shown that tech firms that don’t comply with their duties can expect enforcement action.”It said the data did not cover the period from this spring when it said it stepped up pressure on Facebook, YouTube, Snap, Roblox and TikTok over child safety issues. It also said it recorded some reductions in harmful content on platforms including the games Minecraft and Call of Duty and YouTube, Pinterest and Facebook. In July it launched aninvestigationinto TikTok over child safety concerns, including how it checks users are adults or children.The continuing risks to children come before a planned Australia-style social media ban in the UK for under-16s which is due, from next spring, to cover platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X, but not messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal.However campaigners have warned that must not overshadow the need to enforce protections under the Online Safety Act.“Children will continue to face risks on services covered by the act but not the proposed ban, including gaming and messaging platforms,” said Mitali Sud, a senior policy manager atInternetMatters, a child online safety campaign. “Sixteen- and 17-year-olds will still use social media. A social media ban cannot replace the need to make online services safer for children.”UK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14Read moreA government spokesperson said platforms needed to do more to protect children from harmful content.“That’s why we are taking bold action to strengthen protections for children from risks of harm online – banning social media from offering their services to under-16s and protecting kids from harmful functionalities like livestreaming and stranger communications on a wide range of services, including gaming services,” they said.“When it comes to children’s safety, we are not and never will be bystanders. Platforms have both a moral and legal duty to protect children and we expect them to work with us to set a new normal for future generations.”TikTok, Meta, X and Google were contacted for comment.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsChildrenOfcomSocial media banSocial mediaInternet safetyInternetDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaign | Emergency planning | The Guardian
description: Government’s emergency planning advice has sparked sales of essentials but no panic stockpiling, say prepping shop owners
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Government’s emergency planning advice has sparked sales of essentials but no panic stockpiling, say prepping shop owners
Content: There is no evidence government’s advice has triggered mass panic stockpiling of groceries and other essentials.Photograph: Simon Leigh/AlamyView image in fullscreenThere is no evidence government’s advice has triggered mass panic stockpiling of groceries and other essentials.Photograph: Simon Leigh/AlamyEmergency planning‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaignGovernment’s emergency planning advice has sparked sales of essentials but no panic stockpiling, say prepping shop ownersJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.The government’snew Be Ready campaignis advising the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.Be Ready documentTwo-page document advises the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use in an emergency.In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.View image in fullscreenAn original copy of Protect and Survive, a government booklet of advice on surviving a nuclear attack issued in 1980.Photograph: sjbooks/Alamy“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700% since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”Explore more on these topicsEmergency planningCyberwarInternetInfrastructureDefence policyHackingClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m gift | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party insiders say they expect initial verdict to be against leader and are preparing to appeal against adverse findings
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Party insiders say they expect initial verdict to be against leader and are preparing to appeal against adverse findings
Content: Reform UK is on tenterhooks over the standards commissioner’s report into Nigel Farage.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenReform UK is on tenterhooks over the standards commissioner’s report into Nigel Farage.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersReform UKReform UK braces for Farage standards verdict over undeclared £5m giftParty insiders say they expect initial verdict to be against leader and are preparing to appeal against adverse findingsRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 23 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s Reform is braced for a negative report from the standards commissioner over his failure to declare a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne and plans to appeal against any adverse findings.The party is on tenterhooks over the report, with multiple Reform insiders saying they are readying for a fightback through the appeals process and fully expect the initial verdict to find against their leader.Any attempt by Farage to oppose a negative verdict could mean the process drags on for months, as an MP under investigation has the right to present further evidence to the standards committee as well as to appeal through the independent expert panel.After any appeals process, and if parliament agrees with a penalty of more than 10 days of suspension from the House of Commons, Farage could end up facing a second byelection in his Clacton constituency. This would require a recall petition, triggered by signatures from 10% of voters in the MP’s constituency over six weeks.Farage was interviewed by the standards commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, last month and the party expects to be notified of the verdict at any time.While it awaits the findings, Reform has been overhauling its HQ operations, having been destabilised by undercover investigations by Channel 4 and ITV in recent weeks and fallen in the polls.The Channel 4 reporting with the investigative group Verbatim has led to apolice inquiryinto alleged attempts to orchestrate illegal overseas donations, as well as the suspension of James Orr as head of policy and Dan Jukes as Farage’s communications chief. They deny wrongdoing and an internal party report has cleared them, but the matter remains under police investigation.The ITV reportinguncovered racist councillorsand election candidates for the party caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.One Reform insider said the ITV documentary in particular was extremely bad and showed the party’s vetting had not been up to scratch, despite its claims to have professionalised.Get in touchContact Rowena Mason about this storyIf you have something to share about this story you can contact Rowena using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreBut they said the party was well on its way to bringing in changes in its organisation. Harvey Griffiths, Reform’s new treasurer, has been taking a central role in handling day-to-day party business, while Tom Waterhouse, its general secretary, has taken on the role of getting to grips with vetting.There have also been departures. Aaron Lobo, its former head of operations, has moved to a new role running a Reform-focused TV channel, which is hiring dozens of “journalists” to increase communications directly to voters.Amar Johal, a former government lawyer who had been working for the party as head of policy, has taken on the role of acting head of people operations and is said to be a rising force within the party.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s polling guru and former campaign lead, has been asked to return to play a role as an informal sounding board on strategy for the party. Raheem Kassam, a former communications chief for Farage now based in the US, has been playing an unofficial role as an attack dog mostly aimed at the Tories, including calling Kemi Badenoch a “Nigerian scammer”, which has been condemned by the Conservative chair, Kevin Hollinrake.While Jukes, who was a longtime aide to Farage, was considered a loss, the party’s communications are now being handled by Ed Sumner, its communications director, and Miles Goslett, a former journalist.The mood at Reform is said to be down but less bad than expected given its polling slide, partly because of the £72m gift from two donors, Harborne and Ben Delo. The Guardian reportedundercover footage from Verbatimthis week in which Orr suggested Harborne could be caught by the forthcoming overseas donor cap, given he has only been a registered domestic voter in the UK since June. However, Reform has insisted the money will not have to be handed back.The party has begun a hiring spree since the windfall and is planning to take on400 campaign managersin target seats. It has also sent a mailshot directly to voters – a move that may be repeated in the coming weeks.Farage has been under investigation over the £5m gift from Harborne just before the last election in 2024 since shortly afterthe Guardian revealed it in May.The Reform leader has said itwas a personalmatter, not a political one, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England
Content: A tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks the pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall, on Friday.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/GettyView image in fullscreenA tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks the pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall, on Friday.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/GettyExtreme weatherThousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west EnglandDozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of EnglandJamie GriersonandYassin El-MouddenFri 23 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of homes are without power and schools were closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores.Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. By 3pm, more than 31,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid.Dozens of schools acrossCornwallwere forced to delay their opening, while others did not open at all. Flights were disrupted at airports in the south-west and on the Channel Islands, and passengers were being advised to check the status of their flight before travelling.Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet having been stranded on the UK mainland. The Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday.Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since it closed to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained. English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair.National Rail reported severe disruption across the rail network, with cancellations acrossEngland, Wales and Scotland.Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaking at a wildfires summit in Aintree, Liverpool, on Friday.Photograph: WPA/GettyA government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked whether the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.“It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”National Grid said engineers had so far restored power to more than 52,000 properties affected by Storm Austen.In Sussex, Southern Water said a power cut had affected a reservoir in the area and that it was arranging deliveries of bottled water for customers affected by the disruption.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.View image in fullscreenStorm Austen hits Newhaven in East Sussex.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersThe Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and it warned of danger to life from flying debris. It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and travel disruption.In anticipation of Storm Boelo, train lines in parts of northern and western Scotland are scheduled to close early at the weekend.Services south and west of Kilwinning in North Ayrshire and the Oban and Mallaig lines will shut on Saturday evening, while the line between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach in the Highlands will be out of service on Sunday. Trains are expected to run at reduced speed elsewhere in the country.The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherUK weatherEnglandCornwallnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
Content: Drone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.Photograph: 34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen'/ReutersView image in fullscreenDrone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.Photograph: 34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen'/ReutersUkraineRussia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisisPeople in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weedsPjotr SauerandPeter BeaumontFri 23 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House has said that Russia andUkrainehave agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.Map showing location of OleshkyThe White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered byMelania Trump, and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council ofEurope. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.Lubinets ⁠told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve ⁠demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient ​quantity of ‌humanitarian ‌aid will be delivered to ‌meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure ‌that this is not just a ​one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” ⁠he said.Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions tothe Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops,began last weekafter Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspendedintelligence-sharingwith Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia andbegin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?Read moreAmong Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.Explore more on these topicsUkraineElon MuskTrump administrationEuropeDonald TrumpDrones (military)US foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl
Content: Scene of a drive-by shooting in Trappes, a suburb near Paris. Over 15 minutes, the gunman fired at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersView image in fullscreenScene of a drive-by shooting in Trappes, a suburb near Paris. Over 15 minutes, the gunman fired at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersFranceMacron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near ParisGunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girlAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 23 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west ofParison Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”.He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”Rabeh said everyone inFrancehad a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night.The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable.The man killed was named as Pengo Bossio Wangi in an Instagrampostby the mixed martial arts academy of which he was a member. The Atch Academy paid tribute to a man who “set an example” and said that memories of “his smile, his energy, and his generosity will remain etched within our walls and in our hearts”.Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from ⁠Yvelines.The ‌shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday sawone of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.Additional reporting byYassin El-MouddenExplore more on these topicsFranceEuropeMarine Le PenParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump again invokes claim he has the ‘right’ to run for third term as president | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledge
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: US constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledge
Content: Donald Trump at a midterm election campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at a midterm election campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump again invokes claim he has the ‘right’ to run for third term as presidentUS constitution unequivocally states that he can’t campaign again, which the president also seems to acknowledgeUS politics live – latest updatesAriana BaioFri 23 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpjoked with rally-goers on Thursday evening that he had “the right to run again” for president, invoking a claim he has repeatedly made thathe may seek a third term despite it being unconstitutional.“I don’t know who is going to be your next president and I think the law said, I’m not 100% sure, but I think the law says I’m not allowed to run again,”Trump said in Sioux City, Iowa.Trump went on to seemingly acknowledge that the22nd amendmentprohibits presidents from seeking a third term but then invoked his familiar false claims that Democrats “stole” the 2020 presidential election from him.What’s up with Trump’s unhinged fixation on male candidates’ bodies?Read more“Well, the one thing is different: they cheated us on the second one because we won it three times. So I think I have the right to run again,” Trump said, laughing.“I think I have the right to run again because they cheated,” Trump added with a coy smile, drawing applause from the crowd.1:14Trump floats unconstitutional third term at campaign rally in Iowa – videoTrump has consistently teased that he will run again for president, which would be a direct violation of the US constitution.In October 2025,Trump told reporters he “would love”to run for a third term. At arally in Texas in February,the president told the crowd, “Maybe we should do one more term,” claiming he was “entitled” to it.Last year, the Trump store started selling “Trump 2028” hats. The US president went as far as towear one during the White House Correspondents’ Dinnerin July.His allies have dismissed the president’s claims as a joke.Mike Johnson, the speaker of the House,told reporters last yearthat Trump “has a good time with that, trolling the Democrats” with claims of a third term. Johnson said he didn’t see a way to amend the constitution to allow Trump to run again.Butopponents have raised concernsthat Trump is being serious.Trump himself has recognized the restrictions imposed by the US constitution.Even during Thursday night’s rally, he said, “I’ve studied that phrase for ever. Unfortunately, it’s quite concise. There’s not a lot of wiggle room. It says something to the effect that ‘under no circumstances and for any reason will you even consider thinking about running for president if you had – ’.”The president, who enjoys wide support thanks to his loyal Maga base, has urged supporters to vote as though he is on the ballot in November’s US midterm elections to help Republicans pick up more seats. The impact of this unconventional strategy remains to be seen as Trump’s approval ratingsfall to new lows.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS constitution and civil libertiesLaw (US)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go? | North Korea | The Guardian
description: Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasons
Content: Residents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River BridgePhotograph: Florence Lo/ReutersView image in fullscreenResidents sit at a viewing platform overlooking the newly opened New Yalu River BridgePhotograph: Florence Lo/ReutersNorth KoreaNorth Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?Kim Jong-un has opened the borders to both his key allies in Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, but for different reasonsJustin McCurryin Tokyo andRebecca BaileyChina correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 19.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.Fast forward 12 years anddozens of trucksare now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.mapThe New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju inNorth Koreaand has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time betweenNorth Korea and Russia. Thefirst road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leaderKim Jong-unthat he is prioritising ties with Moscow.map“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to supportVladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, and has heldtwo summitswith the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.View image in fullscreenTrucks adorned with Chinese flags cross the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge into North Korea’s Sinuiju.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersIn return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional allyChina.North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’snuclear weapons programme.In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”View image in fullscreenThe newly opened New Yalu River Bridge could be of more geopolitical importance than economic for China.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersThe North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it wouldsever all rail and road linkswith its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “principal enemy”.But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.“Both countries understand thatKim Jong-unwould rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.View image in fullscreenBeijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence.Photograph: Florence Lo/ReutersTertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”Explore more on these topicsNorth KoreaChinaRussiaAsia PacificKim Jong-unfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom | BBC | The Guardian
description: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Content: Creatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoView image in fullscreenCreatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoBBCBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomBBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers sayTara ConlanFri 23 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDavid Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hitBBCseries is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.View image in fullscreen‘No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame,’ said the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyThe executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.View image in fullscreenThe hit BBC series returns with cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed ‘stonefish’.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoThat includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II,‘iguana v snakes’sequence.Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. Episodes show how the climatecrisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”Asked if the BBC’s£500m cost-cutting drivewould affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1November on BBC1 and iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBCNature documentariesScience and nature TVBBC OneDavid AttenboroughMarine lifeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: As midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subject | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Despite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this election
Author: Callum Jones
Headline: Despite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this election
Content: Voting booths at the Silver Spring civic building for the first day of early voting, on Thursday in Maryland.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APView image in fullscreenVoting booths at the Silver Spring civic building for the first day of early voting, on Thursday in Maryland.Photograph: Allison Robbert/APThe Stakes 2026US midterm elections 2026AnalysisAs midterms loom, Trump and his allies try to change the subjectCallum JonesDespite distraction and distortion, voters know what issues will be informing their votes in this electionThis was originally published in The Stakes 2026, a newsletter about the midterm elections. Sign up to get it in your inboxFri 23 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTShareElections too often get pigeonholed. The hot take, or simplistic analysis, would have it that just one issue – often the issue the source so happens to be most animated about – will decide the entire result.Tens of millions of Americans will go to the polls next month. Will they be galvanized by affordability? Maybe it’s Iran. Or healthcare? Taxes, perhaps. Or crime.It depends, of course, on whom you ask. The US electorate is not a monolith. Just as different voters are grappling with different pressures and realities, they have different priorities and concerns.Take a look at our voter panel. For Justin Daniels, 45, in Detroit, Michigan, the most significant issue in this election is economic malaise. For Yajaira Martinez, 43, in Pharr, Texas, it’s labor. For Scott Akridge, 60, in Marietta, Georgia, it’s the administration’s brutal crackdown on immigration.The Democrats taking the fight to Republican strongholdsRead moreThe challenge for any one party trying to win over such a sprawling country is whether it can address enough of these concerns, and obtain the trust of enough voters, to build a coalition.Which makes the latest polling all the more disconcerting forRepublicans, less than two weeks before election day.The headline takeaways from the most recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey were damning enough: asmy colleague Shrai Popat reported, most Americans think Donald Trump is using the US presidency to enrich himself, and his approval rating has fallen to a new low.Beneath the surface, though, the numbers are yet more dismal for Republicans.Presented with a dozen issues, from affordability and corruption to taxes and transgender issues, respondents were asked which of the two main parties they trust to do a better job of handling them. On all but one – crime – a greater share picked Democrats than Republicans.On the economy, as the White House continues to hail a “new golden age”, Republicans have lost ground significantly over the past six months. While they commanded a one-point lead over Democrats in April, they are now nine points behind on the issue voters consistently rank as a top concern.And on immigration, which Trump and his officials have put at the heart of his second presidency, the five-point Republican lead in April has reversed. Almost two years into the administration’s deadly and controversial crackdown, Democrats are now ahead by two points.View image in fullscreenThe Republican senator Roger Marshall, right, and the Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton debate in Kansas City, Missouri, on Wednesday.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APIn Kansas, where voters have not sent a Democrat to the US Senate since 1932, the party’s candidate, Adam Hamilton, has beenpledging to turn down the heat, and ignore partisan battles, amid rising political polarization. Some recent polls have put him ahead.Midterm elections are almost always tough for Washington’s governing party. There is a conventional playbook for navigating this: senior figures fan out nationwide to reassure the people who backed them two years prior that they get it. They hear them. They’re on it. They just need more time.The president is indeed fanning out across the country. This week alone, he was inKansason Monday and North Carolina on Tuesday, before South Carolina on Wednesday, Iowa on Thursday and Florida on Friday. Georgia and Michigan follow this weekend. JD Vance is on a cross-country tour of his own.But this is where Trump and his allies depart from convention. Rather than acknowledge the golden age has yet to shine for much of the country – let alone concede that some of his priorities since taking office, like the beautification of Washington, or adding his name to the Kennedy Center, were not among the campaign promises his base had found so appealing in 2024 – Trump has opted for an altogether different response.He has tried to change the subject.This summer, as questions over Iran, the cost of living and hardline anti-immigration policies loomed large, the most powerful elected officials in the US tried tostoke fears that communism was rifeinside the Democratic party.In September, the president dangled a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen, a proposal that waswidely criticizedas a pre-election bribe.Now, in the final stretch of the campaign, those questions very much remain. Rather than address them, Republicans appear to be resorting to a volatile mix of distraction and distortion.Having spent much of the Iran war, which he launched in February, claiming it was about to end, the president is now pivoting to Ukraine – striking astunning deal to buy Russian diesel,pausing some sanctions on Moscowand suggesting the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, should quit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd as France was gripped by fresh unrest this weekend, Vance entered the chat. Demonstrations that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the soaring cost of living were, in fact, evidence of “western liberals” having “imported the third world” into their countries, according to the vice-president.“And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” added Vance. Not to be outdone, Trump himself hasused public appearances to echo such warningsin recent days, as my colleagues Joseph Gedeon and David Smith reported.Many Americans are paying close attention – not to France, necessarily, but to the issues that dominate their daily lives. In November, we’ll find out whom Americans trust to address them.Your questions answeredThe US politics team hosted a series of reader Q&As leading up to the midterms. In our final session, Guardian immigration reportersanswered your questionsabout how ICE and Trump’s mass deportation agenda could shape election results.See our other conversations here:The makeup of the Democratic party, plus key races to watchWho are the groups financially backing the candidates in the midterms?Will the Iran war cost Trump in the US midterm elections? Your questions answeredWill Trump’s economy sink Republicans in the US midterm elections? Our reporters answered your questionsMeet the candidate: Mary PeltolaView image in fullscreenMary Peltola at an primary election watch party on 18 August 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska.Photograph: Mark Thiessen/APHow Democrat Mary Peltola is on the verge of flipping right-leaning AlaskaRead moreMary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the huge state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades.She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. She’s heard of communities along the Arctic Ocean where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights.“Nobody can afford that,” Peltola said in an interview.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026The Stakes 2026Donald TrumpJD VanceRepublicansUS politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV show | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
Content: In the hood … Claudia Winkleman, host of The Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/Euan CherryView image in fullscreenIn the hood … Claudia Winkleman, host of The Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/Euan CherryThe Traitors‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV showCelia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owlMichael HoganFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628. No, really. When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia. As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other. About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity. It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know asThe Traitors. It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.Co-creator Jasper Hoogendoorn joined Pos to develop the idea, The Mutineers. After 20 rejections, they fine-tuned the game further. Filming it on a boat was too limiting, so they shifted the action on to dry land – and looked for more aesthetic inspiration. Pos was once a choirboy in a 14th-century cathedral, gazing up at its spooky gothic architecture. This became the template for the show’s setting: cue cloak-clad figures walking silently down torch-lit corridors to a secret tower. The Traitors was finally born in 2021, now known as De Verraders.UK production company Studio Lambert – maker of superior reality TV from Gogglebox to Race Across the World – soon clocked this new Dutch show. “We watched it in the office and couldn’t stop talking about it,” says creative director Mike Cotton. “Reality TV goes in cycles. At the time, it was in a phase of dating shows. This felt totally different. It wasn’t about love, it was about trust.” He and executive producer Sarah Fay visited the Netherlands to witness the phenomenon first-hand. “We went straight to the set,” says Cotton. “All these people in a castle were discussing how someone had been murdered and taking it very seriously. Even unedited, it was fascinating to watch.”Snapping up the UK and US rights, Studio Lambert began adapting it. “The Dutch version was smaller, so we supersized it,” says Cotton. “We tweaked the format. Changed the endgame. We decided to film the British and American shows at the same castle in the Scottish Highlands.” Each episode is estimated to cost £1m, almost double a normal reality show, enabling it to splash out on cinematic flourishes such as exploding pirate ships and creepy cabins.Now all it needed was a worthy host. Enter Claudia Winkleman, clad in covetable knitwear. “[BBC One controller] Kate Phillips said she had a show for me,” recalls Winkleman. “It was in Scotland for four weeks. But I don’t leave the kids or my bed, so I said no thanks and forgot all about it. Then Kate said: ‘You should rethink. I’m going to send you the original series they made in Holland.’ I watched two episodes and called back to say I was booking my train to Inverness.”View image in fullscreenCaped crusaders … Maya Jama and Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PA“Once we had Ardross Castle and Claudia, everything fell into place,” says Cotton. “The UK version quickly became its own thing.” Launching in 2022, it pulled in ratings of about 4 million. As buzz spread and punters caught up on iPlayer, audience figures grew exponentially. The second series leapt to 7 million, the third to 9 million, the fourth to 11.5 million. The inaugural celebrity edition last autumn peaked at 14.9 million, making it the year’s most-watched show.Did Winkleman ever imagine such stratospheric numbers? “Not a chance,” she laughs. “But I don’t like knowing about ratings. My BBC boss Ed [Havard, director of entertainment] called me a couple of weeks ago to say ‘10 million’. I told him it was a clerical error and never to call me again.”Fay believes Winkleman is key to the show’s success. “As much as possible, we wanted The Traitors to feel like a drama,” she says. “That was our approach in every department, be it set design, music or Claudia’s wardrobe. It needed to feel like a premium show. Claudia’s integral to that. It’s not your usual reality host role, where they’re slightly removed from the action. She’s embedded as queen of the castle and obsessed with the game. Right from the start, she begged to have screens in her dressing room so she could watch the footage.”Ever modest, Winkleman plays down her importance. “I disagree with that quite viciously,” she says. “At first, I couldn’t bear being mean or cold. I loathed not smiling and telling everyone they were amazing. But under Sarah’s guidance, I learned to trust that I could be a bit strict. It’s hard because I feel protective and maternal – is that weird? – towards all our players. I want them to know they’re smashing it. Then again, I’m dressed like Chewbacca and throwing portraits on the floor, so I’m hard to take seriously.”Now airing in more than 40 countries, The Traitors has officially become the most successful TV show on the planet. It has won Baftas and Emmys, while spawning board games, stage shows, escape rooms, even a Prom. Did TV insiders expect the show to strike global gold?“Nobody saw it coming,” says Deadline’s TV expert Jake Kanter. “Viewing figures growing steadily is always a good sign because it means word of mouth is strong. The best definition of a hit is that you don’t need to tell anyone how well it’s performing, they just know. Your friends, family and colleagues are talking about it.”When Pos and Hoogendoorn shopped the show around, they resisted pressure to compromise and dug their heels in over certain core principles. One was that gameplay should take place in a self-contained bubble with minimal interference.View image in fullscreenDead end … Claudia Winkleman arrives in style in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio Lambert“The Dutch always talked about it as a game, not a TV show,” says Cotton. “This is the game, these are the rules. After that, they’re very hands-off. That’s something we’ve adopted. We set up the game and just let it go. That’s rare nowadays. We never want producers to come up at the round table or be the reason someone’s suspected as a Traitor. If you interfere, they’ll latch on to it. We plan certain elements but have no way of controlling what happens.”Another cardinal rule was that the identity of the Traitors isn’t hidden from the audience. Wouldn’t it be better if viewers played detective, too? “We did dabble with the audience not knowing with the Secret Traitor twist in series four,” says Fay. “But what’s delicious for the viewer is that they’re in on it all. They see the strategies and paranoia on both sides. Imagine if you didn’t know Alan Carr was a Traitor last year. You’d have missed out on the hilarity of him sweating, panicking and going: ‘What am I doing?’”Winkleman finds the psychology of the game endlessly fascinating. “It’s about gut instinct,” she says. “Turns out it doesn’t exist. It’s about what happens when we try and ‘read’ people. It’s about trust, betrayal, friendship, all of it.” It’s no coincidence that The Traitors was conceived during the era of fake news and social media manipulation. In a post-truth world, it offers insights into conspiracy theories, herd mentality and groupthink.“What still wows me is that every series is completely different,” says Fay. “That’s the beauty of a murder mystery. We’re just back from filming the seventh UK series and, again, there are things coming up that you’ve never seen before.”When did the makers realise they had a smash hit on their hands? “For me, it was episode four of the first series,” says Fay. “The Red Breakfast, when Tom stood up and went: ‘Alex isn’t a Traitor, she’s my girlfriend!’ We were watching the rushes with our mouths wide open.”“It’s rare to find a format that’s multi-generational,” says Fay. “Remember when we walked down the street and pubs were showing the series one final on big screens, like a football match?” grins Cotton. “That blew our minds.”What have been Winkleman’s highlights? “There are so many I could bore you for 18 months straight. I often have to stop myself gasping out loud at the round table. When the Faithful catch a Traitor, it’s electric. If Traitors turn on Traitors, I always think my head is going to fall off. And I still get a total buzz from going into the turret. It feels very special to be allowed in there.”For its award-garlanded host, The Traitors has been transformative. “It’s the greatest job I’ve ever been given,” says Winkleman. “It has changed my life and my career, no question. I’ll be there with Barry the owl long after they’ve fired me. I’ve also told the peacock to make room in the shed where he roosts.”View image in fullscreenFlying friend … Claudia Winkleman in The Traitors castle.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryThe Traitors has overtaken Strictly Come Dancing as the BBC’s crown jewel but it’s a mutually beneficial relationship. From Celia Imrie’s guff to Richard E Grant’s gaffe, from Ross Kemp’s twitching paranoia to James Acaster’s trembling terror, the franchise thrives on communal talking points. It wouldn’t work nearly as well being binged on a streamer. “The Traitors demonstrates the power of television to bring people together,” says Kanter. “At a time when there’s lots of existential hand-wringing about the health of the broadcast industry – and the BBC particularly – it’s a reminder that when terrestrial TV is good, it’s something to treasure.”The chaotic second celebrity series reaches its climax this week, with 17 million expected to tune in. What can they reveal about Friday’s final? Fay laughs. “I’m trying to work out what we can tell you without ruining anything.” “It’s stressful and unpredictable,” says Cotton. “Genuinely surprising, even for us,” adds Fay. “With real heart-in-mouth moments.”“I always cry at the endgame, regardless of who wins,” concludes Winkleman. “Whoever is left standing has played the best game. I feel incredibly proud of them. This series is no different. It feels momentous.”The Celebrity Traitors climaxes at 8pm on Thursday 29 October and Friday 30 October on BBC One and iPlayer.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How I Shop with Bill Bailey: ‘Could be a life-saver in an apocalypse’ | Bill Bailey | The Guardian
description: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The comedian and musician talks medieval instruments, hiking socks and coffee rituals with the Filter
Author: Monica Horridge
Headline: Always wondered what everyday stuff celebrities buy, where they shop for food and the basics they scrimp on? The comedian and musician talks medieval instruments, hiking socks and coffee rituals with the Filter
Content: Composite: Jordan Carter/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Jordan Carter/Guardian DesignGuardian journalism is independent.
