The comedian and musician talks medieval instruments, hiking socks and coffee rituals with the FilterDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereFri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Bailey has been entertaining fans for more than four decades as an award-winning comedian and multi-instrumentalist, blending comedy and music in his performances. After cutting his teeth on the 1980s standup circuit, Bailey went on to forge a successful career as a television regular and presenter on shows including Never Mind the Buzzcocks, QI and Bill Bailey’s Australian Adventure; in 2020 he won Strictly Come Dancing.This autumn and winterhe is touring the UK with his live showVaudevillean.What was the last treat you bought yourself?It literally arrived this morning – a medieval instrument called a psaltery. It’s a bit like a dulcimer or zither, a kind of V shape you hold and pluck. That’s the sort of thing that I buy.View image in fullscreenPluck of the draw: a traditional psaltery in action.Photograph: Alla Chesnokova/GettyPlucked psaltery with padded case£350 at the Early Music ShopWhere do you buy your food?Some of it online, but we’re lucky where we are in west London, with a great greengrocer, butcher, fishmonger, a little Korean store and a Thai shop called Sriracha supermarket, where I can get spices from.What’s the best present you’ve given?A Gibson Les Paul guitar to my godson. It was brilliant seeing someone really immerse themselves in playing it. I think giving a musical instrument is a great present generally.View image in fullscreenString of good ideas: Keith Richards with a Gibson Les Paul, the type of guitar Bill Bailey chose for his godson.Photograph: David Redfern/RedfernsShop Les Paul electric guitars at GibsonShop Gibson Les Paul guitars at Gear4music… and what’s the best present you’ve received?That was a guitar as well, from my wife as a birthday present. I was doing a standup residency in the West End, and there was a bit in the show where I would pick up an electric guitar and start playing it. Unbeknown to me, in the interval, she colluded with the crew to switch the standard guitar for a rare vintage white Gibson. I went [to pick it up] in the second half and thought: “Wait, what’s this?” Then I noticed there was a bow tied around the neck. I was completely overwhelmed; it was a brilliant way to have it delivered. It almost completely derailed the gig.View image in fullscreenBirthday surprise: a vintage white Les Paul, similar to the one Bailey found on stage mid-show.Photograph: titoslack/GettyWhat’s your favourite online store?A music store called Thomann. They sell all kinds of interesting instruments, but also accessories, guitar leads and all the extra stuff you need when you’re playing or writing music at home.Shop music gear at ThomannWhat’s your favourite bricks-and-mortar shop?I buy a lot of outdoor stuff – boots, camping equipment – from Cotswold Outdoor in Kensington. I recently bought a LifeStraw, which apparently you can stick in almost any water source and it will filter it into drinking water. I haven’t tested it in rivers, but it might be a life-saver in an apocalypse.View image in fullscreenLifeStraw water filter bottle£48.95 at Cotswold OutdoorWhat’s the gadget you use most often?A Chemex coffee system, a simple glass flask and filters. It makes the best-tasting coffee.View image in fullscreenChemex coffee maker£34.99 at Coffee Friend£44 at AmazonWhat’s the purchase you regret the most?It was a semi-computerised accordion. It weighed an absolute ton, so it was impractical to play on stage because I could only hold it for very short periods, and it was festooned with cables and things trailing from it. In the end, it sat in the cupboard and gathered dust until I bought a much lighter one.What item do you buy on repeat?Big hiking socks – I do a lot of walking, so you work your way through them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenWalk this way: lots of hiking calls for a steady stream of socks.Photograph: SimpleImages/GettyShop hiking socks at Cotswold OutdoorWhere do you buy your underwear?The last lot I bought was from TK Maxx – a bargain.Shop men’s underwear at TK MaxxWhat would you buy with £20 – and £200?£20: I would probably buy a multipack of socks. For £200, art materials for my dad because he paints a lot and brushes, oils, acrylics and paper are not cheap – we go to Chiswick Arts & Crafts.View image in fullscreenBrush with greatness: Bailey would spend £200 on art materials as a present for his dad.Photograph: Guido Mieth/GettyShop supplies at Chiswick Arts & CraftsWhat’s your ‘saved search’ on eBay/Vinted?I don’t have one, but I buy secondhand furniture from eBay.What’s your greatest vintage find?A Turkish saz, a long-necked lute. I love those instruments that, on the face of it, seem pretty simple and limited, but then you get to know them, and you realise you can play all kinds of things.View image in fullscreenSaz you like it: a Turkish long-necked lute was a standout find.Photograph: UCG/GettyWhat’s your biggest splurge?Day to day, I love a decent coffee. It’s become something of a ritual.View image in fullscreenWorth a shot: good coffee is money well spent.Photograph: Guido Mieth/GettyHow do you make your coffee at home?I bought a little Krups coffee grinder a few years ago, which I use with the Chemex.View image in fullscreenKrups coffee grinder£18.76 at AmazonAnd what everyday item do you scrimp on?I drink more coffee, so probably teabags. I get a big multipack from the Co-op or cash-and-carry, because we have lots of people coming around all the time; you can’t be too precious about the teabags in our house.View image in fullscreenAny old brew: just keep the tea coming.Photograph: RapidEye/GettyShop tea at Co-opBill Bailey’s Vaudevillean is touring from5 November to 13 December, then will be at the Theatre Royal Haymarket from16 December 2026 to 6 February 2027. title: Crowded nest? How parents and their adult kids can live together in peace | Parents and parenting | The Guardian
description: With record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the experts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the experts
Content: Illustration: Justin Metz/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Justin Metz/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Parents and parentingCrowded nest? How parents and their adult kids can live together in peaceWith record numbers of adult children living at home with their parents, how can this arrangement work for everyone? Set ground rules from the off, respect each other’s privacy, and don’t revert to type, say the expertsRebecca CopeFri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether they are fresh out of university and looking for a job, have recently been made redundant, are saving to buy a home or newly divorced, it’s becoming increasingly common for adult children to live at home with their parents.According to the Office for National Statistics(ONS), 35% of men and 22% of women aged between 20 and 34 were living with their parents in 2025.I speak from experience: my younger sister lived at home with my mother for two years while she did her PhD, and I moved home for almost three years after becoming a single mother postpartum. In both of our situations, it would have been good to have some practical advice to make it work, with tensions sometimes running high and arguments inevitable.Talk about itbeforehandIf parents and their adult children are going to coexist successfully, honest communication is essential from the outset. How long do children expect to stay? Will they contribute financially? Will they do any housework? Are guests allowed? Difficulties will arise if you aren’t clear about these boundaries from the off.“You won’t be able to anticipate every point of tension in advance, but you might want to discuss typical frictions like noise and overnight guests,” saysAnita Cleare, a parenting expert and author ofHow to Get Your Teenager Out of Their Bedroom. “Parents should aim for a balance between making adult children feel welcome and maintaining their own mental and financial wellbeing.”double quotation markNow your child is an adult, voicing your opinion on how they should be going about life differently will send you right back into parent-teenager dynamicsParenting expertSue Atkins, whose grownup children have both lived with her for periods, recommends writing down everything you want to say first, so that you can stay focused – and, crucially, to pick your moment. “It’s all about your tone of voice and your attitude,” she says. “If you do it when you’re angry or frustrated, that’s the wrong time. I always say: ‘Strike when the iron is cold.’”Don’t revert to past behavioursBoth parents and adult children can fall into the trap of reverting to childhood dynamics. Parents find children annoying and untidy, and feel free to comment on their lifestyles (“You’re not going out in that?” “What time will you be back?” “That’s a waste of money,” etc), while children regress into teenagers, expecting Mum and Dad to do the laundry, housework and cooking.Adolescence lasts into your 30s – so how should parents treat their adult children?Read more“The biggest trap adult children fall into when returning to live with parents is to demand the rights of adulthood while still expecting to enjoy the privileges of a child,” says Cleare. “For example, expecting their parents to provide household comforts while insisting on sticking to their own separate daily schedule. Vice versa: now that your child is an adult, you don’t have the right to know where they are at all times, what they are doing or what they are thinking. Voicing your opinion on how they should be going about life differently will send you right back into parent-teenager dynamics.”Instead, conceive of it as more of a housemate situation. “It can help to think of your adult child as a friend who is staying with you, rather than as your child,” says Cleare. “Parent-child dynamics have a power imbalance – parents tell children what to do (and children assert their power by not cooperating). Friendships tend to be more equal. Aim for discussion and collaboration rather than rigid rule-setting. Set your parameters, but then treat your adult child as a problem-solver by inviting their views and ideas.” For the adult child, they can also consider what being a good housemate means: chiefly, pulling their weight by doing chores without being asked.Finda practical way to store excessbelongingsIf an adult child is moving back home after living away for some time – perhaps even in their own home – then they will have accumulated a lot of “stuff”.Kate Edmondson, the founder ofHome Edited, a professional organisation service, recommends first agreeing on where belongings will be stored and how much space is realistically available. “Ask them to go through their belongings and make decisions about what is genuinely worth storing,” she says. “Make sure they know what they have and where it is. Clearly labelled, categorised boxes make belongings much easier for them to access without having to pull apart an entire storage area. If you’re storing a larger volume, encourage them to keep their own simple inventory on their phone.”Find shared interestsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Justin Metz/The GuardianWhile you might not agree on politics, what to watch on TV, or other hot topics, see this as an opportunity to spend quality time together.“Build some new family traditions,” suggests Cleare. “Families are glued together by spending time together – whether that’s eating or cooking, watching TV or sport, or shopping. So try to find new ways to spend time doing things you all enjoy.”There’s no reason you can’t view the experience as a positive one. “I think you have to see living together as a springboard, not a destination,” advises Atkins. “When you come through the other side, you may realise you gained a lot from it and are closer.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMake plans for romanceWhether you are already in a relationship, or looking to date, there’s no denying that living with your parents puts a dampener on romance. Elinor Harvey, a psychotherapist at The Relationship Therapy Practice, says communication and boundaries are key.“A family might agree that Friday night is the adult child’s night to go out and date, and that they can bring someone home afterwards,” she says. “Another family might be more flexible, but simply want advance notice if someone is coming back. There doesn’t have to be one set of ground rules that works for everyone. What matters is agreeing to the rules early and making sure everyone understands them.” It’s also important to remember that if the adult child’s parents are in a couple – whether with each other or a new partner – then they will want time alone for their relationship too.If parents don’t want their child to bring anybody back, and that’s a deal-breaker for the adult child, the arrangement is simply not going to work.Respect everyone’s privacyIf there’s one thing that adult children and parents are likely to fall out over, it’s privacy. After all, many have been living away from home – whether at university halls, in shared housing, or with an ex-partner – and won’t appreciate parents walking into their room without knocking. The same goes for asking about their whereabouts or who they are seeing – though it is always considerate for adult children to check in and offer a little reassurance, rather than turning up half-cut at 3am after a night out and waking everyone up.double quotation markDon’t just walk into their bedroom because they’re your children. Respect their personal space and remember that they may have been independent for years“They’re adults now,” says Atkins. “You don’t just walk into their bedroom because they’re your children. You have to respect their personal space and remember that they may have been independent for years.”Don’t try to be a heroAs tempting as it is to try to swoop in and save adult children living at home in less than ideal circumstances, Cleare advises against playing the hero. “When adults move back home, it is often because something isn’t going right in their lives,” she says. “They might have lost their job or relationship, or be struggling to cope in some way. The temptation is for parents to see these issues as something their adult child needs our advice on and to overstep the mark.”Instead, parents can try to boost their child’s confidence by taking an interest without meddling. “Be mindful not to rescue them – empower them,” says Atkins. “If it’s budgeting and money, you might say: ‘Can I give you a hand? This is how we do it.’ You’re helping them develop the skills to move forward rather than taking over. Don’t judge them or patronise them. Ask open-ended questions: ‘What can we do to support you?’ And use ‘I’ statements. Say: ‘I’m feeling … ’ rather than: ‘You always … ’”Find a way to make it fair for divorced parentsWhen an adult child moves back in with a parent, it can cause undue pressure on household budgets, particularly for single parents.And as more than 38% of people who married in England and Wales in 1995 had divorced by 2015,according to the ONS, this is clearly an issue for many families.Beverley Sayers, a mediator who works with theFamilyMediation Council, has encountered parents who are struggling to support an adult child after a separation or divorce. “There’s an unrealistic idea that you don’t have to continue paying for children once they reach 18,” she says. “I often advise the young person to have a conversation with the parent they don’t live with and ask: ‘Can I have some funds to help with this situation so I can contribute to the household?’”Explore more on these topicsParents and parentingFamilyYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender | Movies | The Guardian
description: The auteur’s new film – a study of class, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says
Author: Rebecca Liu
Headline: The auteur’s new film – a study of class, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says
Content: Lee Chang-Dong … ‘I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story?’Photograph: Chae Dae-han/NetflixView image in fullscreenLee Chang-Dong … ‘I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story?’Photograph: Chae Dae-han/NetflixMoviesInterview‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contenderRebecca LiuThe auteur’s new film – a study of labour, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he saysFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAquintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize atVenice film festival, and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markI am dependent on capital to get my films made but trying to protect my own voice. It is almost the fate of all film-makersIn his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980sSouth Korea, then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”Classics of modern South Korean cinema – ranked!Read moreYou could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.Possible Love is incinemas now, and on Netflix November 6.Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalSouth KoreainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas | Movies | The Guardian
description: When thousands of dead crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: When thousands of dead crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups
Content: ‘We just knew that there was something wrong’ … fisherman Stan Rennie in his boat in Hartlepool.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘We just knew that there was something wrong’ … fisherman Stan Rennie in his boat in Hartlepool.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverMovies‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seasWhen thousands of dying crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverupsRobyn VinterFri 23 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 05.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activismRead moreEnvironmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.View image in fullscreenRelentless campaigner … Stan in All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.Photograph: Courtesy of Andy MartinIn All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like theHorizon Post Office scandal, it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.They includeSeahorse (2019), following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.View image in fullscreenJeanie FinlayPhotograph: Phil  SharpBut it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.Another key figure, snippets of whom we see interspersed throughout, is the Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen, now the Conservative Lord Houchen. He led the concerningly fast demolition of the old steelworks – featuring the largest UK explosion in 75 years – and rapid construction of the Teesside Freeport project in its place.His denials, as evidence grows that this work may be what caused the die-offs, are a constant frustration for Rennie and the gang. Many of them believe he was involved in corruption and a cover-up, while Houchen denies this, labelling the fishers “activists” and refusing contact with them.“You can say it’s done,” says Finlay. “It’s not done for Stan. It’s not done for Sue. It’s not done for the scientists … or for Simon Gibbon, the chemist who’s trying to get the dredge licence put on hold.”That is something the viewers have understood better than the authorities, as money has poured into an NEFC £100,000 fundraiser for the next round of scientific testing. “Someone in Glasgow donated £1,000 during the Q&A on the night, and people have been putting £5 in the pot, it’s pretty amazing.”Rennie says audience members have been angry on their behalf, and some have cried. “For strangers who aren’t from the area to have that same reaction, it blows your mind.”Finlay says: “People are becoming infuriated by elected officials who use their enormous platform, their enormous loudhailer, to tell you stories that are greatly at odds with lived experience. Our lives are dominated by tech bros and platforms and conglomerates and people that shout very loudly. And that can often feel disconnected from real life.”On top of that, Finlay says, people are simply disgusted by the state of the UK’s waterways. “You can sell off all the utilities in the country, and now we’re living with the consequences of that. You can make as many promises as you like, you can promise as many jobs as you like. But the reality is, the trains aren’t working and there’s poo in the river and everyone’s pissed off with that.”All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in cinemas from 23 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Taika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet
Content: ‘Put on ice’ … Taika Waititi at a screening of his new film, Klara and the Sun.Photograph: Steven/AFF-USA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Put on ice’ … Taika Waititi at a screening of his new film, Klara and the Sun.Photograph: Steven/AFF-USA/ShutterstockWeek in geekMoviesTaika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movieBen ChildWaititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feetFri 23 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTShareMovie-making these days is a very expensive endeavour. In 1977, George Lucas’s Star Wars cost $11m to make, which would be approximately $60m in today’s money, and has since amassed $775m at the global box office, including rereleases. Fast forward to 2026 and the most recent film in the long-running space saga,The Mandalorian and Grogu, cost a reported $165m and brought in $346m worldwide. If there was ever a Hollywood gold rush, the mines ran dry long ago.Perhaps this is one of the reasons why Disney-owned Lucasfilm seems to be so terrified of making newStar Warsmovies. Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film, the aforementioned Mando and Grogu movie, has actually made it into cinemas. But that has not stopped the studio announcing a small armada of other projects – sometimes via press release, more often at various high-profile celebrations, conferences or other corporate jamborees – that have so far failed to reach multiplexes.This week, Taika Waititi revealed inan interview with Inversethat his proposed Star Wars film,announced six years ago, has been “put on ice”. No clear explanation was offered, but frankly nobody should be surprised. It now joins mooted projects from Patty Jenkins, Kevin Feige and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and DB Weiss on the list of Star Wars movies that we were once told we were definitely (probably) getting, but that we never actually did. Some, such as Rian Johnson’s proposed trilogy, have spent years receding into the distance, while others – Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy’s film about Rey’s new Jedi order, anyone? – have never been officially cancelled.The failure of Waititi’s project may be the most damaging of the lot. Why hire a film-maker with such distinctive, punky sensibilities, only to leave them announcing to the world that their movie is now frozen in carbonite? Surely Lucasfilm teed up this film in the first place because it thought it might be an idea to shift away from dynastic daddy issues and planet-sized weapons with inexplicable design flaws, towards something whose plot couldn’t be guessed halfway through the opening crawl?View image in fullscreenNot exactly the Outer Rim … Ryan Gosling and Flynn Gray in the forthcoming Star Wars: Starfighter.Photograph: Shawn Levy via InstagramThere is every chance that Waititi’s movie would have focused on an annoyingly genial Kiwi stormtrooper who insists on interrupting vital lightsaber duels to ask whether anyone fancies a sandwich. Johnson might have delivered 500 minutes of space opera in which the Jedi council are eventually forced to admit that the feeling of a disturbance in the Force is usually just trapped wind. But at least nobody watching the opening crawl would have known what kind of Star Wars movie they were about to witness – and that alone would have been worth the price of entry.This isn’t the film you are looking for: the Star Wars franchise is hamstrung by a massive identity crisisRead moreAt some point, Lucasfilm has to let somebody make one of these films that might go wrong. Familiar faces and established audiences did not guarantee Mando and Grogu the kind of triumphant return we all wanted to see, and bringing back the saga’s big bad, Emperor Palpatine, more than three decades after he fell down an Imperial reactor shaft, was very far from a smart move. The forthcomingStar Wars: Starfighter, starring Ryan Gosling, may yet surprise us, but any film that already has Star Wars in its title and still needs one of Hollywood’s most famous faces to get us through the door isn’t exactly venturing into the Outer Rim.Surely somewhere out there in a galaxy far, far away is a film-maker who can bring something fresh to this venerable old saga. Disney needs to find them, commission them to make a movie, and then actually let them get on and do it.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekStar WarsTaika WaititiRian JohnsonStar Wars: The Mandalorian and GroguFilm industryScience fiction and fantasy filmscommentShareReuse this content
