title: ‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood out | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: With his first drivers’ title all but secure a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but the Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: With his first drivers’ title all but secure a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but the Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus
Content: Kimi Antonelli, then and now. He first went karting at age five and was taken on as a Mercedes junior driver at 12.Composite: Guardian Picture Desk;  DPPI Media/Alamy; LAT Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli, then and now. He first went karting at age five and was taken on as a Mercedes junior driver at 12.Composite: Guardian Picture Desk;  DPPI Media/Alamy; LAT Images/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood outWith first drivers’ title all but secure, a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focusGiles Richardsin AustinFri 23 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven as Kimi Antonelli may be world champion-elect, it is sometimes hard to equate the young man who has drivenwith such exceptional skilland no little verve to touching distance of an historic first Formula One title with the smiling, wide-eyed kid with tousled hair who still almost looks out of place in the F1 paddock. Yet what has become clear in this extraordinary season is that Antonelli’s talent and his personable, endearing character are inextricably entwined.Whether the Italian seals his place as F1’s youngest world champion, at 20 years old, at this Sunday’s US Grand Prix in Austin or the next round in Mexico or even beyond that is moot – that he will do so is all but assured and for all that he is still in only his second season in the sport, a more rounded, well-liked champion than the Mercedes driver would be hard to find.Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Giles RichardsRead moreEngage with Antonelli and it is almost impossible not to still see the three-year-old child who insisted on taking to his father Marco’s knee to try out the racing simulator the former driver had brought home. Marco would control the pedals and his son the wheel with an irrepressible enthusiasm that could barely be contained and is still there in every dart, feint and incisive pass he makes today.Pictures from his childhood in Bologna, a couple of hours’ drive from where his father runs a racing team in San Marino, show whenever Antonelli has a wheel in his hands there is a smile on his face and his eyes alight. His joy is clear and it is a passion that has run clearly through his career. From going karting at the age of five, a meteoric rise through the ranks, being taken on as a Mercedes junior driver aged 12, then making his debut for the team in 2025 after a whirlwind of three years moving from F4, to Formula Regional and then F2.The faith Mercedes placed in him, not least in that he was stepping into the shoes of the departing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, was huge, yet the team principal Toto Wolff had no doubts as to his talent and his character.View image in fullscreenTwelve year old Kimi Antonelli (centre) on the podium at the 2019 Karting Winter Cup OK-Junior at Lonato, Italy.Photograph: Jacky Foulatier/DPPI Media/Alamy“In the past, there was the opinion in F1 that in order to be winning, you need to be an asshole, you need to be ruthless and opportunistic,” he observed this season as Antonelli made a stunning startwith five wins on the trotand the entire world was paying attention to the kid who, for many, had come from nowhere. “I don’t think that Kimi is that. It’s just down to driving faster than the others, and being a nice person also.” It is an opinion often echoed by those close to the young Italian. Gwen Lagrue, the talent scout who led Mercedes’ junior driver programme, remembers more than just his remarkable talent from their early encounters.“With Kimi, I saw almost from day one that I was dealing with a different kid,” Lagrue said. “First, what impressed me, well, amazed me, was his natural presence. He was already having such an impact on everyone in the paddock, you noticed this kid has something different than the others. Everyone liked Kimi, everyone was hugging him. He was like the Kimi you see today when he was 11. He was so passionate about what he was doing, about racing, about F1, everything.”At the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing hismaturitàschool exams just after coming third – his first podium –at the Canadian GP last year.“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli ended Italy’s 60-year wait for a home F1 win with his triumph at Monza from 19th on the grid.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty Images“My dad is always going to give me his point of view, he’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well,” he said. “We always have a strong relationship but this is the same with my mum and my sister. The way I am I don’t think I could cope with having a bad relationship with my family member, it’s something that I would really struggle to cope with, that’s why I couldn’t see myself, you know, just taking distance from them.”Intriguingly, racing was not a direction his father had initially wanted him to go in. Marco had been a quick sportscar driver and almost signed as works driver for two German touring car teams but was unlucky in not getting a shot. “I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation,” he said. “At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli with his father, Marco, who has guided him carefully throughout his racing career.Photograph: Peter Powell/EPAHowever, having decided to let him pursue the dream, Marco has been there ever since. He is at the track on many weekends and clearly the pair share an easy, close bond with echoes of the one Hamilton shared with his father, Anthony, in his early years. In Hungary, the race after he had risked receiving a penalty for exceeding track limits on his way to a brilliant win in Belgium, Antonelli laughingly recalled his father’s reaction: “He said: ‘Congrats, but …’ Always a but … ‘If I see you doing another track limit for nothing, I’m gonna stretch your neck like a chicken.’”Antonelli’s boyish honesty has been as engaging as his talent. Wolff has noted his ability to switch into a “race mode”, a zone where he is wholly focused on the task, where he has a daring, aggressive driving style, pushing to the limit and past it, on occasion, but which he always learns from. “We had to teach him instead of always being at 110%, just be at 100%,” Lagrue said which, as Wolff has remarked, is a trait he would rather indulge than having to “take a stick to a donkey”.Kimi Antonelli tightens F1 title grip with Belgian GP win after Russell crashes outRead moreYet alongside that verve Antonelli has shown a maturity beyond his years belied by his character when out of the “zone”. He has displayed the judgment of a veteran while being able to manage the endless adjustments of touch and feel of the car and its balance – especially of these fiendishly complex modern rides – such that he, like many of the greats, has made it look easy.F1 driver standingsWatching him do so this season has been a pleasure not least because he is a driver who has taken such untrammelled and infectious joy in doing so. A feeling perhaps summed up by his father, who told La Gazzetta dello Sport just after his son turned 20: “I hope he remains who he is, sweet and generous, and continues to do what he loves for as long as possible.”Before hisextraordinary victory from 19thon the grid at the Italian GP, Antonelli said he wanted to win the championship but that it was important for him to do so by being himself. The latter he can consider a job most admirably well done. The former is only a matter of time.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Change captain? Play the kids? How to solve the problems at Manchester United | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The beleaguered Michael Carrick’s job is on the line, but there are steps he can take to revive the stricken club
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: The beleaguered Michael Carrick’s job is on the line, but there are steps he can take to revive the stricken club
Content: Manchester United's woes: featuring Michael Carrick, Bruno Fernandes, fans and young players such as Shea Lacey.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Shutterstock; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United's woes: featuring Michael Carrick, Bruno Fernandes, fans and young players such as Shea Lacey.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Shutterstock; Getty ImagesManchester UnitedChange captain? Play the kids? How to solve the problems at Manchester UnitedThe beleaguered Michael Carrick’s job is on the line, but there are steps he can take to revive the stricken clubJamie JacksonFri 23 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTake captaincy from Fernandes, then try to sell him and MartínezThe big question as Bournemouth arrive for Sunday’s 2pm kick-off at Old Trafford is whether Michael Carrick will show his authority by stripping the captaincy from Bruno Fernandes and/or dropping Manchester United’s five-times player of the year. On Friday, Carrick refused to deny he may do so, but the bigger picture concerns whether cashing in on the Portuguese and his fellow mutineer, Lisandro Martínez, in the winter window would be prescient to initiate a new era. Fernandes and Martínez are out of contract in the close season (the club has an extra year’s option in both cases) and, judging by recent behaviour, intend to leave. So yielding, say, £40m and £25m respectively for them in January would allow investment as the rebuild begins. Even a few days on, Fernandes’s words in Como seem incredible: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,” he said after Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation. Fernandes’s open questioning of the tactics is a challenge to the head coach’s authority and we wait to see how/if Carrick will face it down. If Carrick acts and proves he is not a lame duck then even if he is removed a favour is done for his successor.Carrick delivers 5min 27sec monologue and says he will hold brolly to keep everyone dryRead moreEnsure the players connect with the fansSeven hundred United supporters made the trip to Lombardy and witnessed a horror show in incessant rain as their team folded against Cesc Fàbregas’s side. Yet, as always, the faithful will be there on Sunday desperate to cheer their men on against Bournemouth and beyond. Carrick constantly talks of how fans are the club’s lifeblood but do all of the players feel this? Performances such as that at Como will surely be averted if a base creed citing how fundamental supporters are to United is laid down to the squad by the manager.Play with joy againSir Alex Ferguson’s flying wingers, Sir Matt Busby’s holy trinity of Best, Law, Charlton, the “attack, attack, attack” mentality: none of this is evident currently on the field; part of what Carrick admitted on Friday had been “lost”. What is needed is a return to this tradition, and this team are capable as was evident in the spirit of Carrick’s first game of his second tenure. Then, on 17 January 2026 at Old Trafford, he sent out an XI that went at Manchester City from the opening whistle, gave Pep Guardiola’s men zero time to breathe, and a rousing 2-0 victory sent all of a United stripe home jubilant. This, basically, was Carrick’s side last season, a proposition that played with a bounce that landed in third place. This term the smile has vanished and a prevailing sense of doom has settled over the club – precisely what Carrick had vanquished after the gloom of Ruben Amorim’s final days. Time to restore the cavalier edge.United have suffered, in part, this term owing to Carrick’s drive to move to a more possession-based proposition. The problem is one of the key midfielders recruited to execute this, Youri Tielemans, does not have the legs for a central role, and so has been fielded at 10, while Kobbie Mainoo, who can run an engine room, is injured, and Fernandes’ penchant for running about, out of position, means gaps appear where a ball receiver should be.Give the young players more of a chanceIn Fernandes, Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire, Diogo Dalot, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo and Martínez there is a core of long-serving senior players who are not performing. To wake this cadre and freshen the mood from what feels a pervasive staleness, why not blood, more regularly, the younger players? The “play the kids instead” trope can be a cliche but it is a truism for a reason: youth has zero to lose, should run around with a smile and can brighten the darkest of times. Shea Lacey, a nippy wide man, Harry Amass, a promising left-back, and the Fletcher twins, Jack, a clever No 10, and Tyler, a defensive midfielder, are 19 and have 22 appearances between them. None could do worse than those senior players ahead of them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGet the attack firingIn seven of their 11 games this season United have scored either a solitary goal or none, a shocking statistic that shows up how dysfunctional the attack is and, as part of the creative collective, the midfield too. United have only 10 goals in seven league outings and in three Champions League games have managed five – four of these against the minnows Sabah. At Como there was, again, zero pattern of play, control and a paucity of chances that has to be a serious concern. This has to change or a relegation fight could be United’s. A more off-the-cuff style, allied to an attacking outlook, would suit Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and others and start menacing teams again as United did when beating City, Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool last year.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Enciso rescues point in storm for Ipswich to deny Nottingham Forest | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Julio Enciso equalised Neco Williams’s goal to give Ipswich a 1-1 draw with Nottingham Forest at Portman Road
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Julio Enciso equalised Neco Williams’s goal to give Ipswich a 1-1 draw with Nottingham Forest at Portman Road
Content: Julio Enciso slots in Ipswich’s equaliser.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/SPP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJulio Enciso slots in Ipswich’s equaliser.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/SPP/ShutterstockPremier LeagueEnciso rescues point in storm for Ipswich to deny Nottingham ForestJohn Brewinat Portman RoadFri 23 Oct 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid a Suffolk squall, winds whipping, a constant drum of rain, an encounter full of half-chances, mistakes, the obligatory refereeing controversy and searching questions. Do Ipswich possess the stones to deal with the big league? Perhaps so. How long can Nottingham Forest’s dip sustain before their president, Evangelos Marinakis, takes his usual course of action. Perhaps not much longer.Ipswich’s Gary O’Neil was the happier manager, Forest had created the cleaner opportunities, only for familiar failings to cost them. “We were never quite good enough with the ball to turn it into a football match,” said O’Neil. Further adding to Forest’s disappointment, Ipswich’s Issa Diop escaped what looked, on first glance, a red card for a last-man foul. A first-half exchange of goals, both owing much to defensive laxness, determined the result.Ipswich 1-1 Nottingham Forest: Premier League – liveRead moreIpswich’s aim is to establish themselves as Forest have in the Premier League. Though Forest and their manager cannot be presumptive of their statuses. “The result doesn’t reflect the performance but I don’t see another solution other than to keep going,” said Oliver Glasner. Forest havesix points from eight matches, just a single win.Glasner admitted he is still “waiting for this click” while saying: “I see great togetherness. The spirit I start to feel … I loved everything I saw today, just not the result.” A record of starting slow only to flourish at previous clubs offers partial protection, though Forest’s ownership is not like other clubs’. Wednesday was the anniversary of Sean Dyche’s appointment. That tenure lasted just 100 days.Liam Delap’s presence in the Forest ranks, the striker barracked at every touch by home fans, served as a reminder of Ipswich’s failed mission two seasons ago. Unloved in Ipswich for decamping to Chelsea, Delap continues to be short of the confidence he showed back then.Forest kicked off as lowest scorers in the division; no side had drawn a blank more often. Their drought did not take long to break but no flood followed. Neco Williams’s goal came via an overlap and then a looping cross from Daniel Muñoz. Williams glided in unmarked, his finish low and true beyond Christian Walton.Another Forest goal appeared likely before home fans, previously exasperated, were lifted by Jaden Philogene forcing a save from Matz Sels and Julio Enciso dancing through red shirts to force another.The equaliser came via a collective loss of concentration characteristic of Forest’s season so far, echoing defeat at Crystal Palace, and at home to Coventry. Jair Cunha gallivanted forward and, adrenaline coursing, lost possession. Dara O’Shea’s punted clearance was poorly dealt with by Nikola Milenkovic, an under-amped back-pass allowed Enciso to show admirable calm when others had surrendered theirs.Forest’s failure to claim the rewards on offer from the first half told a familiar story. So too do repeated refereeing controversies, and howls of conspiracy among their supporters. How the officials, led by Thomas Bramall, the referee, did not view Diop’s clattering of James McAtee as a foul defied belief. Play was waved on. More understandable, if still highly debatable, was the verdict via video assistant that McAtee had conceded possession with a heavy touch as the collision came. “Leif [Davis] was there to cover,” said Diop, shown a yellow card. “I don’t think it’s a red.”“I think they came to the right conclusion, a good process,” O’Neil said. As well he might. “It looks like the VAR was not from the East Midlands today,” said Glasner. “It felt like it was a red card.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInjustice fuelled Forest though did not make them any more clinical, the best of their second-half flurry of chances involved Murillo missing a free header from a corner. That asked for staying power from Ipswich. So far this season, they have not been the soft touch under O’Neil they became in Kieran McKenna’s survival attempt. “We had to show another side to get something,” said O’Neil. “We can play better but if we think we’re going to be dominant in every game … we’ll be fighting for scraps a lot of the time.”Luck was definitely ridden. Callum Hudson-Odoi, as eight messy minutes of injury time were being added, received more than enough time and space to do far better than drag beyond the far post. The story of the night encapsulated for Forest. And of their season.View image in fullscreenNeco Williams runs off in triumph after giving Forest the lead.Photograph: Richard Heathcote/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueIpswich TownNottingham Forestmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Bavuma’s nine-hour masterpiece was art we risk losing in Test cricket’s great purge | South Africa cricket team | The Guardian
description: T20 franchise cricket is trash sport and killing the red-ball game is cultural vandalism. What would George Orwell have made of this?
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: T20 franchise cricket is trash sport and killing the red-ball game is cultural vandalism. What would George Orwell have made of this?
Content: Temba Bavuma has 12 wins from 14 games as South Africa captain, stretched over three broken years of Test cricket.Illustration: Cameron LawView image in fullscreenTemba Bavuma has 12 wins from 14 games as South Africa captain, stretched over three broken years of Test cricket.Illustration: Cameron LawSouth Africa cricket teamBavuma’s nine-hour masterpiece was art we risk losing in Test cricket’s great purgeBarney RonayT20 franchise cricket is trash sport and killing the five-day game is cultural vandalism. What would Orwell have made of this?Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTShareHave you read George Orwell’s review of Mein Kampf? This might not sound like a grabby reference, or a killer hook for the algorithm. But Hitler is always hot. Hitler is legacy brand. Hitler is eyeballs. Also, it’s just a great review, even more so because it was written at a time when the world didn’t quite know what Hitler was “all about”.True, you get a vibe off people. The invasion of France. The ranting, visceral hatred. There were signs, clues, indications that this guy, this guy isnot my kind of guy.But the full Hitler-verse had yet to reveal itself. And for a while you worry Orwell’s going to get it wrong, not go hard enough, misread the full history as we now know it. He writes about how much he likes Hitler’s face because he looks pained and sad, like a wounded dog, giving off that sense of eternal injustice the German people really went for.South Africa beat Boland and weather to force series decider against AustraliaRead moreBy this point you’re trying to catch his eye, coughing loudly, saying “Holocaust” into your fist. No, George. Don’t start talking about charisma.Luckily, it all turns out fine. Orwell says that he would definitely kill Hitler if he got within arm’s reach of him. Then he describes, better than anyone before or since, the terrifying nature of the world Mein Kampf is proposing, above all its utter boredom, the eternal grey repetitions, same struggle, same triumph, same boot stamping on same face, same pitch of willed and empty hysteria.And yeah … you’re thinking about T20 franchise cricket, aren’t you? I didn’t say it. You did. It’s fine. The mind goes where the mind goes.You’re picturing a year-round cycle of brain-flooding noise. An endless will to power. The Kansas City CheeseSteaks v the Reykjavik Unmentionables live from the Jakarta T5 Megascream, injected straight into your eyeballs by a robot replicant Danny Morrison.It’s fine that you want to make this connection. It’s even deeply fitting given the greatest story of the sporting week by an absolute mile, a story so big, so sweeping, so viscerally personal, that most people seem to have completely ignored it, comes from the polar opposite place.This is of course Temba Bavuma’s match-winning nine-hour hundredin the second Test against Australiain Gqeberha, one of those episodes where sport and the life of the nation seem to cross, blend and become indistinguishable.Mainly Bavuma in Gqeberha was an incredible feat of skill, resilience and constant adaptive intelligence, in the way only TestCricketcan deliver. Bavuma walked out to bat with the summer running away from him. Thrashed in the first Test, South Africa were 12 for two, faced with one of the great bowling attacks.Bavuma has been a transformative Test captain, with 12 wins in 14 matches, four hundreds,a world championship mace, all stretched over three broken years. But he is still always, always chasing legitimacy and affirmation, in a way that is unique to cricket, but also unique to this man in this role in this sporting nation. First black middle order batsman. First black captain. How is this going to fall? How strong is that ice underfoot?View image in fullscreenTemba Bavuma’s brilliant, resiliant 179 took 334 balls, and set the stage for a memorable South Africa victory in the second Test.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APTwo days later Bavuma was last man out for 179 in a total of 425 for nine, sprinting off with a kind of light around him, waving his bat giddily, 36 years old, wife and kid in the crowd, the greatest moment of his sporting life.There were so many parts to this. First, the survival period, with that endearing tic of gently jutting his chin out at the bowler, mixed in with the odd deliciously clean whip or push or clump. Bavuma has really quick hands. I remember seeing him in east London in a white-ball game against dark skies and low stands, and all you could really see was his hands whizzing with thrilling speed, like fireflies in the night.In Gqeberha he was all poise and measured severity. When he plays a cover drive he seems to lean at 45 degrees, knees bent, entire body easing into the oblique, perfectly contained in his own little square of time and space.The game changed with thepartnership of 106 with Marco Jansenbefore lunch on the third day, brilliant counterattacking Test cricket, but also an amazing tableau. At one end the gangling Dutch farmer with the easy, guileless stride, a cricketer who always seems to be running in with a bushel of radishes over one shoulder and a bolt-action rabbit gun in his waistband. At the other the tiny, super-smart black captain. It’s no more than an optic, unrelated to the nation’s real-world struggles. But it’s also real. Sport is, as ever, saying: how about this version of things?Bavuma got to his hundred with a release of pent-up power, swivel-pulling Pat Cummins through midwicket, holding the shot, one of those moments where the batter feels what has happened a second before anyone else, allowed in that microsecond to exist all alone inside his own little pocket of private triumph.But then Bavuma has always had to be aware, to hold himself a certain way. There was surprise in some corners that he turned out to be such an unflappable captain. Try being Temba Bavuma for a bit. You think this stuff is going to faze you?Bavuma is a child of the transition period, born three months after Nelson Mandela left Victor Verster Prison, the same day (get this) the government finally opened up all its public hospitals to black citizens. He grew up a township boy in Langa, playing in the street, learning which strips of local tarmac had the most carry and bounce.Plucked out aged 10 on a scholarship to one of South Africa’s top schools, he struggled. Ten is relatively late to start trying to become an elite batter. How about still perfecting your English, learning how to act, what to put on your plate at dinner? Even his height, which we must always talk about, is a thing. Bavuma is the 10th shortest man ever to play Test cricket. Yeah, pour it on. What else have you got?There was the slow-burn start to his career. For years the quota talk circled, the weird dual burden of innate outsiderdom and suspicions of favour. Then suddenly you’re the first township captain of what has always been an anglophone, military-elite kind of sport.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt sounds overwhelming. Right up until you hear him speak, at which point you just want him to talk about all the stuff in that soft voice, gentle but deliciously insistent. It’s no surprise to learn Bavuma has a normal life away from this, that his wife is founder of a luxury real estate firm, he takes his kid to school, doesn’t do celebrity, that he’s never really made a point of making a point, but made it all the same by being relentlessly himself.Why talk about this here? Why bring endless grey, smothering repetition into it? First because even without the Bavuma story this was just an epic piece of sport, one of those occasions where every detail feels meaningful.Steve Smith getting actual whiplash, literally wearing a foam neck-brace after whirling around to see if an edge had carried. Marnus Labuschagne whirling at the crease, acting out his own thoughts in the air like a tortured pantomime horse, while his career self-suffocates in real time. Here is Anrich Nortje, the perfect composite of shoulders, glower and vengeful moustache, looking on like the hand of fate from a deserted balcony, groin-knacked but somehow still profoundly present.View image in fullscreenTemba Bavuma (centre) is embraced as his team enjoy victory in the second Test. The series decider begins in Cape Town on Tuesday.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APThe whole thing heads on to Newlands on Tuesday and the sandpaper reunion game, an impossibly fine piece of narrative work, slow-cooked over eight years, the kind of storytelling the human brain just thirsts for.Although now it is also time to zoom out and feel the whiplash. On the fifth day of the first Test in Durban, as Australiawrapped up their own victorythe TV commentator talked about the fine sporting spirit of the contest and how “it’s credit to the people of South Africa”, at which point the camera panned back with perfect comic timing to show: a completely empty stadium.So, back to Orwell and being on the right side of history. Because a great thing, a carefully woven cultural exhibit, is being overtly encouraged to die here. South Africa hadn’t played a Test before this series for 11 months. They played eight last year, two a second-string trip to Zimbabwe.The hard game, the actual game that still produces the short-form TV offshoot, is being sacrificed mercilessly. And the thing that is replacing it is not just demonstrably inferior, but self-dooming in its basic inanity.double quotation markMoments of beauty, gold, legend … T20 cricket can’t produce these. It’s throwaway content, parasocial celebrity fawningIn the intervals of the Test, South African TV showed a mouthwatering banter-table chat-along featuring all of South Africa’s craggy modern greats, Polly, Makhaya, AB, the Steyn Gun, sat around just telling stories, doing everything but hug each other, conjuring up moments of beauty, gold, legend.This will not be allowed to happen in the future. T20 cricket can’t produce these stories. It’s throwaway content, parasocial celebrity fawning. What are we going to have 20 years from now? Lhuan-dre Pretorius telling bardically embroidered tales about the time he slash-hoicked 37 off 12 balls in the now defunct North American Mega-Lurch?There is still a fear of saying this out loud, of making the unarguable observation that a form of sporting hyper-capitalism is dictating that nothing can matter if it’s not monetisable right here and now. Half-understood arguments about demand and supply will justify an act of cultural vandalism. Well, yeah, but look at the way this entity in a state of managed decline appears, believe it or not, to be in a state of managed decline.The reality is something beautiful is being extinguished. It feels like the sporting arm of a process that has been called the enshittification of modern life, where the bottom line is the only line, where everything must be reduced to stupidity and profitable chaff.Orwell was also good on the “machine worship” of the early 20th century. He was, in the best way, a luddite. Inefficient, human-scale elements have a right to exist too. The mechanised loom made a few things better. But mainly it made a few people quite a lot richer.We can resist this, and not just in the realm of trash sport, but trash life generally. Humans still know what’s good. We crave these things, still hunger for stories like the Bavuma supremacy, which may never happen again, not in the current timeline, because its structures are being peeled away even as it plays out.Explore more on these topicsSouth Africa cricket teamTwenty20CricketcommentShareReuse this content

title: Premier League news: Spurs’ nine injuries ‘normal’, says De Zerbi; ‘emotional control’ keeps Blues red-free | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Tottenham manager insists medical team not to blame as more key players drop out while Alonso happy with Chelsea’s new-found discipline
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tottenham manager insists medical team not to blame as more key players drop out while Alonso happy with Chelsea’s new-found discipline
Content: Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi faces numerous selection issues at Chelsea when Spurs will attempt to win for only the second time in 42 matches.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenTottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi faces numerous selection issues at Chelsea when Spurs will attempt to win for only the second time in 42 matches.Photograph: John Walton/PAThe talkSoccerPremier League news: Spurs’ nine injuries ‘normal’, says De Zerbi; ‘emotional control’ keeps Blues red-freeTottenham manager insists medical team not to blame as more key players drop out while Alonso happy with Chelsea’s new-found disciplineGuardian writers and agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.‘Big confidence’ in Tottenham’s injury teamRoberto De Zerbi has insisted Tottenham’s medical staff bears no responsibility for the numerous selection issues he faces against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday where his club will attempt to win for only the second time in 42 matches in all competitions.The head coach has been boosted by the return of Pedro Porro from injury while he reported that Andy Robertson, Omar Marmoush and Dominic Solanke were “good” in light of fitness concerns. De Zerbi had bad news elsewhere, however, saying Destiny Udogie was still out and Tosin Adarabioyo was a doubt.James Maddison did not train for three days after the home win over Coventry on Monday and may not be ready, while caution will remain the watchword with Dejan Kulusevski, who played his first minutes since May 2025 against Frank Lampard’s side. De Zerbi could be without nine players due to injury when the longer-term absentees are factored in, including Lucas Bergvall and Savio. Rodrigo Bentancur is suspended.Spurs appointed a new performance director last season in Dan Lewindon and he oversaw a clutch of new hires in the performance department in July. De Zerbi made the point that the club would make a “total report” on injuries at the end of the season but “so far we can’t say anything bad about the medical staff”.“I am convinced our medical staff this season is high level. I have big confidence because I know how they are working and they are good enough to believe in. We are suffering a normal situation in football.”De Zerbi went into detail on the cases of Porro, Bergvall and Robertson to reinforce his argument. “Pedro won the World Cup with Spain,” he said. “Maybe with the head or body he didn’t recover enough to start this season without a pre-season. He already suffered in the World Cup the muscular problem of the hamstring. He felt it in training and played anyway against Aston Villa [on 29 September] because he pushed to come back before the right time and he suffered another injury. What is the responsibility of the medical staff?“Bergvall turned his knee and felt pain in the first minute against Manchester United [on 10 October]. He finished the game and the day after he felt pain. What is the responsibility of the medical staff? Nothing. Robertson played four games in a row for Scotland [during the recent international window] and after that felt a small problem and did not play in Manchester. He played 65 minutes against Coventry and was fatigued. It’s normal fatigue for a player who played [so much].”On Spurs’s terrible record at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi said: “What is the problem? We didn’t play in the past for Tottenham and I was not the Tottenham coach in the last seasons. We have already many problems and this is not a problem.”David Hytner2.Alonso: ‘We keep calm, don’t lose our heads’Xabi Alonso has said greater emotional control is behind the improvement of Chelsea’s disciplinary record, one that saw them picked up 11 red cards last season.Alonso focused on the problem after becoming manager last summer and has been rewarded with better behaviour from his new side. Chelsea, who can expect a feisty encounter when hosting Tottenham on Saturday evening, have not had a red card this season and showed intelligence when theywon 2-0 at Everton last weekend.“For me it comes a lot with emotional control, with the control of the game,” Alonso said. “If you are focused on what you have to do, you are prepared for what’s going on. Normally you don’t make that many mistakes and don’t overreact to certain situations.“This is a fundamental part of the game, to have that emotional control. The momentum is coming – we keep calm, I don’t lose my head and I don’t get stupid yellow cards, make stupid penalties.”Alonso pointed to Chelsea signing more experienced players last summer. “I think it helps,” he said. “Absolutely. It helps for that composure that you need in certain moments. You have players that sometimes, even during the game, they take a step back to see this is happening and now we need to keep focused and calm.”Stamford Bridge is usually at its loudest when Spurs turn up at a ground where they have not won since 2018. Alonso expects an “electric” atmosphere but admitted that playing with control in the Premier League can be tough when crowds feed off duels and end-to-end football. “It is really difficult,” he said.View image in fullscreenChelsea manager Xabi Alonso has played down the impact of his influence from the touchline: ‘I have from the touchline some kind of input but the real one is from the players.’Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters“To find a total dominance in a game when you are in full control and you have few problems like in other leagues, it’s difficult to find it in the Premier League unless you have become a top, top, top team. That’s why you can’t rest on your laurels when you are 2-0 up.”Alonso played down the impact of his influence from the touchline. “It is people on the pitch,” the Spaniard said. “I can say many things but sometimes I don’t reach [the players], I don’t control. I can do it in advance. I have from the touchline some kind of input but the real one is from the players. Normally the most experienced ones. It’s the ones that feel it.”Chelsea are without Emiliano Martínez after the goalkeeper broke his jaw against Everton. Mike Penders will start and Alonso sees similarities between the young Belgian and his compatriot Thibaut Courtois. “I spoke with Thibaut as well when he was in the World Cup, asking about Mike, and he even said that he could see resemblances with Mike,” Alonso said.Jacob Steinberg3.Go easy on Ngumoha, says IraolaAndoni Iraola has insisted Rio Ngumoha must be allowed to make mistakes and not have his development stifled by “impossible” demands.The 18-year-oldsparkled for Liverpool in their Champions League comebackagainst Villarreal on Tuesday while still adapting to playing on the right wing. It was only a fifth start under Iraola for Ngumoha, who last month became the third-youngest player to make his competitive debut for England, after Wayne Rooney and Jude Bellingham.The Liverpool head coach has described it is a “privilege” to coach the teenager but is wary of too many expectations being heaped on such a young talent.“I feel very lucky to have him but this is a moment when, because he has played well, we cannot straight away put expectations on him super high because it is not fair for him,” Iraola said. “He will still have to make mistakes, he will still have his moments where it is up and down, because this is a natural process that every player goes through.“We cannot straight away put demands on Rio that are impossible to beat. No, we have to help him in this process knowing that he will have good games and probably some games when it is not so good.”Iraola believes Ngumoha’s personality offers reassurance that he will not be unduly affected by the growing attention. The winger has two years remaining on the contract he signed on turning 17 but is expected to be rewarded with a new deal.“I haven’t felt that he’s very affected, positively or negatively, by all the things that are said about him,” Iraola added. “He’s very focused on the football side, on improving his performances and trying to get the things that we need from him. It’s not easy when you are 18 and everyone is talking about you but he knows that what matters is what is happening today in training and the things that he can add to his game. He’s very focused on that.”Liverpool will again be without the injured Dominik Szoboszlai when hosting in-form Brighton on Sunday and Victor Muñoz is doubtful with a knock sustained in last weekend’s win at Brentford.Andy HunterView image in fullscreenThe 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha sparkled for Liverpool in their Champions League comeback against Villarreal on Tuesday.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA4.Farke faces triple injury blowDaniel Farke has been dealt a blow before Sunday’s Premier League game at Sunderland after revealing Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Anton Stach and Noah Okafor are all injury doubts.Calvert-Lewin, whose fourth league goal of the season earned Leeds a 1-1 home draw against Manchester United last week, and midfielder Stach both sustained foot injuries in that match. Winger Okafor is struggling with a thigh strain and all three players are rated “major doubts” after missing out on team training this week.Farke confirmed Daniel James is in restraint after recovering from his recent injury, while Lukas Nmecha, Harry Wilson and Jean-Mattéo Bahoya will also be hoping to feature. Nmecha has made six league appearances off the bench this season and Farke added: “Overall you have to say for a back-up striker, Lukas has scored I think seven goals last season,” said Farke.“Of course, if he doesn’t play each and every minute due to the fact that Dominic was so outstanding, I think this is a really good record and I would have to say in the last game he looked sharp.”Press Association5.Nothing has changed for us, says ArbeloaAlvaro Arbeloa maintains “nothing has changed” as his Fulham side look to build on a first Premier League win. The Spaniard – who took over as head coach at Craven Cottage in the summer – has come under scrutiny following a testing start to the campaign before easing some of the pressure with a1-0 victory over Hull at Craven Cottage.Fulham come up against another promoted side at Coventry on Saturday and Arbeloa wants his players to continue to show the same focused mindset. “Nothing has changed for us,” Arbeloa said. “When we were not winning games, we believed that we were doing so many things well, and now we have the same targets, so we should come in and try to win a tough game.“Yes, now we have the reward that we were looking for, and now it is another week, another game, so we need to fight again for the win.”Arbeloa added: “When you are working and you are not winning, it is not easy, so everything is easier when you play well, in the way that you want and you win matches. That is the most important thing, and it is very important for your confidence, and I think we deserve it.”Press Association6.Richest clubs face £1.8m bill for regulatorThe highest-earning Premier League clubs will pay up to £1.8m towards the cost of the independent football regulator (IFR) from next summer, but could face paying much higher amounts in the years ahead.The IFR has opened a consultation proposal on the levy needed to fund it, and has projected a total cost to the 116 clubs in the top five divisions of English football of £20.3m in the first year of its licensing regime – 2027-28 – rising to £20.9m in 2028-29. That figure is double the government’s original estimate of £10m a year being required for the IFR.It is thought Premier League clubs will cover around 85% of the total annual IFR costs, though the amount each club repays will be designed to be proportionate to their revenues. The highest-earning clubs will pay up to £1.8m in year one, the IFR said, but it added that most Premier League teams would pay £600,000.However, costs could rise significantly in the future, with the consultation document confirming that set-up costs for the regulator ran to around £45m. Only £1m of that is being recovered in 2027-28, and £2m the year after, leaving some £42m to be recovered over the next eight years. A further £1m of the 2027-28 levy is a contribution to building up reserves for any future litigation costs.David Kogan, the IFR chair, confirmed last week that clubs would ultimately foot the bill for any legal action it may be involved in against Manchester City,depending on the outcome of their Premier League disciplinary case, which could be a significant amount.He said that any legal costs incurred by the IFR in that matter would in the first instance be covered by the government and then recovered from clubs, but stressed that legal action would only be instigated if the advice was that it would succeed, meaning costs could be recovered from the other side.City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period, but have appealed against the verdict. The IFR has the power to force owners to divest from clubs in cases of serious wrongdoing.The IFR’s media release compared its running costs with the Premier League’s administration costs of more than £200m for the 2024-25 season, a comparison is understood to have caused surprise within the top flight.The Premier League has more than three times the IFR’s staff, generates more than £4bn annually, and its administration costs include all operating expenses plus investments in other areas aimed to help the league grow further, such as the set-up of new production studios. It also includes its legal costs related to the City case and others.The IFR said Championship clubs not in receipt of parachute payments would pay around £45,000 for 2027-28, with clubs in Leagues One and Two paying around £9,000 and £6,000 each. National League clubs would pay around £600 a year each, the IFR said.Richard Monks, the IFR chief executive, said: “I am aware of the £10m figure [originally estimated by the government] and, to be clear, that is not a number we believe reflects either the current financial reality or the task ahead of us. The levy we are proposing today represents a fair and balanced approach and will ensure that most clubs pay around 0.1% of their annual revenues.“We are confident football will see this is a relatively modest investment to help achieve a more sustainable ecosystem which will provide peace of mind for fans, clubs and the communities they serve.”Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsFootballThe talkTottenham HotspurChelseaLiverpoolLeeds UnitedFulhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: World and Olympic marathon champion Jepchirchir suspended after positive doping test | Marathon | The Guardian
description: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended for doping after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended for doping after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for EPO
Content: Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir won the Sydney Marathon back in August.Photograph: Mark Baker/APView image in fullscreenKenya’s Peres Jepchirchir won the Sydney Marathon back in August.Photograph: Mark Baker/APMarathonWorld and Olympic marathon champion Jepchirchir suspended after positive doping testAIU investigates after sample tested positive for EPO33-year-old won Olympic marathon in 2021Agence France-PresseFri 23 Oct 2026 08.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a fresh blow for Kenyan athletics, the women’s world marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir, has been provisionally suspended for doping, theAthleticsIntegrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday.The highly decorated 33-year-old, who won Olympic gold in the Covid-delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, was suspended after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for the banned blood booster EPO.Six-year ban for top marathon runner who submitted fake prescriptionRead moreThe athlete is provisionally suspended while the case is investigated, while the AIU said Jepchirchir’s out-of-competition sample had been collected in Kenya before her recent SydneyMarathonvictory.More than 140 Kenyan athletes, including thewomen’s marathon world record-holder, Ruth Chepngetich, have been suspended or banned by the AIU since 2017.Jepchirchir’s lauded career includes a world record in the half-marathon, while she is a four-time World Marathon major winner, having captured the 2026 Sydney Marathon, the 2024 London Marathon, the 2022 Boston Marathon and the 2021 New York Marathon.The decision of World Athletics to award Nairobi the 2029 world championships is likely to increase the scrutiny of the east African nation’s anti-doping policies.Barnabas Korir, Athletics Kenya’s youth development director and vice-president of the national Olympic committee, said he was left feeling shocked by the news of the suspension. “It’s a big disappointment coming soon after we were awarded the World Athletics Championship in 2029,” Korir told AFP. “We are in shock, especially in the calibre of Peres Jepchirchir after a stellar career. We don’t know what is happening with our athletes.”Jepchirchir’s manager, Gianni Demadona, said she had tarnished her reputation. “When I learned from the AIU three days ago that she had been tested positive for EPO, I was confused and shocked,” Demadona said. “I can’t say anything because I was trusting her after 13 years working together that she was one of the most trustable athletes around. I was completely wrong. She spoiled her long and amazing career and she closes her career in the worst way.”Kenya played host to a three-day visit from the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) this month, with the body’s president, Witold Banka, telling the country that it had to strive for zero tolerance on doping.“Kenya proudly calls itself the home of champions. But for that home to remain respected and credible, it must also be clean,” Banka said. “That is why Kenya needs a strong culture of clean sport, zero tolerance for doping, and a more determined approach to preventing and fighting doping.”Banka said that joint cooperation with Kenyan authorities would help lay the foundations for a cleaner sport. “Wada or Adak [Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya] alone cannot achieve its vision if we do not cooperate with those who have the power to go against those who are producing, smuggling and trafficking dangerous steroids to your athletes,” he said.“We’ve found a common understanding and we are on the same track and there’s a clear goal within Kenya for zero tolerance for doping policy and it has to be established immediately with joint actions and a more aggressive approach to those who are destroying the image of the country and the reputation of the athletes.”Explore more on these topicsMarathonDrugs in sportAthleticsKenyanewsShareReuse this content

title: Will Borthwick’s autumn England squad embrace Prem chaos or prioritise prudence? | England rugby union team | The Guardian
description: Scoring spree will be forgotten at the Rugby World Cup, and a return for Courtney Lawes may hint at coach’s thinking
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Scoring spree will be forgotten at the Rugby World Cup, and a return for Courtney Lawes may hint at coach’s thinking
Content: Courtney Lawes claims a lineout for Sale. The veteran lock’s defensive grit and set-piece prowess could be valuable at the Rugby World Cup next year.Photograph: Nigel French/PAView image in fullscreenCourtney Lawes claims a lineout for Sale. The veteran lock’s defensive grit and set-piece prowess could be valuable at the Rugby World Cup next year.Photograph: Nigel French/PAEngland rugby union teamAnalysisWill Borthwick’s autumn England squad embrace Prem chaos or prioritise prudence?Gerard MeagherScoring spree will be forgotten at the Rugby World Cup, and a return for Courtney Lawes may hint at coach’s thinkingFri 23 Oct 2026 08.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTShareIt says much about Steve Borthwick’s approach to England’s coming autumn campaign that he is due to name his training squad within minutes of the full-time whistle at Harlequins on Sunday. Simply put, there is no time to waste.Borthwick will have his squad for only a couple of days after the Prem’s derby weekend before they return to their clubs for a domestic fixture. In years gone by there was an extra week with the players but this time, as 12 months ago, Borthwick’s preparations are truncated.Maro Itoje seals England future by agreeing new deal with SaracensRead moreWhen it comes to naming squads he does not spring too many surprises. But what fascinates is how he may interpret what he has seen in the Prem and the solitary round of Champions Cup matches. Feasts at domestic level, famine on the continent.Will Borthwick look to employ the attacking abandon that has taken hold of the Prem or write it off as bubblegum sport, unsuited to the Test stage and, with only 12 matches left before England’s World Cup opener, rely on players he knows can perform on the international stage? Without getting too reductive, Sunday’s squad will give a clue. If players such as George Hendy, Will Joseph and Fitz Harding are included, it would suggest Borthwick is embracing the chaos. A recall for Courtney Lawes, meanwhile, would hint at a more prudent approach.He may do both or neither. But whether he sees the try-fests as something to harness, or a hindrance, will be revealing. It calls to mind Thomas Tuchel’s insistence before the summer’s World Cup that he wanted England to play like a Premier League side. Does Borthwick want his England team to play like a Prem side? According to Rassie Erasmus he is a coach who “chases trends”.This cuts to the heart of something Borthwick has never really mastered. What is England’s identity? Does Borthwick pick players who best fit his vision for England, or the best players available, creating a gameplan around them? “Your identity comes from the pool of players you have and what it looks like and over time,” the England assistant coach, Richard Wigglesworth, said last month.“The style of English rugby has changed and the profile of player has changed considerably. We’re dynamic, skilful, we want to play fast. When someone mentions identity, they’re incorrect because there’s playing well and there’s not. You can have an identity and lose, who is bothered about that? It’s about playing well and then you’ll see an identity. I think there’s a bit too much made of that.”The dilemma facing Borthwick is all the more acute because the suspicion is the coming month of Nations Championship fixtures will be high-scoring if the weather holds. While the international game is not all-singing, all-dancing in the way that the Prem is, there is evidently a trend towards attacking dominance. And as much as the Nations Championship title is coveted, the stakes are nowhere near as high as they will be in Australia next year.View image in fullscreenNorthampton’s talented squad provide the spine of Steve Borthwick’s England.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianBorthwick will be aware that in the knockout stages of the World Cup, tries do not come for free. South Africa became champions in 2023 without scoring more than 16 points in either the semi-final or final. Of eight knockout matches, only New Zealand scored more than 40 – in a mismatched semi-final against a poor Argentina. The next highest was England with 30 against Fiji, but no one else made it out of the 20s. At the 2019 World Cup in Japan both semi-finals were won with 19 points. The expectation is a significant drop-off in scoring in Australia, once the pool stage – which will witness numerous blowouts – is out of the way. It is all the more relevant next year because the new format means an extra knockout round.“It’s set-piece and defence when the stakes are so high,” says Saracens’ Brendan Venter, who won the World Cup with South Africa in 1995. “You end up having two teams with the best set-piece and defence. The All Blacks often play some cracking stuff but when you go through to the knockouts it’s just low-scoring games.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorthwick is under pressure. Do not be fooled by his recent contract extension, if England are beaten by Australia in their opener, the heat will get more intense. Playing in a manner that excites supporters would help his cause and the best international sides tend to have a strong spine from the dominant domestic club.It is hard to argue against Northampton’s hegemony in England and in Alex Mitchell, Fin Smith, Tommy Freeman and George Furbank – even if he is no longer at Saints – Borthwick has the players to showcase the best of the Prem. “Lots of those skills are relevant,” says Northampton’s director of rugby Phil Dowson. “Are international players better decision-makers in defence? Yeah, I think they probably are but that’s international level isn’t it? Everything is going to be a little better. We always talk about Prem being slightly differently refereed but the ability to run at a defender, sit him down and make him make a decision because I’ve got the ball in two hands is still going to be relevant.”Borthwick sought to bring officiating in the Prem closer to the international game this season but judging by the first few weeks, it is yet to bear fruit. It is a concern that seven of the eight Prem sides failed to win in the opening weekend of the Champions Cup and the manner in which they were outgunned at the breakdown is all the more reason to worry. Again, that is one of Lawes’s strengths, and it felt significant that Borthwick watched Sale’s rearguard action invictory over Saracensearlier this month.Borthwick must sift through the sediment. Find the nuggets that he can employ both in the autumn and next year’s World Cup.Cherrypick the best bits but ignore the bells and whistles. As George Skivington, whose Gloucester side went into the weekend’s fixtures top of the table, puts it: “Steve’s job is to take from what we’re doing well what he thinks can translate … that’s the challenge of being an international coach.”Explore more on these topicsEngland rugby union teamRugby unionanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Cheltenham’s racing return provides romance over jumps and 20-1 shock | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Kingofthefrontier was a surprise winner of the Sharp Novice Hurdle as Cheltenham held its first meeting since March
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Kingofthefrontier was a surprise winner of the Sharp Novice Hurdle as Cheltenham held its first meeting since March
Content: Conor O'Farrell on board Kingofthefrontier after winning the Sharp Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenConor O'Farrell on board Kingofthefrontier after winning the Sharp Novices' Hurdle at Cheltenham.Photograph: David Davies/PAHorse racingCheltenham’s racing return provides romance over jumps and 20-1 shockOutsider Kingofthefrontier wins Sharp Novices’ HurdleTrainer John Dawson gets better of Dan SkeltonGreg WoodFri 23 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe jumping game increasingly resembles the Flat when it comes to the concentration of racing power in ever fewer trainers’ hands, but the opening day of Cheltenham’s new season –the first, in fact, since Gold Cup day in March– brought a reminder that romance has not been drained entirely from the winter code.Dan Skelton, who dethroned Willie Mullins to become the new champion over jumps last season, had already trained 115 winners in the current campaign before racing on Friday, nearly halfway towards Martin Pipe’s all-time record of 243. John Dawson, by contrast, had sent out a total of six winners from his yard in North Yorkshire since May 2023.Cheltenham jumps into action after fixing its troublesome holeRead moreHowever, it was Dawson’s Kingofthefrontier, a 20-1 outsider and only the trainer’s third runner at the home of jumping, who led the field home in the Grade Two Sharp Novices’ Hurdle, with Skelton’s Cooltobecareless, the 13-8 favourite, only third. The winner was nearer last than first turning in but showed an impressive turn of foot to run out a two-and-a-quarter length winner from Nicky Henderson’s Planters Punch.Dawson rode into the famous winner’s enclosure aboard Sine Nomine after the Hunters’ Chase at the festival meeting here in March 2024, but his firstCheltenhamwinner as a trainer was an even better moment in what is still a young racing career.“We’ve always loved him since the word go,” Dawson said. “I just felt we had a horse to come and have a go with.He’s still got a lot to learn and the way he went through the race, Conor [O’Farrell, his jockey] said he was a bit stumbly and he had to balance him a couple of times. But speed wasn’t a problem for me, he was always going to have enough boot to get there, and he picked up really well.“He’s actually a little bit horse-shy and when that big horse of Dan Skelton’s came running towards him, I think he was edging away from him, but he’ll learn a lot from that and he could still be anything.”Dawson and Kingofthefrontier’s owner, George Critchley, opted to run in Friday’s Grade Two feature event in preference to a novice handicap hurdle at Carlisle.“He’d never disappointed us,” Dawson said. “George puts a lot into the game, I wanted to bring him here and I thought he had a horse good enough to do it. I just can’t believe it came off.We’re ambitious [but] we only want the horses to have a go with and hopefully we’ve showcased ourselves [today] to do that. I don’t want to be a massive Dan Skelton in numbers, but I just want real quality.”Irish stables have been dominant at the festival meeting in March in recent seasons and Gordon Elliott is already looking ahead to a possible run in the Grand Annual Handicap Chase for Bowensonfire after the six-year-old’s win in the card’s two-mile novice chase.View image in fullscreenBowensonfire ridden by Jack Kennedy on the way to winning the Novices’ Chase.Photograph: David Davies/PABowensonfire was the first leg of a double for Elliott, completed when Cosmos D’Ainay took a novice hurdle later on the card, while Cian Collins sent out a third winner for Ireland on the day when Brandt, at 10-1, took the final race on the card.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Saturday tipsShowDoncaster12.55 Ancient State 1.30 your feedback.Breacher can provide Futurity Trophy valueAidan O’Brien and Andrew Balding field four of the seven runners in Saturday’s Futurity Trophy at Doncaster, the final Group One of the British season, but the focus on their neck-and-neck tussle for the trainers’ title could mean that the improvingBreacher(1.30) sets off at a value price on ground that promises to suit.William Muir and Chris Grassick’s colt has progressed by the run in three starts to date over seven furlongs, while also looking sure to thrive at middle-distances next season.Cracksman, his sire, was at his best with some cut in the ground and a demanding mile on heavy going could well see Breacher outrun his early odds of around 10-1.Doncaster 12.55:Ancient Stateseems to save his best form for this track and trip and He has gone well fresh in the past, remains fairly weighted on his winning form at the end of last season and his prominent run-style is ideal for this track and trip.Cheltenham 1.45:Olly Murphy’sRoad To Wembley– part-owned by Sir Alex Ferguson – was better than the bare result when fourth on his handicap debut at Worcester in September and should appreciate this move up to three miles.Doncaster 2.05: Bengal Tiger’s 12-length win in a maiden at Naas last time was backed up by an excellent time and he should handle this step up to Listed company without too much fuss.Cheltenham 2.20:James Owen’s string remains in strong form whatever the season or code andIdaho Fireposted a new career best at Uttoxeter last time out – a performance that suggests he could cope with a subsequent 10lb hike in the weights.Cheltenham 2.55:With further rain expected before Saturday’s card,Katate Dori’s form when second over track and trip off a 3lb higher mark in January looks as strong as anything on offer.Cheltenham 3.30:Four of the seven runners in this four-year-old event were in the field for the Triumph Hurdle at the festival and whileIndian Riverwas only 10th, he finished third in the equivalent event at Aintree.
