title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration, says the Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration, says the Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionImmigration and asylumImagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigrationGaby HinsliffOur economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integrationFri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.42 EDTShareMy mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.Under the latest attempt by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to ratchet immigration numbers ever further down, “low-skilled” foreign workers will now have towait up to 15 yearsfor the right to become permanent residents. The new rules would be backdated to 2021 to catchwhat the right dubbedthe “Boriswave”, that unexpected surge of workers who came to Britain in the Boris Johnson years – many on health and care visas – and would under the old five-year rule have started qualifying for settlement in 2027. What has unsettled some of Mahmood’s own cabinet colleagues is the sense of the state reneging on what was understood to be the deal when those workers came here. Having to be continuously employed for 15 years instead of five without a break means in practice that some will have to leave, while others will live in mortal fear of losing a job. A growing cabinet revolt against Mahmood’s reforms is now becoming the first real challenge to Andy Burnham’s authority as prime minister, but also more broadly a test of where he really stands on immigration.This month’s budget throws a problem that governments have been trying to ignore for a decade into sharp relief: kneejerk hostility to foreign workers is costing Britain dear, and not just because public services would fall apart without them. Last month, theInstitute for Fiscal Studies warnedthat falling immigration would inevitably mean falling tax revenues, shrinking John Healey’s headroom at the budget by about £4bn. So much for the rightwing myth that migrants are a drain on their host country: if anything, they’ve been bailing Britain out.It’s not just taxes, either. Immigrants pay a surcharge on top for the right to use the NHS if needed while they’re here, which is now raising£2.5bn a year, according to new research from the Nuffield Trust. It seems all those pesky liberals who argued that migrants are generally healthier than the average Briton – and therefore less likely to need a GP – were right after all: the trust estimates that migrants are on average paying in 60% more in surcharge per year than they take out in healthcare services, a handy little revenue stream that for some reason we never talk about. But immigration crackdowns threaten that income too. The trust notes that falling immigration can lead to “a sharp drop in income” for the NHS, much as slashing foreign student visas has hurt universities that were reliant on their fees.As the Office for Budget Responsibilityspelled out in 2024– when it calculated that the surge of immigration under Johnson that so offended Tory voters at the time would help knock more than £7bn off projected government borrowing by 2028-29 – economically speaking, immigration is basically good news. If the country really wants it to fall, then something else – higher taxes, lower spending or more borrowing – is going to have to plug the resulting hole in the finances. Yet for years now, successive governments, fearful of confronting leave voters, have tried manfully to pretend that that choice does not exist.Mahmood’s plan is essentially yet another attempt to square the same old circle, gearing the system around letting in as few people as possible – in keeping with what a furious public has for the last decade seemed to want – while trying to cherrypick those most likely to make an outsize economic contribution. Under her reforms, the highest paid workers (who are likely to pay lots of tax over their lifetimes) would befast-tracked to settlement, while those judged more likely to be an economic burden on the state overall would be pushed away. What she doesn’t seem to have bargained for, aside from the fact that the rest of the world is in hot competition for high-skilled migrants, is the sense of deep disquiet that engenders. As the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has pointed out, endlessly prolonging settlement risks undermining social cohesion. A country that makes very clear its foreign workers are here at best on sufferance, even if they do hold lives in their hands at work every day, does nothing to encourage them to integrate and put down roots.The logic of Burnham’s announcement that a future Labour government might considerrejoining the EU, meanwhile, leaves Mahmood’s reforms looking strangely like the relics of a bygone era. If rejoining the single market or customs union would inevitably mean accepting freedom of movement again, what’s the point?The truth is that grimly ratcheting immigration down to next to nothing has come at extraordinary fiscal and social cost, and if the aim was to destroy Reform’s raison d’etre then it hasn’t worked. The mainstream right has switched seamlessly from the pre-Brexit days of complaining that Polish plumbers were taking Britons’ jobs, to a much darker post-Brexit stage of painting migrants as rapists and criminals. The far right, meanwhile, has simply moved on from cheerleading for deportations to insisting that even people who were born here aren’t English unless they’re white.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLegal migrant numbers are at a historic low and small boat crossingshave halved, yet that didn’t stop anger at asylum seekers spilling on to the streets again this summer. There is no level of migration low enough to satisfy some people. There is, however, very much a level of migration low enough to make us all even poorer, and the angry somehow even angrier. And right now, we’re living with it.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumOpinionAndy BurnhamShabana MahmoodSocial careNHSLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: This man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the same  | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s future, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s future, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andrew Boff, chair of the London Assembly, at City Hall, London, January 2025.Photograph: See Li/Picture Capital/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAndrew Boff, chair of the London Assembly, at City Hall, London, January 2025.Photograph: See Li/Picture Capital/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionConservativesThis man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the samePolly ToynbeeThe London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s futureFri 23 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTShareThe chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports theEuropean convention on human rights(ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch thatothers would follow himover the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent.In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She alsobars anyone supporting net zero.When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race.In a statementhe pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me,the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.The time may come, he warned, when extremists win an election on an even smaller vote sharethan Labour’s 34% in 2024– and overturn all human rights legislation without the protections the ECHR affords. “That’s what authoritarian governments do,” Boff said. But he insisted that the committee, which vets Conservative candidates, didn’t listen. “They just repeated the same tropes, that activist judges are using the ECHR against parliament.”Now he is free of the party straitjacket, Boff is planning to stand for London mayor as an independent, allowing him to say what he thinks about Badenoch.He complains to me that the energy and resources that should promote the party “all go to promoting Kemi, Kemi, Kemi”. Thinking well of her in 2015, he says he had encouraged her to stand for the London assembly, where she served until 2017 before being elected to parliament. He says he found her “lazy and combative”.Few will be surprised by Boff’s departure. But many will be wondering what took him so long.He was ejected from the Tory conference in 2023for quietly heckling the then home secretary Suella Braverman’s speech, accusing her of homophobia and transphobia. “It is a signal to people who don’t like people who are LGBT+,” Boff, who is gay, said at the time as he condemned her speech as “trash”. Boff said that Braverman “was basically vilifying gay people and trans people by this attack on LGBT ideology”.View image in fullscreenAndrew Boff being escorted out of a speech by Suella Braverman at the Conservative party conference in Manchester, 2023.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesHe was not alone in voicing criticism over the party’s direction. The former Tory MP Robert Buckland, fellow one-nationer and director of the Tory Reform Group, hurried out to defend Boff after his ejection from the conference, saying heckling was “part of the democratic debate” and that his treatment by security staff was “heavy-handed”.Buckland was among the many one-nationers who lost their seat at the 2024 general election. But that traditional strand of Conservatism has not vanished – nor have those who used to vote for the Tories but now turn to the Liberal Democrats or simply boycott the ballot box.Boff’s views represent a growing centre-right moderate strand that has been expelled or silenced under Badenoch’s leadership. Facing this hostile climate, one nation Tories have gone to ground in parliament; but outside the Commons, Prosper UK, a centrist Tory grouping led by the former mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson quietly gains strength.Its mission statement is to win back moderate voters who snubbed the Conservatives at the last general election, and this message seems to have struck a chord, with the group attractingnearly 30,000 supporterssince its launch in January.It is worth examining Boff’s views, as many Conservatives who have signed up to Prosper UK are likely to share them. He calls himself a Thatcherite, strongly opposing Labour’s renationalisation plans, backing low taxes and a small state. He voted for Brexit, believing the words of the likes of Daniel Hannan,who claimed“absolutely nobody is talking about threatening our place in the single market”. But instead the Tories delivered a hard Brexit after what he calls an “atrocious” campaign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTimes have changed; as the political analyst Peter Kellnerpointed out this week, Britain’s pro-Brexit majority has literally died out. Any so-called betrayal of the referendum is only betraying the dreadful legacy of the departed.If the Conservative party has any future as a government, it won’t be under its present leader. A small bounce for improved performance in parliament will never overcome Badenoch’s growing distance from voters, including those who should be natural Tories.Boff may be a throwback to an irretrievable, more moderate Conservative brand, like that of the Macmillan era – a voice from the good old days when traditional party allegiances were clearly defined. Or possibly he and Prosper UK are the vanguard of a reconstituted centre-right able to attract new voters as well as those who have deserted the Tories.That won’t be easy: already there are gloating Spectator-aligned Tories who say thatthe party is better offwithout the likes of Boff, or any real concession to centrism. But we should have a care. The success of a respectable right matters to all in the left bloc of progressive parties, too. A centre right is needed to fight off the dark forces of the hard right and worse, here and across Europe. That Overton window framing politics needs a firm shunt towards a more rational debate on our future in Europe – and on saving the planet.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservativesOpinionKemi BadenochEuropean court of human rightsHuman Rights ActcommentShareReuse this content

title: Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: London’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River Thames, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: London’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River Thames, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Hammersmith Bridge in west London, which has been closed to traffic for seven years, in April 2019.Photograph: Johnny Armstead/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHammersmith Bridge in west London, which has been closed to traffic for seven years, in April 2019.Photograph: Johnny Armstead/REX/ShutterstockOpinionLondonHammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’tSimon JenkinsLondon’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River ThamesFri 23 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.41 EDTShareLondon’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge alsonow closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be5,107 homes a year, up from a previoustarget of 1,381.The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion isofficially ratedthe worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation ofcomputer-assisted“smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just27 seconds offindividual bus journeys. A Guardian investigationlast monthtimed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circuswas under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word inLondon.In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter ofsparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with thetotal for 2024at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness | Emma BrockesRead moreHammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but ithas decidedit “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent£54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’sSadiq Khanappears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, theCity of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn.The foundationcurrently spends lavishly oncauses that havenothing to do with bridges.This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLondonOpinionSadiq KhanArchitectureMotoringcommentShareReuse this content

title: Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubts | Devi Sridhar  | The Guardian
description: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Author: Devi Sridhar
Headline: Take a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignored, says public health expert Devi Sridhar
Content: ‘The question is whether it’s actually useful in daily practice beyond what clinicians are already doing by using experience and years of training.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The question is whether it’s actually useful in daily practice beyond what clinicians are already doing by using experience and years of training.’Photograph: Andrzej Rostek/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Can AI really predict cancer survival better than a doctor? I have my doubtsDevi SridharTake a selfie to see how healthy you are: the idea is enticing and this new research is promising. But so many factors have been ignoredFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.37 EDTShareThe idea that a single selfie could predict how long someone with cancer may live sounds like an incredible breakthrough. AI is getting better at spotting patterns in medical data, but can it be used to reliably predict what will happen to an individual patient? I asked a clinical colleague what she thought about therecent headlines. She found it an interesting development given that doctors have long used facial appearance to assess patient health. For example, she noted that they may write “appears stated age” or “appears older than stated age” as a proxy for general health.Now, researchers from Mass General Brigham, a healthcare institution in Massachusetts, have taken this idea a step further. They have developed an AI model trained on more than 40 million facial images – called FAHR-Face – to assess biological age and predict survival in cancer patients. For biological age, they developed FAHR-FaceAge, which estimates age from certain facial features such as the forehead, the wrinkles between the nose and mouth and the temples. For cancer survival, they developed FAHR-FaceSurvival, trained using almost 35,000 photos of cancer patients. This model focused more closely on the area below the eyes and the bridge of the nose – regions of the face “linked with dying”.Dr Raymond Mak, one of the study’s authors, noted that these parts of the face are the same as those referenced by Hippocrates in 400BC as signs of muscle wasting and mortality risk: “the nose sharp, the eyes sunken, the temples fallen in”.The results, published in The Lancet Digital Health this month, are intriguing – but far from conclusive. Researchers found that AI-estimated facial age was significantly associated with survival in 18 of 28 cancer categories. So, basically, it works for some cancers, but not for others. In addition,Prof Miroslaw Bobernoted, “The tool still needs testing against doctors’ own judgments and across different hospitals and patient groups. For example, the facial-age measure was not significantly associated with survival for Black patients after adjustment for other factors.” That finding adds to thegrowing concernthat AI models can exhibit racial bias based on the data used to train them and underlying assumptions. For example, racial bias has been shown when AI models analysecardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) scans– used to diagnose and monitor heart disease.Let’s go back to what the published study does and doesn’t tell us. These models are built on retrospective data looking at statistical associations across thousands of patients, and it’s a jump to then accurately predict future survival from this. A selfie may contain clues about a patient’s health, but that is a long way from being able to predict their future – and a longer way still from proving that the prediction is useful in clinical practice.I also worry about how unreliable selfies are. Just think of the times you’ve met people in real life and compared them with their profile photos. Anyone who has tried one of the online AI “guess your age” tools will know how much the result varies with lighting, camera angle, facial expression or even time of day. And then there’s botox, fillers, facelifts and even GLP-1 drugs, which alter facial fat and shape. How much can a single photograph really tell us about someone’s underlying health?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPrepare for more website shutdowns in the age of AI – but human inaction is the real culprit | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreAs anti-ageing treatmentsbecome the norm, visible age and underlying health will become an increasingly complex relationship. A face in a selfie that looks younger may not be necessarily healthier. The researchers do note that they tested their age model against lighting, expression and cosmetic surgery – but if predictions are based on specific signs of ageing in parts of the face that those all affect, I can’t see how it would be possible to avoid a certain degree of error in AI estimates.None of this means the research isn’t promising. This new tool and the research team behind it are impressive. Alongside other tests that a doctor may perform to assess a patient’s health and future prognosis, it could take some of the guesswork out of “looks stated age”. But the question is whether it’s actually useful in daily practice beyond what clinicians are already doing when using experience and years of training.If you’re tempted to go to the project’s public website to find out your biological age, even just to brag to friends about how young it says you look, be aware that by uploading your selfie, you will become part of the study too, as their consent forms indicate. Your face is not only being assessed, it’s contributing to the data used to develop the technology. Currently, the tool will only tell you your biological age, but I would be sceptical of what that may tell you about your overall health.Finally, a pop quiz (I’m in the middle of the teaching semester): what top three things did the researchers find made people’s face age? Alcohol, drugs and smoking. No surprise there, but possibly an explanation as to why doctors can broadly read someone’s health status from their face. Something that perhaps we didn’t need AI scanning 40m faces to tell us.Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of EdinburghExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionCancer researchMedical researchcommentShareReuse this content

title: A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obvious | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general
Content: ‘If there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one.’Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘If there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one.’Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obviousMoira DoneganRepublicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney generalFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareIt’s a bit like Lucy with the football. Every few years,Democratsconvince themselves that a Texas Senate seat might finally switch from red to blue. On paper, it makes sense. Texas is a large and urbanizing state with an increasingly educated – and increasingly non-white – population.Other one-time Republican strongholds that have undergone similar demographic shifts have turned purple or even blueish – think Georgia, for example. The border counties along the Rio Grande valley, with their deep poverty and big Latino populations, were long thought to be fertile ground to nurture a kind of anti-Trump populism that could be converted into pro-Democratic sentiment. The state Democratic party is anemic there, but a few talented candidates have emerged.Who else remembers Beto O’Rourke, the formerTexasDemocratic congressman and onetime presidential hopeful, who appeared on a 2019 cover of Vanity Fair, photographed in muted Annie Leibovitz tones along a desert dirt road, promising to deliver his home state, and a crucial Senate vote, from the clutches of Republican control?Donald Trump’s Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa MahdawiRead moreDoes that hope seem naive now? Even almost childish? Given what we know of O’Rourke’s subsequent success – or of the voting trends in the Rio Grande valley – does the past hope of a blue Texas begin to seem at all arrogant?Forgive me, then, for harboring doubts about whether Texas will vote, as some pollsters and many hopeful Democrats now say it will, for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, over his Republican opponent, the odious state attorney general,Ken Paxton.The excitement of Democrats in the TexasUS Senaterace this year carries with it the aftertaste of past disappointments. Lucy swears that this time, she’ll let Charlie Brown kick, and Charlie Brown – a slave to his own optimism – draws back his leg.But if there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one. Polls have put Talarico, a former seminarian, at a steady, though narrowing, lead. And there is reason for his appeal: Talarico speaks in eloquently religious terms that are well-tailored to his Bible belt audience; at 37, his relative youth will probably appeal to voters fatigued by gerontocracy.But the real deciding factor in the election may well be his opponent: Paxton is an uncommonly dishonorable man, even by the very low standards of a Republican Senate candidate. He’s been indicted on various fraud charges by Texas grand juries (he denied wrongdoing and eventually paid $300,000 in restitution).He was sued over similar fraud claims, subjected to multiple whistleblower complaints, nearly disbarred, and impeached in his capacity as attorney general by members of his own Texas Republican party. (He was later acquitted.)He is also going through a messy, public divorce after his wife of several decades, Angela, finally began proceedings against himafter an alleged extramarital affair.He subjects women to systematic mistreatment in public life, too: as Texas AG, he has presided over one of the most maximalist and sadistic abortion ban regimes, leading to one of the highest maternal and infant mortality rates in the country. He is unlikable, and unliked. Republican Texans who would have come out to vote for another candidate are more likely to stay home rather than vote for him.If winning a Texas Senate seat has long been a pipe dream for Democrats, the possibility that they might do so seems to be frighteningRepublicans.A loss in Texas would not just be a strategic defeat for the GOP, but a psychic one – a failure to hang on to unified power in a state that is supposed to be both the geographical center and the cultural linchpin of conservatism. It presents a risk to the emotions and morale of the Republican party much more than other potential losses in states such as, say, Maine, Michigan or Alaska.In a word, it would be emasculating. And in characteristic fashion, Republican power players have sought to assert masculinity as their central line of attack in the race.Over and over, Republicans have sought to keep Texas by insinuating that Talarico is gay, a woman or a pedophile – sometimes all three – and persistently linking him to the issue of gender transition treatment for minors. They have implied that he’s weak, that he’s either asexual or sexually threatening, depending on the occasion, and, weirdly, that he’s vegan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJD Vance, who has used the midterm cycle to informally launch his 2028 bid for the Republican presidential nomination, has seemingly decided to imitate Trump in vulgarity even where he lags him in charisma and humor. Like many, he’s been trying to get a 2016-style nickname for the Democrat to stick: “Talafreako.” It doesn’t quite roll off the tongue.But Vance has also suggested that Talarico is gay – and that he would somehow be disqualified from the Senate if he was. At a rally inTyler, Texas, Vance told a male audience member that he loved him. “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico.” He paused and waited for the crowd to laugh.Before that, he hadinsinuatedthat Talarico was a pedophile. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’sweb browser history,” Vance said.Elon Musk – nominally a resident of Texas, though billionaires don’t really “reside” anywhere – has looked to rescue Paxton’s candidacy with a massive infusion of cash,dumping $158minto the race late last month on the Republican’s behalf. On his social media platform, X, he has taken on a similar tone to Vance in attacking Talarico, alternating between casting vaguely sexual aspersions about Talarico’s character – Musk has repeatedly called him “creepy” – and making specific, incendiary and false claims about the Texas Democrat. “Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them,”Musk wrote.“Not just in Texas, but nationwide. Pure evil.”These kinds of low-brow, sexualized smears are the kind of thing Republicans do to make themselves look tough. The name-calling is supposed to evoke the power of the schoolyard bully in the form of a man in a suit, to conjure the image of someone so powerful that rules, and decorum, don’t apply to him.But I think that really, these kinds of juvenile taunts are a sign of the party’s weakness. Republicans have no answer to mainstream Americans’ economic pain; all they can offer are titillating little libidinal gratifications for their base.They are betting that the grim satisfaction of dominance, of cruelty, will be more important to voters than $5 gasoline. They’re leaning into being mean, in short, because they don’t have anything else.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTexasKen PaxtonUS politicsUS SenateDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Finally gen Alpha discovers Nicole Kidman – via Adéla’s corset lyrics | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Plus, King Charles’s unusual gift to Aung San Suu Kyi, Larry David’s provocative essay and Andrew Scott in Elsinore
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Plus, King Charles’s unusual gift to Aung San Suu Kyi, Larry David’s provocative essay and Andrew Scott in Elsinore
Content: Adéla’s song Nicole Kidman, on her debut album Prima, was inspired by the actor’s corset in the film Mouline Rouge!.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarView image in fullscreenAdéla’s song Nicole Kidman, on her debut album Prima, was inspired by the actor’s corset in the film Mouline Rouge!.Photograph: 20th Century Fox/AllstarDigested weekNicole KidmanDigested week: Finally gen Alpha discovers Nicole Kidman – via Adéla’s corset lyricsEmma BrockesPlus, King Charles’s unusual gift to Aung San Suu Kyi, Larry David’s provocative essay and Andrew Scott in ElsinoreFri 23 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTShareMonday“Who’sNicole Kidman?” asked my 11-year-old. For God’s sake. “You know Nicole Kidman,” I said. “She’s in ...” I tried to think of a single thing she might have seen her in. “She’s that witch queen with the hair in Aquaman.” Blank stare. “She’s in … she’s an icon, she’s really famous. She used to be married to Tom Cruise.” A pause. “Oh for God’s sake, Tom Cruise, from Top Gun.” “Oh yes.” “She was the villain in Paddington!” Thank God.Kidman had come to her attention, and that of every other 11-year-old girl in the land, via Adéla, the Slovakian singer whosesong, Nicole Kidman, from her debut album, Prima, has caused a minor TikTok sensation and went to No 1 on Spotify earlier this month.“Do you mean Adele?” I said, when we got to this part of what already seemed like a very long conversation. Excoriating, alright-grandma look. “It’s Adéla. With an ‘a’. She was in Dream Academy, she went out in the first round.” I knew what this meant and got briefly excited. “So she’s a Katseye reject!” More stern looks. “She’s in trouble for mocking Christians.” I gave up at this point.The Nicole Kidman song,given a discreet nod by Madonna in a TikTok, was inspired by a corset Adéla wore to the Golden Globes and contains the lyrics: “Babygirl in control / I feel like Nicole,” and: “Every single night / I pray that my tits are sittin’ right / Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight.” Hmm.Kidman has graciously accepted the compliment and this week, when the song played at a runway show for Victoria’s Secret in LA, the actor, in the front row,laughed and put her head in her hands. I thought the whimsy of the song was quite clever, then made the mistake of watching the video and, after having a fullMary Whitehousemoment, am rehearsing remarks I intend casually to launch over dinner on the relationship between thongs and UTIs.TuesdayWhat do we think of King Charles sending Aung San Suu Kyi, the imprisoned Burmese leader,two books about soil? Suu Kyi, who is 81 and has been under house arrest at an undisclosed compound since her government was ousted by a military coup in Myanmar in 2021, was pictured receiving the books and smiling in a photo apparently staged by her captors.Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five yearsRead moreIt’s either a genius move on the part of the king – bringing to the gated leader visions of rolling English countryside and vistas she has, at present, zero chance of enjoying – or else, a little tactless. Soil to Table bygardeners Bridget Elworthy and Henrietta Courtauld, has been described as “a celebration of soil and its connection to the food we eat”. And the second title, Soil: The World at Our Feet, is a catalogue froman exhibition held in London last year.Gift diplomacy is, of course, always tricky. You may recall the king’s father’s blunt knockback of a gift from a wellwisher during a walkabout with his wife in 2016. Offered a framed picture of Elizabeth II, the then Duke of Edinburgh snapped: “I don’t want that and neither does the queen. She knows what she looks like.” (The Lady Mayor of Windsor briskly stepped forward to accept the gift and smooth things over.)View image in fullscreenThe king may be a keen gardener and lover of the outdoors, but do his passions translate to a de facto prison in Myanmar?Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/GettyWednesdayLarry David’snew essay in Air Mail, the online newsletter, caused enough division this week to provokecoverage in the New York Times. “In our Socialist America,” David went after the Democrat Socialists of America (DSA), aping the style of Jonathan Swift’sA Modest Proposalto write: “Everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes. Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner. Fresh berries will be provided.”It’s a weaker effort on David’s part than when he went after Bill Maher in the New York Times last year, savaging him in an essay entitledMy Dinner with Adolffor approving remarks made after a meeting with Donald Trump. (“This private Hitler was a completely different animal. And oddly enough, this one seemed more authentic, like this was the real Hitler. The whole thing had my head spinning.”) Predictably, it’s David’s final section on the Middle East that has triggered a lot of take-the-phone-off-gramps fury from gen Z.“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” David writes in his mock manifesto. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty.” Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are great advocates for the DSA, but for a fuller picture it’s worth returning to DSA co-chair Megan Romer’sside-splitting efforts to explain her party’s policiesto David Remnick, earlier this year. “Yeah. You know, again, I don’t have, like, a solid …”ThursdayAndrew Scott is everywhere promotingElsinore, his Oscar-bait movie about the Shakespearean actor Ian Charleson, who died of Aids in 1990, and which I can’t wait to see. (Even though, occasionally, I feel about Scott the way I have come to feel about Nicola Walker – that the acting tics are visible enough to pull me out of the performance.)Elsewhere in gay content, it’s worth stopping by a much-overlooked and very good show,Fellow Travelers, currently airing on Channel 4, in which Matt Bomer and Jonathan Bailey’s characters fall in love in 1950s Washington, right in the middle of Senator Joe McCarthy’s various purges. Alongside the well-known anti-communist witch-hunt, McCarthy also went after gay and lesbian federal workers in what came to be calledthe Lavender Scare, ruining lives as he went. Bailey, who looks like a young Gregory Peck and as an actor just gets better and better, is heartbreaking in this show about an underdocumented episode of history. Highly recommended.FridayNews this week ofAndy Burnham’s appearance on Goggleboxraises the happy, theoretical spectre of what previous incumbents at No 10 might have looked like on equivalent shows. Thatcher on The Weakest Link? Churchill on Bake Off? One feels that Blair would have actively enjoyed scaling the bouncy houses on It’s A Knockout. Someone alert the AI!Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreen‘You only get these guns from sticking to a rigorous programme of pint-lifting, I’m-a-regular-guy exercise.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenYour country needs YOU (to suspend all critical faculties when voting in the midterms)!Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Might overnight this hard hat to Meghan.’Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/GettyExplore more on these topicsNicole KidmanDigested weekAung San Suu KyiKing Charles IIIPrince PhilipLarry DavidAndrew ScottAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too
Content: French students protesting over school conditions at the beginning of October.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenFrench students protesting over school conditions at the beginning of October.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAOpinionParisThe Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutionsEditorialAn electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, tooFri 23 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareFrance sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and thenspread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence inMilan,BrusselsandTiranaas well as in French cities.French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minorityhijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macronutterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, withGreek protestersechoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal,housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possiblereintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAUnderlying all these is thebreakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.This unrest also echoes thewave of gen Z protestsseen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, areseeking to capitaliseon the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections,threatening a radical rightwards shiftthat could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’sinternal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Caryl Churchill’s Triumph: a play for today | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: At barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacency
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: At barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacency
Content: Kate O'Flynn in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London. The play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor.’Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenKate O'Flynn in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London. The play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor.’Photograph: Marc BrennerOpinionTheatreThe Guardian view on Caryl Churchill’s Triumph: a play for todayEditorialAt barely 20 minutes, this satire on strongman politics serves to jolt audiences out of their complacencyFri 23 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.23 EDTShare“Is this theatre for the TikTok generation?” one criticaskedof the latest play by 88-year-old Caryl Churchill, lauded as Britain’s greatest living playwright.Triumph, her blistering satire on contemporary strongman politics, is barely 20 minutes long.Cleverly spliced with Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, the play takes the form of a press conference given by a blond-wigged apparatchik, who smilingly extols the barbarities of an unnamed narcissistic emperor. If “Triumph” were a crossword answer, the clue might be “To greet a populist US leader in confusion – a win (7)”. Even given Churchill’s reputation for prescience, the play was uncannily timely. It premiered in London and New York on the same day that President Trump’s short-lived press officerKatie Zachariawas forced to resign. As the American comedian Robin Williamsquippedof an earlier administration, “People say satire is dead. It’s not dead; it’s alive and living in the White House.”Churchill is a playwright of ideas who, throughout her long career, has played with structure. Her 2012 playLove and Informationdepicted the fragmentation of modern life through 57 scenes and more than 100 characters. With just three actors, this new play is a triumph of form and content: as short and direct as a press conference, its purpose is to alert us to a global crisis. This is the theatrical equivalent of a political sketch.View image in fullscreenCaryl Churchill.Photograph: Scott Wintrow/Getty ImagesA story arc in one act, it is not a highbrow version of the 60- to 90-second schlocky microdrama episodes for mobile phones, which have become so popular that Channel 4 islaunchingits own series. Short plays go back to Suetonius’s time. Chekhov, Beckett and Albee were all masters of the dramatic sprint. Churchill started out writing short radio plays, and in later years her work has become an increasing feat of compression.But this brevity goes against a trend for theatrical maximalism. To persuade audiences back to theatres and cinemas after the pandemic, plays andfilmshave been getting longer, perhaps to justify the price of a ticket. The Oscar-winning movieThe Brutalistrequired a 15-minute interval in 2024. A two-part RSC dramatisation ofMiddlemarchhas just opened at Stratford, where an epicGame of Thronesended last month. However, areduciospell has been cast on the six-hour, two-part Harry Potter and the Cursed Child juggernaut, which hasreopenedat half its original length.A play in your lunch break or after a night out is not practical for many. And while mini dramas make use of empty theatre hours and fit around evening performances, only a playwright of Churchill’s stature could guarantee a sellout, weeklong run for a show briefer than an interval without audiences feeling short-changed. Triumph could be seen as a curtain raiser for a revival of her 1979 classicCloud 9at the National Theatre next month, andThree and a Bit, a new collection of “biting short plays” at the Almeida in January.The Guardian’s Michael Billington called Churchill “theatre’s great disruptor”. With Triumph she is disrupting the conventions of theatregoing itself: a play isn’t always something to be enjoyed between an early supper, interval drinks and the last train home. She has turned the attention economy on its head. Like a Covid-era emergency press conference, Triumph interrupts its audience’s day to make them listen. It jolts us out of our complacency.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram | Instagram | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithms
Content: ‘My mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me.’Photograph: Ink Drop/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘My mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me.’Photograph: Ink Drop/AlamyInstagramLettersWe are reclaiming real life after getting rid of InstagramReaders on taking back their lives – and brains – from social media algorithmsFri 23 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTShareI couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October).Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away fromInstagramresonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience.This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 bookTen Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy.His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being.In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them.Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen.A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind.Guy EdmondsonHipperholme, West YorkshireGeorgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted.I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor.After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram.It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming.I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will.Laura DobieGlasgowI deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful.I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works!Stefanie Withey-JonesLondonI enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation.However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation.There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it.It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind.The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences.Nicky AtkinsonShoreham-by-Sea, West SussexI lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there.Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself.Dr Hilary ReddenAberdeenThe one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids!Cecilia ScottWoking, SurreyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A tender sporting moment with Alex ‘Hurricane’ Higgins  | Alex Higgins | The Guardian
description: Letter: Paul Mitchell recalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughter
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Paul Mitchell recalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughter
Content: Alex Higgins holding his daughter after winning the World Snooker Championship in 1982.Photograph: Phil Spencer/Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex Higgins holding his daughter after winning the World Snooker Championship in 1982.Photograph: Phil Spencer/Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesAlex HigginsLettersA tender sporting moment with Alex ‘Hurricane’ HigginsPaul Mitchellrecalls snooker champion Alex Higgins tearfully celebrating his win with his young daughterFri 23 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTShareWhile I enjoyed your photo feature with its “groundbreaking images [that] have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power” (Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad), 17 October), I felt that a more fitting sporting example than Gazza’s tears would have been Alex “Hurricane” Higgins at the 1982 World Snooker Championship.On winning the title, Higgins, a notoriously erratic and divisive figure, broke down in tears and pleaded for his wife and infant daughter to join him. It was not an act of image management, popularity-seeking or virtue- signalling. Rather, it was the spontaneous reaction of a man who simply wanted to share the greatest moment of his career with his young daughter.The scene was made all the more poignant by what followed. With the benefit of hindsight, and in light of Higgins’s subsequent decline into sporting wilderness and personal hardship, that moment stands as a fleeting glimpse of unguarded joy and human vulnerability. In that respect, it remains one of sport’s most moving displays of emotion.And ifAlex Higgins, a man renowned for his toughness, volatility and refusal to conform, could openly weep in public and clutch his baby daughter at the pinnacle of his career, perhaps it serves as a reminder that showing emotion diminishes neither the man nor the achievement.Paul MitchellBelfastHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Remembering a time when Afghan women had a voice and agency | Afghanistan | The Guardian
description: Letter: John Griffiths says in the 1960s he witnessed women discussing politics with men in Afghanistan’s parliament
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: John Griffiths says in the 1960s he witnessed women discussing politics with men in Afghanistan’s parliament
Content: Afghan women's rights defenders and civil activists call on the Taliban for the preservation of their achievements and education, in front of the presidential palace in Kabul in 2021.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenAfghan women's rights defenders and civil activists call on the Taliban for the preservation of their achievements and education, in front of the presidential palace in Kabul in 2021.Photograph: ReutersAfghanistanLettersRemembering a time when Afghan women had a voice and agencyJohn Griffithssays in the 1960s he witnessed women discussing politics with men in Afghanistan’s parliamentFri 23 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTShareYour article, with its account of forced marriage, illustrates how Afghanistan’s 22 million women and girls need to be freed from Taliban-imposed misogyny (‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides, 15 October). It was not ever thus.Under Russian suzerainty in 1965, four Afghan women were the first to be elected to the Wolesi Jirga, or lower house of parliament. In 1966, I watched two of them, bare‑headed and wearing western-style clothes, discussing a political topic with three of its male members and the future president Babrak Karmal.I also saw several post‑puberty girls not wearing the burqa. This, and reforms such as secondary education for girls, was supplemented by highly visible aid. The two-mile Salang tunnel through the Hindu Kush mountains, linking north and southAfghanistanby road for the first time, is a good example. The problem is: how can we restore such freedom without the use of force, which seldom works.John GriffithsAuthor,Afghanistan: Land of Conflict and BeautyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Delving into the subtext of Winnie-the-Pooh | AA Milne | The Guardian
description: Letters: Ian Arnott recommends the joyous spoofs in The Pooh Perplex, while Dr Peter Glanvill recalls Mary Plain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Ian Arnott recommends the joyous spoofs in The Pooh Perplex, while Dr Peter Glanvill recalls Mary Plain
Content: The drawing by EH Shepard of Winnie-the-Pooh, as the bear plays Poohsticks with Piglet and Christopher Robin.Photograph: Philip Toscano/PAView image in fullscreenThe drawing by EH Shepard of Winnie-the-Pooh, as the bear plays Poohsticks with Piglet and Christopher Robin.Photograph: Philip Toscano/PAAA MilneLettersDelving into the subtext of Winnie-the-PoohIan Arnottrecommendsthe joyous spoofs in The Pooh Perplex, whileDr Peter GlanvillrecallsMary PlainFri 23 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTShareOne of the best books about Winnie-the-Pooh (Editorial, 16 October) isThe Pooh Perplex, a 1963 work by the American academic Frederick Crews. This is 12 essays written in the style of various schools of literary criticism, such as The Sacramental Meaning of Winnie the Pooh, where Eeyore is the Christ figure; À la Recherche du Pooh Perdu, which claims the book is permeated withWeltschmerz; and Another Book to Cross Off Your List, as it contains not one working-class character. Many of these spoofs are strangely plausible – but very funny.Ian ArnottWerrington, PeterboroughI was surprised that your editorial mentioned Paddington, but not Mary Plain from the bear pits of Berne, who had a mentor in the form of the Owl Man (named for his horn-rimmed spectacles). Created by the Welsh writer Gwynedd Rae in the 1930s, she was the subject of more than a dozen tales. The stories were regulars on Children’s Hour and Jackanory. Paddington was a latecomer to my childhood reading.Dr Peter GlanvillChard, SomersetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
