title: The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t have | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: What happened in Wangaratta this week has horrified Australia. But around the world, politicians – and women in particular – face raised safety threats
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: What happened in Wangaratta this week has horrified Australia. But around the world, politicians – and women in particular – face raised safety threats
Content: In the days since the alleged attack on Helen Haines, Australian politicians have detailed their own experiences of abuse and threats.Photograph: James Ross/ReutersView image in fullscreenIn the days since the alleged attack on Helen Haines, Australian politicians have detailed their own experiences of abuse and threats.Photograph: James Ross/ReutersHelen HainesThe alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t haveWhat happened in Wangaratta this week has horrified Australia. But around the world, politicians – and women in particular – face raised safety threatsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBen DohertyFri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Thoughts and prayers.” After each soul-destroying mass shooting in the United States, this is the platitude invariably trotted out by every impotent politician unable to confront the stranglehold reality of the country’s gun lobby.“Turn the temperature down,” risks becoming Australia’s equivalent. The plaintive cry to hold back a rising tide of hatred and anger, incubated, amplified and legitimised online, now spilling into grotesque real-world violence.Helen Haines, the independent member for Indi, remains in hospital. She haslost both legsafter a driver allegedly deliberately drove into her twice, outside her electorate office. A manhas been charged. The motivation for his alleged attack remains unclear. But the horrific incident has sparked an urgent national reckoning about the safety of public figures, especially women.View image in fullscreenHelen Haines, the member for Indi in Victoria in the House of Representatives.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/ReutersHaines’s life will never be the same. But what of political life? What of the lives of women who seek to claim their place in shaping the future of their country?‘Targeting women because they are women’In the days since the alleged attack on Haines, politicians have detailed their own experiences of abuse and threats.The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, has had her children threatened. A man told Pauline Hanson online he would “hunt her down and kill her”.View image in fullscreenFloral tributes outside Helen Haines’s office in Wangaratta on 21 October 2026.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesThe social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, received an anonymous note slipped under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children “die of painful cancers”. The number of death and rape threats she has received over years in public life is beyond counting, she said.Male politicians face threats too. ACT senator David Pocock has moved house several times because of safety concerns for himself and his young family. Barnaby Joyce says a driver performed a u-turn to drive directly at him.The Helen Haines tragedy has shocked Australia. Its horrors highlight the crumbling foundations of our system | Tom McIlroyRead moreBut the attacks and threats are overwhelmingly gendered.Last year, then AFP commissioner, Reece Kershaw, told senate estimates that “the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high office holders is particularly troubling, with a common feature being offensive material centred on derogatory language about their appearance”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Some of this material also contains extremely violent themes, including threats of graphic, sexual violence,” he said.“These threats, which are being made online or are being sent in the post or over the phone, are sometimes also directed at their children.”View image in fullscreenTanya Plibersek in the House of Representatives.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPKershaw said politicians were targeted because of their public profiles or policy positions. “However, in some cases, it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women.”A parliamentary report last year found85% of surveyed parliamentariansand their staff reported dealing with constituents “behaving in a violent, threatening or volatile manner”.Threats to Australian politicians are at an all-time highAustralia is not alone. The Inter-parliamentary Union (of more than 180 parliaments around the world) found “parliamentarians around the world are facing growing levels of intimidation,harassment and violence from members of the public”. A global survey found the odds of a politician experiencing online violence were more than twice as high for women as for men.While members of Australia’s political class are the victims of a rising hostility online erupting into the real world, they are part of establishing a baseline for the tenor and tone of political debate.Helen Haines vigil sparks calls for greater safety for women in politics – videoThe week before Haines was allegedly attacked, the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, stood in the House of Representatives and said that the small business minister, Anne Aly, and the prime minister,should be “stoned in the square”for a decision made by the tax office.That evening, Aly posted on Instagram a devastated, wearied, riposte.“This is not just something that we should just turn away from.”Aly then, almost as an afterthought, revealed: “this past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: ‘stone her’.” Bell withdrew the comment and has since apologised.‘An environment has been created’There is a bleak irony that Aly took to social media – responsible for incubating and amplifying so much violent political rhetoric – to speak out against the attack made against her on the ostensibly more dignified floor of the parliament.The chair of the Centre for Journalism & Democracy at City St George’s University of London, Prof Julie Posetti, is lead author of a series of UN Women reports, which began with last year’s publication,Tipping Point: The chilling escalation of online violence against women in the public sphere.Surveying more than 600 women across 119 countries – with a particular focus on human rights defenders, activists and journalists – the report found more than 70% of respondents had experienced online abuse in the course of their work, and 41% had experienced real-world attacks, abuse, or harassment that they linked to online abuse.View image in fullscreenSmall business minister Anne Aly.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPBritish-Australian Posetti, familiar with the political culture of both countries, says attacks on politicianswere both “entirely predictable and utterly shocking”.“Women are being forced out of public-facing roles … including representative office, because of the serious threats that are being delivered at scale with virtual impunity.”This pressure comes after years of hard-fought improvements for women in political power. While women’s representation in government has increased dramatically over the past decades, and in Australia women make up about half of federal parliament, globally women hold just22% of cabinet level positions, and that proportion is now falling.More than100 countries have never had a female leader.Posetti describes the online-to-offline trajectory of violence as a “vicious, self-perpetuating” cycle. Online threats beget offline attacks, and offline abuse – such as politicians attacking female journalists during press conferences – can trigger a tsunami of online harassment, further exacerbating the risk of offline attacks.“It’s a fire where fuel is just continuously loaded into the mix. It elevates perpetually and it’s amplified online … through those algorithmic drivers, which are tuned to do what they do for profit, because we know that engagement is more likely to be driven by anger and rage than it is by support for some kind of positive action, for example.”1:44AFP charging almost one person a week for targeting politicians, says commissioner - videoThe rising tide of violent rhetoric and action is occurring alongside a broader democratic erosion, one being witnessed around the world.Posetti said decades of progress on gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls were backsliding at an alarming rate under a rising tide of authoritarianism, in which “strong man” leaders decry everything from diversity, equity and inclusion, to low birthrates, and whose acolytesjoke about male control over female bodies.“An environment has been created where there is tolerance for slut-shaming women in politics who are routinely threatened with being ‘raped to death’, for threatening violence against women journalists, and for threatening the families of women human rights defenders with violence,” Posetti says.“If you push women out of public life, you are less likely to get women’s issues represented effectively, you are less likely to see nuanced stories about women covered empathetically: there are real implications for women’s participation in democratic deliberation, not just in being elected to office, but women are being driven out of public debate entirely because there is no safe way to engage.”Posetti argued misogynistic rhetoric “which just five or 10 years ago would have been viewed as repugnant and unpalatable” was being legitimised and reinforced online.In the US, so often the grim indicator of the direction of Australian politics, in 2024 the president threatened a female political opponent with “nine barrels shooting at her …when the guns are trained on her face”. Violence is celebrated: this week Donald Trump congratulated a supporter at a rally for punching a protester.Law follows language. Rhetoric has real-world consequences.The case that established abortion rights in the US,Roe v Wade – settled law of the land for nearly 50 years – was overturned in 2022. Even now, a decade-old tenacious right-wing movement has swung back into vogue in that country –#Repealthe19th– which overtly argues that women be banned from voting.Addressing the crisisFuelling so much is the isolating duality of the online world: the platforms that promise connection but offer only an ersatz counterfeit, while peddling invitations to the darkest corners and reinforcement of the basest of instincts.Users are bombarded all by relentless “feeds” that feel public but are, in fact, uniquely private, carefully curated by deliberately arcane algorithms.Violent memes are posted for all the world to see, but the algorithms hold each viewer in an individual self-reinforcing silo.If those violent posts generate “engagement”, even a moment’s attention, more and more like it are offered, are imposed. Each feed is its own incubator, under constant singular refinement, making social media ever more isolated, more idiosyncratic, more dangerous to vulnerable people.Australia’s digital duty of care bill a ‘global reckoning for big tech’, minister says – videoPosetti says there were two key elements to addressing the deepening crisis. The first is the human element: “There needs to be a commitment from organisations, from political and corporate leaders, and from others in public life, to treat other human beings with decency and dignity”.The second is regulation of the technology platforms on which vitriol is allowed to flourish, amplify and spread. “No matter how effective the political leadership is, unless you address the technological drivers for the escalating hate towards women, minorities, other marginalised groups in society, then you are … sticking a used Band-Aid on a gaping wound, trying to address the aftermath.”Australia, the global vanguard on social media bans for children, and the development of a proposeddigital duty of care, “has a rare opportunity to take some global leadership on this”.Focus on misogynyAfter the alleged attack on Haines, New Zealand MP Tamatha Paul saw parallels in the killings, 10 years apart, of female British politiciansJo CoxandAnn Widdecombe. (Male MP Sir David Amess wasmurdered in 2021).“These were women in politics who were walking down the road, standing outside of their electorate offices, walking to their homes, being in their homes, when they have been attacked or murdered.”View image in fullscreenBritish MP Jo Cox was murdered in 2016.Photograph: Jo Cox FoundationPaul argued the well-meaning counsel from security agencies on how politicians could keep themself safe – don’t advertise social engagements, change routines and routes to work and home – undermined democratic engagement and missed the fundamental problem.“Focus on the fact that misogyny and rape culture, and allowing it to manifest and fester in our society, is what normalises violence against women: either violence against high profile women in politics and all of the invisible violence that happens behind closed doors.“Why do women have to pay with our lives?”Paul said she had a message for men: “this is on you to call out your friends”.“When they make jokes, when they say that politicians look like pigs, when they make comments that they would never make about another man, call them out.“Call them out because this is what happens.”Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesViolence against women and girlsAustralian politicsSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed? | Labour | The Guardian
description: New PM has prioritised small fixes to show voters Labour can make a real difference, and government insiders are delighted at the public’s reaction
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: New PM has prioritised small fixes to show voters Labour can make a real difference, and government insiders are delighted at the public’s reaction
Content: The everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office, one government insider says.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyView image in fullscreenThe everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office, one government insider says.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyLabourPotholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?New PM has prioritised small fixes to show voters Labour can make a real difference, and government insiders are delighted at the public’s reactionAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press.“So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file aboutthatfucking thick of that back in the office.”After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahsblaring out TikTok videos onpublic transport,outlaw “rip-off” private car park finesand – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads.Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan toremove VAT from electricity bills, a £2cap on single bus fares across Englandand take action on“auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas.The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.”Government insiders say the policies are not the product of standing around in a circle, throwing a stress ball and shouting out ideas. “There isn’t someone with a whiteboard brainstorming new bicycles for special constables,” says one, furthering the Thick of It comparison. Instead, the everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office. “We did this sort of thing under Keir too,” said another source. “But under Andy it’s a whole different thing; he’s put rocket boosters under it.”View image in fullscreenBurnham has given his close ally Louise Haigh the job of establishing taskforces for three areas: cost of living, public control and regeneration.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/GettyIn the first days of his premiership, Burnham gave his close ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, the job of establishing taskforces for three core areas – cost of living, public control and regeneration. One government source said: “There is a very intentional drumbeat of those because they do make a difference, but also it’s constantly showing people that we understand where those frustrations and low-level pressures are.”Ideas are “kicked around” between the cost of living taskforce in the Cabinet Office and the policy unit in No 10, with all departments encouraged to feed in. “There’s a sort of filtering up process,” the source said. “It’s quite a sprawling sort of cross-government approach.”Another said that while some departments were better placed to find “not hugely spendy” fixes, every minister was encouraged to contribute. “I think a lot of people had sort of resigned any hope that the government can actually get things done – and this is showing them that, yes, actually, we can,” another source said.The small policy announcements have been, one delighted adviser said, a roaring success. Another source said: “Some people are very snotty about it, but in a world where it’s really hard for a government to cut through, this is working. You put some ideas through the grid and you often don’t know if they’re going to fly. But when you see one go gangbusters, it’s kind of like Christmas morning.”One single fact policy idea dominated the news cycle for an entire day. Another generated tens of thousands of posts on X. Burnham’s faintly hokey video on antisocial phone use garnered 2m views. “It helps that he’s just really good at it,” the source said.View image in fullscreenReform UK and the Tories have criticised Labour for focusing on small-fix policies, including cracking down on people who listen to music without headphones on public transport.Photograph: John Williams/AlamyThe small-fix policies have not been appreciated by everyone. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said the UK was “going down the pan and our prime minister is faffing around tweaking parking tickets” – despite trying to implement the policy himself when he was a Conservative minister. The former Olympian Sharron Davies said: “As Paris burns our prime minister has stopped people playing loud music on buses & trains,” leading some to question whether she expected Burnham to invade the French capital.Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, has been dismissive, saying in a speech this week that cracking down on loud music on public transport was a “job for ticket inspectors, not the prime minister”. Reprising the theme at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the leader of the opposition implicitly accused Burnham of fiddling while Rome burns. “We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined,” she said. “Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.”Across the dispatch box, Burnham hid his delight at her response behind a disappointed look. “I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives,” he said sombrely, while his advisers likely high-fived in private.‘We’ve lost a basic sense of politeness’: UK readers reveal daily reality of public transportRead moreRegardless of the reaction of Burnham’s opponents, the focus on minor grievances is a canny strategy that appears to be working, said the pollster Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. In recent polling, when people were asked whether Burnham understood the pressure of high energy bills on ordinary people, 45% said he did. When the same question was asked about Starmer, that figure was 23%. “I think the Tories and Reform have got it dead wrong on this,” Tryl said. “People bring this sort of stuff up in focus groups all the time. It cuts across left- and rightwing voters. People care about immigration, about the NHS – but they also care about everyday frictions.”But behind the scenes there is an acknowledgment that a focus on ticking off small things from the PM’s to-do list will be significantly more challenging in moments of crisis. There has to be a “twin-track” approach, said one insider. “It’s combining a big picture, long term, dismantling 40 years of neoliberalism and addressing questions about ownership and control, but at the same time tackling more immediate daily bugbears,” they said. “What you’ve seen so far is these smaller level interventions, but the bigger structural, longer term piece will be in the 10-year plan.”While the everyday fixes may be popular, the sugar-high they produce could be short-lived, said Ed Shackle, the head of qualitative research at the policy consultants Public First Global. “The government should be under no illusion that as soon as any real substantive event rears its head, any small popularity boost will be instantly blown away,” he said. “Quick fixes are popular, but they are a poor substitute for fixing the big issues the public care about.”Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamTransport policyUK cost of living crisisTransportMotoringBus faresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Free Speech Union hit by internal allegations of racism and sexually inappropriate remarks | UK news | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Key figure in campaign group accused of saying she would ‘never hire a black person’, and second figure discussed Sydney Sweeney’s ‘assets’
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Exclusive: Key figure in campaign group accused of saying she would ‘never hire a black person’, and second figure discussed Sydney Sweeney’s ‘assets’
Content: The Free Speech Union was founded by the Conservative life peer Toby Young.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Free Speech Union was founded by the Conservative life peer Toby Young.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyUK newsFree Speech Union hit by internal allegations of racism and sexually inappropriate remarksExclusive: Key figure in campaign group accused of saying she would ‘never hire a black person’, and second figure discussed Sydney Sweeney’s ‘assets’Aisha DownFri 23 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Free Speech Union (FSU) is reeling from internal grievances involving allegations of racism, workplace discrimination and sexually inappropriate remarks by senior members of staff, the Guardian can reveal.A key figure in the campaign group, the chief operating officer, Sigrun Olafsdottir, departed late last week after employees alleged that she told a junior member of staff she would “never hire a black person” as a part of a one-on-one meeting late last year.The organisation’s legislative affairs director, Sam Armstrong – who is also head of communications for the Reform MP Robert Jenrick – has meanwhile been accused of making staff members uncomfortable by discussing the American actor Sydney Sweeney’s “assets” in a meeting with more than a dozen staff.The claims cap a difficult period for the FSU, which was founded by the Conservative life peerToby Young, and which critics see as a partisan rallying point for anti-woke grievance.And they may complicate how the organisation seeks to publicly present itself, as a nonpartisan group that seeks to defend “free speech” from the overreach of censorious authorities – one which often raises money from its 50,000 members to do so.View image in fullscreenFSU staff visited 10 Downing Street this week to deliver a petition on saving jury trials.Photograph: Free Speech Union/FacebookIn July, the Guardian reported that theUS state department had allocated $5mto the international umbrella organisation that oversees the FSU, part of a larger effort by the Trump administration to promote rightwing causes in Europe. The state department appeared to withdraw this grant after the Guardian reported on the allocation.In August, the Guardian reported on questions about the organisation’s practices around charity crowdfunding, centred on an instance in which the FSUappeared to raise £60,000for a legal case that was ultimately fought pro-bono. Much of the FSU’s work consists of raising money for people who it argues have faced inappropriate consequences for exercising their right to free speech.Lord Young told the Guardian that that case was “not handled on an exclusively pro bono basis”, saying there was another lawyer involved and the person whose case it was had separate legal costs.These revelations have come alongside a period of internal turmoil. Eight members of the FSU’s small staff have departed within the past year. The Guardian understands that a crucial part of this disquiet has been the allegation of racism against Olafsdottir. The Guardian has spoken to multiple sources about these allegations and viewed documentation related to parts of the claims.Employees complained that Olafsdottir was frequently “hostile” towards younger members of staff. This alleged hostility was said to occur during the FSU’s in-person gatherings.Get in touchContact Aisha Down about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Aisha using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailaisha.down@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.For other options, see our guide attheguardian.com/tips.Show moreThe staff of the FSU work remotely but meet regularly for in-person events. These often take place at pubs and hotels, with some personnel said to drink heavily late into the night. Employees of the FSU described blurred boundaries and instances of aggression and discriminatory behaviour on the part of some senior staff during these sessions.Olafsdottir and Armstrong declined to comment. Young told the Guardian he could not comment on “internal employment matters”. On the incident in which Sydney Sweeney was discussed, he said it related to an FSU member’s case, adding: “There was therefore nothing untoward or unprofessional about the conversation.”Sources who spoke to the Guardian described Olafsdottir as a prominent presence in an organisation that employs slightly more than two dozen people across the UK and Scotland, and close to Young.View image in fullscreenSam Armstrong – pictured in 2017 – talked at length about Sydney Sweeney’s ‘assets’ on a staff call, FSU colleagues said.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/AlamyShe was not the only senior leader alleged to have made staff members uncomfortable. Several FSU staff members described discomfort at Armstrong’s behaviour. They described an all-staff video meeting during which Armstrong discussed Sweeney’s physique, shortly after Sweeney had appeared in the controversial American Eagle“good jeans” ad. More than a dozen staff were present, and more than half were women. Armstrong joked that Sweeney was the “biggest” story in free speech that week.“He [went] on to talk about her ‘assets’ at length. It was this continuous joke about her ‘assets,’” said a staff member who was on the call. “It was really stupid and really weird.”The Guardian has seen FSU text messages referring to the Sweeney episode. In one of them, the FSU’s engagement director ribbed Armstrong and others as “a bunch of chaps so alpha in appreciation of Sydney Sweeney’s assets”.Armstrong, whose webpage describes him as a political consultant and journalist, attended one high-profile meetingbetweenYoung and Sarah B Rogers, a US state department official who has aggressively mocked the UK in public appearances.The group remains active in raising funds from its 50,000 members, and this week representatives visited 10 Downing Street to deliver a petition on saving jury trials.Staff who have left the organisation – many of them early in their careers – expressed a sense of betrayal to the Guardian over the workplace climate in the FSU. One suggested the prospect of funds from the state department, and blurred lines around crowdfunders, had eroded internal checks further.The FSU was “getting a bit cowboy” with “too much money sloshing around”, they said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsToby YoungnewsShareReuse this content

title: Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: People succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating toll
Content: Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenHot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyExtreme heatHeat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warnPeople succumbed to heat at highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, with health issues, loneliness and poverty exacerbating tollAjit NiranjanFri 23 Oct 2026 00.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 00.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeat killed a record 50,000 people in European cities this summer, newresearchsuggests, with scientists blaming climate breakdown for two in every three of the deaths.Morgues and funeral homes filled with bodies from June to August as the heat added by planet-baking pollution cut short an extra 32,000 lives in urban areas, the researchers found. Hot days pushed vulnerable bodies into overdrive and warm nights prevented them from recovering.The “staggering” death toll, modelled using historical relationships between heat and health in 854 cities, was the worst on record, the study found. Hot weather marked by relentless heatwaves killed nearly twice as many people as it did in each of the two next most dangerous years.A bar chart showing heat deaths in European cities from 2000 to 2026, split by the share of deaths attributable to climate change.“In some sense, the absolute numbers of the heat-related deaths estimated across the 854 urban areas are indeed staggering,” said Malcolm Mistry, a climate and health scientist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who co-authored the study. “But perhaps what is even more alarming is the proportion of these deaths that we attribute to anthropogenic climate change.”The share of deaths due to climate breakdown has risen from about 40% at the start of the century to 65% this summer, the study found.People succumbed to heat at the highest rates in Malta, Italy and Hungary, while absolute death tolls were greatest in Italy, France, Spain, Germany and the UK. Because death certificates rarely record contributing factors – such as dangerous temperatures that push a stroke victim or lung cancer patient past their limits – families rarely know that heat and human activity hastened their relatives’ death.“These shocking figures represent thousands of families who have lost a loved one this summer due to the climate crisis,” said Katie White, the climate transition minister for the UK, where scientists estimated 4,354 heat deaths this summer.”In Naples, the hardest-hit city on the continent, 815 people per million died from the heat, according to the study’s age-standardised estimates. Mario Guarino, an emergency doctor at Ospedale CTO in the north of the city, said he witnessed a 15% increase in emergency room visits during the hottest weeks.View image in fullscreenNaples was the hardest-hit city in Europe, with 815 people per million dying from the heat, according to the study.Photograph: Ansa/Ciro Fusco/EPAThe “defining characteristic” of the period was the complexity of health problems exacerbated by heat, he added, with loneliness and poverty worsening the situation further.“We took in a terminal cancer patient who lived in a hot attic simply because his family couldn’t find a company to install air conditioning during the summer,” said Guarino. “An elderly man with dementia was abruptly abandoned by his Ukrainian caregiver who returned home to say goodbye to her son, who had been called to war. Emergency services found [the man] lying on the floor one night with a fractured pelvis, desperately trying to call the tenant next door.”The study found people over the age of 85 made up almost half of the death toll, though younger people were not immune, with 833 people between the age of 20 and 44 also thought to have died due to the heat. The scientists said the death toll from the cities studied, which account for about 40% of the European population, could not be easily extrapolated to estimate the full death toll including those in towns and villages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDoctors have urged governments to encourage people to drink water and seek shade.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyThe scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, the EU’s climate monitoring serviceannounced this month, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C. Slightly less punishing temperatures in eastern Europe brought the continental average to its third-hottest level on record.Greenhouse gases have warmed Europe about twice as fast as the global average, exposing more people to intolerably hot summers and fewer people to dangerously cold winters. While cold is a bigger killer than heat, scientists expect rising temperatures to claim more lives than they save, as heat deaths are projected to rise faster than cold deaths fall.The study combinedestablished relationships between heat and mortalitywith temperature data for 2026 to rapidly estimate the fallout from this summer’s heat. The death tolls for individual countries differ from what national public health agencies have calculated using their own methods.David García-García, a researcher at the mortality monitoring system at the Carlos III health institute in Madrid, who was not involved in the study, said it was a “valuable contribution” that allowed for comparisons across the continent. “However, it is important to bear in mind that these are estimates based on observed temperatures and epidemiological models, which do not incorporate actual data on deaths occurring in the summer of 2026,” he said.Doctors have urged governments to burn fewer fossil fuels – the core driver of rising temperatures – while bolstering health systems, greening cities, rolling out air conditioning and encouraging people to drink water and seek shade. They have also stressed the benefits of people checking in on vulnerable neighbours and family members so they can get help before tragedy strikes.“The real epidemic these days is loneliness,” said Guarino. “Many elderly people are left alone during the summer, abandoned by their families, and due to their low income, they can’t afford air conditioning or, if they do have it, avoid turning it on because of the cost of electricity.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatClimate crisisEuropeOlder peopleEurope weatherLonelinessClimate sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economies
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economies
Content: People selling merchandise that expresses support for the presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in Boa Vista over the weekend.Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economiesByTom Phillipsin Mucajaí; photographs by Raphael AlvesFri 23 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the night beforethe first round of Brazil’s presidential electionand Rosimari Monteiro was so excited she couldn’t sleep. The 38-year-old spent hours tossing and turning at her home in the Amazon town of Mucajaí before rising at dawn to cast her vote.“I was the first person to vote at my polling station … I voted 22, so we got off to a positive start,” recalls Monteiro, as she stands in her sitting room with her two young daughters.Twenty-two is the number Brazil’s electronic voting system uses to identify the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who is hoping to beat the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in this year’s election.“To us, he represents the future. We want a light at the end of the tunnel. We want a better future for ourselves and for our kids, who are the future of our nation,” enthuses Monteiro, who was far from the only person in Mucajaí to vote Bolsonaro.View image in fullscreenRosimari Monteiro, a driving instructor, with her daughters Lauana, three, and Louise, 10.In fact, this sun-baked roadside settlement is where Bolsonaro secured his biggest proportional victory in Roraima, the northern state where the would-be president also registeredhis best nationwide result. Nearly 79% of 11,734 votes in Mucajaí went to Bolsonaro.Map of northern BrazilMonteiro gave several reasons for her decision, including Bolsonaro’s pledges to fight crime and create jobs. But one issue explains why the son of the disgraced former presidentJair Bolsonarois so popular here and across Roraima, where 14 of 15 municipalities backed the far-right politician.View image in fullscreenIllegal mining takes place in Yanomami Indigenous Land in the Amazon rainforest in November 2019.Photograph: João Laet/The GuardianMucajaí was the launchpad for much of the illegal gold rush in which tens of thousands of minersinvaded the nearby Yanomami Indigenous territoryduring Jair Bolsonaro’s environmentally calamitous 2019-2022 presidency. Prospectors used the meandering Mucajaí River to sneak into those protected Indigenous lands near the border with Venezuela, bringing malaria, mercury poisoning, hunger and destruction to its 32,000 Indigenous people. Ranches carved out of Mucajaí’s rainforests conceal clandestine airstrips from which helicopters and planes ferried supplies, miners and sex workers into jungles that the Yanomami’s ancestors are thought to have occupied for at least 1,000 years.View image in fullscreenThe town of Mucajaí in Brazil’s northern state of Roraima.View image in fullscreenAn unidentified aircraft, allegedly used in illegal mining and potentially drug trafficking, was seized by police in Boa Vista last week.When Lula beat Bolsonaro’s father in the 2022 election, the leftwinger launcheda crackdownto evict those miners and cripple a multi-billion dollar illegal industry he blamed fora “genocide” against the Yanomami. A broader environmental offensive across the Amazoncut deforestationto its lowest levels since the late 80s.‘A war society doesn’t see’: the Brazilian force driving out mining gangs from Indigenous landsRead moreNow, nearly four years later, Mucajaí’s electorate hopes a Bolsonaro victory in Sunday’s second round runoff will end that clampdown and allow the 21st century gold rush to resume. “The closure of the mines brought complete penury. It became really hard to find jobs,” complains Monteiro, a driving instructor whose brother-in-law worked in the mines.Like many people in the area, Monteiro believes that, if elected, Bolsonaro will move to legalise mining on Indigenous lands “so people can get back to work”. Speaking in the Amazon on Tuesday, Bolsonaro vowed to be a president “who will turn the riches God has given us into riches for every single one of you”, adding: “Lula couldn’t give a shit about the Amazon.”View image in fullscreenThe presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro greets supporters during the ‘Bloquinho 22’ campaign event in Manaus, Brazil last week.The prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency hascaused panic among Indigenous leaders and conservationists– here in Roraima, and all over the Amazon. From January, when the new president takes power, at least seven of the nine Amazon states, including Roraima, will have pro-Bolsonaro governors. Congress will featurea record number of rightwing politicianshostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.“By voting 22, Brazilians are signing a death certificate for the Yanomami, and Indigenous people in general,” says the Yanomami leader Júnior Hekurari, 40, who was on the frontline of efforts to protect his people duringthe humanitarian crisisthat unfolded under Bolsonaro.View image in fullscreenJúnior Hekurari, 40, the president of the Urihi Yanomami Association, at his home in Boa Vista earlier this month.Already, Hekurari sees signs the miners are again preparing to flood Brazil’s biggest Indigenous territory. In the days after the 4 October first round, whichBolsonaro won by 47% to Lula’s 45.1%, Yanomami villagers reported receiving calls from illegal prospectors ordering them to clear remote runways so they could return.Nilton Tubino,who has led Lula’s anti-mining crusade since 2023, says “strange movements” have been detected on the outskirts of the territory, reinforcing suspicions miners are gearing up to pillage precious metals andtin ore used to make mobile phones.View image in fullscreenNilton Tubino explains his team’s efforts to combat illegal gold mining in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory.Tubino, who calls Mucajaí the “nerve centre” of the illegal trade, believes Lula can recover from his first-round loss. “The election isn’t over until it’s over,” says Tubino.But speaking at his group’s headquarters in Roraima’s capital, Boa Vista, Tubino admits his unit will close if Bolsonaro prevails. He fears environmental and Indigenous protection officials who have led Lula’s crackdown will be sidelined and persecuted, as happened under Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after the 2022 election. The consequences for the Yanomami will be dire.“This is a lethal threat … to the very existence of these people, to their culture and cosmovision, and way of life,” Lula’s former environment minister, Marina Silva, has warned.Gold mining is not the only reason Roraima’s voters back Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old evangelical Christian twice baptised in the Jordan River. The evangelical church’s rapid advance into the Amazon has also bolstered support, with prosperity theology striking a chord among those on Brazil’s fast-growing agricultural frontier.Leandro Gentil, a political activist and pastor in Boa Vista, considers Bolsonaro a champion of the Christian values his church fights “tooth and nail” to defend. “Bolsonaro is practically a unanimity within our congregation … He’s the fresh oxygen we need to breathe,” Gentil adds, citing the politician’s opposition to same-sex marriage, abortion and drugs.View image in fullscreenLeandro Gentil, 42, a fire department lieutenant in Boa Vista, is a Bolsonaro supporter.Similar views are heard in Mucajaí, where small evangelical temples are found on most streets.Marinalva Ferreira Barbosa, a 40-year-old cleaner who worships at a local branch of the powerful Assemblies of God church, says she opposes Lula because he champions “things forbidden by the Bible”. “Like men getting with men, women with women – this kind of filth,” adds Barbosa, who works in the Paradise Pousada, a 15-room hotel that, because of the mining crackdown, is empty.Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaignersRead moreBolsonaro’s hardline pledge to eliminate “narco-terrorists” – despite his own well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld – has also seduced voters in the Amazon, whereorganised crime groups are tightening their grip.“Drugs could destroy our future,” says Bolsonaro activist Luciano Gomes, as he stares out across Mucajaí from a tourist view point. Several of the rundown streets below are scrawled with graffiti celebrating Brazil’s biggest criminal organisation, the PCC, or threatening to shoot rivals from the Red Command gang dead.View image in fullscreenA wall featuring graffiti from rival criminal organisations in the city of Mucajaí.But Gomes’s main reason for supporting Bolsonaro is his desire for mining to be unleashed. “Our state has a wealth of mineral resources … gold, diamonds and rare earths that were discovered recently,” he says, insisting they can be exploited responsibly. “Bolsonaro champions the idea that miners aren’t crooks, they’re workers.”On Sunday, Gomes will return to the polls to vote “22”, sporting a garish shirt emblazoned with images of the Bolsonaros and their ally, the US president, Donald Trump.View image in fullscreenLuciano Gomes, 40, an alternate city councillor in Mucajaí, hopes Bolsonaro will revive mining operations.If Bolsonaro triumphs, Gomes will lead a procession of cars draped in Brazil and US flags 50 miles north to Boa Vista, to attend an all-night shindig in a square centred around the statue of a gold panner.The most famous Yanomami leader, Davi Kopenawa, has other ideas. “I’m going to vote for my friend Lula … The Lula government is a friend of the native peoples,” says Kopenawa, 70, warning of conflict and resistance if Bolsonaro wins.“There will be a war between Indigenous people and non-Indigenous people. Violence, death, bloodshed,” predicts Kopenawa’s 44-year-old son, Dário, whose association’s offices in Boa Vista resemble a prison, encircled by high walls, security cameras and an electric fence to guard against attacks.View image in fullscreenDário Kopenawa, 44, is president-elect of the Hutukara Yanomami Association.Photograph: Raphael Alves/The GuardianOne recent evening, scores of students and Indigenous activists hit Boa Vista’s streets to denounce Bolsonaro’s plans. Among them is Joênia Wapichana, a lawyer and politician who ran the Indigenous protection service, Funai, under Lula.View image in fullscreenJoênia Wapichana at a pro-Lula demonstration in Boa Vista last week.Photograph: Raphael Alves/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLeft-leaning voters gather in front of the Workers’ party (PT) headquarters in Boa Vista to show their support for Lula.Photograph: Raphael Alves/The Guardian“Roraima isn’t the back yard ofbolsonarismo,” says Wapichana, 53, who insisted that Indigenous communities will not give up without a fight.“No people in Brazil are more resilient than the Indigenous people … that’s why in 2026 we still exist,” Wapichana says. “We are born fighting, we are born resisting.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilAmazon rainforestAmericasDeforestationMiningLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Severe flooding in eastern Spain and UK hit by first named storm of winter  | Europe weather | The Guardian
description: Storm Adam brings torrential rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen strikes England and Wales
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Storm Adam brings torrential rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen strikes England and Wales
Content: A firefighter pumps out water from a flooded garage in Guardamar de la Safor, Valencia, Spain.Photograph: Natxo Frances/EPAView image in fullscreenA firefighter pumps out water from a flooded garage in Guardamar de la Safor, Valencia, Spain.Photograph: Natxo Frances/EPAWeather trackerEurope weatherAnalysisSevere flooding in eastern Spain and UK hit by first named storm of winterMegan Davies, Claire Jones and Magdalena Shopova for MetDeskStorm Adam brings torrential rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen strikes England and WalesFri 23 Oct 2026 04.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.29 EDTShareStorm Adam brought torrential rain to easternSpainearlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours, with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours.The severe flooding led 145 municipalities across Valencia and Alicante to impose a temporary lockdown on about 850,000 people on Monday. At least five people have died, 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated.The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport causing some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions are improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.The first named storm of the winter for the UK is tracking through the Channel.Storm Austenis bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.View image in fullscreenA car is surrounded by fallen branches in Falmouth, England, after Storm Austen made landfall.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty ImagesFollowing quickly on from Storm Austen is another deep low-pressure system, Storm Boelo, which is expected to track across northern Scotland on Saturday into Sunday. Much of the UK and Ireland will experience very unsettled conditions with further damaging winds, and heavy and prolonged rain. Western Scotland will face the strongest gusts, but the rest of the UK and Ireland can expect 40-55mph winds. Western parts of Ireland will experience 50-60mph winds with up to 70-80mph in exposed parts of north-west Ireland, similar to western Scotland. Again, heavy rain associated with Storm Boelo will reach 10-20mm, with as much as 30-60mm in western parts of Ireland, Wales and south-west England. This, on top of the rainfall from Storm Austen, will increase the risk of flooding.Super Typhoon Champi is heading towards China and Japan over the weekend after passing north-easternTaiwanon Friday. It has weakened since Wednesday, but is still a significant typhoon with the equivalent strength of a category 5 hurricane, producing 185mph gusts and sustained winds of 121 mph. After torrential rain from the typhoon this week, up to 900mm of rain is forecast to fall in the mountainous regions of northern and eastern Taiwan from Tuesday to Saturday. As a result, there are school closures, cancelled flights and six-metre waves, with damage expected over the next few days.Explore more on these topicsEurope weatherWeather trackerSpainUK weatherEuropeChinaJapanTaiwananalysisShareReuse this content

title: At Cop17, the pressure is on to rescue a deal that could end the destruction of nature  | Environment | The Guardian
description: ​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stake
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: ​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stake
Content: Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, speaks at Cop17.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAstrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, speaks at Cop17.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockDown to Earth newsletterEnvironmentAt Cop17, the pressure is on to rescue a deal that could end the destruction of nature​As world leaders struggle to meet deadlines to halt nature loss set four years ago, a rare leopard in host country Armenia offers a symbol of what is at stakeDon’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereRebecca RatcliffeFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Armenian capital Yerevan is chock-a-block right now with officials, scientists and environmentalists from all over the world gathering for Cop17. Everyone is here to try torescue a historic dealto end the destruction of nature.The pressure is on. Targets set for 2030 arewoefully off track, and the nearly 200 countries present need to agree on a plan to speed things up. All this is happening at a time when national budgets are tight andleaders are distractedby conflict, protests and the global energy crisis.But first, this week’s most important reads.Essential readsThis Norwegian village is one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. How can its people save it?What does the UK’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?US extreme weather survivors are a growing group – now they want to be a political forceIn focusView image in fullscreenThe Persian leopard, spotted on a camera trap in Gndasar Community Conserved Area.Photograph: Gndasar Environmental-Social NGOThere have been snippets of positive news. Just a week before the conference began, a Persian leopard, one of Armenia’s rarest and most endangered animals, was spotted in the southern-central region of the country.“It was late, we came home and then one of my caretakers [rangers] called me and said, ‘I have amazing news,’” Syuzi Karapetyan, a teacher who also leads the Gndasar Social-Environmental NGO, explained when I visited her village on Saturday. She had goosebumps when she heard the news, she said.Persian leopards, also known as Caucasian leopards, were once widespread across western and central Asia, but their range has shrunk dramatically. There are thought to be no more than 10 leopards in Armenia, as poaching and habitat destruction have devastated its population.The discovery of a new individual, never spotted before in the country, has delighted Karapetyan and local people, who in partnership with WWF have rebuilt the population of bezoar goats, one of the leopard’s key prey species, and found ways to protect its habitats.The question of how to save our most endangered species is a critical issue being discussed at Cop17. Scientists have warned of the rapid annihilation of wildlife, far above natural background levels, with some saying we are in themidst of a mass extinction event, driven by human overpopulation and overconsumption.A commitment to protect endangered species was one of 23 targets that governments set four years ago, and whichthey are not on track to meet.Lots of governments still haven’t mobilised resources, partly because they don’t know where to focus, says Dr Kira Mileham, who co-chairs the Reverse the Red Action Partnership, which supports governments to tackle species loss.There might be hundreds of species at risk within a country’s borders; which should they prioritise?This week, Armenia and Colombia announced an initiative, the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species (Cares), a government coalition that aims to help countries assess where to focus their efforts. Some species might not need much dedicated action, as long as parallel efforts – for example to protect their habitat – are under way. Others might need more focused, species-specific interventions such as protection from disease or, if their numbers are very low, help to enable them to breed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Cares alliance will help governments to assess which of the species in need of specific support are already receiving attention from NGOs or research institutions, and which are falling through the cracks, and connect them with experts, says Mileham. Reverse the Red will serve as the secretariat of Cares.It’s then up to governments to develop a plan, and find resources to support it. So far, 17 countries, including the UK, have joined the Cares alliance to share best practice.Separately, nine private funders and organisations, including Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re:wild, have said they will commit more than $500m over the next five years to recover the world’s most threatened species.The money has been welcomed, but it also matters how it is spent. There is still a huge bias inhow conservation funding is allocated, with larger, charismatic animals such as leopards, tigers and elephants sweeping up the majority of resources. “Decisions need to be taken based on the scientific information that is available, and not just because some are cute, which unfortunately is what happens,” says Benoit Guénard, associate professor at the University of Hong Kong, who has researched the distribution of conservation funds.Many conservationists hope money will be better targeted, with resources spread more evenly – and that fungi, algae and amphibians might see some of the success enjoyed by the Persian leopard.Read more:‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in declineWorld must cut emissions by 18% in four years ‘to find our way back’, UN saysAs a former minister who once climbed a tree to save it, I know there is passion to protect nature. We just have to show it | Steven GuilbeaultTo read the complete version of this newsletter –subscribe to receive Down to Earthin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentDown to Earth newsletterCop17 biodiversity summitArmeniaBiodiversityConservationWildlifeClimate crisisnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Which is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debate | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest dates from 1400s
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest dates from 1400s
Content: Dr James Wright declared The George Inn in Somerset, which has been serving ale continuously since the early 1430s, to be the oldest pub in England.Photograph: Jane Tregelles/AlamyView image in fullscreenDr James Wright declared The George Inn in Somerset, which has been serving ale continuously since the early 1430s, to be the oldest pub in England.Photograph: Jane Tregelles/AlamyHeritageWhich is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debateHistoric England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430Helena HortonFri 23 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons.But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate.While many claim origins dating back 1,000 years, Dr James Wright, a buildings archaeologist, said it was difficult to verify whether any pubs were built and used as inns or ale houses and kept in continuous use prior to the 1400s.After painstaking investigation, including tree-ring dating on the wooden beams of pubs – a process known as dendrochronology – Wright named the George Inn, of Norton St Philip, Somerset, as the oldest pub in England. It has fabrics dating from the late 14th century.View image in fullscreenInside the George, set up in the 14th century by the monks of Hinton Priory.Photograph: PRHe told the Guardian: “Not one of the claimants to be the oldest pub (and there are over two dozen of them) are even vaguely close to being so in reality.”I stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all? | Simon JenkinsRead moreOf the George, he said: “The architectural history of the George Inn’s stone and timber suggests that this building has been in continuous service for over 600 years.” He said the pub was set up in the 14th century by the monks of nearby Hinton Priory.Tree-ring dating had helped “to understand scientifically exactly how old the timbers are,” he said. “Because we know medieval carpenters didn’t muck around at all and they would fell the timber when it was green and build almost immediately afterwards, the actual date of felling gives us the near date of construction.”Ye Olde Fighting Cocks in St Albans, Hertfordshire, claims to have been established around AD800, and the Bingley Arms in Bardsey, West Yorkshire, declares on its site: “It’s the original English pub – officially the oldest in Britain – dating back over 1,000 years to a time when Vikings were conquering parts of the country.” Similarly, the Royal Standard in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, boasts that it was a favoured watering hole of King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in around AD880.View image in fullscreenThe Royal Standard in Beaconsfield claims to have been frequented by King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in the ninth century.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyWright said most of these claims seemed to be “modern marketing strategies”. “The Fighting Cocks is often said to date to AD793. This date was probably not arrived at until 1926 when it appeared on a postcard. Prior to that, it was speculated to date to 1030, 770 and 672,” he said. “There does not seem to be a basis in reality for any of those claims. Instead, the building started as a monastic dovecote, built around 1400. The earliest date when we can say for sure it was active as a public house is the first decade of the 19th century.”Many of the pubs claiming to be the oldest say they were mentioned in the Domesday Book, but the historian said: “There are no pubs mentioned – at all – in the Domesday Book, so any pub claiming to be in it is having you on.”Wright added: “The claims are likely to originate less in folklore and more in canny marketing strategies by landlords, tenants, breweries and pub companies. The claims potentially rely upon the public not being aware of how to accurately date historic buildings.”View image in fullscreenThe King’s Head in Shrewsbury is a serious contender for the title of one of England’s oldest pubs.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamyHe provided the Guardian with a list of the pubs he believes to be the oldest in the country. His methodology was to determine that it was purpose-built as a public house, that it had been in continuous service and that there was archaeological, archival or dendrochronological evidence for the existence of significant primary fabric remaining from the original construction.Pubs, bars and hotels report ‘Burnham bounce’ in optimism but call for further tax reliefRead more“I did consider buildings which had been converted and others which had periodically changed in land use,” he said. “Even with those taken into consideration, there are only about 12 to 16 genuine contenders which have been doing trade since the medieval period. Of these, the oldest date to the 14th and 15th centuries.”Revealed: Wright’s list of oldest pubsGeorge Inn, Norton St Philip, Somerset: late 14th century and 1430-32.Bull Hotel, Ludlow, Shropshire: 14th and 15th centuries.King’s Head, Shrewsbury, Shropshire: 1426, 1430-31.New Inn, Gloucester, Gloucestershire: 1432.White Hart Inn, Hook, Hampshire: 1419-51.George Hotel, Dorchester-on-Thames, Oxfordshire: mid 15th century.Angel Inn, Andover, Hampshire: 1445-55.Kings Head, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire: 1445-55.Angel, Grantham, Lincolnshire: circa 1450.George and Pilgrims Inn, Glastonbury, Somerset: 1461-83.Saracen’s Head, Southwell, Nottinghamshire: 1460s.George Hotel, Odiham, Hampshire: 1486-87.This article was amended on 23 October 2026. A previous version said the Saracens’s Head is in Lincolnshire; it is in Nottinghamshire.Explore more on these topicsHeritagePubsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tommy Robinson ‘threatened people and acted like a bully’, jury told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Prosecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Prosecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’
Content: Tommy Robinson at Southwark crown court in London on Friday. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson at Southwark crown court in London on Friday. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAUK newsTommy Robinson ‘threatened people and acted like a bully’, jury toldProsecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’Ben QuinnFri 23 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Robinson is guilty of harassing two journalists because we do not live in a “vigilante world”, jurors have been told, as the prosecution sought to use the far-right activist’s words against him.Robinson had posted a video in which he told Daily Mail journalists he would find them after they wrote about his alleged role influencing England’s 2024 riots. He told them he had obtained details of where they and their families lived and warned them to abide by “men’s rules”.Ben Holt, prosecuting, told the jury: “Let’s get real, shall we, and not live in a vigilante world where ‘men’s rules’ apply? Whatever they are. Let’s ground ourselves in a country where there is law and order.”Summing up the case, Holt said Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had accepted that sharing images of journalists’ homes and partial photos of their loved ones was intended to exert pressure.However, he rejected Robinson’s insistence that the journalists on the receiving end of what the prosecution described as “bullyboy and intimidatory” conduct would not have been in fear of violence as a result.Robinson, 43, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence in 2024 to two journalists who were working for the Mail, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies the charges.Robinson said in evidence that he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified a hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk.But Holt said Robinson had never asked for the image to be taken down in calls and messages to the journalists and the Daily Mail’s editor. “Instead, he just threatened people. He acted like a bully,” he said.Holt repeated the words Robinson had directed at the journalists: “Good for the goose, good for the gander. You are coming for me, I am coming for you.” Holt described this as “straightforward retaliation”.Such was the concern of the journalists that the police had to be called on a number of occasions, said Holt, who pointed to “unpleasant” comments made by Robinson’s supporters online after some of his posts. Robinson had close to 1 million followers on X at one point, and some of his supporters are “unpredictable”, Holt said.Alisdair Williamson KC, for the defence, said Robinson’s actions were justified because the “fear for him is real”.“When you judge whether what he did was reasonable, you might think that he showed some restraint,” he told the jury. “I know what language I might use if people put my family in that position. The fear for him is real.”Williamson said the journalists did not care about Robinson’s concerns about the article, nor the stress it caused him, adding: “They don’t care to pick up the phone.”A series of agreed facts that were read out to the court before the closing speeches included a reference to four threat-to-life warning notices that police had given to Robinson in 2018, 2019 and 2024, shortly after the Daily Mail article.The court also heard that a video had been posted online in August 2024 by a man named Omar Abdirizak in which he said: “Tommy Robinson I got a message for you … we got pirates in every corner. Muslims in every corner,” before making a rifle gesture.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

Headline: Victim left with life-threatening injuries after incident in Frances Street, Woolwich, south-east London
Content: The Metropolitan police said they were called to the scene at 8.09pm on Thursday where they found a man with gunshot wounds.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenThe Metropolitan police said they were called to the scene at 8.09pm on Thursday where they found a man with gunshot wounds.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PALondonMet police searching for suspect after man shot near Royal Artillery barracksVictim left with life-threatening injuries after incident in Frances Street, Woolwich, south-east LondonRachel HallFri 23 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are searching for a suspect after a man was shot near the Royal Artillery barracks in south-east London.The victim has been left with life-threatening injuries after the incident, which took place in Frances Street, Woolwich, located 600 metres from the barracks.The Metropolitan police said they were called to the scene at 8.09pm on Thursday where they found a man in his 30s with gunshot wounds. title: Criminals recruiting children to damage Greater Manchester HMOs, police believe | UK news | The Guardian
description: Houses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeks
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Houses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeks
Content: Pictures of damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments on social media.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPictures of damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments on social media.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesUK newsCriminals recruiting children to damage Greater Manchester HMOs, police believeHouses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeksHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCriminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe.In recent weeks, dozens of properties have been targeted across Greater Manchester, mostly in Salford, but also in Stockport and Tameside.The houses that have been attacked are either HMOs (houses in multiple occupation), or properties that have been mistaken for HMOs. Police have received at least 46 separate reports of criminal damage, with cars also targeted alongside houses.Windows have been smashed, and walls and doors have been sprayed with graffiti reading “fuck off” and “no HMO”. Houses are being targeted because they are believed to hold immigrants or refugees.Ch Supt Marcus Noden said: “We suspect vulnerable people are being exploited and paid to damage buildings they believe are HMOs. Some of those being exploited are believed to be children.”“This recent spate of damage is not being tolerated,” he added. “A 42-year-old man has today been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage at an address in Salford overnight. He remains in our custody for questioning.”Previously Noden said that officers were “taking this spate of damage extremely seriously and are continuing to relentlessly target offenders, including those who we believe are using and exploiting children to orchestrate the criminality”.Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.”In a statement, the council said: “We have serious concerns that the impact of the banners is highly likely to spread misinformation, escalate cohesion issues in communities and the potential for inciteful behaviour.”Police have also said that social media is fuelling the attacks, which began on 5 October, with online platforms being used to “push the message out across different areas”.Posts with pictures of the damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments, many of them praising the attacks and predicting further violence.However, some have also been critical of the criminal campaign of damage, including domestic abuse survivors who had recently been housed in HMOs.Four people have been arrested this week in relation to the attacks. On Monday, a 46-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, and on Wednesday a 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.Police have also made previous arrests in relation to the spate of criminal damage, including a 13-year-old boy.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Severe flooding in US west triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation orders | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: At least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: At least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah
Content: Floodwaters from the San Juan River rising in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on 23 October 2026.Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/ReutersView image in fullscreenFloodwaters from the San Juan River rising in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on 23 October 2026.Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/ReutersExtreme weatherSevere flooding in US west triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation ordersAt least one injured after flooding in Four Corners region – which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and UtahMaya Yangand agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 14.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 17.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSevere flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues – some from rooftops – and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado andNew Mexicoand others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees on to houses and downed power lines inArizona. At least one person was injured.An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued on Friday by New Mexico guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, Devin Neeley, a San Juan county spokesperson, said.“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4ft (1-1.5 metres) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.View image in fullscreenFlooding in Hurricane, Utah, on 22 October 2026.Photograph: Chelsey Field/APSkies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.About 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.“We are kind of all hands on deck,” Intoppa said.In a Facebookposton Friday morning, Farmington police said: “Agencies have been working through the night and are doing everything they can to respond as quickly as possible.”Additionally, a flood warning in Rio Chamasaid: “The current extent of the flooding along the San Juan River in New Mexico has not been observed since before the completion of Navajo dam in 1962.”On Friday, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning across west central Montezuma county in southwestern ColoradoFarmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the US where four states – Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona andUtah– come together.National guard members also were deployed to assist with flooding in south-west Colorado. Rising waters prompted mandatory evacuations along four rivers, including the San Juan River through Pagosa Springs.
