The resort town famous for its riverside hot springs suffered flooding from a similar weather pattern a year ago.“Please shelter in place, water levels are beginning to recede, but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel,” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office posted online on Friday.In nearby Rio Grande county, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.Some homes along the Conejos River in the San Juan Mountains experienced up to 7ft of interior flooding, while homes in the South Fork area saw water levels reach 4-5ft, the Colorado Sunreported.The small mountain town of South Fork reported a missing bridge that extended over Forest Service Road 380, the outlet added.Meanwhile, the sheriff’s office of Archuleta countywarnedresidents on Friday to shelter in place, saying: “Water levels are beginning to recede but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel.“The evacuation check-in center is not currently accessible, if you need an evacuation location the PLPOA Clubhouse at 230 Port Ave, Pagosa Springs CO is open and available,” it added.Photos posted online by the Colorado Department of transportation showed a road washout near Silverton on Highway 550, where brown floodwaters surged across a large section of the damaged roadway, Colorado Public Radioreported.View image in fullscreenFloodwaters from the San Juan River rise in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on 23 October 2026.Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/ReutersJared Polis, Colorado’s governor, had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the south-west part of the state.The city of Hurricane in far south-western Utah was cleaning up after declaring a state of emergency on Thursday. Reddish-brown flood water lapped into and about 80 homes in a neighborhood and 50 recreational vehicles in an RV park.Surreal scenes included a shipping container drifting slowly down a street.An evacuation order wasissuedfor the Willow Wind RV Park in Hurricane.Othervideosposted online showed people in Hurricane leading horses to safety through murky floodwaters.“The full extent and severity of the damage, as well as the potential displacement of residents, remain under assessment,” Hurricane officialssaid, adding that the floods have damaged or affected bridges, culverts, public roads and electrical power boxes.The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the south-west are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”The severe flooding follows weeks ofextreme weatheracross the south-west, including Thursday’s storms in Arizona, which brought golf ball-size hail and tornadoes, and aprolonged heat domethat pushed temperatures across the region into the triple digits.Meanwhile, California wasgrippedby an unprecedented heatwave last week, with downtown Los Angeles reaching a record 104F, surpassing the previous high of 101F set in 1953.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherFloodingColoradoNew MexicoUtahNatural disastersUS weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Content: Faisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAView image in fullscreenFaisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAMiddle East and north AfricaUS and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on IranMultinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisisPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 23 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForeign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes onIranwhile talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey andGermany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed theMecca defensive security pactin August, a grouping Egypt may join.The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”He made no criticism of the US but accused “theHouthisand Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”Explore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaEuropeIranMiddle East peace talksUS-Israel war on IranHouthisIran nuclear dealnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed | Israel | The Guardian
description: Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight
Content: Israeli forces patrolling Hebron as Benjamin Netanyahu visited the area on Friday.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenIsraeli forces patrolling Hebron as Benjamin Netanyahu visited the area on Friday.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIsraelIsrael launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killedBenjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfightEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andLorenzo TondoFri 23 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city.Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting.The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted avideoof himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight.The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers.Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead more“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of theWest Bank,” Dahleh said. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli lawyer, said Smotrich’s video was a “direct admission” that the demolitions were a collective punishment. He noted that deterrence had been used as an excuse for collective punishment since antiquity.The defence minister, Israel Katz, promised further mass demolitions and forced displacement. He drew an explicit comparison with Gaza and said Hebron would be targeted in the same way as Jenin refugee camp, where nearly 20,000 people have been forced from their homes. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, with about 250,000 residents.Katz said: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron. Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.”Netanyahu announced that plans had been drawn up for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967, when Israeli forces occupied the Palestinian territory and forcibly displaced about 300,000 Palestinians.No date had been set “but it is on the way”, he said in a statement that also pledged mass forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron and the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.The attack was launched by two men armed with an assault rifle and a handgun, according to the Israeli military. The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.An AFP photographer who was on the way to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.Prominent Israelis, including a candidate for the far-right Amcha Yisrael party, shared conspiracy theories groundlessly accusing the AFP photographer of links to the gunmen after he documented the Hebron attack.The Foreign Press Association (FPA) said it was deeply alarmed by claims the photographer had been tipped off, describing them as “dangerous and defamatory”. “He is a longtime professional who was on his way to another assignment and courageously documented what he saw in keeping with his professional duties,” the FPA said in a statement.The incident came a week aftersettlers severely injured the photographer Heidi Levineas she documented attacks on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also denied entry to several European journalists and an academic.Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.Attacks have intensified further since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September. Israeli settler militantshave used violenceto stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.Israel holds elections on Tuesday. The current far-right coalition, which backs settlers politically and financially, is seeking to shore up voter support in the face of polls that show it is likely to loose its majority.Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, also travelled to Hebron on Friday and demanded the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement, which is already heavily curtailed by Israeli controls, checkpoints and roadblocks.Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Opposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of election | Spain | The Guardian
description: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Content: Pedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPAView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPASpainOpposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of electionVideo shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoingAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 23 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.Launchedthis weekacross the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks aboutreceiving a university postthanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks abouthiding jewelleryin a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenA still from the People’s party AI-generated video featuring a deepfake of Begoña Gomez.Computer-generated: @ppopular/XThe Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister,told the broadcaster TVEon Friday.While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.A majority of the nine legal expertsconsulted by the newspaper El Paísconcurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – tocrack downon the impact of disinformation.“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticutidentified more than 200such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.Explore more on these topicsSpainPedro SánchezAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports
Content: A snowy London street. Great Britain has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on production from the North Sea.Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA snowy London street. Great Britain has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on production from the North Sea.Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty ImagesEnergy industrySome of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winterOfficial forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure importsJillian AmbroseFri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreat Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs inEuropethis winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports.The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing.National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut.The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted.In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies.Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent.Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler monthswith gas stores at their lowest level in 13 yearsowing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis.The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision toapprove the new Jackdaw gasfieldin the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month.Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter.The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July.The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid.Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed.National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels.Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnergy storageEnergyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bites | Consumer spending | The Guardian
description: Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget
Content: Fort Kinnaird retail park in Newcraighall, south-east of Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFort Kinnaird retail park in Newcraighall, south-east of Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianConsumer spendingUK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bitesEconomic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budgetRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 03.25 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConsumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urgedRead moreThe latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East.Petrol and diesel priceshave surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost£14,000 on average in additional costsfor mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach£2,000 a year from Januaryfor the typical household.Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to3.5% last month, while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeezeRead moreSeparate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”The Treasury has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsConsumer spendingEconomicsRetail industryUK cost of living crisisEconomic policyConsumer affairsJohn HealeynewsShareReuse this content

title: Boom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubs | Hospitality industry | The Guardian
description: World’s second largest brewer says use of drugs such as Wegovy can reduce desire to drink alcohol
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: World’s second largest brewer says use of drugs such as Wegovy can reduce desire to drink alcohol
Content: Heineken offered advice to pubs, including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food.Photograph: william87/Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenHeineken offered advice to pubs, including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food.Photograph: william87/Getty/iStockphotoHospitality industryBoom in weight-loss drugs could lead to fall in beer sales, Heineken warns UK pubsWorld’s second largest brewer says use of drugs such as Wegovy can reduce desire to drink alcoholMark SweneyFri 23 Oct 2026 06.33 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 05.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.The world’s second-largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month that said the use of GLP-1 medication – such as Ozempic and Wegovy –could reduce the desire to drink alcohol. This in turn could result in “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars, it added.The document, revealed by Reuters, said the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” said a Heineken spokesperson. “Consumer behaviour is evolving in response to a range of broader trends. GLP-1 is one of the developments we are monitoring.”GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek aquick solution to weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.Heineken said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits were evolving.Trends the brewer has identified in GLP-1 users include opting for smaller serves, lower alcohol drinks and more premium products.“Our latest consumer research suggests GLP-1 users are not simply replacing alcohol,” said the spokesperson. “They are becoming more purposeful in their choices and broadening their preferences. These behaviours are not unique to GLP-1 users. They reflect broader consumer trends towards health and wellbeing, moderation, choice and more intentional consumption that we are seeing across our markets.”As well as its eponymous lager, Heineken also owns brands such as Amstel, the Mexican lager Sol and Strongbow cider.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guinness maker, Diageo, has told investors that any impact from GLP-1 drugs becoming mainstream should be manageable, while Carlsberg told Reuters that data did not support the view that the use of weight-loss drugs affected beer consumption trends.However, surveys by research companies including Circana, NIQ and KAM have pointed to reduced drinking by GLP-1 users.According to Heineken, there was almost £14bn in sales of beer in British pubs, bars and restaurants in the year to February, with less than £300m of that from no- and low-alcohol products.Explore more on these topicsHospitality industryBeerWeight-loss drugsFood & drink industryPubsAlcoholPharmaceuticals industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week
Content: Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall in sales.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTextile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall in sales.Photograph: Maureen McLean/REX/ShutterstockRetail industryRetail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut backLatest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next weekMark SweneyFri 23 Oct 2026 06.35 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor,John Healey, announces his budget next week.TheOffice for National Statistics(ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK hasfallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic.While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East.In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict.Stripping out the increase from fuel, retail sales fell 0.7% in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City.“October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics.“This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in [the final quarter of this year and the first quarter of next]. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.”Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector.Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather.The only sector to record an increase in sales last month – apart from automotive fuel – was department stores, where the volume of goods bought rose 0.2%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe fall in monthly sales follows a bumper August, with the ONSrevising figures up from a 0.5% monthly rise to 0.7%.This helped fuel a 0.7% increase in sales over the three months to the end of September compared with the previous quarter.“Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel, which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East,” said Hannah Finselbach, a senior statistician at the ONS. “Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryBudget 2026John HealeyBudgetOffice for National StatisticsPetrol pricesUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ring | Television | The Guardian
description: Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game
Content: High stakes ones and zeros … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenHigh stakes ones and zeros … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MaxTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ringHuman heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation GamePhil HarrisonFri 23 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe begin with the audio of a horrifying call made to the French police in 2020. Two men are driving home when their car is attacked. The police ask for the caller’s name as bullets ricochet around the vehicle. “Who cares what we’re called?” the man shouts. “I’m going to die!” Seconds later, his companion is dead. This killing (of a mechanic called Houcine Hakkar) was planned and discussed in detail on an app called Sky ECC. The police were at the tip of an enormous iceberg.Showing modern law enforcement on screen can be a challenge: in the online era, it’s less cops and robbers; more zeros and ones. So it’s a surprise to be confronted with something as thrilling as The Narco Hack. This three-part documentary explores an extraordinary investigation by French, Belgian and Dutch police, during which they undermined several massive criminal organisations via methods at once impressively logical and completely mind-boggling by compromising Sky ECC’s encryption software.Sky ECC was developed by a company called Sky Global, apparently with lawyers and journalists in mind. The app was designed to strip phones of all their normal features, leaving just itself. When the app was shut down, the phones deactivated. Oh, and the phones could be wiped remotely, which was a handy feature. “At Sky, they knew very well that it wasn’t going to be choirboys buying it,” says “Albert”, a drug dealer. “You weren’t going to be talking to your mum on Sky.” Thomas Herdman, who worked for the company, is interviewed and offers an unconvincing defence constructed around the idea that a luxury hotelier wouldn’t ask their guests how they could afford to stay at the hotel.View image in fullscreenEngaging … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MAXAnd so begins an epic tale of brave detective work and tech wizardry. This kind of material is undeniably hard to render visually – but while The Narco Hack does feature an awful lot of scrolling computer text and close-ups of smartphones being turned on, it also hears at length from the cops involved. From shrewd, single-minded prosecutor Johanna Brousse to eccentric cybercrime whiz “Bertillon” (his name is protected and he appears via a series of AI-rendered face-swaps), they’re an engaging bunch.Furthermore, the investigation grips hard, and the stakes are extremely high. As Bertillon walks us through the decryption process (server locations, cryptographic keys: you’re glazing over already, aren’t you?), most viewers almost certainly won’t fully understand. However, what unfolds on the ground is approximately The Wire meets The Imitation Game. The various police jurisdictions involved aren’t singing from the same charge sheet – the Belgians want to stop the drugs and guns moving, while the French want to identify suspects and follow them.Then there’s the issue of how much to reveal to their quarries. As the detectives realise they’re looking over the shoulders of drug kingpins, they also understand that if they act hastily, they’ll only land small fry. How much further could access take them? This dilemma is sharpened by the sheer horror of what is being revealed as indigestible chunks of gibberish text become comprehensible. Sexual torture. Skin flayed with scorching hot skillets. An innocuous-looking pink house in Serbia which turns out to contain meat grinders into which informants are fed. Surely, at some point, the police have to stop intelligence-gathering and start smashing down front doors?Police raids across Europe after encrypted phone network shut downRead moreSoon enough, they do. They uncover billions of euros (mainly laundered via cryptocurrency) and Dubai-resident drug lords calling themselves things like Saddam Hussein, Putin and Hitler. It’s hugely satisfying to witness but feels like a sisyphean task all the same. Underpinning everything is perhaps the crucial conversation of our era. About the thin line between innovation and crime. About who polices tech companies and how. And about where responsibility ultimately lies.This documentary is specific in its field of interest but it’s more widely thought-provoking, prompting consideration of everything from social media companies that enable the creation of child sexual abuse material to AI companies and their laissez-faire attitude to intellectual and creative theft. Sky ECC is what happens when tech finds its ideal users and, for reasons of commercial expediency, simply shrugs its shoulders.Still, there’s a very human heroism being celebrated here. The consequences of the hack were significant in all sorts of smaller, more profoundly personal ways too. In the wake of Houcine Hakkar’s horrible fate, there were mutterings about the unlikeliness of smoke without fire. In revealing the conversations around his killing, the hack unequivocally cleared his name. His murder had been a terrible mistake. The look on his sister’s face as she talks about her brother suggests that’s no small consolation.The Narco Hack is on HBO Max nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewCybercrimeHackingDocumentaryFactual TVOrganised crimeEncryptionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films | Movies | The Guardian
description: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
Author: Danny Leigh
Headline: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
Content: ‘You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria StevensView image in fullscreen‘You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria StevensMoviesInterview‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest filmsDanny LeighNew film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movieFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says.We are talking about Fatherland. Directed by acclaimed Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski, Hüller plays the German polymath Erika Mann, who in the film drives her novelist fatherThomas Mannthrough newly divided postwar Germany. The Nazi past shadows everything – but the movie is also tied up with the birth of East Germany, where Hüller grew up. (She still lives in what was once the GDR.) I tell her I’ve never before seen a film that acknowledged the utopian dreams of that place and time, however damaged they became. Yes, she replies: German directors don’t know how to approach it.“But Fatherland has a grief that you feel clearer coming from the East.”Toni Erdmann’s Sandra Hüller: ‘Everybody knows the German clichés. Maybe they’re true’Read moreAnd then her voice cracks, and she cries. We reflexively apologise to each other. “I’m just grateful Pawel gave space to this political idea that didn’t survive inGermany, but is one maybe people can still think about. The socialist idea.”Hüller wipes her eyes. Finally, she laughs. “You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you? I can see the headline.”View image in fullscreenIn Fatherland Hüller plays Erika Mann, who drives her father through newly divided postwar Germany.Photograph: Agata GrzybowskaAnd yet she has always been open about the nuance to the East Germany she remembers from childhood – a place defined by more than the Stasi men of cold war thrillers. “What fascinates me is that in East and West were two systems that for a certain time could have learned from each other.” She apologises again; I’m not sure why. “It is this situation we live in now. I feel like I’m on thin ice.”Inevitably, we come to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The subject is doubly unavoidable in light of Fatherland. The Manns originally fled the country in 1933 and they would end up in the US. “It’s no secret there are similarities now,” Hüller says. “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.” Her tone turns businesslike. “The question is what we do about it.”We all contain multitudes, but Hüller more than most. At home in Leipzig, she is a co-founder of the experimental Farn Kollektiv theatre group; a politically engaged woman of 48, she is the single mother to a teenage daughter. She is also deadpan funny. An account of her excellent safety record as a driver is a comic treasure. “Thatshould be your headline. ‘Sandra Hüller – a clean licence.’”She is also a movie actor with snowballing momentum. In 2024, she astonished twice over as the wife of the commandant of Auschwitz in The Zone of Interest and a woman suspected of murdering her husband in Anatomy of a Fall. The latter saw her Oscar-nominated. Now, after Project Hail Mary, Digger and Fatherland, there will also be Rose, a stark 17th century fable in which she plays a war veteran – who is, in fact, a woman passing as a man. Oscar talk is simmering once more. America is freshly excited.“OK, so what is happening is that I made very different movies at different times, but they’re all coming out together. It’s nothing I control.” What is good, she says, is that, with her as the common thread, Hollywood marketing budgets end up spotlighting the likes of Fatherland too. “On the other hand, I struggle with seeing myself as someone special. I still consider myself part of a group. That is actually the highest praise I can give myself.”Curiously, a collective spirit might also apply to the fifth film Hüller is strongly rumoured to be in this year: Marvel relaunch Avengers: Doomsday. Whatever else Marvel movies represent, they have a reputation for an oddly egalitarian vibe on set. I wonder aloud if that’s true. “Me too!” She gives an impish tilt of the head. Ah. For the record, then, Hüller still may or may not be part of the new Avengers.But in theory, a Marvel film might feel unexpectedly non-hierarchical? “I heard that as well! Which would show having a lot of money available doesn’t have to mean abusing your power. And that would be a great thing. In theory.”If the thought of Hüller doing Marvel takes getting used to, it makes more sense after Project Hail Mary. In a deft piece of Hollywood feelgood, she proved the perfect foil for Ryan Gosling’s reluctant spaceman as stone-faced mission controller Eva Stratt. The air of ultra-competence was very Sandra Hüller for Beginners. The film even harked back to her 2016 breakthrough in skewed German comedy Toni Erdmann. Hüller has a glorious singing voice. Then, she karaoked Whitney Houston’s Greatest Love of All. Now, it was Harry Styles’ Sign of the Times.View image in fullscreen‘I love watching people invent’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria Stevens“But I think Eva Stratt made some people uncomfortable. It can feel unusual to be governed by a woman.”Still, making Project Hail Mary was another pleasant surprise – her first Hollywood set where the directors – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller – actually lightened the mood. “They made sure we could actually play. Have fun.” She did, though, find it strange being wrangled by runners on the kind of blockbuster where producers want to know where a star is at all times. (Unlike almost every actor on her level, Hüller doesn’t even have an assistant.) “But you can always hide in the bathroom.”Would she spend more time in the US than necessary? “Not right now. No. It’s a workplace.” Anyway, she says, she likes where she lives. “It’s simple. America is just very far away.” And she smiles.She believes audiences embraced Project Hail Mary because the film-makers sought to unite them, inside a cinema at least. “And entertain them without the usual things – death and weapons. So you have a story about a human with a task that lets them be bigger than themselves. That inspired people.”But what about their response to Digger? Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, with Tom Cruise as a cartoonish oil tycoon, the movie got poor reviews, then did cataclysmically at the box office. Can we talk about it? “Sure!” she says brightly. “I mean, we expected a strong reaction. It’s a polarising movie. And a political movie, which we weren’t able to say in interviews. For whatever reason.” A beat. “But personally – I was surprised by the harshness of the rejection. People really hated it!”Hüller, though, says she loves it. “Years from now, it will be seen as a document of our times.” But time won’t be able to fix a problem like the thinness of her role as the sister of Cruise’s character. There should have been more of her, I say. “Well, there was.” Naturally, she smiles. Ah. (Again.) More rumours put forward that her role was heavily cut by Iñárritu. “You’d have to talk to Alejandro.” Are they still friendly? “Of course!”At the movie’s royal gala premiere in London, the audience spent hours watching on screen the introductions of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, to the cast and many others. I tell Hüller a cameraman briefly focused on her, waiting in a red carpet frock with a look that suggested a looming medical procedure. The memory clearly tickles her.So what was she thinking? “Well, I thought of the people in the cinema, waiting for us to start the movie, and not being able to leave. Also, my feet really hurt.” But she has a surprise in store. “I mean, I’ve never met any royalty in my life, so I was also fangirling.” Really? Hüller seems an unlikely monarchist. “I don’t find the monarchy interesting. But they are fascinating, remarkable personalities.” So what did she finally talk about with the royal couple? “Oh, I can’t remember. I was in shock!” Would she like to meet them again? “Of course! I want to have tea with them! I want to talk abouteverythingwith them!”‘This is a film to make us unsafe in the cinema. As we should be’: Sandra Hüller and Christian Friedel on The Zone of InterestRead moreHüller is now hooting with laughter.If we do include the Avengers, her fifth film of this most productive year is Rose. Like Fatherland, it is a story of the German past, in black and white. And yet, after fun with royals and Ryan Gosling, Rose now brings her back to modern Germany. It was filmed in Saxony-Anhalt, “where a certain party recently won power”. (This is the German state where the AfD claimed 43.8% of the vote in September.)In preparation to play a character passing as male, Hüller says she watched men more closely than she ever had before. The result was a study of all that goes into being read as male. “Honestly, it left me astonished. I realised that as a woman, I rarely enter a room and think of it as a battleground. But male behaviour is so related to that. Where is the enemy and how can I defeat him?”So do men make bad socialists? “No! Some of the most famous socialists have been men.” Could that be why we don’t have socialism, though? She grins and wags a finger. “You forgot Mamdani?” She also has a related point. “One advantage of being born in the GDR and seeing it fall apart, or reunified, however you want to call it, is you learn no system is for ever. And that is interesting in a time when the things we’ve done so long don’t work any more. So maybe it is good to think of different ways they could work in future.”Hüller is having to rethink the present too. Despite still seeing herself as a theatre actor who sometimes makes films, her German stage career is now on hold – at least in front of the curtain. Fame complicates. “If you are part of an ensemble but people come to see you as if the others matter less, I don’t enjoy that.” But she has a workaround. Farn are now creating two new plays she will instead direct. (“One is about revenge. The other goodbyes.”) So far, she says, the new role has been a pleasure. “I love the discussions. I love watching people invent. And we will see how long this wave continues.”She tells me she is also curious how my piece will turn out. In Germany, she says, interview subjects give notes on a draft before anything goes to print. We don’t do that in the UK, I say. “I know. But as the interviewed person, it gives you a feeling of being respected. Not that I don’t feel respected here. Anyway, I never change much.” She smiles. “Sometimes just a comma.” So will she read this? “No, because I have no say.”And yes, she agrees, laughing, that means I can write whatever I want.Fatherland is out in the UK and US on 23 October, and in Australia on 17 November. Rose is out on 11 December in the US, and 5 February in the UKExplore more on these topicsFilmGermanyPeriod and historical filmsThomas MannEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Robson Green stars in a rural culture-clash cosy crime drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Northumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch today
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Northumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch today
Content: Familiar faces … Robson Green (right) as Joe Ruby in The Northumbria Mysteries, with Simon Callow as Father David Rutherford.Photograph: Alex Telfer/BBC/Lonesome Pine ProductionsView image in fullscreenFamiliar faces … Robson Green (right) as Joe Ruby in The Northumbria Mysteries, with Simon Callow as Father David Rutherford.Photograph: Alex Telfer/BBC/Lonesome Pine ProductionsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Robson Green stars in a rural culture-clash cosy crime dramaNorthumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch todayHollie Richardson,Alexi Duggins,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesFri 23 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Northumbria Mysteries2pm, BBC OneIf you enjoyedSally Phillips’s recent Hairdresser Mysteries, here’s another daytime cosy (if slightly less camp) crime drama with a familiar face. Robson Green plays ex-con and gambler Joe Ruby, who finds himself solving crimes on the Northumberland coast with Liz White’s Oxford-educated DI Rose O’Connell. First up, the body of a monk is found in a priory.Hollie RichardsonOur Great Yorkshire Life7pm, Channel 5More northern countryside goodness, this time with ex-Emmerdale actors Matt Wolfenden and Roxy Shahidi exploring Nidd Valley without any gadgets. Elsewhere, chef Matt Healy is catching lobsters in Flamborough Head and conservators restore Wentworth Woodhouse.HRGardeners’ World9pm, BBC TwoAfter this instalment of the horticultural show, there are only two more episodes before the end of the series. With Monty Don having confirmed his departure, it’s worth soaking up every moment of his tips, centred on Don’s luscious Longmeadow garden.Alexi DugginsWar9pm, Sky AtlanticThe big divorce seems to be heading for a settlement but, in this cheerfully vicious drama, nothing is ever straightforward. A taut episode centres on St John (a frozen-blooded Pip Torrens) trying to bully opposing lawyer Nick (James McArdle) into submission. With his weak spot hit and hundreds of millions on the table, Nick starts to disintegrate.Jack SealeThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneIf the apocalypse had never happened, could farm girl Maggie and drawling killer Negan have been friends, or more? That’s the premise of this alternate-universe episode of the horror drama, which gives the characters (and long-serving actors) a fascinating meet-cute in contemporary, non-zombified New York.Graeme VirtueThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneOne of the nation’s favourite celebrities du jour, Hannah Waddingham, makes her debut on the red sofa. She’ll be sitting next to Cate Blanchett, fresh from her London theatre run, and Steve Irwin’s son Robert. Jorja Smith provides the live music.HRFilm choiceHow to Make a Killing ( John Patton Ford, 2026)9.05am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereEven attempting to remake 1949 black comedy Kind Hearts and Coronets, that undisputed British classic in which Alec Guinness has a virtuosic turn as all eight members of the doomed D’Ascoyne family, is an audacious act of American cockiness. But then “audacious American cockiness” is exactly the vibe that star Glen Powell specialises in. He plays Becket Redfellow, the orphaned son of an estranged heiress, who believes himself entitled to the family fortune and will stop at nothing to secure it – not even serial killing in a succession of silly wigs.Ellen E JonesParalyzedBy Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (Judd Apatow and Neil Berkeley, 2026),NetflixIf you’ve ever wondered how Maria Bamford got that way, here’s the answer: a documentary about the life of this true one-off – your favourite standup’s favourite standup – featuring interviews with Conan O’Brien, Tig Notaro and Stephen Colbert. Bamford also appears, of course, in an intimate interview recorded in her California home, and her singular voice guides us through archive footage, from home movies of her Minnesota childhood through to the basement comedy venues of her early career.EEJLive sportPremiershiprugby: Gloucester v Bath,7pm, TNT Sports 1At Kingsholm Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Junk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstep | Drama films | The Guardian
description: The Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused tone
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused tone
Content: David Schwimmer in Junk.Photograph: MUBIView image in fullscreenDavid Schwimmer in Junk.Photograph: MUBIDrama filmsReviewJunk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstepThe Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused toneAdrian HortonFri 23 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou could be forgiven, upon watching the first scene of Junk, for believing that this debut feature will boldly, perhaps ill-advisedly, dare to satirize the industry it’s purporting to join. At a swanky restaurant in LA, four people aglow with self-importance embark on the time-honored ritual of discussing the screenplays they’re working on – specifically, the screenplay Martin (David Schwimmer), is “working on”. It’s classic industry navel-gazing, underscored by a tight focus on Martin’s clammy face as he sputters poorly through a confidence game.Clayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very goodRead moreSchwimmer, of course, is still best known for playing a perpetually and comedically exasperated sitcom character; it’s hard to square that extremely familiar voice with Martin’s dark bluster on how “drug-addled gen Zers” have “no respect for the communal aspect of the cinema”, an off-putting rant that is also a tad intriguing – who is more pretentious here, the sweaty character or the picture starkly sending him up?But Junk, directed by Jack Begert from a script co-written with Dani Goffstein, swerves quickly and, for too long, inexplicably to a different stratum of Hollywood. Somewhere else in the city, two burnouts, played by Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder, find themselves without their car, pills or plans once a house robbery goes awry. The sharp pivot is confusing, though not unwelcome; Begert, a prolific director of surrealist music videos for artists such asOlivia Rodrigo,Doja Catand Kendrick Lamar, has an eye for LA’s seedy beauty, the way a night can unwind like the city’s endless roads. You could, like the chihuahua nicked from the house and hot potatoed while the thieves flee to the scene to the modest synths of Caroline Polachek’s So Hot You’re Hurting My Feelings, just be along for the ride.Alas, it’s a bumpy and unsatisfying one. Junk is molded from another feature by a different name, Little Death, that premiered at the Sundance film festival back in 2024. According to press notes, that earlier movie was “a different shape entirely” from the new picture released byMubi, though “at heart it’s the same movie.” I unfortunately missed Little Death on its festival run, where it picked up a Sundance innovator award, so I cannot speak to what, exactly, has changed, though the new shape is an odd one: two loosely connected stories of addiction and desperation in LA, one far more compelling and visually stimulating than the other, and only one deserving the film’s billing as a “slacker odyssey” across the city.That section, as AJ (Fike) and Karla (Ryder) struggle to score and strive in nearly equal measure, beguilingly conveys, for a too brief stretch, the feeling of an unplanned evening in LA, hazy and sprawling and peopled by unpredictable characters who are at once assertive and stoned. There’s something appealing, if derivative, to lurking with two kids as they hurdle roadblock after roadblock of their own making. The appearance of Euphoria alum Fike, as another optimistic addict endearing even as he’s lying through his teeth, recalls the audacity of that now-cursed show – an impression unfortunately underscored by a visit to an antiseptic, sinister apartment owned by a drug dealer with “school shooter vibes” (an off-putting Karl Glusman) that undercuts the film’s woozy naturalism.Unfortunate, too, that the 110-minute film’s middle section returns to Schwimmer’s screenwriter, sweatily withdrawing into fantasy with a molten core of self-loathing. The title card, presented 35 minutes in, presents an art exhibit that teases Junk as “a search for meaning in the post-post-modern dilemma” – a line surely meant as a joke, though it more or less describes the film’s grating meta ambitions, as Martin maybe or maybe not writes the other half of the story. It is, I assume, supposed to be ironic that Martin, stymied by a male protagonist deemed too “unlikable” by broadly drawn film executives, resorts to increasingly repellant behavior and flights of fancy. But whatever the intentions (and impressive flourishes of surrealist animation), it is certainly a slog to witness. The fact that, in taking the exec’s notes that he switch his protagonist to a woman in order to get made, Martin is played, for a time, by Gaby Hoffman, scans as unduly cynical. (And the less that is said about a recurring fantasy sequence involving a beautiful woman, played by Angela Sarafyan, in a barn described by his therapist as his “mother’s womb”, the better.) That Jena Malone, as Martin’s beleaguered fiancee, gets a well-earned tirade puncturing his absorption is only fair, though of little comfort.If this sounds like the review of two entirely different movies – well, though connections between the two are eventually revealed, Junk never coheres into one picture. There’s admirable ambition here, and plenty of sumptuous visuals to spare, but the clash between one section’s biting cynicism and another’s ragged heart proves too discordant to overcome. Which is a shame; as a whole, the film may be a mess, but there are little treasures within this Junk to perhaps be reimagined down the road.Junk is now available globally on Mubi nowExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsDavid SchwimmerMubiComedy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Backrooms to The Monkey: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television | The Guardian
description: Chiwetel Ejiofor stars in a heart-poundingly original horror, while Theo James plays twins cursed by a killer wind-up monkey. Happy Halloween week!
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: Chiwetel Ejiofor stars in a heart-poundingly original horror, while Theo James plays twins cursed by a killer wind-up monkey. Happy Halloween week!
Content: Mall trawl … Chiwetel Ejiofor in Backrooms.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenMall trawl … Chiwetel Ejiofor in Backrooms.Photograph: PRThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevisionBackrooms to The Monkey: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekChiwetel Ejiofor stars in a heart-poundingly original horror, while Theo James plays twins cursed by a killer wind-up monkey. Happy Halloween week!Ellen E JonesandSimon WardellFri 23 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekBackroomsDirector Kane Parsons was just 20 when he shot this genre-redefining horror, based on the “creepypasta” YouTube series he’d been developing since his mid-teens. Chiwetel Ejiofor stars as Clark, a failed architect who discovers an apparently endless liminal space behind the strip mall store where he works and, depressingly, also lives. Renate Reinsve is Clark’s therapist, Mary, a woman working through her own traumas around enclosed spaces, who nonetheless follows him into these backrooms to attempt a rescue. The wallpaper may be monotonously yellow, but there are scares of every shade here and, underlying it all, the heart-pounding thrill of pure originality.EEJMonday 26 October, HBO MaxThe Seventh SealView image in fullscreenKiller moves … Max von Sydow and Bengt Ekerot in The Seventh Seal.Photograph: Moviestore/REX/ShutterstockThe scene where the knight (Max von Sydow) plays chess with Death (Bengt Ekerot) is among the most recognisable in the history of cinema, and endlessly parodied by the less cultured likes of Bill & Ted’s Bogus Journey and The Muppets. But that shouldn’t eclipse the rest of Ingmar Bergman’s 1957 classic, worth seeing in full for its allegorical depiction of plague-ravaged medieval Europe, the austere black and white cinematography of Gunnar Fischer, and a climatic rendering of the Danse Macabre, performed before slowly dissolving dark clouds.EEJSaturday 24 October, 9.30pm, BBC FourCat PersonView image in fullscreenSituationship … Geraldine Viswanathan and Emilia Jones in Cat Person.Photograph: Courtesy of Sundance InstituteIs Cat Person a romantic comedy? Or is it a psychological horror? The erratic tone shifts of this 2023 film, adapted from Kristen Roupenian’s viral short story of the same name, are entirely in keeping with its subject matter: what it means to be a single, straight woman and, in the internet parlance, “date your only natural predator”. Emilia Jones stars as Margot, a 20-year-old college student who begins an ambivalent relationship with Robert (Nicholas Braun, AKA Greg from Succession), a harmless if slightly pompous nice-guy lunk. Or is he?EEJSaturday 24 October, 11.40pm, BBC OneThe Boston StranglerView image in fullscreenConfession … Tony Curtis and Henry Fonda in The Boston Strangler.Photograph: Ronald GrantTony Curtis turns up halfway through, playing against type as the now DNA-linked killer, Albert DeSalvo. The real stars, though, are the dogged detectives of Boston PD, featuring a host of reassuringly craggy-faced character actors such as George Kennedy and Murray Hamilton, and headed up by John S Bottomly (Henry Fonda). They run down seemingly every creep and kook in eastern Massachusetts before eventually landing on their man. Director Richard Fleischer’s use of split-screen adds to both the pacing and the period feel.EEJSunday 25 October, 10.10pm, Talking Pictures TVskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll of Us StrangersView image in fullscreenTowering drama … Andrew Scott and Paul Mescal in All of Us Strangers.Photograph: Parisa Taghizadeh/APAndrew Haigh’sfilm is an emotionally complex, fable-like story of regret and redemption. Andrew Scott, never better, plays Adam, an introverted, gay screenwriter who lives alone in a tower block. In search of inspiration, he revisits his childhood home, only to come upon the ghosts of his parents (Claire Foy and Jamie Bell), who died in a car crash when he was 12. He also meets Harry (Paul Mescal), seemingly the only other person in his building, and starts a tentative romance. These two encounters draw Adam out of himself, giving him the chance to reassess his childhood, his sexuality and his present. A heart-rending but hopeful tale.SWWednesday 28 October, 9pm, Film4The MonkeyView image in fullscreenScreamer …  Tatiana Maslany stars in horror comedy The Monkey.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyOsgood Perkins made 2024’s scariest movie in Longlegs, but his 2025 follow-up, based on a Stephen King short story, is a raucous comedy horror with more laughs and more life wisdom. Theo James plays twins whose traumatic family inheritance continually resurfaces in the form of a cursed wind-up monkey. Whenever someone is foolish enough to turn its key, a spectacularly gruesome death ensues. This leaves the twins with a dilemma: how to go on living when death is all around?EEJWednesday 28 October, 10.40pm, BBC OneApocalypse Z: New WorldView image in fullscreenGoing viral … Carlos Alcaide stars in Apocalypse Z: New World.Photograph: @AndreaResmini/AmazonThe Spanish-language zombie flick Apocalypse Z: The Beginning of the End was a huge international hit for Prime Video in 2024. In this sequel, also directed by Carles Torrens, much of the population has taken refuge in the Canary Islands, following the outbreak of the blood-borne TSJ virus. Roberto (Carlos Alcaide) joins a special return mission to the mainland, which soon becomes a scramble for survival as the infected hordes march on. Perhaps returning fan favourite Lúculo the cat (still played by Pedrito the cat) can come to the rescue?EEJFriday 30 October, Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsTelevisionThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lupin review – the French super-thief is magnetic in his blockbuster return | Television | The Guardian
description: The bizarrely salient French crime smash is higher stakes than ever – and its Houdini-style thrills are complemented with some interesting questions around race and infamy
Author: Micha Frazer-Carroll
Headline: The bizarrely salient French crime smash is higher stakes than ever – and its Houdini-style thrills are complemented with some interesting questions around race and infamy
Content: Smooth operator … Omar Sy as Assane Diop in Lupin.Photograph: Selly Sy/NetflixView image in fullscreenSmooth operator … Omar Sy as Assane Diop in Lupin.Photograph: Selly Sy/NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewLupin review – the French super-thief is magnetic in his blockbuster returnHoudini-style thrills, Marvel-style set pieces and relentless twists? The stakes are higher than ever in the hit crime series – but beneath the action, it asks some big questionsMicha Frazer-CarrollFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSomething strange has happened with Lupin. Two years after the French jewel heist thriller’s third season aired, its series one plotline played out in real life, in the form of a global news story turned viral sensation. The Louvre heist of 2025 happened by day – while Lupin’s main character Assane Diop (Omar Sy) stole jewels from the Louvre at night. The real-life robbers posed as construction workers – Diop posed as a caretaker. You couldn’t help but draw comparisons.So it returns for the fourth series with a salience the makers could never have predicted – amid a renewed appreciation of the power of a cleverly crafted disguise to dupe even the world’s most revered cultural institutions.Things are higher-budget, higher stakes and more cinematic from the title card onwards. The show’s central question seems to be: what happens when a mastermind finds themselves a victim of their own intelligence? We meet master criminal Diop, four years after he surrenders to the police at the close of the third season, in a maximum security prison. Diop is a week away from release, hoping to fulfil his fatherly promise to put the life of crime behind him and join his family in Senegal, when technology across Paris is hacked, and warnings of imminent heists signed with the name “Lupin” appear. Things are not looking good for Diop, who has modelled his life on fictional master criminal Arsène Lupin. He is swiftly straitjacketed and locked in a panopticon-style glass cell, allowing surveillance and mockery by prison guards and prisoners alike. We are only 12 minutes in to episode one. I repeat, things are not looking good.View image in fullscreenA bit of a bind … Lupin.Photograph: Emmanuel Guimier/NetflixDiop’s Blackness has often served as his strength – the racial stereotypes still rife in supposedly“colourblind” Franceallow him to camouflage as a janitor or delivery person for his crimes. But when he becomes a suspect, his racialisation is his downfall; blurry security footage shows that a robber was a Black man, which is taken as unequivocal evidence that Diop is guilty.So Diop is hoisted by the petard of his own notoriety: despite being imprisoned in a high-security facility, the police still believe he was somehow involved in the jewel theft. He must have found a way to become invisible, to break out. He is implicated in a crime that doesn’t seem to bear his fingerprints, before it even happens.Lupin eschews exposition and offers up Houdini-style thrills right from the start. I find myself wanting to believe that Diop is not responsible for the robberies, but it is hard to know what to trust in this show. The twists have been relentless: last season concluded with Diop’s nemesis, Hubert Pellegrini, revealing himself as the secret mastermind behind much of the series’ conflict.How France’s Lupin became the surprise Netflix hit of the seasonRead moreLupin asks complicated questions about what it means to attempt to leave things behind when you have achieved a certain level of infamy. Other thieves (in the show and in real life) become copycats. To those investigating, it becomes unthinkable that anyone else could have pulled this off. Yet Diop is no longer the puppet master – now, he is at the mercy of others. “I want to be done with Lupin once and for all,” he remembers telling his son. But there is an irony here: Diop embarked on his life of crime to avenge the death of his father, who was falsely accused of a jewel theft.
