Now, Diop finds himself falsely accused, while the potential impact on his son hangs in the balance.This is all compelling enough to justify another series of the Netflix hit, which has been subject to delays that some fans have bemoaned as making it as drawn-out as the end of Stranger Things. Much like that show, Lupin has been scaled up from a five-episode series to eight. Sy, whose performance is magnetic as always, has graduated to co-showrunner and wants to lean harder into the show’s “superhero”-like qualities. These include tech and set pieces which undoubtedly add a sprinkling of Marvel.Certain moments do feel over-dramatised – and it relies on that cliche of the old pro getting roped back in for one last hurrah. But will Lupin manage to shapeshift from a French drama punching above its weight on the global market to a big-budget thrill-ride? Watching on Netflix’s default US English setting (which is sacrilege, anyway) would certainly tip this Hollywood feel over the edge. Make sure you switch to French.Lupin is on Netflix now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the gloriously boisterous grime-metal of Native James and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Filtering alt influences and eskibeats through a distinctly Black British point of view, the Ipswich rapper’s scorched-earth rage sounds like a lot of fun
Author: Olive Pometsey
Headline: Filtering alt influences and eskibeats through a distinctly Black British point of view, the Ipswich rapper’s scorched-earth rage sounds like a lot of fun
Content: Quick-witted … Native James.Photograph: Sophie WebsterView image in fullscreenQuick-witted … Native James.Photograph: Sophie WebsterAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the gloriously boisterous grime-metal of Native James and the week’s best new tracksFiltering alt influences and eskibeats through a distinctly Black British point of view, the Ipswich rapper’s scorched-earth rage sounds like a lot of funOlive PometseyFri 23 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromIpswich, UKRecommended if you likeLinkin Park, Kano, Bob VylanUp nextNew single Dumb Bruddah released via SharpTone Records on 30 October“Laaa!” growls Native James on his 2025 track Fallen, stretching a wicked fried scream over more traditionally poppy “la-la-la” chants like a hair-raising metal frontman. Because, well, that’s what he is. But James is also a pretty deft rapper, the kind of artist who grew up listening to Evanescence during school lunchtimes then went home and studied first-wave grime on Channel U. The preceding verse on Fallen rattles through quick-witted bars over bouncy nu-metal riffs, blending Jamaican Patois with The Lion King references for a scorched-earth unmasking of his “demon within”. He’s raging in every sense of the word – and it sounds like a hell of a lot of fun.Last year’s EP Confessions of a Sinner is full of similarly – gloriously – boisterous grime-metal crossovers. A student of fellow rap-rockers Linkin Park, James (real name Aaron James) filters his alt influences through a distinctly Black British point of view, from his rapid-fire, staccato delivery to his sly sense of humour. His latest single, July’s Never Been Scared, fine-tunes that blueprint, introducing metallic, eskibeat-style synths before its final drop crashes down like a roaring clap of thunder. A guest verse from Boy Better Know’s Frisco earns him bonus grime kudos, not that he really needs it. James had already brought out Double S and Professor Green during his 2025 Glastonbury set to perform their collaboration Block (RR), then he reunited the trio at Download festival this summer. Last month, he won One to Watch at the Independent Music Awards, following in the footsteps of Arlo Parks and Nia Archives. No wonder he’s never been scared. At 140bpm, he’s barely got time.Olive PometseyThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenGorgeous chamber drone … Wendy Eisenberg.Photograph: Eleanor PetryWendy Eisenberg–Mmeeaanniinngg BbuussiinneessssKeen to test the transcendence and infinite potential of their songs, Eisenberg stretches a highlight from this year’s self-titled record into gorgeous 37-minute chamber drone with a lot to offer lovers of Dirty Three.LSBassvictim – White FlagTeeing up the duo’s second album of compacted electrotrash this year, this is an almighty bassline house wobbler reeking of stale cigarettes and spilled energy drinks, featuring some appealingly out-of-tune vox.BBTMatilda Tjäder – The Phone CallThe Swedish artist’s project Shelf Life began as a short story, then became an opera. Now it’s an album of zonked experimental pop about a woman who collects items with the same expiration date. This shimmering ballad sits at its heart.BBTThreshold – StillwaterAngling for more of Alex G’s hangdog beauty? Find it in the tumbling, glistening piano and weary barroom anthemics of Isaac Eiger, who has also co-written for Adéla, Frost Children and Chanel Beads.LSGyrofield – BurlsA hero in drum’n’bass circles since her teens, Hong Kong native Kiana Li goes down some less-travelled wormholes in the dub bass continuum with new album Great Jobs, ending up at muscular techno-skank on Burls.BBTBjarki – Isn’t It Nice(to Be Somebody)For all that the Icelandic producer’s comeback is ultra-regimented, running on bass that flickers like a mechanised hummingbird wing, it’s also somehow alluringly frisky, suggestive of transcendent pleasures.LSGiGi FM – AscendaIt’s difficult to do minimal techno with as much drama and genuine propulsion as GiGi FM does here, inspired by the Greek goddess Astraea, who left corrupted humanity to go and live in the stars.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistRapMetalGrimePop and rockHip-hopBlack British culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Loidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail | Electronic music | The Guardian
description: Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound design
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound design
Content: Shimmering sounds … Loidis, AKA Brian Leeds.Photograph: Kei MurataView image in fullscreenShimmering sounds … Loidis, AKA Brian Leeds.Photograph: Kei MurataElectronic musicReviewLoidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers review – epic 111-minute album is a teeming universe of detail(Incienso)Brian Leeds, AKA Huerco S, keeps raising the temperature on his once-chilly ambient on an ambitious record full of delightful detail and ASMR-inducing sound designBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 23 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sun barely seemed to rise in the earlier work of US electronic producer Brian Leeds. As Huerco S he put out the audio equivalent of 5pm November gloaming: lo-fi, low-lumen ambient and house music, flickering as if through a thicket of pine. But the light sharpened on his 2022 album Plonk, and for his project Loidis – on 2024 album One Day and this year’s stunning remix of James K’s Peel – the temperature seemed to rise along with the tempos. It wasn’t quite Balearic summer, but certainly Baltic spring or Adriatic autumn.View image in fullscreenLoidis: From the Toolkit of Lovers album cover.Photograph: Kei MurataHis new album is his grandest statement across either project: 111 minutes of music across six sides of vinyl, a scale he goes a long way towards justifying. In tracks reminiscent of the microhouse sound of early 00s acts such as Luomo, the synth chords have Leeds’ trademark degraded shimmer, paired with ticklish snares and delightful ASMR-inducing sound design, stereo effects panning from right to left with quicksilver physicality. It’s hugely pleasurable to let your mind zoom in and out of these arrangements, marvelling at the microscopic detail then appreciating the overarching sense of groove, further enhanced by big melodic motifs: the playful echoing notes in TT Stunt, or the Afrobeat bassline of Running Rich. A couple of tracks in the second half lack the adventure elsewhere, but at least 90 of the minutes here are riveting, psychedelic even on nothing stronger than a cup of tea.Explore more on these topicsElectronic musicDance musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season | Music | The Guardian
description: Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
Author: Safi Bugel
Headline: Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
Content: Swampy sounds … Basma (centre) and Temir Alcy.Photograph: ChloesassiView image in fullscreenSwampy sounds … Basma (centre) and Temir Alcy.Photograph: ChloesassiExperimental album of the monthMusicReviewBasma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season(Stroom)Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tensionSafi BugelFri 23 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe new album from French-Moroccan vocalist Basma and Paris-based group Temir Alcy comes just in time for the changing of the clocks. It’s a dark and disorientating listen, exploring themes of loss and new beginnings over swampy, downtempo rhythms. The 11 tracks here linger somewhere between folk, shoegaze and ambient, with skulking percussion, droning passages and plucked strings soaked in reverb. Opening track Belati sets the tone with its spacious, shapeshifting composition, where ghostly drones and Basma’s layered calls give way to a sluggish beat. Most of the tracks follow a similar non-structure: amorphous but with an intermittent, sultry groove, like the winding bass on Khti Sarah, or the slow, swinging rhythm on Aji M3aya.View image in fullscreenBasma and Temir Alcy: NAD album cover.Basma’s performance is always captivating. Singing in a mixture of Darija (vernacular Arabic) and French, she delivers poetic snapshotsin sensory terms that chime with the shifting seasons: “shy light”, blowing wind and bonfires. On Rised, breathy fragments are looped and reversed into a dreamy haze, while her lilting chants on La Tourne have a hypnotic effect. On standout Al Atlal, which lumbers along like a haunted lullaby, she drifts between soft wails and stoic spoken word.Accentuating the murky atmosphere are the textural elements which lurk between Basma’s vocals and the sub-bass, often so subtle they are barely perceptible. On Belati, traces of oscillating electronics emerge; Khti Sarah features muted flecks of oud. Disembodied field recordings shimmer and glitch like static on Aji M3aya. Cha3ouka is immediately thrown off-kilter by the percussive krakeb, offering dissonant clatter over dubbed-out whorls. On Ana Jaya, where the experimentalism peaks, the line between instruments and vocals blurs as the sound dissipates. The effect is bodily: tension you can feel, but can’t quite pin down. It’s a brilliant, heady formula.Also out this monthDalga(Zel Zele) is an exciting compilation of wonky pop productions made in 1980s Turkey, most of which have never been reissued before. Across these nine tracks, traditional Anatolian psych and pop sensibilities combine with robotic samples, hi-NRG drum programming and delirious, glitching synths.Hysterical Love Projectare part of an ever-expanding pool of artists making atmospheric, trip-hop-inflected pop. The Melbourne duo’s second LP, February’s Album (Motion Ward), is a gorgeous meditation on love and longing, channelled through mumbling vocals and warm, reverb-heavy instrumentals. The quietly pulsing Thinking Woman’s Lament is a highlight. The second album from experimental dubwise groupHoly Tongueis an invigorating listen, propelled by Valentina Magaletti’s ritualistic drums and scattered with haunting samples and effects(AD 93). Ecstatic, echoing guest vocals from Dali de Saint Paul add to the whirlwind on two of the tracks, but it’s the rolling instrumentals that stand out most.Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental album of the monthExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I wrote my first novel at 12 – it has not yet found a publisher’ | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May Alcott
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May Alcott
Content: ‘The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides is extraordinary’ … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Christopher L Proctor/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides is extraordinary’ … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Christopher L Proctor/The GuardianThe books of my lifeFictionLessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I wrote my first novel at 12 – it has not yet found a publisher’The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May AlcottBonnie GarmusFri 23 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryI have a very clear memory of reading Fun With Dick and Jane. I was four years old, and my dad wrote each word on a chalkboard. I memorised them, then opened the book and read them back to him. I couldn’t believe it. It felt like magic! When I was older, I stumbled across the book and was surprised to find Dick and Jane didn’t really have all that much fun.My favourite book growing upHarriet the Spy by Louise Fitzhugh. Eleven-year-old Harriet Welch wants to be a writer, and her nanny encourages her to keepa notebook so she can practise writing every day. But when the other kids at school find her book (which is filled with her meanest, most vulnerable thoughts), she quickly becomes the school pariah. I must have read this story a hundred times. Harriet Welch was the reason I started writing stuff down. She was also the reason I understood that no matter how hard it feels, it is imperative to own and apologise for your mistakes.The book that changed me as a teenagerTo Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. Scout’s voice grabbed me from the start. It was a deep dive into racism, poverty, hatred and social justice, and it had a direct impact on how I saw the world.The writer who changed my mindHenry David Thoreau. “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately,” he wrote in Walden, “to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.” I was 18, loved the outdoors, craved adventure, and desperately wanted to see what I was made of. But it’s hard to get work from a mountaintop, so I settled for living deliberately in my tiny, overpriced, noisy, too-hot apartment. Survival comes in many forms.The book that made me want to be a writerFun With Dick and Jane! Seriously. I was in love with reading from the very beginning, and writing a story seemed like the obvious next step. At age five I wrote my first book. It was a page long and included an illustration. It has not yet been picked up by a publisher. I also wrote an entire novel by 12. For some reason, that, too, remains unsigned. All offers considered.The book I came back toLittle Women by Louisa May Alcott. I was supposed to love it (I was nine; I fitted the demographic), but it didn’t speak to me. Fast forward 15 years. I was trekking in Nepal’s Annapurna range and found it on a hikers’ bookshelf. I reread it in my tent by candlelight. I couldn’t believe how great it was. Jo is amazing!The book I rereadThe Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides. The writing is extraordinary, and the point of view is one of a kind. There isn’t a wasted word in the entire book. I also love to read essays and often return to The White Album by Joan Didion to study the way she crafts sentences. She has an amazing ability to capture the energy of an age, a movement, a fad, just as it begins to slide.The book I could never read againThe Gormenghast Trilogy by Mervyn Peake. I loved this when I was a teenager and maybe I would love it again, but I don’t want to run the risk of spoiling my good memories.The book I discovered later in lifeSo Long, See You Tomorrow by William Maxwell. It’s told from the point of view of a man in his 60s looking back on a childhood upended by murder and the loss of his mother. It’s a brilliant study of how impossible it is to make sense of our memories, because they have a bad habit of rewriting themselves.The book I am currently readingMay We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy comfort readGrimms’ Fairy Tales.Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus is published by Manilla. title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more
Content: Dogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle.Photograph: John DevolleView image in fullscreenDogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle.Photograph: John DevolleChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersReviewChildren’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novelsA sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 23 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDogs, Dogs, Dogsby John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99“Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes.More!by Ged Adamson, Moon and Bird, £12.99Best friends Squirrel and Mouse are on a blissful walk together, but Squirrel keeps wanting more – a hat, a tie, a boingy stick! – until he realises it’s all pointless without Mouse to share it. A slyly hilarious anti-consumerist picture book that encourages small readers to pore over its delightful background details.The Tale That Time Sewsby Sita Brahmachari, illustrated byJane Ray, Templar, £12.99A little girl waits for her new sibling to be born while Nana stitches together family stories in a quilt that will wrap them both in this 5+ picture book; a lyrical, beautiful account of displacement, migration and learning to flourish in new places while remembering your roots.Little Minotaurby Gaia Alessi, Walker, £14.99In ancient Crete, a boy with a bull head is cherished by his sister Ariadne and mother Pasiphaë. Though he struggles to form words, he rejoices in the natural world. But when fearful rumours rise up, he must find his place – and a better ending to his story – in this dreamy, beguiling picturebook Minotaur retelling for 5+.Pomona: Stories of the Cat Witchby Tor Freeman, Guppy, £14.99Pomona the cat witch lives in the forest, surrounded by pals including Ratso, Elfis and Prince Frog. It’s here that she discovers empathy while dusting her house, finds a friend for a lonely caterpillar and helps Ratso break an annoying curse. These daft, whimsical, highly illustrated stories are perfect for 5+ readers with a taste for thoughtful silliness.View image in fullscreenA Year of Fairy Talesby Sophie Anderson, illustrated by Elisa Paganelli, Usborne, £25This sumptuous hardback collection – one story for every month – features retellings of classic fairytales like Jack and the Beanstalk as well as original tales rooted in world folklore. Anderson’s lively, adventurous writing marries with Paganelli’s swirling, soaring artwork to create a treasure trove for 7+ readers to share at bedtime or explore solo.Lumi and the Wolfby Lottie Saahko, Hachette, £14.99Sent to stay with relatives in Lapland, autistic Lumi struggles to adapt, and her family warns her that a dangerous white wolf is lurking. When she befriends the wolf, Lumi and local boy Oskár set out on a perilous journey to the national park where Wolf can be safe – though she will have to use all her sharp senses and stored knowledge to get him there. Atmospheric and fast-paced, with intricately drawn illustrations, this tense, heartfelt 9+ animal adventure deals both with the impact of climate change on traditional Sami ways of life, and the deep human need to find where you belong.View image in fullscreenThe Rambler’s Curseby Mikey Please, HarperCollins, £14.99Things are going well for the magical Café at the Edge of the Woods until a terrifying customer arrives: a human. His appearance sets off a chaotic chain reaction, involving a temperamental wizard’s staff, a red motorbike, a stolen gold hoard and a blanket of carnivorous moss. Can chef Rene and waiter Glumfoot defend the Woods from catastrophe in this laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook? Developing the world and characters of Please’s Waterstones prize-winning picture book, this is the first in a trilogy for 8+.Girl With a Sabretooth Tigerby Jasbinder Bilan, Chicken House, £7.99In prehistoric England, 11-year-old Swallow, afraid her baby sister will die, undertakes a dangerous quest: to fetch a piece of green jadeite from the heart of a mountain god. Ishi, a village boy, insists on coming too – but it’s the spirit of the great tiger whose tooth she wears that will guide and protect her in this poetic, powerful, pared-back 9+ story of love, determination, courage and shared resource.View image in fullscreenAnger Is Only a Shadowby Elizabeth Acevedo, Hot Key, £8.99Lil is on probation. She needs to be New Lil – staying head down and out of trouble until her next court hearing – but Old Lil, barely contained, is desperate to make bad, impulsive decisions. Then her brother Aldwin, hundreds of miles away at college, starts talking about hearing voices, and Lil realises she’s the only one who can help. But can she get to him without sacrificing her freedom? A poignant, complex, thought-provoking YA novel by a Carnegie-winning author.Nightcurseby Emma Hinds, Usborne, £9.99Revenant Emrys Swift has been 17 for 157 years, living a cloistered life in a secret magical library and trying to remember his own death. When three important books go missing, he must collaborate with his nemesis, charismatic shapeshifter Aubrey Vale, to figure out where and why, but as spectral warnings rise around them, and the secrets of Emrys’s death and Aubrey’s life are laid bare, could their antipathy be changing to attraction? A gorgeously readable queer enemies-to-lovers romantasy, set in a richly realised magical world.Flarestormby Moira Buffini, Faber, £9.99In a world where telepaths called Torches are either oppressed or exalted, an uprising is under way, seeking equality for all. The rebels are marching on the Capital, but Torches Elsa and Kaira are struggling to break out of their underground prison, while Rye, in captivity, is being forced to track powerful Torch Petra as she flies into the unknown. And where will conniving Zara Swan decide her ultimate loyalty lies? Messy, explosive, bloody and brutal, the concluding volume of the bestselling YA Torch Trilogy resolves multiple storylines and perspectives in a blaze of pain, fear, loss and glory.Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersChildren's book roundupChildren's books: 8-12 yearsChildren's books: 7 and underFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Under Fire by Humza Yousaf – a deeply affecting story of being stranded in Gaza | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so lucky
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so lucky
Content: Humza Yousaf with his wife, Nadia, and daughter in 2023.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHumza Yousaf with his wife, Nadia, and daughter in 2023.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewUnder Fire by Humza Yousaf – a deeply affecting story of being stranded in GazaThe former Scottish first minister writes of his in-laws’ plight and the tragedy of those who weren’t so luckyFiona SturgesFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAweek into Israel’s bombing of Gaza in 2023, which followed Hamas’s deadly terrorist attack on Israel, Scotland’s then first ministerHumza Yousafreceived a text from his mother-in-law, Elizabeth. “Humza, I think we are about to die. I need you to promise me that you will take care of my girls.”Elizabeth, a retired nurse from Dundee, and her Palestinian husband, Maged, had been visiting family inGazaand become trapped there when the bombing began. Not only were people dying all around them, but their house was filling up with friends and neighbours whose homes had been destroyed, and they were running out of food. On the night Elizabeth texted, they had been told to leave their neighbourhood of Deir al-Balah ahead of a fresh wave of Israeli strikes. They later learned the evacuation order was a false alarm. Even so, Yousaf reflects, “in the four weeks from hell, this felt like the lowest point”.Under Fire is a short yet deeply affecting book detailing Yousaf and his wife Nadia El-Nakla’s month-long nightmare as Elizabeth and Maged remained stranded in Gaza, during which they made repeated attempts to flee. The Israeli government had said it would let foreign nationals leave, though for Yousaf’s in-laws this appeared to be an empty pledge. More than once they made the perilous journey to Rafah, on the border with Egypt, only to be turned away when they got there. Meanwhile, Nadia’s brother was working in a Gaza hospital and sending desperate updates about civilian casualties, the lack of clean water and medical supplies and how he was performing surgeries without anaesthetic, often lit by the light from a mobile phone.double quotation markHe doesn't mince his words about Rishi Sunak, who failed to provide updates for worried British citizens with family in GazaYousaf and his family’s agonising plight unfolds as he goes about his duties as the newly elected first minister. The text from Elizabeth arrived during the SNP conference, on the eve of his first speech. As a result, much of the narrative concerns his efforts to meet his responsibilities in Scotland while trying to comfort and support his wife and children. All the while, he and his aides plead with the Foreign Office in London to help get Elizabeth and Maged out.Yousaf is a natural communicator and, though his writing sometimes lacks flair, he effectively conveys the stress and torment that comes with attending meetings and delivering speeches while wrestling with what to make public and what to keep private regarding his family. In the end he decides to share what is happening to his in-laws to raise awareness about the horrors being visited on Gaza’s civilian population. The title Under Fire has a dual meaning, describing the terrifying ordeal of Palestinians in Gaza and the scrutiny and criticism that comes not just with being Scotland’s first minister but the first Muslim leader of a country that is 95% non-Muslim and overwhelmingly white.There is another narrative here concerning Yousaf’s struggles to make his way politically and step out of the shadow of his mentor and predecessor Nicola Sturgeon, which sits awkwardly in a book that is primarily about a family in crisis. Similarly, his diatribe about Kate Forbes, his rival for the top job, and her “clumsy” leadership campaign would suit a straightforward political memoir, but here feels out of place.More pertinent are Yousaf’s criticisms of the then British foreign secretary James Cleverly for initially failing to pick up the phone to him, even after he had spoken publicly about his parents-in-law being stranded. Neither does he mince his words about Rishi Sunak, whom he chastises for failing to provide updates for worried British citizens with family in Gaza.Under Fire is most powerful when Yousaf – who resigned as first minister after 13 months – gives full vent to his anger at the unfolding genocide in Gaza and articulates not just the plight of his in-laws, who eventually crossed the border into Egypt in November 2023, but the trauma of those left behind and the barbarity of Israel’s actions. “The scale of what those still in Gaza have had to endure is impossible for us to truly comprehend,” he writes. “At times, I can’t understand how there is anyone left alive.” Yet he insists he is hopeful that “what is broken can be mended … That flame of hope must be for each of us to carry; it is one we cannot allow to be extinguished.”Under Fire: My Family’s Escape from Gaza and the Cost of Leadership by Humza Yousaf (£25) is published by The Bridge Street Press. title: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft  | Games | The Guardian
description: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Content: Strong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareView image in fullscreenStrong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareGamesEA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereftLucy JamesThe closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi seriesFri 23 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTShareEarlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today.It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to aleaked trailer, was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release.The three games that comprise original space-faring Mass Effect trilogy count as my favourites of all time. I first played in 2010, shortly after buying my Xbox 360 and being reassured by my friends that the game was a worthy investment, and have replayed them countless times since. Depending on the day, the top spot fluctuates; more often than not it’s the character-driven sequel Mass Effect 2, which ends with one of the most iconic missions in gaming, that takes the top spot.Released over a five-year period from 2007-12, the trilogy follows the adventures of Commander Shepard: a lawless Spectre special agent who is empowered by the galactic Citadel Council to use any means necessary to protect its interests and get the job done. Shepard’s appointment as the first human Spectre in a galaxy where humans are the new kids on the block aligns with the arrival of the Reapers, an ancient synthetic race that raze all organic life every 50,000 years. Shepard must convince the galaxy that the threat is real and gather its top soldiers, scientists and scoundrels to defeat it.View image in fullscreenComing together to save the galaxy ... Mass Effect 2Photograph: EA/BioWareWhen I played Mass Effect for the first time, I didn’t get it. Its controls felt janky and awkward, and I was thrown headlong into a galaxy full of history and politics that I didn’t understand: the game didn’t spell things out, throwing out names and jargon and expecting me to follow. After one exceedingly frustrating encounter with the Mako, the game’s infamously awkward land buggy, I quit entirely. Some months later, something drew me back: the feeling of a job left half done. The galaxy was in peril, and I had to save it.The second time I tried, something clicked. I focused less on the gameplay quirks and went all-in on its story and characters: the naive archaeologist, Dr Liara T’Soni; the browbeaten Citadel security guard Garrus Vakarian; and Kaidan Alenko, a human enhanced by the military, and suffering because of it. Mass Effect’s story was simple – save the galaxy from a tormenting synthetic race with guns and space powers – but you got to determine how it played out. Players were given the opportunity to make meaningful choices that hugely affected how the story unfolded, and that stuck with me (and millions of others).Throughout the course of the game, you can shape not only Shepard’s gender and what they look like, but how they react to situations. Would they be friendly, and use some inter-species cooperation to defeat the Reapers? Or take the renegade route, tersely shutting down dissenters, sometimes resulting in hilariously out-of-pocket responses? (My apologies to the intrepid space reporter Khalistah al-Jilani.) Regardless of how you played, it was thrilling to have such agency over how Shepard moved and was perceived in the world. But the real fun was in making decisions that altered the story not only in Mass Effect, but its sequels.I agonised over every choice, large or small. Across three games and the far flung reaches of the galaxy, my influence was felt. Races lived and died at my whim, and the consequences of my actions showed up in the most unexpected ways. It made my playthrough feel truly mine, guided by the stern hand of its development team, but shaped by me, and me alone. Shepard’s plight was mine, and I would save the galaxy. I hadn’t played anything like it at the time, and even now, I struggle to think of moments that compare. Its missions and story beats are so ingrained in my mind that you’d think I actually lived them. Such is the wonder of a video game, the freedom to explore and affect the world you’re playing in.View image in fullscreenMass Effect’s unlikely fan favourite, Garrus.Photograph: EA/BioWareMass Effect’s story wouldn’t have hit as hard if it weren’t for its characters: a motley crew of the galaxy’s toughest and cleverest, drawn to your cause for their own, complex reasons. It questioned whether AI had a soul, the sins of the father, and the heaviness of duty. BioWare wrote missions personalised to your squadmates’ causes, asking you to make agonising decisions that could benefit or harm them, and then forcing you to deal with the results. The writers went one further, allowing you to date some of these characters, slowly building from nervous flirting to ratings-friendly romance scenes. Saying goodbye to your squad, who’d been with you through hell, before the third game’s devastating final act brought me to tears over a decade ago. It still does.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s been over a decade since Shepard’s story concluded, and the trilogy is still lauded as among the greatest ever made. I play dozens of games a year, and few have stuck with me as Mass Effect has. Its influence is impossible to shake. It set the standard for action-RPGs for years to come, and despite a furore at its original ending (since changeddue to public outcry), is still beloved and widely referenced in gaming culture.BioWare’s ending feels so final, so abrupt. Despite missteps and mismanagement in recent years, most publicly in the form offailed sci-fi shooter Anthem, getting a glimpse at what the new Mass Effect might have been has left fans bereft. The foundation of the universe was so strong, and in the right hands it could have been another genre-defining story. The loss of BioWare is an enormous one for gaming, a bastion of western role playing games brought down. Its influence will continue to be felt throughout the gaming galaxy.Lucy James is founder and curator oflookingfor.gameand co-host of the Friends Per Second gaming podcast.Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamescommentShareReuse this content

title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game | Games | The Guardian
description: From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
Content: Gung-ho Hollywood fantasy … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 screenshot.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenGung-ho Hollywood fantasy … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 screenshot.Photograph: ActivisionGamesReviewCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a gameActivision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxFrom parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the gameKeith StuartFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was asales disappointmentfor Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure.As you may haveread, this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.View image in fullscreenStories ‘ripped from the newspaper headlines’ … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionNevertheless, it’s a bombastic, thrilling airport novel of a game, crammed with classic CoD set pieces, including but not limited to parkour over Manhattan rooftops, a car chase in Paris and a shootout in a train yard that somehow feels like a cross between Frogger and Time Crisis. A climactic battle at a North Korean airbase throws absolutely everything at you from sniper firefights to helicopter gunship attacks.There are also moments where you’re forced into stark unethical actions, faintly recalling the notorious “No Russian” mission from 2009’s Modern Warfare 2. Elsewhere, a whole open-world section lets you explore a snowy landscape, carrying out story missions and side quests to improve your armoury. It’s a nice break from corridor shooting, and somehow it doesn’t stall the game’s momentum. Throughout the six-hour campaign, bullets fly and buildings collapse, friends become enemies, enemies become friends, and a breathless story of geopolitical skullduggery emerges. It’s a shame, though, that the Capt Price arc gets a little overlooked toward the end and his denouement lacks the intended emotional clout, but it’s fun and at least a little bit emotional while it lasts.View image in fullscreenBullets fly and buildings collapse … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionThe multiplayer mode is a refinement of the turbo-paced, ultra-lethal experience of Black Ops 7. Players are still extremely agile, able to vault over obstacles and skid around corners, blasting their guns like John Wick on a recently polished vinyl floor. But movement is a touch more naturalistic here, and weapons have a heft to them that makes you feel deadly, even if you’re getting shot in the face every five seconds.Alongside all the classic modes there are decent newcomers, such as the epic, up-to-64-player, Combat Outpost, and Collateral, a round-based shootout where you buy new weapons and items at the start of each bout (the better you do, the more cash you get to spend on goodies). The highlight though is Kill Block, which takes place in a modular training centre where three landscape types are randomly selected from dozens of possibilities, then slotted in to a play space at the start of the round so you’re never sure how everything will fit together. You might have to move from a train yard to a storage depot to a trench network, and weapons are randomised too, so you could all be fighting with pistols or sniper rifles, adding to the unpredictable challenge.The last part of the package is a reconstructed take on Call of Duty’s extraction shooter mode, DMZ. Taking place in and around Hajin City, abandoned during the events of the campaign, you parachute in with up to two teammates, then carry out various PvE missions to earn cash and gear, before calling in for air rescue – all while avoiding or attacking other players on the same map. New to this version is the Forward Operating Base, a safe house you return to after each expedition where you can upgrade your weapons, 3D print new gear and get info on the current roster of boss characters. There’s also a three-branch skill tree for your character, which you populate by earning in-game XP. This gives you a range of new abilities and improvements including taking more loot from downed enemies, faster revives and reducing damage from explosives.DMZ, then, is a huge mode with lots to do, set in a dynamic world with a real-time weather system. So far, we’ve only been able to play an early access version, but exploring the world and gambling on just one final side quest before extraction promises to offer the sort of tension and excitement this genre thrives on. However, its success will depend on how many players Activision can attract and retain, and to survive it’ll surely have to tempt people over from established rivals such as Arc Raiders and Escape from Tarkov. That could be the toughest mission of all.Infinity Ward and its co-developers have thrown everything they have at this game, and it shows. The campaign is short but polished, the multiplayer still grabs you by the neck and DMZ is richly detailed and exhaustive. It’s all rendered in incredible audiovisual detail, delivering the spectacle we expect from the series. I’m not sure it’ll bring in a vast new audience, especially with GTA 6 on the way – Call of Duty remains a gung-ho Hollywood fantasy of armed conflict that glorifies the military-industrial complex. But if it’s a glossy, bombastic thrill ride you’re after, there is plenty here to keep you locked and loaded for months to come.Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is out nowExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyPlayStationPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XPCNintendo Switch 2reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Snowman gets a hi-tech rebuild – with help from Raging Bull and a ‘Hot Santa’ | Christmas shows | The Guardian
description: More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint Nick
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint Nick
Content: In from the cold … Andrew Ashton (The Snowman) and Tate Masuku (The Boy) at Birmingham Rep, with production design by Anna Fleischle.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenIn from the cold … Andrew Ashton (The Snowman) and Tate Masuku (The Boy) at Birmingham Rep, with production design by Anna Fleischle.Photograph: Johan PerssonChristmas showsThe Snowman gets a hi-tech rebuild – with help from Raging Bull and a ‘Hot Santa’More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint NickLyndsey WinshipFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Top of the show!” says Will Tuckett. On the grand piano, musical director Andy Massey strikes up an arpeggio that could melt the most frozen of hearts: “We’re walking in the air …” It is The Snowman, of course. Raymond Briggs’ 1978 picture book was animated for the screen in 1982 with a score by Howard Blake and became a hit stage show in 1993, an annual outing for Birmingham Rep ever since. Now it’s getting a reboot, directed by Tuckett, former Royal Ballet dancer turned choreographer and director of everything from the National Ballet of Japan’s Nutcracker to a stage adaptation of In the Night Garden.We’re in a studio in Birmingham. As the overture plays, a large wooden box in the centre of the room opens like the cover of a book, to become a house. There’s a kitchen, a couple at the table with a pot of tea and an endearing puppet cat winding round their legs. Upstairs, a boy wakes up, looking forward toChristmas.View image in fullscreenTaking flight … The Snowman at Birmingham Rep.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe Snowman is a perennially popular show but “it needed a bit of a refresh,” says Tuckett. “Theatre’s changed a lot in 30 years – expectations have changed.” Audiences are so used to the latest effects that the scenes where the Snowman takes the boy flying, for example, were starting to lack the wow factor. The old show used a one-point harness to lift the actors, and if you drifted in the wrong direction “you had to swim back,” says Tuckett, miming the breaststroke in mid-air. Now they have a fancy automated system that lets them dance through the air against a backdrop by video designer Nina Dunn. “I was blown away,” says Tuckett. “She made all the snow feel 3D, the landscape 3D.” The effect will be much more filmic and immersive.Puppetry is also much more sophisticated and ubiquitous than it was in 1993, from the trailblazing War Horse to the Paddington musical whose designer Tahra Zafar has created a Snowman costume, which can blink and smile as well as dance. Daisy Beattie has designed a menagerie of puppets, which the dancers manipulate: the curious cat, two pheasants on wheels, a lone fox and some sweet rabbits. Other things you can’t change too much. “The score is the score,” says Tuckett, although there are always tweaks. The original used lots of synth-y samples on keyboards, but the quality of sound you can generate electronically now is completely different.View image in fullscreenPerennially popular … The Snowman at Peacock theatre, London, in 2013.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMost important, though, is the story. “And it’s a story told through dance, it’s not a ballet with a story,” Tuckett clarifies. We might think of The Snowman as a bit saccharine, but “it’s a book about loneliness, and ultimately, it’s a book about loss”. He’s rejigged scenes to show that there’s lots of love, too. The simplicity of this story is the antidote to the fast-cut craziness of modern kids’ entertainment where “there’s a glitter shower – and then all the pyros go off,” he says. “This is very simple, very honest. It’s really about human relationships and family, but none of it is too heavy.” His job is “to slow things down, but keep things moving”.Tuckett and the team had multiple visits to pore over Briggs’ original artworks. “It’s really emotional seeing it, because I was given the book as a kid at Christmas,” says Tuckett. “Going back and seeing his original marks and little notes on it, and the original cover – he used Tippex for some of the snow – it was just amazing.”Tuckett opens his laptop and brings up an illustration of the boy and the Snowman flying. “It’s really hard to look at it and not well up and remember when you were small and when your kids were small.” He zooms in on the details. “I don’t want [the show] to look like a panto – it should feel like the drawings.” He and Zafar had been discussing how the simplest things are often the hardest. “Have you seen Raging Bull?” he asks, a reference I was not expecting. He describes how in Martin Scorsese’s film, all the boxing rings were different sizes and shapes, to give different visual effects, even though it’s ostensibly the same setting. The video projections will do some similar changing of perspective, but there are painted sets too. In the workshop, I find a giant snowy tree taking up the whole room.View image in fullscreenLoss and loneliness … The Snowman, 1982.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThe book is only around 30 pages long, the film was 26 minutes, and the stage show will be around an hour, so Tuckett’s job is to expand on the material, yet stay true to it, while making it all a bit less gendered. “Like, could the dad not just sit in his chair smoking a pipe and falling asleep while his wife does the washing up and the ironing?” says Tuckett. The biggest change will be more proper dancing. There are some new characters “who are really zoomy” and a Father Christmas who is “a beautiful classical dancer,” says Tuckett. “His jacket is a bit like one of those huge North Face ones, and when he takes it off, he looks like Hot Santa,” Tuckett laughs. “And it means then he can properly dance.”In the previous show, they cast actors in the role of the young boy, but Tuckett has brought in dancers. Four of them, aged 11-14, will rotate the role. “We tried the flying the other day and it was really fun,” says one dancer, Tristan, while Tate, another, adds: “We get all those features from the film and the book and make them come to life.” Jake says: “It’s really cool being part of a new production and seeing how it’s made.” He watches the Snowman film every Christmas with his mum.Tuckett felt that the show, as it was, had become increasingly something for little kids. “I felt there was a bit of a disconnect with the adults in the audience.” The book, he says, is “so well observed, and the humour in it works if you’re a kid, but as an adult, it’s really clever”. Briggs’ illustration of the melted snowman still brings a lump to the throat. Is it going to be a Toy Story vibe, I ask: the kids will be laughing, the parents crying? “It’s totally that,” smiles Tuckett.The Snowman is atBirmingham Repuntil 1 November, thenPeacock theatre, London, 21 November-3 January 2027Explore more on these topicsChristmas showsTheatreDanceBirmingham RepRaymond BriggsSadler's WellsChildren's theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stranger things turn an English village upside down in Max Porter’s rural noir Lanny | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emerges
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: A family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emerges
Content: Broken and furious … Hanora Kamen as Jolie in Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenBroken and furious … Hanora Kamen as Jolie in Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewStranger things turn an English village upside down in Max Porter’s rural noir LannyBristol Old VicA family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emergesArifa AkbarFri 23 Oct 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOverheard in the auditorium during the interval: it’s like Tales of the Unexpected meets Jackanory. But if those references are dated by several decades, they go some way to summing up the strange mix of elements in this drama about a boy who goes missing from a village, and the ancient myth of a “green man” who might have something to do with it.But then,Max Porter’s novel, on which it is based, weaves so many seemingly incongruent parts together to create its own beautiful brand of rural noir. It might be better described as The Missing meets This Country meets Stranger Things, except the Upside Down here is English countryside.The story follows townie couple Robert (Raj Bajaj) and Jolie (Hanora Kamen), who move to the sticks and are just settling in when their otherworldly son, Lanny (Lucian Thomas on press night), goes missing. A local artist (Richard Cant), dubbed “Mad Pete” – for his bohemianism or, as a gay man in these parts, for his sexuality? – had formed a friendship with Lanny and is now considered prime suspect. The myth of a pagan figure, Dead Papa Toothwort, looms over the human drama as the police procedural unfolds.It is a lot to transpose to the stage, alongside Porter’s multi-voiced portrait of a village and satirical social observations of country life. Bea Roberts does a deft job of adapting the mixer-blend of reality, imagination and hallucinatory bucolic lore. The production is full of pace and creepiness when it could so easily slide into the ridiculous.View image in fullscreenHaunted set design … Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayIt is much helped by Rebecca Jane Wood’s haunted set design, incorporating the village and its woodland. Screens show scratchy images of bare branched trees and antler-figured silhouettes, reminiscent of a Brothers Grimm storybook. Together with Zeynep Kepekli’s contrasting of warm/cold lighting design, the optics capture the chilling magic of Dead Papa Toothwort’s parallel world.It is smartly directed by Nancy Medina too. Horror and humour squat at close quarters although the story is heavy on green man mythology at first and it does not give enough space to domestic realism. But there is an accomplished bridging of the dark and scary with the satirical and light. The book lends itself to dialogue and the many voices of the village and the babble of modern life criss-cross in disembodied audio, sometimes accompanied by floating sentences written across the set.Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Read moreThis seems, ultimately to be a story about the pain, responsibility and sometimes the emotional disconnect in parenthood. As Robert reflects, “who can have children and not go completely mad?” In this production he is not an emotionally numbed dad but seems a little generic. Jolie is excellently played by Kamen as a mother left broken and furious by her loss, while Thomas does a great job of bringing Lanny to life.Village homophobia is made more emphatic and there is an added racial element: Lanny is a brown boy, we are told, but this does not feel fully developed. Some of the underlying anxieties of the book are lost among the many strands: the sense of dislocation for these urban folk in a village environment and its spikier, more judgmental neighbours; the question of who belongs here, and whom the land itself belongs to, ultimately. Some of these inquires are subsumed by the fever and gothicism of the plot.It swings into the surreally hallucinatory in its final scene. The happy ending might be a story, a song or a miracle – a pagan god showing mercy to the humans that occupy his land.AtBristol Old Vicuntil 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBristol Old VicMax PorterFairytalesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lowry kicks off, pop goes kinky and the wild man of Florence is tamed – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: The painter of industrial England heads south, the Hockney of Soho displays all and debauched artist Filippo Lippi lays his sins at the altar
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The painter of industrial England heads south, the Hockney of Soho displays all and debauched artist Filippo Lippi lays his sins at the altar
Content: Heads up … A Football Match, 1932, by LS Lowry.Photograph: Crane Kalman Gallery, LondonView image in fullscreenHeads up … A Football Match, 1932, by LS Lowry.Photograph: Crane Kalman Gallery, LondonArt Weekly newsletterArt and designLowry kicks off, pop goes kinky and the wild man of Florence is tamed – the week in artThe painter of the industrial north heads south, the Hockney of Soho displays all and debauched artist Filippo Lippi lays his sins at the altar –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 23 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekLS LowryThe strangest and perhaps most truthful painter of modern Britain gets a thorough looking at.MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, 24 October to 28 FebruaryAlso showingAllen JonesKinky pop art from the diehard naughty boy of 1960s British painting – the Hockney of Soho?Gazelli Art House, London, until 18 DecemberMultiplied WondersWoodcuts by Jacopo de’ Barbari, Albrecht Dürer and more reveal the power of the reproduced image in the Renaissance.British Museum, London, until 21 MarchBeyond BayeuxYinka Shonibare, Hurvin Anderson and others design tapestries in collaboration with Edinburgh’s Dovecot Studios, in a somewhat opportunistically titled show.Guildhall Art Gallery, London, until 21 MarchAnne RedpathLandscapes on Skye with white houses and bright green fields tenderly depicted in gouache and watercolour.National, Edinburgh, until 6 DecemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Justin Theodore Benttinen/Nikon Small WorldSheep dung, snails and mouse brains are all beautiful … if you look closely enough. This artwork could be a newly discovered planet or an abstract piece by Stanley Donwood for Radiohead’s A Moon Shaped Pool, but the truth is tinier: it is the tip of a ballpoint pen, a winning entry fromthe Nikon Small World photography competition.What we learnedBowie, bodybuilders and a blubbering Frenchman have changed the way we see masculinityLight and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography at Tate Modern will stop you in your tracksPhotos of bustling dancefloors show a changing America through the decadesFrieze art fair is open, and we’ve identified 10 things worth seeingBondi beach in Sydney is alive with sculptureDesigner Kate Faulkner is stepping out of William Morris’s shadow in a show that celebrates her influence on Morris & CoOlivier Mourgue, whose Djinn armchairs featured in 2001: A Space Odyssey, has diedGreat Pottery Throw Down judge Keith Brymer dressed up for a trip down memory laneFederico Veronesi’s best photograph is a devastating portrait of a grieving elephantArtist Tony Albert is reappropriating racist artefacts of Aboriginalia for his show Not a Souvenir in Sydneyskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA new book documents the key players in Cameroon’s vast visual art historyA Paris exhibition explores Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialismMasterpiece of the weekSt Jerome and the Lion: Predella Panel by Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, 1455-60View image in fullscreenPhotograph: piemags/AlamyFilippo Lippi was the wild man of early 15th-century Florentine art, if the stories told about him in the Renaissance are anything to go by. It was even said his patron Cosimo de’ Medici had to lock him in the Medici palace to stop his debauchery. There is a core of fact behind the tales, as Filippo – a friar – is known from legal records to have had children with an escaped nun, Lucrezia Buti. Their son Filippino also became an artist. But whatever his life was like, there’s no lack of piety in this painting of the early Christian Jerome, a real historical figure who translated the Bible into Latin. The lion tamely lets the holy man pull a thorn from its paw, in an intricately painted mountainous landscape with a pink church. Jerome concentrates on his work, as you would if you were de-thorning a dangerous big cat. This is just a small panel from the base of an altarpiece but it packs in the emotion and humanity that makes Lippi a great artist, in spite of, or because of, his sins.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ comments | US television | The Guardian
description: After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye
Content: Adam Brody in season three of Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marchinowski/NetflixView image in fullscreenAdam Brody in season three of Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marchinowski/NetflixUS televisionNobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ commentsAfter Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eyeOwen MyersFri 23 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has responded to star Adam Brody’s recent support of Palestine amid theIsrael-Gaza war.“Everyone is entitled to a different opinion,” Erin Foster said in aninterviewwith the Not Skinny Not Fat podcast when asked about Brodycalling fora free Palestine.Nobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different coupleRead more“You know, it’s complicated,” said Foster, who also has an acting role in the new season. “I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing.“While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s OK.”Nobody Wants This, which returns for its third season this week, chronicles the unexpected love story between agnostic podcast host Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) and rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody).The story was inspired by Foster’s own real-life love story after she converted toJudaismafter meeting her husband.“As the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” Foster said. “The show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person.View image in fullscreenAdam Brody and Erin Foster in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix“Sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”Last month, Brody opened up about his political views for the first time. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he toldGQ. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”Nobody Wants This’s third season sees Joanne and Noah move in together while their siblings continue to look for love. In a four-starreview, the Guardian’s Jack Seale said the new episodes will make fans of the show “fall in love with it all over again”.Foster has often posted about theIsrael-Gaza waron social media.“Nothing that is happening in Israel/Palestine is acceptable or comfortable to look at,” shewrotein 2021. “Innocent lives lost as casualties of war, as well as the atrocious lack of human rights that exist under a Hamas run government.“There is a chance for peace here, and it involves a two state resolution where both exist next to each other, respecting each other’s beliefs, and sharing the holy land that all three major religions call sacred. Palestinians deserve to live in peace without fear. So do Jews.”An independent UNinquiryin June found that Israel continues to commit genocide by targeting children in Gaza.The Guardian has reached out to representatives for Foster,Netflixand Brody for comment.Explore more on these topicsUS televisionTelevisionIsrael-Gaza warJudaismNetflixPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing? | Music | The Guardian
description: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
Author: Oliver Keens
Headline: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
Content: Rave on … the dancefloor at The Hacienda in  Manchester, 1989.Photograph: Peter J Walsh/PYMCA/Avalon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRave on … the dancefloor at The Hacienda in  Manchester, 1989.Photograph: Peter J Walsh/PYMCA/Avalon/Getty ImagesMusicMurder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should beOliver KeensFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTowards the end of summer, a debate began raging in clubland, kick-started by an Instagram post from the esteemed DJ Jane Fitz. Ahead of the Houghton festival, where she is a regular fixture, she posted a request asking people to stop chatting so much during DJ sets.“What I wrote was super respectful,” she tells me. “A bit of talking is obviously OK. But why would you stand completely still, where the sound is super loud, just to ask your mate about a new boyfriend or what they had for lunch? It’s called a dancefloor for a reason.”View image in fullscreenJane Fitz at Rural in 2025.Photograph: ToshimuraFitz’s plea exploded. It chimed with many, while others were up in arms, claiming that paying an entry fee allowed them to do whatever they wanted. “People were accusing me of being the fun police,” she says. “I’m not trying to stop your fun, mate. I’m trying to give you a better night out.”“I think the dancefloor is dead,” Charli xcx sang on her tongue-in-cheek comeback single Rock Music this spring. Was she right? Many DJs and clubbers are worried it goes further than the yappers Fitz complained about, citing the rise of certain drugs – insular ketamine, chew-your-ear-off cocaine – and TikTok-boosted star DJs bringing in passive fans used to consuming dance music through a screen, who end up standing still filming the DJ and their visuals. Then there is the rising cost of clubbing, prohibiting younger, potentially bouncier dancers from attending raves.As fewer purpose-made clubs have been built in recent years, clubbers have got used to squeezing into one-room raves often in converted arches, warehouses and garages. Josh Aitman, an organiser of the sober-friendly London queer party Good As You, complains that “some parties can be so packed in that I get looks just for dancing”. Separate bar areas are scarce and the 90s concept of a dedicated chill-out room is long gone, so thesmoking areais often the only safe – if smelly – bet for a chat away from the music.View image in fullscreenPaul M’s “The dancefloor is for dancing” card and reasons for it on the reverse.While the audiophilia boom has improved sound quality in many clubs, stricter council licensing demands often result in quieter dancefloors, making chat more liable to cut through and annoy other punters. One diehard group of clubbers detailed the science on cards they handed out this summer on dancefloors including at Houghton. One side read: “The Dance Floor Is For Dancing” with “Please take your conversation to the back” written underneath. The flipside featured a diagram of EQ curves. “Dance music is very bassy, meaning there’s loads of room on the top end of the EQ spectrum for vocals to punctuate,” says Paul M, one of the instigators of the cards.“The sadistic side of me wishes I could just turn the music off for 10 minutes and give these people a lecture on all this so they understand,” says Paul. “The cards were a jokey way of doing that – but it’s no joke. I was watching a DJ I’d wanted to see for ages and two men next to me were having a 20-minute discussion about mortgage rates.” Astonishingly, this group of dancefloor activists wasn’t alone – someone else at Houghton gave out cards that just said: “Stop Talking.”Not everyone in clubland wants the dancefloor to be treated as a sacred space. James Ronald, who plays as Hot Cross Fun and is a resident DJ for the nomadic party Disco Disco, posted a heartfelt rebuttal to Fitz’s post titled: “Please Talk on the Dancefloor.” It garnered a similarly huge reaction. “I get that you should be respectful,” says Ronald. “But she talked about treating it like a church, cinema or a theatre – places where you just observe and nobody communicates.”View image in fullscreenA sign at Gaffe in London tells clubbers to keep chat off the dancefloor.Ronald tapped into an important reason why club culture is such a powerful force: the dancefloor is a place for people to connect. “Community is a really big part of clubbing,” he says. He defends the right for clubbers to get deep. “There’s been instances with a particular friend, for example, who only really opens up when he’s a bit wasted. We’ve had important chats about family and personal issues, chats we wouldn’t have had anywhere else.”It’s a fairly new discussion and, apparently, an intractable one. Dan Beaumont, a DJ who is writing a history of London’s queer club culture, sees it like this: “Gossip is the glue that holds clubbing together. You need an equilibrium of yappers and dancers.Clubbingdoesn’t work when it’s one and not the other.”One possible way forward is for venues to set more direction for what they expect from punters. At Gaffe, a DIY space in north east London, a sign shows two arrows pointing in different directions. One says “Dancing”, the other “Yapping”.View image in fullscreenMichael Peacock having fun on the dancefloor.Photograph: Warehouse Project“The sign is a bit tongue in cheek,” says founder Luca Marchal. “But the arrows point in different directions for a reason. We’re asking people to take the longer chats off the dancefloor. Having a proper catch up is a massive part of going out, so we want that to happen somewhere good.”Until more venues spell it out quite so clearly with signs, interpersonal skills have become more important than ever in this delicate standoff, a challenge for conflict-averse Britons. Compare that with Berlin, where there is far less social stigma around asking someone to take their chat outside. “There’s a certain etiquette that leads to more satisfying and transformative experiences on the dancefloor,” says the British DJ Pandora, who is based in Berlin. “You’re more able to get into a flow state without the distraction of nearby conversations.”British clubs have started to follow Berlin’s lead in banning phones on the dancefloor, a change that many have credited with restoring a bit of life. Michael Peacock, an almost ambassadorial figure for British clubbing, is one of those leading the charge. The 68-year-old likes to arrive at clubs barefoot, often wearing little, and proceeds to have the most fun in the room; he says his peak this summer was dancing for 30 straight hours.In 2022, a video of Peacock going for it at Fabric in London was shared online by a punter with mocking intent. There was a huge outcry: not only are people not dancing because they are filming the DJ (or each other) but they may be worried about someone else filmingthem. “A lot of the debate on social media is about how phones destroy the vibe for the DJ,” says Peacock. “But there’s still scant regard for ravers who are filmed without their consent.”Peacock now campaigns for less phone use in clubs. He praises Amber’s in Manchester which goes further than most “no-phones” clubs with a strictly enforced zero tolerance policy. “There are still times when I have to remonstrate with people,” he says with a sigh.Sheffield DIY venue Plot 22 staff place a sticker over your phone camera on the way in, and will have a word if they catch you breaking the rules. “Our space is small and intimate,” says the venue’s manager, Mike Thompson. “Even just one person filming with a flash would really disrupt the vibe”. Co-owner Adam Seymour agrees: “People say they feel free to enjoy the dancefloor when you take away the ability to use their phone.”If clubbing’s heyday was defined by ecstasy, today’s most popular drugs can pull the dancefloor in disparate and equally destructive directions. Many feel that the rise in ketamine use – a drug that creates a profound sense of dissociation – has made dancefloors markedly less buoyant in recent years.View image in fullscreenLuke Una … ‘For me, music has to be about connection. A night club should be about transcending and escaping together.’Photograph: Sophie FarrellManchester DJ Luke Una stresses that he doesn’t want to be judgmental about drug use, but calls ketamine a “very solo” drug. “It breaks any sense of communal togetherness. For me, music has to be about connection. A nightclub should be about bringing people together and transcending and escaping together. The one time I had it, I’ll be honest with you, I thought I was listening to Underground Resistance for 12 hours until I came round and realised that I was listening to the air conditioning unit.”‘Nobody’s going out!’ Why is Britain’s nightlife in such decline – and can anything save it?Read moreThen there’s cocaine, the cost of which has plummeted in recent years and is now as omnipresent as ecstasy used to be. Clubbers have “gone from a drug that makes the music sound amazing, to a drug that makes you think you’re amazing and people need to listen to you instead,” says the DJ Wes Baggaley, a resident on NTS Radio, a London music station.But Luke Una is keen to point out how a revival of a different drug is having the opposite effect. “In the last 12 months, there’s been a lot more unity, love, warmth and smiling – down to people taking mushrooms again. I played a party in Belfast and said to the person running it, ‘Why is everyone so fucking happy?” And he said, ‘Luke, they’re all on mushrooms.’ I’m not advocating using them – but you can see the difference.”Now Jane Fitz feels optimistic: “We started a debate, which was a great first step. I have seen differences, I think people have realised there should be some kind of etiquette. During the breakdowns in songs, the dancefloor has been feeling quiet with people listening again.”When a party pops off, Luke Una also sees optimism: “I believe something is going on which feels like a reaction to what has become a brutal, toxic world out there. It feels like people are coming back to life in 3D again, showing a need to be together and – without being cringe about it – to kind of transcend together too.”This article was amended on 23 October 2026 because an earlier version located the nightclub Gaffe in south London rather than north-east London.Explore more on these topicsMusicMusic festivalsFestivalsClubbingClub culturefeaturesShareReuse this content
