title: Experience: I’ve climbed Mount Everest 20 times | Life and style | The Guardian
description: In 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-Sherpa
Author: Deborah Linton
Headline: In 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-Sherpa
Content: ‘The mountain has given me everything, and I feel humbled by that’: mountaineer Kenton Cool.Photograph: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The mountain has given me everything, and I feel humbled by that’: mountaineer Kenton Cool.Photograph: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I’ve climbed Mount Everest 20 timesIn 1996 doctors told me I wouldn’t walk again unaided, but in 2022 I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non-SherpaKenton CoolFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIgrew up in Slough, Berkshire, in a bungalow beside a farm. My father was a scout leader, and I was always outside, building dams and dens, sleeping out and hiding in trees.In my teens, family holidays were two weeks in Wales. At home, nature was my playground.When I was 17, a school friend took me to a climbing wall where he was a regular. I loved the physicality of it and trying to work out where to put my hands and feet next. We would go there twice a week. In sixth form, we headed to the south coast in Dorset for my first real climbing outing. The waves were crashing and it felt scary and exhilarating. I thought it was magical.We would go climbing there or in the Peak District whenever we could. After A-levels, we caught a bus to Chamonix, in the Alps, for five weeks of camping; we climbed Mont Blanc and made stupid mistakes like starting too late in the day. It was a huge learning curve, but it was fabulous.I did a geology degree at the University of Leeds and joined the climbing club. I wanted to see the Himalayas, so organised a trip to Pakistan. That was a turning point. The climbing was wonderful, but it was the people I fell in love with.double quotation markThere have been testing times, like when we encountered a catastrophic oxygen delivery failure and had to share tanksOver the next decade, I spent half my year working in ski and climbing shops, and the other half climbing across Europe, New Zealand and Asia. It was treacherous at times. In 1996 I fell from a rock face, shattering both heel bones, and was told I wouldn’t walk again unaided. After several surgeries and three months in a wheelchair, I defied doctors to climb – and even ski – some of the world’s highest peaks.A group of us took on harder and higher routes and were nominated for a Piolet d’Or – the Oscars of the climbing world – after establishing a trail on Annapurna III, a 7,555-metre peak in Nepal, in 2003.That caught the attention of a Sheffield adventure company, which asked if I would guide an expedition of two to Everest. I was an accomplished climber, but I had never been to 8,000 metres or led at high altitude; it was a huge leap of faith.Experience: I survived being buried in an avalancheRead moreThe ascent took eight weeks and I relied heavily on Sherpa expertise. We climbed through the night, with thunderstorms and stars lighting the sky, and I soaked in the feeling of being on the summit at the highest point on the planet, looking down at the Himalayas spread below.I loved facilitating someone else’s journey. I did three more Everest ascents for the company before setting up my own in 2006. Now I take on one client a year, preparing together for up to three years.I’ve climbed Everest most years since that first time. This May, I clocked up my 20th summit. There have been testing times – once, we encountered a catastrophic oxygen delivery failure and had to share tanks.But there have been beautiful moments, too. The best was in 2017: we had summit day to ourselves – warm, no wind and just the right amount of snow. I could see Kangchenjunga and Makalu, the third and fifth highest peaks, respectively, and into Tibet. In 2013, I climbed Everest’s neighbouring peak, Nuptse, looking back from 7,900 metres and recalling years of memories.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat same year, I encountered my hardest night when I came across a dying climber who passed away in my arms. Another time, I pulled a dead Sherpa off the fixed line ropes, the barriers designed to stop people falling. The mountain doesn’t respect whether you have climbed it 20 times or once – anybody can die there.In 2022, I took the record for the most Everest summits by a non‑Sherpa after my 16th ascent. Meanwhile Kami Rita Sherpa holds the general record. I still hold mine, although it has never been about numbers; it’s about experiences.There will be a time when I stop climbing Everest, but it won’t be soon. It has given me everything and I feel humbled by that. But it’s the place and its people that mean the most to me – Sherpas I have climbed with; locals who fed me in their homes or nursed me when I was ill; people who have become my friends. The mountain is simply the vehicle that got me there.As told to Deborah LintonDo you have an experience to share? title: Something crunchy, something sharp, something sweet: Sam and Sam Clark’s autumn meze recipes | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: A plate of seasonal flavours and colours – tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A plate of seasonal flavours and colours – tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms
Content: Sam and Sam Clark's autumn meze (clockwise from top): tabbouleh; oyster mushrooms with garlic and dill; beetroot, apple and mint; Syrian lentils; roast squash, tahini and chickpeas; and fried aubergines, chilli, yoghurt and mint in the middle.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark's autumn meze (clockwise from top): tabbouleh; oyster mushrooms with garlic and dill; beetroot, apple and mint; Syrian lentils; roast squash, tahini and chickpeas; and fried aubergines, chilli, yoghurt and mint in the middle.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.Autumn food and drinkSomething crunchy, something sharp, something sweet: Sam and Sam Clark’s autumn meze recipesTabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms … a riot of colour and autumnal flavours with every forkfulSam and Sam ClarkFri 23 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAutumn is a time of year when our meze plate becomes more comforting and generous, with earthy beetroot, sweet squash and woody mushrooms. The cooking is simple, but the flavours and textures are layered and kept lively with sharp vinegars and citrus. Each one of today’s dishes is considered individually, but also in the context of the plate as a whole, and how each element relates to the others to achieve balance and harmony. And, of course, always serve with pitta or flatbread to scoop up every last morsel.Served together, this meze selection should feed four generously.Beetroot, apple and mintView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s beetroot, apple and mint.Raw beetroot has an earthy sweetness and plenty of crunch that works particularly well with the acidic sharpness of a granny smith. Mint lifts and toasted walnuts bring richness. A good, sweet-sharp vinegar and olive oil are really all the dressing this needs. Serve at room temperature.Prep15 min1½ tbspsweet aged red-wine vinegar(we useForum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar), or good red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilSalt and black pepper250g raw beetroot, peeled and coarsely grated1 large granny smith apple, unpeeled, quartered, cored and cut into very thin matchsticks2 tbsp thinly shredded mint leaves50g lightly toasted walnuts, slicedIn a small bowl, whisk the vinegar and olive oil, season to taste and set aside.Mix the beetroot and apple in a large bowl with half the shredded mint and half the walnuts, pour on the dressing and toss gently. Check for seasoning, then serve with the remaining mint and walnuts scattered on top.Autumn tabboulehView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s autumn tabbouleh.We tend to think of tabbouleh as a summer dish (cucumbers, tomatoes, lemon, parsley, mint), as something fresh and light for when the weather is warm. But the idea of tabbouleh lends itself well to the changing seasons. What matters most is the balance of herbs, grain, fruit or vegetables, something crunchy and something sharp, and all those things can change to suit whatever’s around. This is a celebration of autumn in one dish. Serve at room temperature.Prep15 minSoak10-15 min40g medium bulgur wheat100g white muscat or sultana grapes, halved2 fresh figs, peeled and cut into thin wedges75g lightly toasted almonds, roughly chopped2 spring onions, cut into thin rounds1 small bunchflat-leaf parsley, finely shredded1 small bunchmint, finely shreddedSalt and black pepperFor the dressing½ small garlic clove, crushed to a paste with a little salt1 pinch ground cinnamon1 tbsp orange juice1 tbsp lemon juice3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilPut the bulgur in a bowl, add cold water just to cover and leave to sit for 10-15 minutes. Meanwhile, put all the dressing ingredients in a jar, season and shake well.When the bulgur has absorbed all the water and is soft (if it’s still al dente, stir in another tablespoon of water and leave for a couple of minutes), gently rub it between your palms to fluff it up. Put all the remaining ingredients in a large bowl, then pour the dressing on top. Add the bulgur to the bowl, toss to mix, check the seasoning and serve.Oyster mushrooms, garlic and dillView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s oyster mushrooms, garlic and dill.The seared and nicely caramelised mushrooms give this dish a great complexity of flavour and texture. Serve at room temperature.Prep5 minCook20 min8 large oyster mushrooms, thicker ends of stalks cut off and discarded3 tbsp olive oilSalt and black pepper2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped2tbsp roughly chopped dillPut a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium to high heat. Toss the mushrooms with a tablespoon of the oil and season. When the pan is hot, lay in the mushrooms gill side down and leave to fry until caramelised and a rich golden colour. Turn over, cook for 30 seconds, then spread out on a platter. Evenly scatter over the raw garlic and dill, drizzle over the remaining two tablespoons of oil, check the seasoning and serve.Fried aubergine, chilli, yoghurt and mintView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s fried aubergine, chilli, yoghurt and mint.A classic Moro recipe that’s also great with salted anchovies. Serve at room temperature.Prep10 minDrain20 minCook30 min1 large aubergine, cut into 1½cm-thick roundsSalt and black pepper100ml olive oil, plus 1 tbsp extra for frying the garlic100ml sunflower oil1 large garlic clove,peeled and cut into thin matchsticks4tsp sweet aged red-wine vinegar(we useForum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar), or a good aged red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar1 heaped tbsp finely shredded mint, plus extra to serve1 long green chilli, cut in half lengthways, deseeded and finely chopped4dsspGreek yoghurt1 pinchblack onion seeds, to finishPut the aubergine slices in a colander, toss with half a teaspoon of fine salt, then leave for 20 minutes to drain off any excess water and to get rid of any bitterness. Dry the slices on kitchen paper.Heat both oils in a wide frying pan until hot but not smoking. Lay in the aubergine slices in a single layer (if need be, cook them in batches) and fry, turning as required, until deep golden brown and crisp on both sides. Transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to absorb any excess oil. Meanwhile, fry the garlic matchsticks in the extra tablespoon of olive oil, until golden, then drain.Put the drained aubergine slices on a platter, sprinkle over the fried garlic, vinegar and mint, then leave to sit for five minutes.Stir the chopped chilli into the yoghurt and season with a little salt.Spoon a small dollop of the yoghurt on top of each aubergine slice, scatter over a little extra shredded mint and the black onion seeds, season and serve.Syrian lentilsView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s Syrian lentils.The keys to this dish are to toast the cumin, to fry the garlic to the darkened side of golden, and to use the coriander stalks as well as the leaves. Serve warm or at room temperature.Prep10 minCook40 min+4 tbsp olive oil2-3 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1 roundedtsp cumin seeds, roughly ground250g cooked small brown or puy lentils(from a tin or pouch)1 small bunchcoriander, stalks and leaves separated and roughly chopped50g caramelised crispy onions(shop-bought or homemade)Salt and black pepperPut three tablespoons of the oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. When it’s hot but not smoking, add the garlic and cumin, and fry until light brown. Stir in the lentils, chopped coriander stalks, half the crispy onions and enough water to loosen the mix to the consistency of a thick soup. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for five minutes, until the lentils are soft. Take off the heat, stir in the chopped coriander leaves, then season. Scatter the rest of the crispy onions on top and serve.Roast squash, tahini and chickpeasView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s roast squash, tahini and chickpeas.Kaboucha squash has an excellent sweetness and dense texture, although its knobbly skin is tougher than other squashes and therefore harder to peel. Make this dish last, because it’s the only one here that needs to be served warm.Prep10 minCook30 min1 small-medium kabocha squash(about 450g), or butternut squash, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm chunks3 tbsp olive oil½ tsp ground cinnamon½ garlic clove, crushed to a paste with a pinch of saltSalt and black pepper4tbsptinned chickpeas, drained1 tsp finely chopped red chilli¼ tsp nigella seedsFor the tahini sauce1 small garlic clove, peeled and crushed1½ tbsp tahini1 good squeeze of lemon1½ tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the squash in a roasting tray, add the oil, cinnamon and garlic, season generously, then toss to coat. Spread out into an even layer, then roast for 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is soft and caramelised.Scatter over the chickpeas and bake for another five minutes, until they’re slightly crisp.Meanwhile, make the sauce. Mix the garlic, tahini and lemon juice in a small bowl, whisk in two and a half tablespoons of water, then whisk in the oil. Check the seasoning.Transfer the pumpkin mix to a platter, drizzle over the sauce and finish with the chilli and nigella seeds.Sam and Sam Clark are chefs/owners ofMoroandMoritoin London EC1Explore more on these topicsAutumn food and drinkMiddle Eastern food and drinkFoodVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkHerbs and spicesSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

Content: Kokum’s spiced tamarind and apple sour.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Kokum’s spiced tamarind and apple sour – recipeA lively tequila sour shaken up with an injection of tamarind and star aniseDhononjoy Roy DipFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRich tamarind chutney gives this vibrant tequila sour a sweet-sour depth that pairs brilliantly with crisp apple juice.Spiced tamarind and apple sourServes145ml blanco tequila– we useOlmeca Altos Plata25ml apple juice25ml fresh lime juice20ml sugar syrup½ tsp tamarind chutney–any decent brand will do1 egg white, or 3 drops cocktail foamer1 star anise, to garnishPut everything bar the star anise in a shaker and shake vigorously without ice to set the egg white and build a smooth foam. title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns | Food | The Guardian
description: I like to get pumpkin into everything – including dessert – at this time of year
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: I like to get pumpkin into everything – including dessert – at this time of year
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for chocolate and pumpkin spice choux bunsWhip winter squash puree into a creamy filling and pipe direct into the heart of a cracking seasonal puddingBenjamina EbuehiFri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this time of year, I aim to get as much pumpkin as I can into my meals, including desserts. If I’ve been organised, I’ll roast and puree some from scratch, but I seem always to have at least one tin of pumpkin puree to hand, which I can use quickly in anything from pumpkin pies to cookies and muffins. Here, it’s whipped into cream with some spices, then piped into crackly puffs of choux for a chic, autumnal dessert.Chocolate and pumpkin spice choux bunsPrep10 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus coolingMakes12For the chocolate craquelin60g unsalted butter65g light brown sugar10g cocoa powder65g plain flourFor the choux50ml milk45g unsalted butter60g plain flour1 tsp sugar1 pinch salt1-2 large eggsFor the filling150g pumpkin puree1 tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground cloves1 tsp vanilla bean paste90g cream cheese75g icing sugar150ml double cream20g pecans, roughly choppedBriefly mix the butter and sugar for the craquelin in a small bowl, until smooth and well combined, then work in the flour and cocoa powder to make a thick paste. Spread this evenly over a sheet of baking paper, top with a second sheet, then roll out to about 2-3mm thick and pop it in the freezer to firm up.Meanwhile, make the choux. Put the milk, butter and 50ml water in a saucepan and heat until steaming and the butter has melted. Off the heat, add the flour,sugarand salt, and stir quickly to bring the dough together. Return to the heat, cook, stirring, for one or two minutes, then transfer to a clean bowl and leave to cool for a few minutes.Meanwhile, whisk the eggs in a jug, then bit by bit work some into the dough, mixing until it’s all incorporated before adding more. The dough will look lumpy at first, but it will come together. Continue mixing in the eggs (you may not need all of them) until the mixture is glossy, falls easily, and leaves a V shape hanging when lifted with a spoon. Transfer to a piping bag, snip off 2½cm from the end and pipe 12 blobs of the choux dough on to a lined tray.Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Take the chilled craquelin out of the freezer and, working quickly, use a round cutter roughly the same width as the piped choux to cut out 12 discs. Gently place a disc on each choux, then bake for 15 minutes. Turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for another 10-12 minutes, until the buns are puffy and firm to the touch. Remove and leave to cool completely.Meanwhile, whisk the pumpkin puree, spices, vanilla and cream cheese in a bowl until smooth, then mix in the sugar. In a second bowl, whip the cream to very soft peaks, then fold into the pumpkin mix.Use a sharp, serrated knife to trim the top off each choux bun just above halfway. Spoon the cream into a piping bag with an open-star nozzle, then pipe swirls into each bun. Sprinkle chopped pecans on top, then gently top with the choux “hats”. Serve at once.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotBakingPastryPumpkinChocolateDessertEggsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A form of anti-status status’ – how much would you pay for a plain tote bag? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The ubiquitous carrier has been given a four-figure makeover. But why has an everyday bag associated with running errands and US supermarkets become so aspirational?
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: The ubiquitous carrier has been given a four-figure makeover. But why has an everyday bag associated with running errands and US supermarkets become so aspirational?
Content: A status symbol? … tote bags from Phoebe Philo (£450), Boat and Tote from LL Bean (£53), and Toteme (£510).Photograph: Phoebe Philo, Boat and Tote and TotemeView image in fullscreenA status symbol? … tote bags from Phoebe Philo (£450), Boat and Tote from LL Bean (£53), and Toteme (£510).Photograph: Phoebe Philo, Boat and Tote and TotemeGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Fashion Statement newsletterFashion‘A form of anti-status status’ – how much would you pay for a plain tote bag?The ubiquitous carrier has been given a four-figure makeover. But why has an everyday bag associated with running errands and US supermarkets become so aspirational?Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereEllie Violet BramleyFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you were in the blessed position of having £500 to spend on a bag, what would you look for? Would it be made of cotton? A nice light shade bound to sully quickly, like “paper white” or ecru? Would you want something that looks a lot like those ubiquitous totes sold by a certain US supermarket chain for a couple of dollars?No, thought not. But there are plenty of options if you do. Phoebe Philo, former Celine designer and quiet luxury pioneer,offers a white canvas shopper, made entirely from cotton except for the silver brass hardware of its internal zipped pocket, for £450. Luxury Swedish brand Toteme’s“effortless tote bag”is made from organic cotton canvas and is available in dark brown, red or classic ecru. It goes for £510.Tom Ford’s version, at £1,600, differentiates itself a little, with a body made exclusively of cotton canvas but trims and handles from calfskin. Prada’s, which featuresleather details and metal hardware, could be yours for over £2,000.These are the kinds of totes that have become a relatively inexpensive staple, thanks to Trader Joe’s, LL Bean, J Crew, museum gift shops and countless other brands stocking this pleasingly simple and in some ways hyper-practical bag. They have become a common sight on the shoulders of people doing their vegetable shopping or in need of a second bag for gym clobber on an office day.So why have they been co-opted by luxury fashion? For Tiffany Hill, the founder ofTrend Suite, “the appeal is partly that the canvas tote has become a form of anti-status status”. The “strange impracticality of their pale colour” is, she says, part and parcel of it. “A cream or ecru tote that costs hundreds, or even thousands, and is inevitably going to mark, almost makes practicality beside the point. You are buying into an aesthetic and a lifestyle rather than simply buying something to carry your belongings in.”These ecru canvas totes are two a penny on the American east coast. Muffy Aldrich is the editor of the blogSalt Water New England: The Thing Before Preppy, where she offers tips on styling her LL Bean tote. (She has a couple of dozen of them in ecru.) If she includes those with different trim/handle colours, “it is embarrassingly in the triple digits”. She has bags in “medium, large, and extra-large. Occasionally the small. Long handles and short. Zip-top and open-top.”Perfect for going from Nantucket beach to lobster roll shack, Aldrich thinks “they may be the single most iconic East Coast Preppy item today. And fittingly, it is almost impossible to walk through any coastal New England town without running into one.” In large part that’s down to design. For Aldrich, their handles are a case in point: “The straps wrap completely around the bag, instead of just being sewn on at the top, so the bags feel secure when you carry them.”View image in fullscreen‘Ubiquitous’ … the inexpensive Trader Joe’s shopping bag.Photograph: PR ImageThe fact they are so symbolic of Martha’s Vineyard is very much the point. “The canvas tote already carries this very specific visual language of boats, summer houses, farmers’ markets, weekends away and slightly old-fashioned American affluence,” says Hill. “Luxury brands don’t have to invent that mythology – they can borrow it.”Where totes were once a symbol of sustainability in an era of disposable plastic bags, they have since become part of the overproduction problem – according to theUN Environment programme, the average cotton tote needs to be used between 50 and 150 times to offset its production. In reality, less than 10% of totes are used more than three times. So there has for some time been an appetite for tote bags that do more than clog up your cupboards, which explainsthe advent of the “forever tote”.And these iterationsare, apart from perhaps their colour, extremely practical. Boxy in shape, Anna Wintour famously carried “the book”(a dummy copy of the upcoming Vogue)in a monogrammed number. In the final episode of theTV show Furious,which depicts the sordid world of an Epstein-esque billionaire, his daughter reaches for hers when she needs a bag in a rush that’s sturdy enough to stash away all the drives harbouring her father’s collection of child sexual abuse images. It’s a smart piece of costume design from Claire Parkinson, who clearly understands that the character is exactly the type to have such a tote to hand.What we could call “the Erewhon effect” may also be at play. Erewhon, a high-end LA supermarketfrequented by the Kardashians and TikTokers– AKA a $19 powdered-beef-organ and unpasteurised milk smoothie kind of place – sells ecru totes. Emblazoned with “Erewhon”, they are about £74 and, in certain circles, aspirational.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Consumers have become very fluent in these quieter lifestyle codes: the right grocery shop, coffee cup, baseball cap or canvas tote can communicate taste and belonging just as effectively as an obvious designer logo,” says Hill. “The status is increasingly in recognising the reference rather than displaying the price.” Even if the reference is a supermarket, albeit an extremely fancy one; fashion has always appropriated the everyday.Marc Jacobs could be seen as playing an early role in this strange new world of expensive totes. In 2019, he launched The Tote Bag collection. The heavily branded canvas bags were hundreds rather than thousands of pounds, and marketed with the pithyslogan “No more Birkins, only tote bags”, they became a mainstream classic.“The fashion houses are riffing,” says Aldrich. “They can add an inner pocket or outer pocket, or different handle lengths. A logo, of course. Zhoosh up the proportions.” But pleasingly for anyone who owns a similar bag that cost them a tenner: “fashion houses are not going to make an appreciably ‘better’ canvas tote than the original, because it is already perfect for what it is.”In fact, Aldrich suggests, these new luxury iterations are antithetical to the tote’s allure. “When we get to a point where a tote bag is so precious – so expensive and made of softer materials – that we are afraid to toss it from boat to boat or let it get covered in sand … we get very close to losing what made it iconic to begin with.” Paradoxically, then, “it becomes temporary. Disposable. And that may be exactly what the fashion houses are counting on as the next season rolls around.”Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletterAccessoriesnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in Europe | Ski resorts | The Guardian
description: From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds
Content: Bad Gastein in Austria.Photograph: Guenter Graefenhain/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBad Gastein in Austria.Photograph: Guenter Graefenhain/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsSki resorts‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in EuropeFrom cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowdsTell us about a conservation tourism experience– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFree travel to a Salzberg gemBad Gastein is a relatively unknown gem. The Austrian state it sits in, Salzburg, offers free local transport (theguest mobility ticket) if you are staying in the state, so you can travel to the resort via train for nothing. The slopes are directly next to the station, too.Rob OwenFamily fun in the French AlpsView image in fullscreenPuy-Saint-Vincent.Photograph: Santiago Urquijo/Getty ImagesPuy-Saint-Vincentin France is a wonderful, small, child-friendly resort. Our grandchildren learned to ski each morning with great instructors on the gentle slopes under amazing azure skies. Three generations then made memories of a lifetime, skiing the wide quiet slopes together each afternoon. We enjoyed dog sleds and cosy hot chocolate in the slopeside cafes. A wonderful trip.BarbaraProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A historic railway and superb skiing in NorwayView image in fullscreenA ski lift in Gausta.Photograph: Alf Jacob Nilsen/AlamyGausta, Norway, is such fun. Stay at Gaustablikk,thehotel built by Kirk Douglas’s stuntman, a wonderfully quirky piece of local history. Explore Vemork, the historic heavy-water plant where British and Norwegian resistance fighters carried out their daring sabotage during the second world war. For families, the on-piste skiing is friendly and accessible; while the cross-country trails are simply stunning. Then there’s the real adventure: an old US military trainclimbs Gaustatoppen, opening up spectacular off-piste skiing with views and terrain that rival much of mainland Europe. It’s a brilliant mix of history, skiing, scenery and adventure, and somehow remains a wonderfully under-the-radar destination.FionaMarkets and glühwein in the Austrian TirolView image in fullscreenSt Johann in Tirol, Austria.Photograph: Animaflora/Getty ImagesAs a family of four, we lovedSt Johann in Tirol. It’s a comfortable Austrian village with Christmas markets, picturesque churches and gorgeous frozen valley walks – with little marmosets and weasels to look out for along the river. Wherever you stay, you can walk to a gondola. It’s really near to Salzburg airport, too. In Austria, kids get all-day lessons, which is a big bonus. Parents can just kick back or wander around and have aglühweinor two. Prices were very reasonable in the Christmas holidays.NickA locals’ favourite on the Italian borderView image in fullscreenMonte Lussari village.Photograph: Jacques Decro/Getty ImagesTarvisio-Monte Lussarion the Italian-Slovenian border covers 24km (15 miles) of skiable terrain interconnected across two main sectors: the historic and stunning Monte Lussari pilgrimage peak and the Priesnig area. Used by local people and those in the know, it offers sufficient ski runs and good value ski passes and restaurants, and is much cheaper than neighbouring resorts in Austria.NeilMagic in the air at La Rosière, FranceView image in fullscreenFamily-friendly La Rosière.Photograph: Real Image/AlamyStay in the attractive resort ofLa Rosièrein France, in the foothills of the Mont Blanc region. Enjoy the short forest walk to the village, with wind chimes and magic in the air, for an après-ski drink and a cheese fondue in a local tavern with the kids.Oliverskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOff-piste heaven in the Norwegian AlpsView image in fullscreenStrandafjellet.Photograph: Glenn Pettersen/Getty ImagesAbout 50km (30 miles) from Ålesund,Strandafjellethas excellent pistes, but also some of the best off-piste skiing in Norway. Strap on a pair ofrandonnéeskis and you can use the lifts to access spectacular backcountry skiing in the Sunnmøre Alps. The views down to the fjord make this truly special. Pistes are illuminated for evening skiing.GrahamA charming village in Les Trois ValléesView image in fullscreenSaint-Martin-de-Bellevile in the French Alps.Photograph: Delpixart/Getty ImagesSaint-Martin-de-Belleville, in the French Alps (Les Trois Vallées), is low at about 1,500 metres, so go mid-season. The single run ends smack in the centre of the village, which has retained its historical features along with small, friendly bars and places to eat. Plus, it gives access to the whole of the Trois Vallées ski area – absolutely amazing from one small but beautiful village. There are plenty of choices for accommodation, both expensive and cheap.Russell WalkerQueue-free skiing for all in Italy’s DolomitesView image in fullscreenChristmas time in Brunico.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyBrunicois tucked away in the Dolomites, just a 90-minute transfer from Innsbruck. I had a great week at the beginning of March. Unlike bigger resorts, queues were nonexistent here. There are runs for beginners through to experts. Great snow and plenty of opportunities to use it.Ian BWinning tip: Bavarian charm and quiet slopesView image in fullscreenA restaurant in Oberstdorf, Germany.Photograph: Harry Laub/Getty ImagesOberstdorfin Germany continues to be my go-to for a quiet and restorative ski week away. There are 130km (80 miles) of pistes for all levels, stacks of Bavarian restaurants, a wide variety of mountain huts, plenty of hotels for all budgets and family sizes, and the novelty of skiing into and out of Austria daily.Neuschwanstein Castleis a short hop away for a day off. Unbeatable value.Daniel StephensView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsSki resortsReaders' travel tipsSkiing holidaysWinter sports holidaysSnowboardingEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Let’s go nuts in the garden – and the cobnut is a great place to start | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: It’s high time we rediscovered these delicious nuts, but be warned: like the Victorians, squirrels can’t get enough of them
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: It’s high time we rediscovered these delicious nuts, but be warned: like the Victorians, squirrels can’t get enough of them
Content: Cobnuts have been foraged for millennia.Photograph: Alastair Wallace/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCobnuts have been foraged for millennia.Photograph: Alastair Wallace/ShutterstockGardening adviceLet’s go nuts in the garden – and the cobnut is a great place to startIt’s high time we rediscovered these delicious nuts, but be warned: like the Victorians, squirrels can’t get enough of themClaire RatinonFri 23 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I think of the crops I’m eager to grow, my mind rarely goes to nuts. But when I spotted the last of the season’s cobnuts at the greengrocer’s, it occurred to me that this could be one to consider. The nuts that come from the hazel – a tree that grows in many a woodland and also my front garden – have been foraged for millennia and cultivated versions have existed since Roman times.It’s the cultivated varieties you want to plant for a decent crop of cobnuts, as wild hazel produces smaller yields. This is a tree that prefers mild conditions, hence their connection to Kent, where they were grown abundantly during the Victorian era (one of the most popular varieties is called the Kentish cob.) They prefer a sunny spot, in free-draining earth – a challenge for me with my clay soil – in a sheltered position where they’ll be protected from frosts that would affect pollination.double quotation markGreen cobnuts have a delicate flavour or you can wait until the husks turn yellow for the full nut experienceAs cobnut trees are monoecious – meaning that the pollen-bearing catkins and the fruit-bearing flowers grow separately but on the same tree – pollination is a key consideration. Some cultivars will not self-pollinate and so rely on the presence of another tree (as well as the wind) for successful pollination. Fortunately, wild hazel can pollinate most cultivars, so if you have some in your garden, as I do, you may well be fine.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoil in need of some TLC? Then it’s time to make room for legumesRead moreAs with most trees, the best time to plant them is when they are dormant, so from November through to late winter works for cobnuts, which are generally sold as one- to two-year-old trees. While it is possible to get a crop of nuts from an unpruned tree, making the effort to prune should result in larger, better quality nuts. Aim for an open structured tree with about 10 leaders growing outwards. Once established, prune to prevent overcrowding in winter. If you do this after the catkins have arrived, this can help distribute pollen for better pollination. Additionally, brutting is a traditional pruning technique that encourages heavier cropping and involves bending that season’s side shoots in late summer, but leaving the broken section still attached.Cobnuts are ready to harvest from August if you like the taste of them when fresh, before they start to ripen. In any case, this might be your only opportunity if you share your garden with squirrels. Green cobnuts have a delicate nutty flavour and a juicy texture, but for those who prefer the more typical nut experience, wait until the husks start to turn yellow a month or so later. Cracking, shelling and then lightly roasting your cobnuts serves to enhance their nutty flavour.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensNuts and seedsFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features | Apple Watch | The Guardian
description: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
Content: The Ultra 4 is Apple’s do-it-all smartwatch, ready to tackle marathons or just the daily commute.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Ultra 4 is Apple’s do-it-all smartwatch, ready to tackle marathons or just the daily commute.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Apple WatchReviewApple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new featuresBiggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AISamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.That’s because several of the key featuresannounced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically thesame as last year’s model.The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to theprevious versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.View image in fullscreenUpgraded sensors sit in a new attractive fan-like design for the dome, which improve reliability during movement.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianUpgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina oftop adventure watch rivals.The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.SpecificationsCase size:49 x 44mmCase thickness:12mmWeight:63gProcessor:S11Storage:64GBOperating system:watchOS 27Water resistance:100 metres (10ATM)Connectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWBSensors:HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeterVitals and readinessView image in fullscreenWhen your health metrics deviate from your baseline, the readiness app gives you a score out of 10 showing how prepared your body is for strenuous exercise.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.watchOS 27 and AIView image in fullscreenThe vitals app spots changes to your metrics overnight and can now update HR and HRV during the day.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra 4 runswatchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to theSeries 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on amodern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while thesound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe action button continues to be exclusive to the Apple Watch Ultra for starting exercise and many other features.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianApple says the battery should last more than1,000 full charge cycleswith at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for£95. Damage repairs cost£539.The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in itsenvironmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.PriceThe Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from£749(€899/$799/A$1,349).For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from£369, the Watch SE 3 costs£219and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from£860.VerdictThe Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.Pros:great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.Cons:no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.Explore more on these topicsApple WatchWearable technologyGadgetsAppleSmartwatchesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Slugs? Dull? This one is pure showbiz | Invertebrates | The Guardian
description: Falmouth, Cornwall: The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-west
Author: Charlie Elder
Headline: Falmouth, Cornwall: The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-west
Content: ‘The extravagant rainbow sea slug comes with a “ta-da!”’Photograph: Paul Naylor/PAView image in fullscreen‘The extravagant rainbow sea slug comes with a “ta-da!”’Photograph: Paul Naylor/PACountry diaryInvertebratesCountry diary: Slugs? Dull? This one is pure showbizFalmouth, Cornwall:The rainbow sea slug is a bizarre and breathtaking animal, and with warming seas it’s gaining a toehold in the south-westCharlie ElderFri 23 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI have never seen a species quite so flamboyant in appearance. A couple of centimetres in length, it was curled beneath the submerged rock like a piece of gaudy costume jewellery.When the cry went up that one had been found, I had to prevent myself from breaking into a run as I navigated the slippery seaweed-covered boulders to catch my first glimpse of this rarity.A sea slug. And yet a species that does everything possible to dispel any idea that slugs are drab and dull. The extravagant rainbow sea slug comes with a “ta-da!”. Typically found along the coasts of Spain and Portugal, this multicoloured member of theAeolid nudibranchsfamily has spreadnorth with warming seas, and was first recorded in the UK off the Isles of Scilly in 2022. It has since secured a toehold in southern bays of Cornwall and Devon.I had joined a “bioblitz”, run bythe Rock Pool Project, on a low spring tide in Falmouth. The community organisation’s monthly challenge engages members of the public in a citizen-science survey of seashore life. The rainbow sea slug was a star find, drawing an admiring huddle of enthusiastic rockpoolers. Breathtaking and bizarre, its outlandish confectionary of candy colours looks almost artificial. The vivid pink body is decorated with a mane of blue finger-like projections known as cerata, which are topped with yellow and orange. A pop-art palette of colours designed to warn predators that it is unpalatable.View image in fullscreen‘This one was found on the underside of a rock beside white circles of recently laid eggs.’Photograph: Charlie ElderThis one was found on the underside of a rock beside white circles of recently laid eggs – the next generation of these sensational little sea creatures.The project volunteer and marine biologist Ellie Maynard told me that she encountered her first rainbow sea slug last Christmas. “Since then I have seen upwards of 20 here,” she said. “It has been really rapid how they have grown in number.”It was far from the morning’s only rarity. Others included the wonderfully namedhair curler slug, which first reached the UK last September and has wavy brown cerata that give it a permed appearance.The rainbow sea slug we were watching eventually trundled off, like an overdressed performer late for a carnival. Show time was over.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order atguardianbookshop.comand get a 15% discountExplore more on these topicsInvertebratesCountry diaryMarine lifeRural affairsCornwallAutumnWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The White House Farm massacre - exclusive: new forensic evidence suggests Sheila Caffell killed herself. Is Jeremy Bamber innocent? | Criminal Cases Review Commission | The Guardian
description: In 1985, Bamber was sentenced to life imprisonment for killing five members of his family. Now analysis of crime scene photographs by a leading forensic biologist could exonerate him. Warning: this article contains graphic photographs
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: In 1985, Bamber was sentenced to life imprisonment for killing five members of his family. Now analysis of crime scene photographs by a leading forensic biologist could exonerate him. Warning: this article contains graphic photographs
Content: Sheila Caffell, Jeremy Bamber’s sister. Did she kill her family and then herself?Composite: Guardian Design; David Thorpe/ANL/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSheila Caffell, Jeremy Bamber’s sister. Did she kill her family and then herself?Composite: Guardian Design; David Thorpe/ANL/REX/ShutterstockThe Bamber filesCriminal Cases Review CommissionThe White House Farm massacre - exclusive: new forensic evidence suggests Sheila Caffell killed herself. Is Jeremy Bamber innocent?In 1985, Bamber was sentenced to life imprisonment for killing five members of his family. Now analysis of crime scene photographs by a leading forensic biologist could exonerate him.Warning: this article contains graphic photographsSimon HattenstoneFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTShareOn7 August 1985,five peoplewere found dead atWhite House Farm in Essex, England:28-year-old Sheila Caffell(familiarly known asBambi); her six-year-oldtwin sons Daniel and Nicholas; and her adoptive parents,June and Nevill Bamber. All five had been shot with a rifle. Caffell’s24-year-old brother, Jeremy Bamber, who was also adopted, had alerted Essex police to a disturbance inside the farmhouse – he said his father had called to tell him – andwas outside with the police for four hours before the bodies were discovered.Caffell, who had recently been hospitalised withschizoaffective disorder and is said to have feared her children were going to be taken into foster care, was found with the rifle lying on her chest, pointing towards her neck. There were two gunshot wounds to her neck and chin, and a bloodied Bible by her side.View image in fullscreenJune Bamber (left), Caffell and her twins Nicholas and Daniel, who were all found dead at White House Farm.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyThe case was initially thought to be open and shut, a tragic murder-suicide committed by Caffell. But a month later, Jeremy Bamber was arrested, after relatives went to the police to voice their suspicions about him, and hisformer girlfriend, Julie Mugford, then told police he had confessedthe murders to her. The relatives went on to inherit from Nevill and June Bamber’s considerable estate after Bamber’s conviction. It was later discovered thatMugford had agreed to sell the story of their relationship to the News of the World for £25,000 if Bamber was convicted. Essex police and Crown prosecutors had also agreed to drop charges against her for burglary, chequebook fraud and selling cannabis, because “prosecuting her could jeopardise her availability or credibility as a key witness”.Bamber has now been in prison for41years, and questions have always been asked about the safety of his convictions. These have grown recently. The proper body to examinethese questions is theCriminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), but it has already taken the CCRC four years to consider less than half the evidence that Bamber has submitted toit, and it has concluded that the four points (out of 10) in the submission that it has so far considered do not meet the high evidentiary threshold to refer the case back to theCourt of Appeal. In the second piece in our series considering discrete pieces of evidence, the Guardian commissionedforensic biologist Sue Carney-Gannonto analyse the bloodstain patterns at the crime scene for the first time.Forty years ago, the jury at Jeremy Bamber’s trial was given a binary choice. Either the 24-year-old son of well-to-do farming stock had killed five members of his adoptive family, including his sister, Sheila Caffell. Or Caffell, 28 – also adopted, but from a different family – had killed their parents and her six-year-old twin boys before turning the gun on herself.What became known as the White House Farm massacre was a horrific case: brutal, chaotic, shockingly policed and, to this day, hugely controversial. On 28 October 1986, Bamber was convicted of the five murders in a 10-2 majority verdict at Chelmsford crown court, Essex, England.View image in fullscreenWhite House Farm, Essex – scene of the massacre.Photograph: Ted Blackbrow/ANL/ShutterstockBut now a leading forensic biologist has presented evidence that Caffell took her own life. After analysing the crime scene’s bloodstains for the Guardian, Sue Carney-Gannon has concluded that the patterns on the clothing and body of Caffell point to suicide. “In my opinion, if Sheila Caffell took her own life using the rifle, as the defence for Jeremy Bamber assert, then this explains the distribution of blood on her nightdress and right arm,” she writes in her report. “In my opinion, these findings are accounted for by her having taken her own life with the rifle; blood from the wound under her chin running down the upper right front of her clothing and splashing on to her right forearm, then veering to her right side as her body and arms fell.”Carney-Gannon’s conclusion challenges the prosecution case, which maintained that Bamber meticulously staged Caffell’s suicide after he shot their parents, June and Nevill Bamber, and her twins Nicholas and Daniel.The crimes occurred in the early hours of 7 August 1985. It was originally reported as a murder-suicide committed by Caffell, who had been diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and had been hospitalised earlier that year after a psychotic episode. Caffell’s delusions included the belief that she was possessed by the devil and her twin sons were evil.Three days after the murders in the picturesque village of Tolleshunt D’Arcy, Bamber’s uncle and cousins went to Essex police to suggest he had been behaving strangely and that they suspected him. His uncle, Robert Boutflour, provided the police with an elaborate theory to explain how he thought Bamber had killed his family. These relatives went on to inherit from June and Nevill Bamber’s considerable fortune.On 3 September 1985, Bamber split up with his girlfriend, Julie Mugford, after she discovered he had cheated on her with her best friend. Four days later, exactly a month after the murders, Mugford gave a statement to the police, implicating him.View image in fullscreenJeremy Bamber being led into Chelmsford crown court at the start of his trial, October 1986.Photograph: Peter Case/Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesIt soon emerged at Bamber’s trial how seriously the crime scene had been contaminated. At least 43 officers had trampled through the farmhouse, clothing and bedding had been destroyed, clumsy reconstructions resulted in bodies and murder weapons being displaced. Alarmingly, the crime scene was not secured for 32 days. The most reliable record of the crime is the series of photos police photographer Detective Constable Bird started taking two-and-a-half hours after officers first entered the farmhouse, although the scene was already heavily compromised.A bundle of crime-scene photos was disclosed to Bamber’s defence before the 1986 trial. Fifteen years later, in 2001, a second bundle was disclosed to his new team, to prepare for his appeal. Finally, in 2011, following decades of legal battles and multiple court orders regarding non-disclosed evidence, Essex police handed over 406 crime scene negatives to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the body tasked with investigating potential miscarriages of justice. When the CCRC refused to pay to have the negatives developed into hi-res photographs, Bamber’s supporters paid £2,295 to have them developed.Late last year Bamber agreed to hand the crime scene photographs to the Guardian so we could get them forensically analysed. We asked Carney-Gannon, who has given expert evidence in more than 2,000 cases, to examine the bloodstain patterns, focusing on the master bedroom. In the 41 years since the murders, these photos have never been analysed in this way before. Bloodstain analysts use biology, chemistry, physics and maths to examine the size, shape and location of blood left at a crime scene, to reconstruct violent events.Once seen, the crime scene photographs cannot be forgotten. Nevill Bamber was found in the kitchen, his head slumped in a coal scuttle. The twins were dead in their beds.View image in fullscreenThe Bible that was found next to Caffell.The Guardian asked Carney-Gannon to focus on the master bedroom. We believed that the crime scene there suggested a struggle had taken place between Caffell and June Bamber.Caffell was found on the far side of the master bedroom with a bloodstained Bible by her side and the rifle on top of her. June Bamber lay in her bloodied nightdress against the door. There were multiple blood drops on the carpet between Caffell and June Bamber.While Carney-Gannon stated she could not tell from the bloodstain pattern whether there had been a struggle in the room, her other findings were more interesting and seem more significant.At Bamber’s trial, the prosecution argued that he had led Caffell into the master bedroom, asked her to lie down, then shot her twice in the neck. The prosecution argued that she must have been murdered, because it was impossible for her to shoot herself in the neck twice. This has long been refuted by scientific evidence showing the first shot, into her lower neck, was not fatal.View image in fullscreenThe master bedroom at White House Farm, where Caffell and June Bamber were found dead. Bloodstains on the bed suggest June sat on it after being shot.At trial, the pathologist Peter Vanezis was called by the prosecution, but the evidence he presented challenges the prosecution case. Vanezis believed Caffell had been sitting up when she received both injuries, and fell backwards immediately after the second shot. He indicated that Caffell could have walked around briefly after receiving the first of her neck wounds. Vanezis told the court that, from the pathological evidence alone, he could not say whether Caffell had been murdered or taken her own life. Despite being a witness for the prosecution, he testified at the trial: “My examination did not reveal anything to contradict the suicide theory.”Carney-Gannon’s analysis of the bloodstain patterns reaches the same conclusion – that Caffell was sitting when she was shot. “In my opinion, the blood stains to Sheila Caffell’s clothing and right arm suggest she was sitting upright as the shot entered under the chin, and blood began to run down her upper front and splashed on to her right forearm. As she began falling backwards, blood on the front of her clothing began to run to the side, and as her arms fell, blood on her forearm adjusted direction due to gravity.”The forensic biologist says the blood pattern analysis cannot help determine whether Caffell shot the rest of the family or whether Jeremy Bamber did. However, throughout the trial Mr Justice Drake laid out the zero-sum nature of the case to the jury. In summing up, he said: “On the facts of this case, the killer was either Sheila or Jeremy Bamber and therefore it follows that if you are sure that Sheila did not carry out the killings, then it must be Jeremy Bamber who did.”Carney-Gannon refutes the theory proposed at trial that Bamber shot Caffell while she was lying down. “If she had been lying on the floor when he shot her, then in my opinion, this would not readily explain the pattern of blood on Sheila Caffell’s clothing, particularly the veering of the blood to her right side, since she would not have fallen after the shot.” She says she assumes that if he had shot her while she was lying down, he would have had to first incapacitate her.View image in fullscreenCaffell was a model known as ‘Bambi’.Photograph: PA Wire/Press Association ImagesAt trial, it was never suggested that Bamber had incapacitated Caffell. The prosecution argued that Caffell was passive and compliant due to the high dose of haloperidol, an antipsychotic drug, that she had been taking. In fact, her dosage had just been dramatically reduced because it was causing severe side-effects, including muscle stiffness and a “zombie-like” state. The defence argued that the sudden reduction had caused a psychotic episode that resulted in the massacre.Carney-Gannon does not rule out the possibility that Bamber shot his sister, but suggests the only feasible way he could have done so is to have shot her under the chin while she was standing up. “The possibility that Ms Caffell was upright and Jeremy Bamber held the rifle barrel under her chin and fired, cannot be ignored.” Even here, though, Carney-Gannon says she struggles to explain the blood patterns she has analysed. “In my opinion, that scenario might result in similar blood patterns to her upper clothing, but might not readily explain the blood on her forearm, if her arms were by her side at the point she received the shot.”At trial, Vanezis, the pathologist for the prosecution, explicitly ruled out the possibility that Caffell had been shot while standing. He pointed out that her nightdress would have been more heavily stained if she had been standing when shot the first time, or if she stood up after having been shot. In his expert testimony, Vanezis said: “The nature of the blood stains to the nightdress suggested that Sheila Caffell was sitting up when she received both injuries. After the second injury she would have immediately fallen back.”Carney-Gannon’s analysis of the blood patterns around June Bamber suggests she suffered a horribly slow, messy death. June received wounds to her chest, arms, upper back and head. Carney-Gannon believes the bloodstains on the bed suggest June sat on it after being shot. “In my opinion, this distribution of blood on this location of the bedding is explained if June Bamber sat in this position while injured and bleeding from wounds in her arms, back, and possibly other areas, and with blood on her hands,” she writes.Her report, which has been peer-reviewed, comments on the “numerous blood drips on the carpet around the body of June Bamber, across the floor at the foot of the bed, and on the floor at the far side of the bed where the body of Sheila Caffell was found ... The number of drips and the extent of the distribution suggest a person (or persons) who was actively bleeding has moved around these areas … In my opinion these findings are explained if June Bamber was the injured person moving around the bedroom whilst bleeding.” The blood staining on June’s feet “supports the suggestion she walked around the bedroom whilst bleeding and dripping blood on to the carpet”.View image in fullscreenThe forensic biologist Sue Carney-Gannon identified bullet holes on the bed.Carney-Gannon has also identified two bullet holes and a cartridge casing on the bed – indicated by green arrows in the photo above – where the shooter appears to have missed their target. She says she cannot discount the possibility that the bullet holes may be the result of bullets that hit and then exited June Bamber, but she believes they are likely to be “the result of shots that did not strike any of the deceased parties”.At trial, ballistics expert Malcolm Fletcher stated that every shot had hit the target area, saying there were “25 hits out of 25”, indicating that 25 bullets and 25 empty cartridge cases had been found. The prosecution argued that Bamber – a skilled huntsman – had to be the killer, because Caffell was insufficiently experienced with a rifle to have a 100% hit rate. The defence argued that Caffell did have limited knowledge of handling .22 rifles because she had grown up on the farm and attended rural shoots.The bullets identified by Carney-Gannon imply that the shooter was less skilled than has been suggested. After all, not only does Carney-Gannon suspect that some bullets missed June Bamber, she believes June probably moved around for some time after being shot.Carney-Gannon’s findings support a forensic investigation the Guardian commissioned from the prestigious forensic physician Professor Jason Payne-James, earlier this year, into whether or not a silencer was used in the shooting of Caffell.The silencer in question was found three days after the massacre, in a downstairs storage cupboard at White House Farm, by relatives who went on to inherit from the Bamber estate. This silencer was crucial in the case against Bamber. The prosecution argued that Caffell’s arms were not long enough to kill herself had the silencer been attached to the rifle, and, if she had shot herself, she would obviously have been unable to replace the silencer in the downstairs cupboard. At trial, it was stated that blood belonging to Caffell was found inside this silencer.Mr Justice Drake told the jury that if they were convinced beyond reasonable doubt that a silencer was used, then Bamber was guilty of the murders. Minutes before they convicted Bamber, the jury returned to ask whether the blood in the silencer definitely belonged to Caffell. The judge told them it did. In fact, it was merely her blood grouping, which she shared with Robert Boutflour, who regularly used the guns. Later testing suggested the blood found in the silencer might not even be human.Payne-James concluded that a silencer had not been used, and that the two shots to Caffell’s neck and chin were either contact or close-contact wounds. This dismantled much of the prosecution’s case against Bamber, and is consistent with Carney-Gannon’s view.View image in fullscreenThe latest analysis of blood patterns suggest that Caffell killed her family and then herself.The new findings will be handed to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the body responsible for investigating alleged miscarriages of justice and referring them to the Court of Appeal if it concludes there is a “real possibility” that a conviction may be unsafe. The commission spent four years examining four out of 10 points in the latest submission by Bamber, before rejecting them.After being criticised for its low referral record in recent years (1.5% of total applications in 2023/24 were referred to the Court of Appeal), the CCRC’s chair and CEO were forced to resign last year. Under the leadership of interim chair Dame Vera Baird KC, there has been a sharp increase in referrals – 45 cases were referred in the 2025/26 financial year, compared with 31 in 2024/25. Baird accused the previous regime of “almost looking for reasons not to refer”.It is hard to see how the commission will not be swayed by Carney-Gannon’s findings, especially under its new leadership. After all, the new evidence regarding stray bullets that were shot at the bed; June Bamber sitting down and walking around after being hit by an unskilled shooter; and, most importantly, the blood stains suggesting that Sheila Caffell shot herself, turns the case on its head.A spokesperson for the Jeremy Bamber Innocence Campaign says: “This report supports what Jeremy has said all along, that he did not murder his family. The report is clear that the blood patterns present at the scene are consistent with the initial conclusion drawn by the police at the scene, that his seriously mentally ill sister Sheila killed her family and then herself. These two terrible tragedies have been compounded by how long it is taking the appeal system to recognise this in the light of the scientific evidence now available.”A spokesperson for Essex police said: “In August 1985, the lives of five people, including two children, were needlessly, tragically and callously cut short when they were murdered in their own home by Jeremy Bamber. In the years that followed, this case has been the subject of several appeals and reviews by the Court of Appeal and the Criminal Cases Review Commission – all of these processes have never found anything other than Bamber is the person responsible for killing his adoptive parents Nevill and June, sister Sheila Caffell and her two sons Nicholas and Daniel.”This article was amended on 23 October 2026. An earlier version of the final paragraph appeared without any attribution. It was amended to make clear that this was a quote from an Essex police spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsCriminal Cases Review CommissionThe Bamber filesJeremy BamberUK criminal justiceShare

title: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus  | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda
Content: Travellers stand next to an Ebola awareness banner at Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos, Nigeria.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersView image in fullscreenTravellers stand next to an Ebola awareness banner at Murtala Muhammed international airport in Lagos, Nigeria.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersEbolaMystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virusSwitzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in UgandaCarlos Mureithiin Nairobi and agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHealth officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading toUganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.The Ugandan government reportedEbolacases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.TheAfricaCentres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsEbolaNigeriaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaSwitzerlandUgandanewsShareReuse this content

Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Meghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police
Content: Meghan Markle said her thoughts were ‘with any children who may have been harmed’.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenMeghan Markle said her thoughts were ‘with any children who may have been harmed’.Photograph: GettyMeghan, the Duchess of SussexDuchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against fatherMeghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met policeCaroline DaviesFri 23 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
