I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”Sources said although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2018, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the Rasp unit within the Met police.It is understood the Met has not previously investigated Markle Sr, nor is it currently doing so. The force said it was making internal inquiries regarding officers from Rasp being involved in the passing on of a letter.A Met spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s royalty and specialist protection command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.”Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.The FBI said in a statement: “The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”The undersecretary for the Philippines’ justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC the matter was being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu.The interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”.Meghan’s father has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”Meghan’s half-sister Samantha Markle has defended their father, accusing her brother Markle Jr of “making up lies” to make money.She told the Mail: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”She alleged her brother made the allegations days after their father cut off his funds, “and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media”.She alleged the computers were not in her father’s possession for two years and he could have been set up. “That leaves a lot of room for tampering,” she said.Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchyPhilippinesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes | Tibet | The Guardian
description: Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded
Content: Rescuers searching through building ruins in Nagqu city after a quake hit northern Tibet.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRescuers searching through building ruins in Nagqu city after a quake hit northern Tibet.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesTibetMagnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homesSearch and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recordedAssociated PressFri 23 Oct 2026 03.53 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 00.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA magnitude-7 earthquake has hitTibet, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and destroying hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media have said.Search and rescue efforts continued after at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed to help rescue efforts. Supplies were also sent into the region, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents, folding beds, torches and winter clothing.The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 119 miles (191km) east-north-east of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 11 miles.The agency recorded at least seven aftershocks of magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 6 miles. Videos posted by CCTV showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.Moment magnitude-7 earthquake strikes China’s TibetChina’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to stop trains passing through the region.More than 300 police officers were dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue services had sent almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported. Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.The earthquake caused rockfalls, forcing local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snow was expected in the region over the next three days, Xinhua said.China’s president, Xi Jinping, called for an all-out effort in the rescue operation and medical relief work.Nagqu is more than 185 miles north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa. Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025,at least 126 peoplewere killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.In August, a disastrous flood hit the border of Tibet and Nepal. China’stight grip on informationprevented international media from visiting the affected regions on the Tibetan side,obscuringthe scale of the damage.In December 2023,a quake in remote Gansu provincein north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.Tibet is a particularly seismically active area. The high-altitude region was taken under Chinese control in the 1950s and its people, who are predominantly ethnic Tibetans, have had a tense relationship with the authorities in Beijing since. As well as being one of the poorest regions in China, many Tibetans reject Beijing-imposed controls on their culture and religion.Agence France-Presse contribute to this reportExplore more on these topicsTibetEarthquakesChinaNatural disastersAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia | Australia weather | The Guardian
description: Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday
Content: The BoM is warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe BoM is warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianAustralia weatherThunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of AustraliaParts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by SundayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdeshola Orewith Australian Associated PressFri 23 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSevere thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenchedQueensland.Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding acrossSouth Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop inTasmaniaovernight into Sunday morning.Cloudy with a chance of moths: bogong swarms are bamboozling weather radars across NSWRead more“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-easternVictoria, Sydney and Brisbane.“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.Explore more on these topicsAustralia weatherQueenslandVictoriaSouth AustraliaTasmanianewsShareReuse this content

title: Jordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlight | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: David Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates looms
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: David Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates looms
Content: Australian Greens leader David Shoebridge (left) and WA senator Jordon Steele-John.Composite: AAPView image in fullscreenAustralian Greens leader David Shoebridge (left) and WA senator Jordon Steele-John.Composite: AAPAustralian GreensAnalysisJordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlightSarah Basford CanalesDavid Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates loomsGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastFri 23 Oct 2026 18.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.22 EDTShareMore than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon Steele-John had behaved inappropriately towards women made headlines, his position in the party remains in limbo and its new leader’s handling of the issue in question.David Shoebridge’s first major challenge at the helm of the federal Greens came earlier this month when the Nine newspapers reporteda three-page letter had been sent to himurging an independent investigation into Steele-John.It referred to secondhand allegations that the Western Australian senator had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.As a progressive party that prides itself on taking such matters seriously and fairly, it made sense that Shoebridge announced the 32-year-old’s leave amid an independent probe into the claims.But the process quickly became more complicated. Days later, a defiant Steele-John rejected the allegations against him,denied he agreed to take leave from parliament, and accused an internal faction within the WA Greens of playing “nasty political games” in its decision to release the letter to the media.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereSteele-John said he made a public statement because he didn’t want his silence on the letter’s claims to be perceived as guilt.While Shoebridge insists Steele-John agreed to take leave, he acknowledges he alone does not have the power to force the senator to do so.Only if two-thirds of the party room – or more than seven members – decided to expel him in a secret ballot would Steele-John have to comply.Such a move would be nuclear. Even if the WA Greens’ independent investigation clears him of any wrongdoing, Steele-John’s standing in the party room would be shattered.The week ahead under scrutinySenate estimates is a time for members of the upper house to have their moment in the spotlight. For the Greens, it’s a chance to extricate answers about government policies from carefully trained bureaucrats to drive home a political point.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGreens leader denies knowledge of ‘secret dossier’ on how to handle Jordon Steele-John misconduct allegationsRead moreWith theNDIS undergoing major changesbetween now and the decade’s end, Steele-John, who is championed and well-liked within the disability community as the party’s disability spokesperson, will not attend.Steele-John issued a statement late Friday saying he had explored attending digitally, but had “been informed that would also be unacceptable”.“As such I have decided not to return next week and will instead focus on the independent and timely investigation I hope is soon commenced by the Greens WA,” Steele-John said.For many supporters within and outside the Greens, the optics of allowing a federal party member accused of sexual misconduct – even though a complainant has not directly come forward to make those allegations – to continue public duties would have been a tough pill to swallow. Particularly as the“manosphere” phenomenonand backlash against the #MeToo movement gain momentum in mainstream society.The question over whether the allegations were politically motivated by adversaries of Steele-John looking to gain advantage in the state’s pre-selection is a part of the equation.But the fact remains that the rumours have persisted over the senator’s time in office. Even if they are malicious, as Steele-John contends, the simpler option would still be to stand aside and settle them while they are investigated.The decision over whether to force Steele-John to take leave will be as much about Shoebridge’s leadership as it is about the party’s processes.The party room, and its membership more broadly, prides itself on being a movement based on consensus decision-making.Shoebridge will need the support of the party room to take the expulsion route. How he handles this issue will also set the tone for the rest of his leadership and, depending on his actions, could prompt an ugly battle with Steele-John.It’s a quagmire – politically, legally and ethically.There are unlikely to be any winners.Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensAustralian politicsDavid ShoebridgeWestern AustraliaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse | Australian economy | The Guardian
description: High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries
Content: Jim Chalmers has revealed his officials are downgrading their forecasts ahead of the mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenJim Chalmers has revealed his officials are downgrading their forecasts ahead of the mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian economyAnalysisJim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worsePatrick ComminsHigh inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worriesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastFri 23 Oct 2026 00.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 00.56 EDTShareJim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busydowngrading their forecastsahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.In other words, things are getting worse, not better.Economy set to worsen, with higher unemployment and weaker growth on the way, Jim Chalmers revealsRead moreOvernight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150,echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fundearlier this month.That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace fora potential fifth interest rate hikeon 3 November.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereMeanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hitsome serious wobbles.Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.Odds of fifth interest rate hike this year shorten as RBA deputy warns inflation outlook ‘worsening’Read moreProductivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editorExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyJim ChalmersAustralian politicsInterest ratesReserve Bank of AustraliaUnemploymentBusinessanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl
Content: Scene of a drive-by shooting in Trappes, a suburb near Paris. Over 15 minutes, the gunman fired at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersView image in fullscreenScene of a drive-by shooting in Trappes, a suburb near Paris. Over 15 minutes, the gunman fired at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersFranceMacron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near ParisGunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girlAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 23 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 15.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west ofParison Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”.He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”Rabeh said everyone inFrancehad a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night.The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable.The man killed was named as Pengo Bossio Wangi in an Instagrampostby the mixed martial arts academy of which he was a member. The Atch Academy paid tribute to a man who “set an example” and said that memories of “his smile, his energy, and his generosity will remain etched within our walls and in our hearts”.Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from ⁠Yvelines.The ‌shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday sawone of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.Additional reporting byYassin El-MouddenExplore more on these topicsFranceEuropeMarine Le PenParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Melania Trump has helped broker ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town, says White House – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: Residents in Oleshky have been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis due to the lack of food, electricity and other resources
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Residents in Oleshky have been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis due to the lack of food, electricity and other resources
Content: 09.40 EDTMelania Trump helps broker ceasefire in Russian-occupied town where residents were starving to deathSmoke rises from a residential neighborhood in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region of Ukraine on 22 September 2026. (Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade “Borysfen” via AP)Photograph: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade “Borysfen”/APThe White House has issued a statement saying Melania Trump has helped broker a ‘ceasefire’ in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where residents have been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis due to the lack of food, electricity and other resources.The small town in southern Kherson has been the centre of an increasingly desperate humanitarian crisis under Russian occupation.Since May, Russia has failed to deliver food, medicine or other essential goods to the area leading to deaths from starvation and disease. There has also been problems with the burial of bodies and sanitation, as the local morgue has been destroyed and there is no running water.Russia andUkrainehave accused the other of blocking supplies to the population of the ⁠town ​which Ukrainian forces ​want to retake.Ukraine has previously appealed for a ceasefire to evacuate the estimated 2,000 civilians left in the town – but Russia hadn’t made any commitments.Earlier this week, Pope Leo called for an intervention while the Kremlin said Putin had discussed the situation with Donald Trump.The White House now say both countries have agreed to pause military action “to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway. A ceasefire is set to come into effect on 29 October.Map“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the ⁠brink of disaster. Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised ​primarily ​of elderly residents ​who urgently need medical attention, medicine, ​food, and ‌clean water,” Melania ​Trump ​said in the statement.“It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she added.There is no comment from Moscow or Ukraine yet. The Guardian’s international correspondents are looking into the statement and attempting to corroborate it with their sources.ShareUpdated at10.21 EDT

title: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis
Content: Faisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAView image in fullscreenFaisal bin Farhan of Saudi Arabia, Ishaq Dar of Pakistan, Hakan Fidan of Turkey, Jean-Noël Barrot of France, Johann Wadephul of Germany, Ed Miliband of the UK and Antonio Tajani of Italy at the summit in Istanbul on Friday.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAMiddle East and north AfricaUS and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on IranMultinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisisPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 23 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForeign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes onIranwhile talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey andGermany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed theMecca defensive security pactin August, a grouping Egypt may join.The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”He made no criticism of the US but accused “theHouthisand Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”Explore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaEuropeIranMiddle East peace talksUS-Israel war on IranHouthisIran nuclear dealnewsShareReuse this content

title: Opposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of election | Spain | The Guardian
description: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Content: Pedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPAView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPASpainOpposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of electionVideo shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoingAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 23 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.Launchedthis weekacross the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks aboutreceiving a university postthanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks abouthiding jewelleryin a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenA still from the People’s party AI-generated video featuring a deepfake of Begoña Gomez.Computer-generated: @ppopular/XThe Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister,told the broadcaster TVEon Friday.While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.A majority of the nine legal expertsconsulted by the newspaper El Paísconcurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – tocrack downon the impact of disinformation.“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticutidentified more than 200such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.Explore more on these topicsSpainPedro SánchezAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
Content: Drone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.Photograph: 34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen'/ReutersView image in fullscreenDrone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.Photograph: 34th Separate Marine Brigade 'Borysfen'/ReutersUkraineRussia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisisPeople in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weedsPjotr SauerandPeter BeaumontFri 23 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House has said that Russia andUkrainehave agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.Map showing location of OleshkyThe White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered byMelania Trump, and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council ofEurope. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.Lubinets ⁠told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve ⁠demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient ​quantity of ‌humanitarian ‌aid will be delivered to ‌meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure ‌that this is not just a ​one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” ⁠he said.Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions tothe Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops,began last weekafter Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspendedintelligence-sharingwith Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia andbegin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row?Read moreAmong Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.Explore more on these topicsUkraineElon MuskTrump administrationEuropeDonald TrumpDrones (military)US foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed | Israel | The Guardian
description: Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight
Content: Israeli forces patrolling Hebron as Benjamin Netanyahu visited the area on Friday.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenIsraeli forces patrolling Hebron as Benjamin Netanyahu visited the area on Friday.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIsraelIsrael launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killedBenjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfightEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andLorenzo TondoFri 23 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city.Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting.The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted avideoof himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight.The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers.Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead more“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of theWest Bank,” Dahleh said. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli lawyer, said Smotrich’s video was a “direct admission” that the demolitions were a collective punishment. He noted that deterrence had been used as an excuse for collective punishment since antiquity.The defence minister, Israel Katz, promised further mass demolitions and forced displacement. He drew an explicit comparison with Gaza and said Hebron would be targeted in the same way as Jenin refugee camp, where nearly 20,000 people have been forced from their homes. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, with about 250,000 residents.Katz said: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron. Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.”Netanyahu announced that plans had been drawn up for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967, when Israeli forces occupied the Palestinian territory and forcibly displaced about 300,000 Palestinians.No date had been set “but it is on the way”, he said in a statement that also pledged mass forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron and the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.The attack was launched by two men armed with an assault rifle and a handgun, according to the Israeli military. The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.An AFP photographer who was on the way to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.Prominent Israelis, including a candidate for the far-right Amcha Yisrael party, shared conspiracy theories groundlessly accusing the AFP photographer of links to the gunmen after he documented the Hebron attack.The Foreign Press Association (FPA) said it was deeply alarmed by claims the photographer had been tipped off, describing them as “dangerous and defamatory”. “He is a longtime professional who was on his way to another assignment and courageously documented what he saw in keeping with his professional duties,” the FPA said in a statement.The incident came a week aftersettlers severely injured the photographer Heidi Levineas she documented attacks on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also denied entry to several European journalists and an academic.Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.Attacks have intensified further since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September. Israeli settler militantshave used violenceto stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.Israel holds elections on Tuesday. The current far-right coalition, which backs settlers politically and financially, is seeking to shore up voter support in the face of polls that show it is likely to loose its majority.Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, also travelled to Hebron on Friday and demanded the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement, which is already heavily curtailed by Israeli controls, checkpoints and roadblocks.Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Content: Tensions in the Middle East have been rising, with Iran claiming to have hit commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz and Washington ordering some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenTensions in the Middle East have been rising, with Iran claiming to have hit commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz and Washington ordering some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersOilOil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on IranBrent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentresLauren AlmeidaFri 23 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched againstIran.Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch$126 a barrelby the end of April.Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to havestruck four commercial shipsin the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leaveSaudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStreeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricaIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’ | Global development | The Guardian
description: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
Author: Amrit Dhillon
Headline: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
Content: From next month, prodded by the findings of India’s supreme court, prices of 137 cancer drugs are expected to fall by up to 70%.Photograph: Rupendra Rawat/AlamyView image in fullscreenFrom next month, prodded by the findings of India’s supreme court, prices of 137 cancer drugs are expected to fall by up to 70%.Photograph: Rupendra Rawat/AlamyGlobal developmentIndia slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosedSupported byAbout this contentAmrit Dhillonin DelhiFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.From next month,137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaperas the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carrieda vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.View image in fullscreenSarojam Radhakrishan initiated the court action after being unable to pay for her cancer drugs.Photograph: FacebookThe judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trademark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.A 30% trade margincap on the price of 42 drugshas been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.Whenever the IndianCancerSociety holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”View image in fullscreenThe supreme court in New Delhi, where judges have asked the government to explain why the price cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not all non-patented drugsPhotograph: APIndia records about1.56m new cancer cases annually– up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battleRead more“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentGlobal healthCancerHealthPharmaceuticals industryIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Blue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boom | BBC | The Guardian
description: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Author: Tara Conlan
Headline: BBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers say
Content: Creatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoView image in fullscreenCreatures filmed in the deep ocean are ‘more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real’, said the Blue Planet III producers.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoBBCBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomBBC series deliberately uses ‘more organic’ shots to assure viewers animals are not AI-generated, producers sayTara ConlanFri 23 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDavid Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III deliberately includes cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hitBBCseries is returning with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed “stonefish” cam.Since the first Blue Planet, TVs and cameras have evolved to give viewers sharper, higher definition pictures. But the combination of the rise in AI and the extraordinary sequences and fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios’ natural history unit for this series led producers to include what they called more “organic” footage and less polished shots, to show that the animals were not AI-generated.View image in fullscreen‘No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame,’ said the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jo HaleyThe executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI, “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it’s completely real”.She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”But now such things are being left in as “we’re really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.For the first time, the BBC’s specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It’s all real photography.”Bootle added that as we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they’ve seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.View image in fullscreenThe hit BBC series returns with cutting-edge technology, including the world’s first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed ‘stonefish’.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jose BrancoThat includes never-before-seen action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV – developed by the programme’s producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.Over the four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton, creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, camera operators wearing leg-mounted scooters to create immersive TikTok-style diving footage and using lasers to film deep-sea creatures.Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and footage involving penguins that echoes the Planet Earth II,‘iguana v snakes’sequence.Threats to the ocean as well as its resilience are addressed in the series. Episodes show how the climatecrisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, and the issue of plastics raised in Blue Planet II continues with a story about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.White added: “What’s wonderful is he hasn’t lost his curiosity … he’s still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”Asked if the BBC’s£500m cost-cutting drivewould affect BBC Studios’ renowned natural history reputation, White said she could not comment on that but pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series.Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1November on BBC1 and iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBBCNature documentariesScience and nature TVBBC OneDavid AttenboroughMarine lifeAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Online safety laws have failed to protect children in UK, Ofcom admits | Children | The Guardian
description: Campaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regime
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Campaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regime
Content: Under the Online Safety Act, tech giants had to protect children from harmful content with a series of duties introduced in summer 2025.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenUnder the Online Safety Act, tech giants had to protect children from harmful content with a series of duties introduced in summer 2025.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianChildrenOnline safety laws have failed to protect children in UK, Ofcom admitsCampaigners call lack of progress ‘staggering’ as online regulator issues review of first nine months of new regimeRobert BoothUK technology editorFri 23 Oct 2026 18.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLandmark online safety measures have failed to limit the proportion of children suffering harm from social media, the UK’s online regulator has admitted, in an assessment branded “staggering” by campaigners.The proportion of children being fed unsafe content that often left them frightened, confused and upset, was almost unchanged, according to anOfcomreview of the first nine months of supposedly strict requirements on social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram.Under the Online Safety Act, the tech giants had to protect children from harmful content including pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny and bullying, with a series of specific duties introduced in summer 2025.But Ofcomfoundthat “at a total level there was no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content over the first nine months after the children’s safety duties came into force in July 2025”.It called the finding “concerning” and said there was no evidence indicating a change in the severity of harm since the flagship regulations, under the Online Safety Act, took effect.Examples of harms included children being shown the murder of Charlie Kirk, graphic pornography and weapon-related content making them feel unsafe in their schools and neighbourhoods. Personalised recommendation feeds powered by “for you” algorithms were repeatedly found by Ofcom to be at the root of the continuing tide of harmful material.The findings come a week after a coroner concluded that access to the suicide-related material on TikTok may have played a significant part in the decision of Adriana Retyte, a 14-year-old pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, to take her own life in May.They come a day after Clavicular, 20, a popular social media influencer who promotes surgery and drugs as part of extreme male beauty regimes and has appeared with Andrew Tate, pleaded not guilty to rape in a US court, raising fresh concerns about the influence of “manosphere” content creators.Ofcom’s research included tracking the exposure of UK children aged eight to 17 to harmful content on user-to-user services, its impact and their use of safety tools and an analysis of children’s wellbeing after exposure to harmful content. The assessment has been shared with Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport.NSPCC, a child protection charity, said the findings showed that children were being exposed to harmful content at an “alarming rate”, which it said was echoed in the flow of calls for help to Childline, its online and telephone support service. Rani Govender, the head of child safety online, said “progress is not happening nearly fast enough”.“Tech companies have had months to act, yet too many platforms are still built to keep children hooked with their algorithms continuing to push harmful content to their young users,” she said. “We urgently need stronger action from tech companies to rein in features that drive harm to children and stop putting business interests over their safety obligations.”Dame Melanie Dawes, the watchdog’s chief executive, this week told MPs: “We do not see a safety culture from these large social media companies.” The regulator is already facing a wave of legal actions from tech companies challenging its powers including the Instagram operator Meta, as well as TikTok and X, owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX group. It haswarnedit risks being “absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms”.Children most commonly reported encountering pornographic content via personalised feeds, and girls, in particular, reported feeling confused or upset after seeing such content, Ofcom found. Suicide and eating disorder content was also driven mostly through personal feeds, with girls most likely to encounter both types of harmful material. The Ofcom review also found that “young men and boys consuming motivational and self-improvement content can rapidly become exposed to more extreme content which includes the promotion of misogyny and racism”. Misspelled hashtags and coded language are often used to bypass content moderation systems that would otherwise block harmful misogynistic content.Ian Russell, the father of Molly Russell, who took her life aged 14 in 2017 after viewing suicide material on social media, told the Guardian the lack of progress was “staggering but sadly not surprising”. He blamed “timidity and lack of action” from the regulator and said: “It is time that Ofcom stood up for children and investigated the major flaws in TikTok and Instagram’s design features, not just small technicalities that have been their focus so far.”An Ofcom spokesperson said: “This is an industry that’s been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years. And so while significant progress is being made – including the introduction of widespread age checks, stronger protections against grooming, and tougher safeguards against child sexual exploitation and abuse – we’re under no illusion that there is much for the industry still to do. We’ve shown that tech firms that don’t comply with their duties can expect enforcement action.”It said the data did not cover the period from this spring when it said it stepped up pressure on Facebook, YouTube, Snap, Roblox and TikTok over child safety issues. It also said it recorded some reductions in harmful content on platforms including the games Minecraft and Call of Duty and YouTube, Pinterest and Facebook.
