In July it launched aninvestigationinto TikTok over child safety concerns, including how it checks users are adults or children.The continuing risks to children come before a planned Australia-style social media ban in the UK for under-16s which is due, from next spring, to cover platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X, but not messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal.However campaigners have warned that must not overshadow the need to enforce protections under the Online Safety Act.“Children will continue to face risks on services covered by the act but not the proposed ban, including gaming and messaging platforms,” said Mitali Sud, a senior policy manager atInternetMatters, a child online safety campaign. “Sixteen- and 17-year-olds will still use social media. A social media ban cannot replace the need to make online services safer for children.”UK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14Read moreA government spokesperson said platforms needed to do more to protect children from harmful content.“That’s why we are taking bold action to strengthen protections for children from risks of harm online – banning social media from offering their services to under-16s and protecting kids from harmful functionalities like livestreaming and stranger communications on a wide range of services, including gaming services,” they said.“When it comes to children’s safety, we are not and never will be bystanders. Platforms have both a moral and legal duty to protect children and we expect them to work with us to set a new normal for future generations.”TikTok, Meta, X and Google were contacted for comment.In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsChildrenOfcomSocial media banSocial mediaInternet safetyInternetDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of England
Content: A tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks the pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall, on Friday.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/GettyView image in fullscreenA tree brought down by Storm Austen blocks the pavement in Falmouth, Cornwall, on Friday.Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/GettyExtreme weatherThousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west EnglandDozens of schools in Cornwall also affected as Storm Boelo heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and north of EnglandJamie GriersonandYassin El-MouddenFri 23 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of homes are without power and schools were closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores.Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. By 3pm, more than 31,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid.Dozens of schools acrossCornwallwere forced to delay their opening, while others did not open at all. Flights were disrupted at airports in the south-west and on the Channel Islands, and passengers were being advised to check the status of their flight before travelling.Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet having been stranded on the UK mainland. The Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday.Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since it closed to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained. English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair.National Rail reported severe disruption across the rail network, with cancellations acrossEngland, Wales and Scotland.Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaking at a wildfires summit in Aintree, Liverpool, on Friday.Photograph: WPA/GettyA government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked whether the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.“It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”National Grid said engineers had so far restored power to more than 52,000 properties affected by Storm Austen.In Sussex, Southern Water said a power cut had affected a reservoir in the area and that it was arranging deliveries of bottled water for customers affected by the disruption.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.View image in fullscreenStorm Austen hits Newhaven in East Sussex.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersThe Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and it warned of danger to life from flying debris. It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and travel disruption.In anticipation of Storm Boelo, train lines in parts of northern and western Scotland are scheduled to close early at the weekend.Services south and west of Kilwinning in North Ayrshire and the Oban and Mallaig lines will shut on Saturday evening, while the line between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach in the Highlands will be out of service on Sunday. Trains are expected to run at reduced speed elsewhere in the country.The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherUK weatherEnglandCornwallnewsShareReuse this content

title: Criminals recruiting children to damage Greater Manchester HMOs, police believe | UK news | The Guardian
description: Houses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeks
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Houses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeks
Content: Pictures of damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments on social media.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPictures of damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments on social media.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesUK newsCriminals recruiting children to damage Greater Manchester HMOs, police believeHouses being targeted because they are thought to hold immigrants, with dozens of properties affected in recent weeksHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentFri 23 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCriminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe.In recent weeks, dozens of properties have been targeted across Greater Manchester, mostly in Salford, but also in Stockport and Tameside.The houses that have been attacked are either HMOs (houses in multiple occupation), or properties that have been mistaken for HMOs. Police have received at least 46 separate reports of criminal damage, with cars also targeted alongside houses.Windows have been smashed, and walls and doors have been sprayed with graffiti reading “fuck off” and “no HMO”. Houses are being targeted because they are believed to hold immigrants or refugees.Ch Supt Marcus Noden said: “We suspect vulnerable people are being exploited and paid to damage buildings they believe are HMOs. Some of those being exploited are believed to be children.”“This recent spate of damage is not being tolerated,” he added. “A 42-year-old man has today been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage at an address in Salford overnight. He remains in our custody for questioning.”Previously Noden said that officers were “taking this spate of damage extremely seriously and are continuing to relentlessly target offenders, including those who we believe are using and exploiting children to orchestrate the criminality”.Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.”In a statement, the council said: “We have serious concerns that the impact of the banners is highly likely to spread misinformation, escalate cohesion issues in communities and the potential for inciteful behaviour.”Police have also said that social media is fuelling the attacks, which began on 5 October, with online platforms being used to “push the message out across different areas”.Posts with pictures of the damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments, many of them praising the attacks and predicting further violence.However, some have also been critical of the criminal campaign of damage, including domestic abuse survivors who had recently been housed in HMOs.Four people have been arrested this week in relation to the attacks. On Monday, a 46-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, and on Wednesday a 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.Police have also made previous arrests in relation to the spate of criminal damage, including a 13-year-old boy.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tommy Robinson ‘threatened people and acted like a bully’, jury told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Prosecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Prosecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’
Content: Tommy Robinson at Southwark crown court in London on Friday. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson at Southwark crown court in London on Friday. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two journalists.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAUK newsTommy Robinson ‘threatened people and acted like a bully’, jury toldProsecution says Robinson guilty of harassment of Daily Mail journalists because we do not live in a ‘vigilante world’Ben QuinnFri 23 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Robinson is guilty of harassing two journalists because we do not live in a “vigilante world”, jurors have been told, as the prosecution sought to use the far-right activist’s words against him.Robinson had posted a video in which he told Daily Mail journalists he would find them after they wrote about his alleged role influencing England’s 2024 riots. He told them he had obtained details of where they and their families lived and warned them to abide by “men’s rules”.Ben Holt, prosecuting, told the jury: “Let’s get real, shall we, and not live in a vigilante world where ‘men’s rules’ apply? Whatever they are. Let’s ground ourselves in a country where there is law and order.”Summing up the case, Holt said Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had accepted that sharing images of journalists’ homes and partial photos of their loved ones was intended to exert pressure.However, he rejected Robinson’s insistence that the journalists on the receiving end of what the prosecution described as “bullyboy and intimidatory” conduct would not have been in fear of violence as a result.Robinson, 43, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence in 2024 to two journalists who were working for the Mail, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies the charges.Robinson said in evidence that he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified a hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk.But Holt said Robinson had never asked for the image to be taken down in calls and messages to the journalists and the Daily Mail’s editor. “Instead, he just threatened people. He acted like a bully,” he said.Holt repeated the words Robinson had directed at the journalists: “Good for the goose, good for the gander. You are coming for me, I am coming for you.” Holt described this as “straightforward retaliation”.Such was the concern of the journalists that the police had to be called on a number of occasions, said Holt, who pointed to “unpleasant” comments made by Robinson’s supporters online after some of his posts. Robinson had close to 1 million followers on X at one point, and some of his supporters are “unpredictable”, Holt said.Alisdair Williamson KC, for the defence, said Robinson’s actions were justified because the “fear for him is real”.“When you judge whether what he did was reasonable, you might think that he showed some restraint,” he told the jury. “I know what language I might use if people put my family in that position. The fear for him is real.”Williamson said the journalists did not care about Robinson’s concerns about the article, nor the stress it caused him, adding: “They don’t care to pick up the phone.”A series of agreed facts that were read out to the court before the closing speeches included a reference to four threat-to-life warning notices that police had given to Robinson in 2018, 2019 and 2024, shortly after the Daily Mail article.The court also heard that a video had been posted online in August 2024 by a man named Omar Abdirizak in which he said: “Tommy Robinson I got a message for you … we got pirates in every corner. Muslims in every corner,” before making a rifle gesture.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter speaks out for first time: ‘I have to go in’ | Oregon | The Guardian
description: Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacher
Content: Kaylub Giamanco, who has children that attend Silver Rail elementary school, fatally shot the attacker who killed three students and a teacher.Photograph: Saskia Hatvany/Oregon Public Broadcasting/APView image in fullscreenKaylub Giamanco, who has children that attend Silver Rail elementary school, fatally shot the attacker who killed three students and a teacher.Photograph: Saskia Hatvany/Oregon Public Broadcasting/APOregonFather who killed Oregon school shooter speaks out for first time: ‘I have to go in’Kaylub Giamanco recounts the day he confronted the Silver Rail elementary school shooter, who killed three boys and one teacherDani AnguianoFri 23 Oct 2026 19.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last weekspoke for the first timeabout the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.”Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter, has received national attention and praise forstopping the bloodshedat Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school.He fatally shot Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school, who broke in andshot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.Oregon man who killed school shooter reportedly took part in military drills with Iraq veteransRead moreIn an interview withOregon Public Broadcasting(OPB), his first since the 15 October shooting, he recounted that day. He told reporters that he was only in the area because he had decided to return home and eat lunch with his wife rather than the meal he brought to work that day.For a moment, Giamanco, who lives near the school, thought it was a prank when he saw a man in black armed with a gun headed toward Silver Rail, he said. Then he saw the man fire the gun and climb over a school fence. Giamanco pulled out a .40 caliber handgun from his center console and headed into the school parking lot, calling 911, before himself hopping over a fence to pursue the shooter.He quietly followed Griffin without the teenager seeing him, at one point crawling on his hands and knees when he heard “children pleading for their lives”.“I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,” he told OPB.Giamanco crawled through a broken window and toward the special education class Griffin had entered, where a teacher was fighting with the shooter. He came into the classroom and fired his gun. Griffin fell and was reaching for his weapon before Giamanco, who said he “was afraid of him shooting anybody else”, shot him two more times.He told OPB that he lies awake at night thinking of what he saw that day and the teenage perpetrator, and wonders if he could have done more.“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told the outlet. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”Giamanco said he wants to see safer schools with school resource officers at every site, and that he would like to raise funding to support school safety efforts.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS school shootingsClassroom violenceWest CoastGun crimeUS gun controlnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ohio man convicted of murder for running over officer after police killed his son | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Rodney Hinton ran over Larry Henderson after he viewed body-cam footage of police shooting dead his son Ryan
Author: Auzzy Byrdsell
Headline: Rodney Hinton ran over Larry Henderson after he viewed body-cam footage of police shooting dead his son Ryan
Content: Rodney Hinton Sr, father of Rodney Hinton and grandfather of Ryan Hinton, speaks at a news conference on 5 May 2025 in Cincinnati.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreenRodney Hinton Sr, father of Rodney Hinton and grandfather of Ryan Hinton, speaks at a news conference on 5 May 2025 in Cincinnati.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APOhioOhio man convicted of murder for running over officer after police killed his sonRodney Hinton ran over Larry Henderson after he viewed body-cam footage of police shooting dead his son RyanAuzzy ByrdsellFri 23 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnOhioman who killed a deputy with his car just hours after seeing video of his son killed by Cincinnati police was found guilty of murder and other charges on Friday, according toauthorities.Rodney L Hinton, 40, faces between 15 years and life in prison after his convictions in the death of Hamilton county special deputy Larry Henderson. His sentencing is tentatively scheduled for 16 November.During his 10-day trial, Hinton’s defense argued that he was so distressed over his son’s killing that he could not legally distinguish between right and wrong at the time of Henderson’s killing. But jurors rejected that defense after deliberations which began on Wednesday, finding him guilty of murder, reckless homicide and felonious assault.Officer who shot and killed Black toddler in Mississippi resigns from police forceRead more“The senseless murder of Deputy Larry Henderson Jr shattered a family and left a community mourning the loss of a dedicated public servant” who had spent 33 years on the job, Ohio’s attorney general, Andy Wilson, said in a statement. “We are thankful to the jury for its verdict, which accurately reflects the evidence in this case.Wilson’s statement added that Henderson’s “death is a painful reminder of the risks that law enforcement officers face every day while working to keep us safe”.Hours before Henderson’s killing, the Cincinnati police department sat down with Hinton’s family and their attorneys to view body-worn camera footage of his son, Ryan Hinton, being shot and killed by the agency’s officers the previous day.Ryan Hinton, 18, was killed after officers responded to a report of a stolen vehicle at an apartment complex. Two officers attempted to detain four people, including Ryan, in the reported stolen car – and all of those in the vehicle in question began to run, police said.Police also said Ryan Hinton was armed.Thebody-worn camera footage, which was published by NBC News, showed an officer exiting his vehicle and aiming his gun at Ryan Hinton, who appeared to be running away. Another recording captured an officer saying, “He’s got a gun!” The firearm was reportedly recovered at the scene.The officer who shot Ryan Hinton fired about four times. It is unclear from the footage if Hinton had aimed a firearm at officers.After seeing that footage, Rodney Hinton left in his own car and took aim with it at Henderson, according to Cincinnati police.Officials say Henderson saw the car coming toward him but could not avoid being hit. Prosecutors contended that Hinton “tracked” Henderson.“He turned his wheel the same direction that Larry moved, and the car struck Larry, throwing him, tossing him into the air, twisting him until he landed,” assistant prosecutor Kate Burroughs said in closing arguments on Wednesday.Rodney Hinton’s attorney, Clyde Bennett II, had asked jurors to find the defendant not guilty of all charges by reason of insanity.Bennett told reporters after the verdict that Hinton planned to pursue an appeal.“The fight is not over,” Bennettsaidin remarks recorded by Cincinnati news station WLWT.Explore more on these topicsOhioUS policingUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump drops some Canada tariffs in bid to boost embattled Susan Collins in Maine | US politics | The Guardian
description: Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Republican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged voters
Content: The Republican senator Susan Collins at a campaign stop in Lewiston earlier this week.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APView image in fullscreenThe Republican senator Susan Collins at a campaign stop in Lewiston earlier this week.Photograph: Robert F Bukaty/APUS politicsTrump drops some Canada tariffs in bid to boost embattled Susan Collins in MaineRepublican senator faces critical re-election battle in state where president’s trade war has outraged votersGaya Guptain New YorkFri 23 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump dropped some of the US’s tariffs onCanadaon Friday to “better serve the public interest” the White House said, handing a win to Susan Collins, the embattled Republican senator for Maine, as she faces a tight re-election campaign that will help determine whether Democrats can flip control of Congress.Collins announced that the exemptions would apply to nine agricultural products, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and seaweed. She added that many of the state’s farmers rely on specialized equipment and materials from across the border that are “unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense”.“In my repeated conversations with Ambassador Greer, Secretary Lutnick, and other senior administration officials, I have asked for tariff relief for these important products, and I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner,” she wrote.The White House also specified that certain processing equipment – such as plywood sheets, packing boxes, paper products, and certain machinery – would be removed from its tariffs. These materials can be crucial forMainebusinesses operating close to the border.“President Trump is further refining the scope of the July 20 and September 8 actions to better serve the public interest, and to ensure these measures continue to effectively offset the burden or disadvantage to US commerce from Canada’s discriminatory measures,” the White House said in a news release.Collins, who has served in the Senate for nearly 30 years, is running for re-election against Troy Jackson, a Democrat who has served in the Maine state senate and is a former logger. The race is crucial for the Democratic party’s hopes of flipping control of the chamber, and is so far considered a toss-up.‘It’s just getting worse’: anger in Maine over Trump’s trade war with close neighbor CanadaRead moreThe trade war between Canada and Maine has touched a nerve in the state, which relies heavily on commerce with Canada. Many of the industries mostentrenched in the state’s history– such as logging, lobstering and fishing – were expected to take a hit after Trump’s tariff announcements this year.Earlier this week, the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney,saidAmerican tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”After Trump placed a 50% tariff on certain Canadian goods, which began on 22 August, Canada announced its own retaliatory tariffs in response, ranging from 15% to 50% on $20bn worth of American goods. Canada later withdrew its tariffs on American seafood, which helped Maine’s fisheries in particular.Maine is considered a purple state, and many within the state – including Collins – consider themselves to have an independent streak. Collins has frequently sought to distance herself from Trump, particularly when it comes to his trade policies, and hasbroken with her party more than any other Republican senatorsince Trump took office, according to a New York Times analysis of her voting record.But her efforts to vote against Trump’s policies have rarely succeeded in his second term so far, the analysis found.Jackson has frequently seized on this line of attack since replacing Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket. At a television debate earlier this month, Jackson also pointed to Collins’s crucial vote to confirm the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh. The court subsequently overturned Roe v Wade.“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in his opening statement.Democrats argued the decision to drop some Canadian tariffs was an admission by the White House that Trump’s policies were unpopular.Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate finance committee, called the move a “desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career”.“The only way to get Trump to reverse course,” he said, “is for Americans to send a message that his sabotage of the American economy has got to go, along with any politician who has supported his agenda.”Explore more on these topicsUS politicsTrump tariffsUS midterm elections 2026MaineTariffsRepublicansCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Content: Tensions in the Middle East have been rising, with Iran claiming to have hit commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz and Washington ordering some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenTensions in the Middle East have been rising, with Iran claiming to have hit commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz and Washington ordering some US diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersOilOil price rises above $117 a barrel amid fears US will renew strikes on IranBrent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentresLauren AlmeidaFri 23 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOil has hit its highest level in more than six months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by about 3.5% on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point – its highest level since April.The jump came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched againstIran.Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”The oil price later eased back slight to sit about 2.7% up at just over $116 a barrel. Brent crude had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to touch$126 a barrelby the end of April.Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to havestruck four commercial shipsin the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leaveSaudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStreeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricaIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’ | US news | The Guardian
description: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
Content: Chase Che, left, poses with his 2004 Mazda6 during the Caffeine and Octane car show in Kennesaw, Georgia, on 4 October 2026. Stevie Dombrowski stands beside his 2007 Ford Mustang, which he affectionately calls the ‘Broke-Stang’.View image in fullscreenChase Che, left, poses with his 2004 Mazda6 during the Caffeine and Octane car show in Kennesaw, Georgia, on 4 October 2026. Stevie Dombrowski stands beside his 2007 Ford Mustang, which he affectionately calls the ‘Broke-Stang’.US newsThe young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loansAndrew Lawrenceand photographs by Jordan Putt in Kennesaw, GeorgiaFri 23 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”double quotation markPeople just want something that’s not going to fail themCharlie SpearsFor generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting forless than 10%of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.View image in fullscreenTrey Kemp looks through the rain-covered window of his 1989 Ford F-150 during the Caffeine and Octane car show.According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is$765 for a new carand $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay$1,000 or more a month, according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”Y2K cars don’t encompasseverythingproduced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect becomemortgage payments on wheels– they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.a man standing by his car and the headlights of a carChristian Handy poses with his 1995 Volvo 850 T-5R. He says the small wipers, designed to keep the headlights clean, no longer work.The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunkfrom 21% of inventory a year ago to 15%, according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlanderwith a screwdriver. “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”‘Kids say they take a quick look at TikTok’: a new kind of distracted driving is on the riseRead moreIn a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access toowners and even independent mechanics. Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.View image in fullscreenA 1990s-era Honda Civic sits in front of a row of newer sports cars as car show attenders wait out the rain. The event draws a mix of older enthusiast cars, daily drivers and newer performance vehicles.Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘Whatis going on?’” Price says. Generally speaking, he says, “the fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”Twenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, orslamming on the brakeswhen sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven, you’ve gotta shut off all these things, and a lot of times it doesn’t completely shut off.”a man in a car and a tongue in the front of a carStevie Dombrowski sits inside his 2007 Ford Mustang during Caffeine and Octane. A tongue protrudes from the front bumper of another car at the show.A few rows down from the Buick were Mike and Kate Landaverde in his-and-hers Honda Civics from the 90s: a barebones CRX coupe called Dirty Gertrude and a slightly less spartan wagon called Tatiana. The couple bought them cheap, in keeping with the Y2K ethos. Mike, 34, treats having to bump-start the CRX and his sweat-soaked commutes in summer traffic as part of the thrill ride. “I’m smiling the whole time,” says Mike, who manages a local Wendy’s. They keep a 2021 Toyota Corolla hatchback in the garage as a backstop.Thatcar’s got AC.When young Wendy’s customers pull up to the drive-through in newer barges he assumes carry huge monthly payments, Mike can’t help feeling a bit smug. The couple’s Hondas, however, haven’t necessarily come cheap. Kate, 39, reckons the money she has put into modifications on Tatiana alone could buy a new car. But the occasional outlays – on an engine swap, most recently – can be done at a self-directed pace. “You can do the mods at your own wallet bracket,” says Kate, a software specialist who does her own wrenching. “You can go eBay parts. But all my friends call me bougie because I’m not gonna do anything cheap.”Meanwhile, making a case for best in show was Alex Jimenez in a 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan tricked out to look like the Scooby-Doo Mystery Machine. “My family is growing,” said Jimenez, a 32-year-old facilities manager, as his 14-year-old daughter Izel sat shotgun scrolling through her phone while a Scooby-Doo cartoon played on the aftermarket infotainment display. Beyond the extra space, he says, “we love it because I can literally fix everything at home. I don’t need special equipment or tools or a computer to diagnose what’s wrong with it. And it puts smiles on people’s faces everywhere we drive. I mean, everybody’s taking pictures.”View image in fullscreenA Scooby-Doo plush hangs from the window of a Volkswagen customized as the Mystery Machine.Y2K cars have their charms, sure. Barry, of Consumer Reports calls it “survivorship bias” – seeing the most durable makes and models still on the road contributes to assumptions that all from the era must be rock solid. But there’s a reason the automotive industry moved on. “If you go back to cars in the 1990s, our road-test data and reliability surveys were showing problems that were unheard of on modern vehicles: defective paint, parts falling off; the steering wheel would be on crooked,” Barry says. Rust is another scourge of Y2K cars, though it’s less of a concern in the Sun belt. Newer models are far better protected against corrosion. “The technology that allows a car’s body and frame to survive longer is just so much more advanced,” says Barry, adding that a modern car from a manufacturer that prioritizes reliability can reasonably be expected to last 200,000 miles or more with proper maintenance. To his point: the average car on American roads is now13 years old.double quotation markCar companies are banks nowChe BidalStill, some young Y2K-car owners welcome the opportunity to get their hands dirty. Che Bidal, a 19-year-old Pit operator who also belongs to the furry community, was idling inside his 2004 Mazda6 as the rain poured on Caffeine and Octane. He takes immense pride in having bought the broken sedan for $900 and getting it running again with another $1,500 in parts and help from AI chatbots and YouTube tutorials. Having Frankensteined a Y2K car back to life, the prospect of taking on a new car payment – in this economy – only to be discouraged by the manufacturer from making his own repairs seems ridiculous. “Car companies are banks now,” says Bidal, who was further emboldened by his positive experience under the hood to start a wrenching group for furries. “Coming from fandom into the [auto enthusiast] community is a whole different thing – pretty amazing.”Nevertheless, there’s a critical difference between a car that’s gratifying to restore and one that can protect you when something goes terribly wrong. Modern cars are subject to increasingly demanding safety standards, and the differences in structural reinforcements and accident-avoidance features between models just three years apart can be dramatic. Consumer Reports has long recommended that drivers prioritize safety as much as their budget allows – advice that its largely Boomer readership can more easily take onboard, naturally.View image in fullscreenChase Che wears his furry mask in his 2004 Mazda6. He bought the V6-powered car for $900 and used it to learn how to perform his own repairs and maintenance, with help from a car-focused group within the furry community.Barry went through an old-car phase too. “When I was driving around in my 1988 Renault Medallion, I’d see someone come across the center line as they’re looking on their phone and think, ‘I would not stand a chance in an overlap collision,’” he says. “You might think that the older car you’re driving is a tank. Well, thecarmight be fine. It’s the things inside the car, the new safety features, that help you survive.” Features like blind-spot monitoring, driver attention monitoring and electric stability control, which intervenes to maintain traction in a skid.The US auto industry has made some effort to address young consumers’ affordability concerns. In 2021, Ford introduced the Maverick, a four-door compact pickup with an available hybrid powertrain and a starting price below $30,000. A startup called Slate, which offers an infinitely customizable electric truck with a starting price of about $25,000, hopes to begin fulfilling orders at the end of this year.The Cybertruck was supposed to be apocalypse-proof. Can it even survive a trip to the grocery store?Read moreIn China, buyers can get new cars with features that would seem extravagant at the same price point in the US – the payoff from decades of Chinese investmentin innovationand American offshoring of manufacturing.An affordable, widely available Chinese carwith modern features would give young US car buyers something truly tantalizing to consider. But Chinese automakers are in effect shut out of the US market. Even if they weren’t, Barry cautions: “We’re still not getting one for $8,000. Think closer to $20,000. You’re still going to have a car payment. And even if the interior is simple, it’s a different kind of simplicity than someone driving a 99 Camry is looking for.”View image in fullscreenFrom left, Ayden Blake, Evan Barclay, Riley Bennett and Stevie Dombrowski stand with their vehicles. The friends said the ability to perform their own maintenance and make modifications draws them to older cars.Ultimately, young consumers just want cars that deliver on the industry’s fabled promise of independence – and right now, Y2K cars are meeting the brief. These days, Price’s Pewter Pebble struggles with a leaky sunroof, and the headliner is still drooping. “It’s a Volkswagen so it’s coming back to bite me in the butt,” he says. “I’ve probably had to put three grand into it this year.” But with more than 150,000 miles on the clock, it’s taken him further than even he could have imagined.The absence of a car note helped him become a homeowner in his 20s. It softened the blow of Alex Vindman’s upset loss to Democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida’s August Senate primary. Rather than scramble for another job, Price took a European vacation to decompress and plot his next move. As it happens, he spoke to the Guardian from the Spanish Pyrenees. “If I had a car payment and I lost my job,” he says, “I wouldn’t have the flexibility to hike a mountain.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsAutomotive industryMotoringRoad transportGeorgiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’ | Global development | The Guardian
description: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
Author: Amrit Dhillon
Headline: Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed
Content: From next month, prodded by the findings of India’s supreme court, prices of 137 cancer drugs are expected to fall by up to 70%.Photograph: Rupendra Rawat/AlamyView image in fullscreenFrom next month, prodded by the findings of India’s supreme court, prices of 137 cancer drugs are expected to fall by up to 70%.Photograph: Rupendra Rawat/AlamyGlobal developmentIndia slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosedSupported byAbout this contentAmrit Dhillonin DelhiFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.From next month,137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaperas the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carrieda vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.View image in fullscreenSarojam Radhakrishan initiated the court action after being unable to pay for her cancer drugs.Photograph: FacebookThe judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trademark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.A 30% trade margincap on the price of 42 drugshas been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.Whenever the IndianCancerSociety holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”View image in fullscreenThe supreme court in New Delhi, where judges have asked the government to explain why the price cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not all non-patented drugsPhotograph: APIndia records about1.56m new cancer cases annually– up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battleRead more“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentGlobal healthCancerHealthPharmaceuticals industryIndiaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood out | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: With his first drivers’ title all but secure a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but the Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: With his first drivers’ title all but secure a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but the Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focus
Content: Kimi Antonelli, then and now. He first went karting at age five and was taken on as a Mercedes junior driver at 12.Composite: Guardian Picture Desk;  DPPI Media/Alamy; LAT Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli, then and now. He first went karting at age five and was taken on as a Mercedes junior driver at 12.Composite: Guardian Picture Desk;  DPPI Media/Alamy; LAT Images/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026‘A different kid’: from karting to F1 champion-elect, Antonelli’s ability has always stood outWith first drivers’ title all but secure, a friendlier champion would be hard to find, but Italian’s eight wins this season speak to his focusGiles Richardsin AustinFri 23 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven as Kimi Antonelli may be world champion-elect, it is sometimes hard to equate the young man who has drivenwith such exceptional skilland no little verve to touching distance of an historic first Formula One title with the smiling, wide-eyed kid with tousled hair who still almost looks out of place in the F1 paddock. Yet what has become clear in this extraordinary season is that Antonelli’s talent and his personable, endearing character are inextricably entwined.Whether the Italian seals his place as F1’s youngest world champion, at 20 years old, at this Sunday’s US Grand Prix in Austin or the next round in Mexico or even beyond that is moot – that he will do so is all but assured and for all that he is still in only his second season in the sport, a more rounded, well-liked champion than the Mercedes driver would be hard to find.Austin GP is about much more than potential for Antonelli’s first F1 world title | Giles RichardsRead moreEngage with Antonelli and it is almost impossible not to still see the three-year-old child who insisted on taking to his father Marco’s knee to try out the racing simulator the former driver had brought home. Marco would control the pedals and his son the wheel with an irrepressible enthusiasm that could barely be contained and is still there in every dart, feint and incisive pass he makes today.Pictures from his childhood in Bologna, a couple of hours’ drive from where his father runs a racing team in San Marino, show whenever Antonelli has a wheel in his hands there is a smile on his face and his eyes alight. His joy is clear and it is a passion that has run clearly through his career. From going karting at the age of five, a meteoric rise through the ranks, being taken on as a Mercedes junior driver aged 12, then making his debut for the team in 2025 after a whirlwind of three years moving from F4, to Formula Regional and then F2.The faith Mercedes placed in him, not least in that he was stepping into the shoes of the departing seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, was huge, yet the team principal Toto Wolff had no doubts as to his talent and his character.View image in fullscreenTwelve year old Kimi Antonelli (centre) on the podium at the 2019 Karting Winter Cup OK-Junior at Lonato, Italy.Photograph: Jacky Foulatier/DPPI Media/Alamy“In the past, there was the opinion in F1 that in order to be winning, you need to be an asshole, you need to be ruthless and opportunistic,” he observed this season as Antonelli made a stunning startwith five wins on the trotand the entire world was paying attention to the kid who, for many, had come from nowhere. “I don’t think that Kimi is that. It’s just down to driving faster than the others, and being a nice person also.” It is an opinion often echoed by those close to the young Italian. Gwen Lagrue, the talent scout who led Mercedes’ junior driver programme, remembers more than just his remarkable talent from their early encounters.“With Kimi, I saw almost from day one that I was dealing with a different kid,” Lagrue said. “First, what impressed me, well, amazed me, was his natural presence. He was already having such an impact on everyone in the paddock, you noticed this kid has something different than the others. Everyone liked Kimi, everyone was hugging him. He was like the Kimi you see today when he was 11. He was so passionate about what he was doing, about racing, about F1, everything.”At the heart of this engaging character it seems is a grounded and emotionally rich relationship with his family. While he was supported in following his racing dreams, he was told unequivocally that if he was to kart on a weekend, school must follow on a Monday until he graduated. He duly did so, completing hismaturitàschool exams just after coming third – his first podium –at the Canadian GP last year.“Which driver has done the A-levels or the baccalaureate? Name me one that has finished school. No one,” Wolff observed pointedly of his prodigy. The role of his family has clearly been crucial. His father as guide, mentor and, both have admitted, stern taskmaster at times, whom Antonelli has described as his “rock”. But there is also clearly a hugely important relationship with his mother, Veronica, and younger sister Maggie.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli ended Italy’s 60-year wait for a home F1 win with his triumph at Monza from 19th on the grid.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty Images“My dad is always going to give me his point of view, he’s going to give me advice and then if I decide to listen, good, but if I don’t decide to listen, it’s OK as well,” he said. “We always have a strong relationship but this is the same with my mum and my sister. The way I am I don’t think I could cope with having a bad relationship with my family member, it’s something that I would really struggle to cope with, that’s why I couldn’t see myself, you know, just taking distance from them.”Intriguingly, racing was not a direction his father had initially wanted him to go in. Marco had been a quick sportscar driver and almost signed as works driver for two German touring car teams but was unlucky in not getting a shot. “I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation,” he said. “At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli with his father, Marco, who has guided him carefully throughout his racing career.Photograph: Peter Powell/EPAHowever, having decided to let him pursue the dream, Marco has been there ever since. He is at the track on many weekends and clearly the pair share an easy, close bond with echoes of the one Hamilton shared with his father, Anthony, in his early years. In Hungary, the race after he had risked receiving a penalty for exceeding track limits on his way to a brilliant win in Belgium, Antonelli laughingly recalled his father’s reaction: “He said: ‘Congrats, but …’ Always a but … ‘If I see you doing another track limit for nothing, I’m gonna stretch your neck like a chicken.’”Antonelli’s boyish honesty has been as engaging as his talent. Wolff has noted his ability to switch into a “race mode”, a zone where he is wholly focused on the task, where he has a daring, aggressive driving style, pushing to the limit and past it, on occasion, but which he always learns from. “We had to teach him instead of always being at 110%, just be at 100%,” Lagrue said which, as Wolff has remarked, is a trait he would rather indulge than having to “take a stick to a donkey”.Kimi Antonelli tightens F1 title grip with Belgian GP win after Russell crashes outRead moreYet alongside that verve Antonelli has shown a maturity beyond his years belied by his character when out of the “zone”. He has displayed the judgment of a veteran while being able to manage the endless adjustments of touch and feel of the car and its balance – especially of these fiendishly complex modern rides – such that he, like many of the greats, has made it look easy.F1 driver standingsWatching him do so this season has been a pleasure not least because he is a driver who has taken such untrammelled and infectious joy in doing so. A feeling perhaps summed up by his father, who told La Gazzetta dello Sport just after his son turned 20: “I hope he remains who he is, sweet and generous, and continues to do what he loves for as long as possible.”Before hisextraordinary victory from 19thon the grid at the Italian GP, Antonelli said he wanted to win the championship but that it was important for him to do so by being himself. The latter he can consider a job most admirably well done. The former is only a matter of time.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Kimi AntonelliMercedes GPFormula OneMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders unionize after years of fighting for fair pay | Dallas Cowboys | The Guardian
description: The Dallas Cowboys voluntarily recognized the cheerleaders’ union, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: The Dallas Cowboys voluntarily recognized the cheerleaders’ union, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining
Content: The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders perform at a game this year.Photograph: Ron Jenkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders perform at a game this year.Photograph: Ron Jenkins/Getty ImagesDallas CowboysDallas Cowboys cheerleaders unionize after years of fighting for fair payTeam elects to voluntarily recognize unionSquad members have advocated for better wagesUwa Ede-OsifoandElla BrockwayFri 23 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheDallas Cowboyscheerleaders have unionized, in a watershed labor victory that comes after years of fighting for fair pay.The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association (DCCA) was voluntarily recognized by the Cowboys as the collective bargaining representative for the cheerleading squad, according to a Friday news release. The recognition came after “meaningful discussion” between the Cowboys organization and the DCCA, and the parties are set to begin collective bargaining.“The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for the talent and dedication they exhibit,” the DCCA said in a statement. “They remain one of the most sought-after opportunities for talented dancers worldwide.”‘A beauty pageant in athletic form’: how cheerleading show America’s Sweethearts became a Netflix megahitRead moreEstablished in 1961, one year after the football team played its inaugural season in theNFL, the Cowboys cheerleaders are among the most recognizable dance groups in the world. The squad’s national profile rose as they were chronicled in a Netflix series, America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, which released its third season in June.For decades, the franchise has faced scrutiny over the cheerleaders’ low salaries, despite their enduring pop culture relevance.The squad’s compensation was largely shrouded in mystery until details spilled into the public view in 2018, when cheerleader Erica Wilkinsfileda federal fair wage lawsuit against the Cowboys. Wilkins claimed she averaged $15,000 during her seasons with Dallas and said she made less money than the team’s male mascot. The Cowboys are the NFL’s most valuable franchise at $17bn, per Forbes.The second season of America’s Sweethearts followed oft-tense contract negotiations – including threats of a walkout – involving the 36-member team. Several squad members spoke of holding full-time jobs in addition to their demanding DCC schedule so they could pay their bills.By the end of the season, the dancers received a 400% pay raise, increasing the hourly rate for some members from $15 per hour for the 2024 season to $75 per hour. One squad membertoldthe New York Times that while the new contract increased wages for game day appearances, it did not provide health insurance.The Cowboys cheerleaders are not the first in the NFL to form a union. In 1995, the National Labor Relations Board ruled that the Buffalo Bills cheerleaders could unionize. The Buffalo Jills, as they were known,joinedthe National Football League Cheerleaders Association. The union was short-lived and the Jills squad disbanded in 2014.Explore more on these topicsDallas CowboysNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Skye Blakely caps remarkable injury comeback with world gymnastics all-around title  | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: The 21-year-old American claimed the world all-around title in Rotterdam, two years after a devastating injury ended her hopes of reaching the Paris Olympics
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The 21-year-old American claimed the world all-around title in Rotterdam, two years after a devastating injury ended her hopes of reaching the Paris Olympics
Content: Skye Blakely celebrates after winning the women’s all-around title at the World Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam on Friday.Photograph: Adam Pretty/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSkye Blakely celebrates after winning the women’s all-around title at the World Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam on Friday.Photograph: Adam Pretty/Getty ImagesGymnasticsSkye Blakely caps remarkable injury comeback with world gymnastics all-around titleAmerican, 21, wins world all-around title in RotterdamBlakely ruptured achilles before 2024 Olympic trialsFirst US champion since Simone Biles three years agoGuardian sportFri 23 Oct 2026 16.14 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSkye Blakely completed a sensational comeback from a ruptured achilles tendon to win the women’s all-around title at the world gymnastics championships in Rotterdam on Friday, claiming the biggest individual prize in the sport outside the Olympics.The 21-year-old American scored 55.733 points across four apparatus to finish ahead of Russia’s Liudmila Roshchina (55.199), with China’s Ke Qinqin taking bronze (55.032).Blakely’s triumph came little more than two years after her Olympic ambitions were shattered when she ruptured her right achilles during floor exercise training, just two days before the US trials for the 2024 Paris Games. The injury required surgery and ended a season in which she had finished runner-up toSimone Bilesat the national championships.It was the second major setback of her career after she tore an elbow ligament while warming up for the Tokyo Olympic trials.“Throughout the meet, I was telling myself ‘Do it for the girl in 2021 and the girl in 2024 who couldn’t do everything, just fight for her,’” Blakely told reporters. “That’s what I kept telling myself: ‘I am capable, I am ready’ and I made every version of myself extremely proud.”View image in fullscreenSkye Blakely celebrates after Friday’s all-around win.Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters“I already cried, but it just means the world to me,” Blakely said after qualifying at the Rotterdam Ahoy arena. “Knowing how much I’ve been through – two major surgeries, a lot of hardships, ups and downs.”Blakely, a Dallas native, entered Friday’s final as the second-ranked qualifier and delivered under pressure, producing assured routines on uneven bars and balance beam before protecting a lead of more than a point on floor exercise.‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failedRead moreHer 14.200 on beam, an apparatus that had caused problems during the Americans’ silver-medal finish behind China in Wednesday’s team competition, gave her a commanding advantage heading into the final rotation. A misty-eyed Blakely became overwhelmed by emotion after completing her floor routine, then wrapped herself in an American flag once the result was confirmed.“It truly means the world to me, knowing how much I have overcome, all of the hardship that I faced and the days that I wanted to give up or didn’t think it was possible,” Blakely said. “To see it really come to be tonight, is just, it makes me so proud of myself and makes me reflect on little me who would dream of this.”Algeria’s Kaylia Nemour, the leading qualifier, finished fourth after a mistake on her opening vault forced her to perform a less difficult attempt. She recovered with an outstanding performance on uneven bars but missed bronze by just 0.034 points. Fellow American Claire Pease finished seventh after falling from the balance beam.Blakely, a University of Florida junior, became the first American to win the world all-around crownsince Biles in 2023, extending a US streak of podium finishes at every Olympics and world championships since 2003.Competition continues on Saturday with the first apparatus finals. Blakely and Pease are set to compete in the women’s vault and uneven bars finals, whileFred Richardwill contest the men’s floor exercise and Patrick Hoopes the pommel horse.Explore more on these topicsGymnasticsUS sportsUSA Olympic teamSimone BilesShareReuse this content

title: Aaron Rodgers says NFL’s Paris game is safe despite PSG cancellation amid unrest | NFL | The Guardian
description: The Steelers quarterback says he trusts the NFL’s security assessment as civil unrest and severe weather disrupt preparations for Sunday’s game
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Steelers quarterback says he trusts the NFL’s security assessment as civil unrest and severe weather disrupt preparations for Sunday’s game
Content: Paris Saint-Germain marketing director Fabien Allègre (left) and NFL Europe and Asia-Pacific chief Brett Gosper attend a press conference in Paris on Monday ahead of the NFL’s first regular-season game in France.Photograph: Johnny Fidelin/Icon Sport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenParis Saint-Germain marketing director Fabien Allègre (left) and NFL Europe and Asia-Pacific chief Brett Gosper attend a press conference in Paris on Monday ahead of the NFL’s first regular-season game in France.Photograph: Johnny Fidelin/Icon Sport/Getty ImagesNFLAaron Rodgers says NFL’s Paris game is safe despite PSG cancellation amid unrestSteelers, Saints still on for NFL’s Paris debut on SundayViolent protests prompt US security warning for fansPSG cancel Sunday match amid escalating Paris unrestGuardian sportand agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 17.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NFL would have cancelled its first regular-season game in Paris, scheduled for Sunday, if the situation were unsafe,Pittsburgh Steelersquarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday, referring to the recent protests in the French capital.France experienced some of its worst urban unrest in years last weekend, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to tighten restrictions on protests on Thursday amid fears that demonstrations planned for Saturday could turn violent.The unrest has already forced the postponement of Sunday’s Ligue 1 match betweenParisSaint-Germain and Lyon, which has been moved to Monday night at the request of local police. Authorities cited security concerns and the strain on police resources over a weekend that will also see the NFL stage its first regular-season game in France.The demonstrations have been driven by anger over the rising cost of living, deteriorating conditions in public schools and teacher shortages. Some estimates put the number of protesters who marched last weekend at 800,000.The Steelers face theNew Orleans Saintsat the Stade de France in Saint-Denis on Sunday, around 10km from central Paris.The four-timeNFLMVP said he was confident the game would go ahead as planned.“I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” he told a press conference on Friday.“This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.”View image in fullscreenNFL France general manager Matthieu Maignal speaks at a press conference in Paris on Monday ahead of the league’s first regular-season game in France between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints.Photograph: Johnny Fidelin/Icon Sport/Getty ImagesThe NFL said last week that preparations were continuing as scheduled despite the unrest. “We continue to work closely with local authorities and partners on all operational and security matters,” the league said, adding that there had been “no disruption or impact at league sites”.The game in Paris has been largely overshadowed by the nationwide protests, with new demonstrations planned for Saturday. The Steelers informed fans on Thursday that a “Steelers House” fan event in the Bastille neighbourhood would not go ahead.The US state department issued a security alert on Thursday night, calling on its citizens to “avoid demonstrations and areas of unrest”.“Americans in Paris for the NFL game on Sunday, October 25 should also exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings,” the state department added.‘Not overly worried’Many Americans and other foreign visitors have travelled to France to watch Sunday’s game despite the protests.Fred Zelt, a 67-year-old Steelers fan at the NFL House set up in Paris, arrived in the French capital a week ago.“We saw [last Saturday] a march of probably several hundred students. It was completely peaceful,” he told Reuters.“Every place we’ve been seemed calm and normal to us. We now see shops boarding up windows.“There are lots of people out. People are having a good time and we’re not overly worried.”Fabian Bauer, a 28-year-old Saints fan, travelled from Germany with his parents.“We had a long discussion about whether we should come here or not,” he said. “In the end, I informed myself, and most of the fans said it’s likely to be safe, especially on Sunday.“It’s not as bad as one might have thought.
