Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The US president accused the NBA superstar of disrespecting the national anthem after footage showed him warming up before Philadelphia’s season opener
Content: Tyrese Maxey and LeBron James react during the fourth quarter of the Philadelphia 76ers’ 114-106 comeback victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night.Photograph: Emilee Chinn/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTyrese Maxey and LeBron James react during the fourth quarter of the Philadelphia 76ers’ 114-106 comeback victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night.Photograph: Emilee Chinn/Getty ImagesLeBron James‘Slow news day at the office’: LeBron James shrugs off Trump’s national anthem attackTrump calls James a ‘TOTAL DISGRACE’ over anthemUS president demands apology for pregame warm-upJames helps Sixers erase 29-point deficit against CavsGuardian sportand agenciesFri 23 Oct 2026 00.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behavior during the playing of the national anthem.Trump posted a video of the basketball legend making apparent warm-up movements while lined up with hisPhiladelphia 76ersteammates before their season opener against the New York Knicks on Tuesday.Rookie Lendeborg jaws at ‘weak ass’ Dončić and admits he didn’t watch much NBARead more“While listening to our National Anthem,LeBron Jamesdisrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” he wrote.The video used by Trump had an on-screen caption that read: “LeBron working on his golf swing pregame.” It showed him making lateral swinging motions and basketball shooting movements.Trump, speakingat a campaign rally in Iowaon Thursday night, renewed the attack, calling James’s actions “a big scandal kind of a story”.Trump and James have traded barbs before, and the NBA’s all-time leading scorer shrugged off the president’s latest criticism.“It must be a slow news day at the office,” he said after the Sixers completed an epic comeback to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in Philadelphia. “Slow news day at the office.”James, 41, is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season with his fourth team.Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Trump’s comments were the kind of distractions he was schooling his team to tune out.View image in fullscreenLeBron James drives past Cleveland center Jarrett Allen during the third quarter of Philadelphia’s 114-106 comeback victory on Thursday night.Photograph: Emilee Chinn/Getty Images“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said. “I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor.“The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”Philadelphia’s win on Thursday marked both the largest comeback by the Sixers in the play-by-play era (since 1996-97) and the largest comeback win of James’s career.James finished with 17 points, 10 rebounds, five assists and three steals, while Tyrese Maxey powered the rally with 32 points and a crucial defensive effort on James Harden. Jaylen Brown, also making his home debut in a 76ers uniform, scored 17 of his 21 points in the second half and 10 in the fourth quarter.Trump has been critical of athletes before – particularly Black athletes – for their behavior during the playing of the Star-Spangled Banner before games.During his first term, Trumpsingled out NFL star Colin Kaepernickfor his decision to kneel during the Star-Spangled Banner to protest against racial injustice and police brutality.Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesDonald TrumpPhiladelphia 76ersNBABasketballUS sportsColin KaepernickShareReuse this content

title: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision
Author: Ramin Skibba
Headline: Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision
Content: Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, and Marc Benioff, Salesforce’s CEO, attend the Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, California, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, and Marc Benioff, Salesforce’s CEO, attend the Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, California, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersReworkedAnthropicExperts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the companyAnthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the visionSupported byAbout this contentRamin SkibbaFri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast year, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, warned that artificial intelligence couldeliminate halfof entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing90% of code. Neither of those predictions came to pass.Now, in areportAnthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents.Anthropic says AI has changed the way work gets done, and as a result, restructured employment at the company. The report suggests its changes foreshadow the future of work more broadly: as more companies adopt AI agents, software engineers could face a tougher job market while entry-level tech workers struggle to build necessary skills and experience.“As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift,” Anthropic’s report reads before offering a potential future. “One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue.”In its report, Anthropic touts its “deep adoption of AI”, which it claims resulted in “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts”. By outsourcing some coding and sales-related tasks to AI agents, Anthropic said it raised productivity within a few months.From May 2026 onwards, AI agents logged more work hours than human employees, the report said. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, based on Anthropic’s analysis of their chat summaries.It also says since March 2025 – soon after the release of its agentic AI coding tool Claude Code – entry-level technical hires dropped from nearly 30% to 9%, and headcount dropped from about 21% to 14%. It attributes the shifts to AI usage, and described its workers as merely “a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents”.While the report provides a small glimpse of the inner workings of the AI heavyweight, some AI researchers are skeptical that it will herald big changes across companies or industries. Instead, they say the findings are probably Anthropic’s attempt to drive its valuation ahead of its initial public offering – similar to how SpaceX boasted about proposed space datacenters to boost its market debut in June.Anthropic’s claims seem to backsome tech executives’ viewthat AI is behind recent waves of corporate layoffs, but research complicates that.Morgan Frank, a Case Western Reserve University researcher on how AI and technological changes affect workers, recently posted apaperthat’s in peer review showing that AI-exposed job markets deteriorated well before the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Claude a few months later. State unemployment claims reveal that job markets tanked starting at the beginning of 2022, months before ChatGPT’s release, according to the paper.“It doesn’t appear that the launch of ChatGPT corresponds to any major increase in loss or worsening outcomes,” he said.Frank said several factors could explain recent job losses, including cutting pandemic-era hires and “AI-washing”, where some bosses credit AI for layoffs they might have made anyway.Julián Posada, a Yale social scientist, also questions Anthropic’s motives for publishing its report.“It is written from the perspective of a company that wants to sell shares, a company that really wants people to invest in it,” said Posada, author of the book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.Unlike an economics study, the report lacked an independent assessment by outside auditors, Posada said. Its figures and graphs only tell part of the story, without revealing how Anthropic’s workers feel about their work or how they are actually engaging with the models, he said.Dylan Baker, lead research engineer at the non-profit Distributed AI Research Institute, was also curious about how Anthropic’s developers feel about the changes. Shifting some software development to AI, while hiring few entry-level workers and having the remaining engineers wrangle AI agents seems “shortsighted”, they said.Baker is also surprised by Anthropic’s human “bottleneck” characterization.“That’s such a strange way to put it,” they said. “It fundamentally misunderstands how software is written, architected and designed. It’s such a social, interpersonal and human process.”Anthropic’s report quotes an unnamed engineer, who described facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention”. That doesn’t sound like a fruitful work environment, Baker said. “I wouldn’t think really thoughtful, well-designed products are coming out of that team.”As generative AI products proliferate, amajority of Americansare wary of AI, with particular concerns about AI-related job losses, according to Pew Research Center. In its report, Anthropic suggests that tech employers should offer their workers stock ownership, posing this as a potential solution to rising concerns. “It is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout,” it said.Anthropic did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.Anthropic, which could debut on the stock market as soon as November, released its employment report one day afterpledging to commit5% of its shares to the “public good”, though it did not provide details. Critics noted that philanthropy has long doubled as a reputation builder used by tech titans like Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg.But Anthropic, and its claims that it is improving how work gets done could face tougher scrutiny as it nears its IPO. A draft of the company’s S-1 filing revealed that Anthropic had an$80bn net lossover the first half of this year, and that it received ajunk credit ratingin June. Considering Anthropic’s slowing revenue growth, investors now project avaluationof $1.5tn, down from earlier estimates of$2tn or more. At the same time, Anthropic’s cloud computing partner, CoreWeave, has become swamped in AI debt and itsstock is plummeting, fueling concerns that the AI bubble may begin to deflate.Regardless of when or whether the bubble pops, software engineers and other tech workers will surely be affected, Baker said. The question is how that will play out.“My hope is that there is a reckoning, a reassessment or re-evaluation of how much this has always been about human work,” they said.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)Dario AmodeiTechnology sectorChatbotsUS work & careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features | Apple Watch | The Guardian
description: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI
Content: The Ultra 4 is Apple’s do-it-all smartwatch, ready to tackle marathons or just the daily commute.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Ultra 4 is Apple’s do-it-all smartwatch, ready to tackle marathons or just the daily commute.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Apple WatchReviewApple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new featuresBiggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AISamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.That’s because several of the key featuresannounced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically thesame as last year’s model.The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to theprevious versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.View image in fullscreenUpgraded sensors sit in a new attractive fan-like design for the dome, which improve reliability during movement.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianUpgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina oftop adventure watch rivals.The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.SpecificationsCase size:49 x 44mmCase thickness:12mmWeight:63gProcessor:S11Storage:64GBOperating system:watchOS 27Water resistance:100 metres (10ATM)Connectivity:Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWBSensors:HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeterVitals and readinessView image in fullscreenWhen your health metrics deviate from your baseline, the readiness app gives you a score out of 10 showing how prepared your body is for strenuous exercise.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.watchOS 27 and AIView image in fullscreenThe vitals app spots changes to your metrics overnight and can now update HR and HRV during the day.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Ultra 4 runswatchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to theSeries 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on amodern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while thesound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe action button continues to be exclusive to the Apple Watch Ultra for starting exercise and many other features.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianApple says the battery should last more than1,000 full charge cycleswith at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for£95. Damage repairs cost£539.The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in itsenvironmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.PriceThe Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from£749(€899/$799/A$1,349).For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from£369, the Watch SE 3 costs£219and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from£860.VerdictThe Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.Pros:great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.Cons:no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.Explore more on these topicsApple WatchWearable technologyGadgetsAppleSmartwatchesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking | Technology | The Guardian
description: After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’
Content: The homepage of the PHP.net website on 22 October 2026 in Singapore.Photograph: Yong Teck Lim/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe homepage of the PHP.net website on 22 October 2026 in Singapore.Photograph: Yong Teck Lim/Getty ImagesTechnology‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hackingAfter discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’Johana BhuiyanFri 23 Oct 2026 14.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a“vulnpocalypse”,or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilityhave already begun.After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,”the warning read.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,”they wrote.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Opposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of election | Spain | The Guardian
description: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing
Content: Pedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPAView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez and his wife at a campaign rally in Fuenlabrada last weekend.Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPASpainOpposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of electionVideo shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoingAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 23 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.Launchedthis weekacross the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks aboutreceiving a university postthanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks abouthiding jewelleryin a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.View image in fullscreenA still from the People’s party AI-generated video featuring a deepfake of Begoña Gomez.Computer-generated: @ppopular/XThe Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister,told the broadcaster TVEon Friday.While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.A majority of the nine legal expertsconsulted by the newspaper El Paísconcurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – tocrack downon the impact of disinformation.“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticutidentified more than 200such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.Explore more on these topicsSpainPedro SánchezAI (artificial intelligence)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’ | US news | The Guardian
description: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
Content: Chase Che, left, poses with his 2004 Mazda6 during the Caffeine and Octane car show in Kennesaw, Georgia, on 4 October 2026. Stevie Dombrowski stands beside his 2007 Ford Mustang, which he affectionately calls the ‘Broke-Stang’.View image in fullscreenChase Che, left, poses with his 2004 Mazda6 during the Caffeine and Octane car show in Kennesaw, Georgia, on 4 October 2026. Stevie Dombrowski stands beside his 2007 Ford Mustang, which he affectionately calls the ‘Broke-Stang’.US newsThe young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loansAndrew Lawrenceand photographs by Jordan Putt in Kennesaw, GeorgiaFri 23 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”double quotation markPeople just want something that’s not going to fail themCharlie SpearsFor generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting forless than 10%of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.View image in fullscreenTrey Kemp looks through the rain-covered window of his 1989 Ford F-150 during the Caffeine and Octane car show.According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is$765 for a new carand $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay$1,000 or more a month, according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”Y2K cars don’t encompasseverythingproduced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect becomemortgage payments on wheels– they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.a man standing by his car and the headlights of a carChristian Handy poses with his 1995 Volvo 850 T-5R. He says the small wipers, designed to keep the headlights clean, no longer work.The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunkfrom 21% of inventory a year ago to 15%, according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlanderwith a screwdriver. “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”‘Kids say they take a quick look at TikTok’: a new kind of distracted driving is on the riseRead moreIn a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access toowners and even independent mechanics. Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.View image in fullscreenA 1990s-era Honda Civic sits in front of a row of newer sports cars as car show attenders wait out the rain. The event draws a mix of older enthusiast cars, daily drivers and newer performance vehicles.Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘Whatis going on?’” Price says. Generally speaking, he says, “the fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”Twenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, orslamming on the brakeswhen sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven, you’ve gotta shut off all these things, and a lot of times it doesn’t completely shut off.”a man in a car and a tongue in the front of a carStevie Dombrowski sits inside his 2007 Ford Mustang during Caffeine and Octane. A tongue protrudes from the front bumper of another car at the show.A few rows down from the Buick were Mike and Kate Landaverde in his-and-hers Honda Civics from the 90s: a barebones CRX coupe called Dirty Gertrude and a slightly less spartan wagon called Tatiana. The couple bought them cheap, in keeping with the Y2K ethos. Mike, 34, treats having to bump-start the CRX and his sweat-soaked commutes in summer traffic as part of the thrill ride. “I’m smiling the whole time,” says Mike, who manages a local Wendy’s. They keep a 2021 Toyota Corolla hatchback in the garage as a backstop.Thatcar’s got AC.When young Wendy’s customers pull up to the drive-through in newer barges he assumes carry huge monthly payments, Mike can’t help feeling a bit smug. The couple’s Hondas, however, haven’t necessarily come cheap. Kate, 39, reckons the money she has put into modifications on Tatiana alone could buy a new car. But the occasional outlays – on an engine swap, most recently – can be done at a self-directed pace. “You can do the mods at your own wallet bracket,” says Kate, a software specialist who does her own wrenching. “You can go eBay parts. But all my friends call me bougie because I’m not gonna do anything cheap.”Meanwhile, making a case for best in show was Alex Jimenez in a 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan tricked out to look like the Scooby-Doo Mystery Machine. “My family is growing,” said Jimenez, a 32-year-old facilities manager, as his 14-year-old daughter Izel sat shotgun scrolling through her phone while a Scooby-Doo cartoon played on the aftermarket infotainment display. Beyond the extra space, he says, “we love it because I can literally fix everything at home. I don’t need special equipment or tools or a computer to diagnose what’s wrong with it. And it puts smiles on people’s faces everywhere we drive. I mean, everybody’s taking pictures.”View image in fullscreenA Scooby-Doo plush hangs from the window of a Volkswagen customized as the Mystery Machine.Y2K cars have their charms, sure. Barry, of Consumer Reports calls it “survivorship bias” – seeing the most durable makes and models still on the road contributes to assumptions that all from the era must be rock solid. But there’s a reason the automotive industry moved on. “If you go back to cars in the 1990s, our road-test data and reliability surveys were showing problems that were unheard of on modern vehicles: defective paint, parts falling off; the steering wheel would be on crooked,” Barry says. Rust is another scourge of Y2K cars, though it’s less of a concern in the Sun belt. Newer models are far better protected against corrosion. “The technology that allows a car’s body and frame to survive longer is just so much more advanced,” says Barry, adding that a modern car from a manufacturer that prioritizes reliability can reasonably be expected to last 200,000 miles or more with proper maintenance. To his point: the average car on American roads is now13 years old.double quotation markCar companies are banks nowChe BidalStill, some young Y2K-car owners welcome the opportunity to get their hands dirty. Che Bidal, a 19-year-old Pit operator who also belongs to the furry community, was idling inside his 2004 Mazda6 as the rain poured on Caffeine and Octane. He takes immense pride in having bought the broken sedan for $900 and getting it running again with another $1,500 in parts and help from AI chatbots and YouTube tutorials. Having Frankensteined a Y2K car back to life, the prospect of taking on a new car payment – in this economy – only to be discouraged by the manufacturer from making his own repairs seems ridiculous. “Car companies are banks now,” says Bidal, who was further emboldened by his positive experience under the hood to start a wrenching group for furries. “Coming from fandom into the [auto enthusiast] community is a whole different thing – pretty amazing.”Nevertheless, there’s a critical difference between a car that’s gratifying to restore and one that can protect you when something goes terribly wrong. Modern cars are subject to increasingly demanding safety standards, and the differences in structural reinforcements and accident-avoidance features between models just three years apart can be dramatic. Consumer Reports has long recommended that drivers prioritize safety as much as their budget allows – advice that its largely Boomer readership can more easily take onboard, naturally.View image in fullscreenChase Che wears his furry mask in his 2004 Mazda6. He bought the V6-powered car for $900 and used it to learn how to perform his own repairs and maintenance, with help from a car-focused group within the furry community.Barry went through an old-car phase too. “When I was driving around in my 1988 Renault Medallion, I’d see someone come across the center line as they’re looking on their phone and think, ‘I would not stand a chance in an overlap collision,’” he says. “You might think that the older car you’re driving is a tank. Well, thecarmight be fine. It’s the things inside the car, the new safety features, that help you survive.” Features like blind-spot monitoring, driver attention monitoring and electric stability control, which intervenes to maintain traction in a skid.The US auto industry has made some effort to address young consumers’ affordability concerns. In 2021, Ford introduced the Maverick, a four-door compact pickup with an available hybrid powertrain and a starting price below $30,000. A startup called Slate, which offers an infinitely customizable electric truck with a starting price of about $25,000, hopes to begin fulfilling orders at the end of this year.The Cybertruck was supposed to be apocalypse-proof. Can it even survive a trip to the grocery store?Read moreIn China, buyers can get new cars with features that would seem extravagant at the same price point in the US – the payoff from decades of Chinese investmentin innovationand American offshoring of manufacturing.An affordable, widely available Chinese carwith modern features would give young US car buyers something truly tantalizing to consider. But Chinese automakers are in effect shut out of the US market. Even if they weren’t, Barry cautions: “We’re still not getting one for $8,000. Think closer to $20,000. You’re still going to have a car payment. And even if the interior is simple, it’s a different kind of simplicity than someone driving a 99 Camry is looking for.”View image in fullscreenFrom left, Ayden Blake, Evan Barclay, Riley Bennett and Stevie Dombrowski stand with their vehicles. The friends said the ability to perform their own maintenance and make modifications draws them to older cars.Ultimately, young consumers just want cars that deliver on the industry’s fabled promise of independence – and right now, Y2K cars are meeting the brief. These days, Price’s Pewter Pebble struggles with a leaky sunroof, and the headliner is still drooping. “It’s a Volkswagen so it’s coming back to bite me in the butt,” he says. “I’ve probably had to put three grand into it this year.” But with more than 150,000 miles on the clock, it’s taken him further than even he could have imagined.The absence of a car note helped him become a homeowner in his 20s. It softened the blow of Alex Vindman’s upset loss to Democratic socialist Angie Nixon in Florida’s August Senate primary. Rather than scramble for another job, Price took a European vacation to decompress and plot his next move. As it happens, he spoke to the Guardian from the Spanish Pyrenees. “If I had a car payment and I lost my job,” he says, “I wouldn’t have the flexibility to hike a mountain.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsAutomotive industryMotoringRoad transportGeorgiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude
Content: ‘In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job.’Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job.’Photograph: Oscar Wong/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisIs a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?Nick RomeoAn old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitudeFri 23 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareIn a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates hasdeclaredthat AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei haswarnedthat the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and thisin itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently,France, India andArgentinaare among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recentglobal surveyfound greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows thesame pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, hereplied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychologicalbenefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Herproposalwould create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit calledUniversal Basic Employment(UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)US work & careersUS economyUS politicsEmploymentEconomicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft  | Games | The Guardian
description: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Content: Strong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareView image in fullscreenStrong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareGamesEA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereftLucy JamesThe closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi seriesFri 23 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTShareEarlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today.It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to aleaked trailer, was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release.The three games that comprise original space-faring Mass Effect trilogy count as my favourites of all time. I first played in 2010, shortly after buying my Xbox 360 and being reassured by my friends that the game was a worthy investment, and have replayed them countless times since. Depending on the day, the top spot fluctuates; more often than not it’s the character-driven sequel Mass Effect 2, which ends with one of the most iconic missions in gaming, that takes the top spot.Released over a five-year period from 2007-12, the trilogy follows the adventures of Commander Shepard: a lawless Spectre special agent who is empowered by the galactic Citadel Council to use any means necessary to protect its interests and get the job done. Shepard’s appointment as the first human Spectre in a galaxy where humans are the new kids on the block aligns with the arrival of the Reapers, an ancient synthetic race that raze all organic life every 50,000 years. Shepard must convince the galaxy that the threat is real and gather its top soldiers, scientists and scoundrels to defeat it.View image in fullscreenComing together to save the galaxy ... Mass Effect 2Photograph: EA/BioWareWhen I played Mass Effect for the first time, I didn’t get it. Its controls felt janky and awkward, and I was thrown headlong into a galaxy full of history and politics that I didn’t understand: the game didn’t spell things out, throwing out names and jargon and expecting me to follow. After one exceedingly frustrating encounter with the Mako, the game’s infamously awkward land buggy, I quit entirely. Some months later, something drew me back: the feeling of a job left half done. The galaxy was in peril, and I had to save it.The second time I tried, something clicked. I focused less on the gameplay quirks and went all-in on its story and characters: the naive archaeologist, Dr Liara T’Soni; the browbeaten Citadel security guard Garrus Vakarian; and Kaidan Alenko, a human enhanced by the military, and suffering because of it. Mass Effect’s story was simple – save the galaxy from a tormenting synthetic race with guns and space powers – but you got to determine how it played out. Players were given the opportunity to make meaningful choices that hugely affected how the story unfolded, and that stuck with me (and millions of others).Throughout the course of the game, you can shape not only Shepard’s gender and what they look like, but how they react to situations. Would they be friendly, and use some inter-species cooperation to defeat the Reapers? Or take the renegade route, tersely shutting down dissenters, sometimes resulting in hilariously out-of-pocket responses? (My apologies to the intrepid space reporter Khalistah al-Jilani.) Regardless of how you played, it was thrilling to have such agency over how Shepard moved and was perceived in the world. But the real fun was in making decisions that altered the story not only in Mass Effect, but its sequels.I agonised over every choice, large or small. Across three games and the far flung reaches of the galaxy, my influence was felt. Races lived and died at my whim, and the consequences of my actions showed up in the most unexpected ways. It made my playthrough feel truly mine, guided by the stern hand of its development team, but shaped by me, and me alone. Shepard’s plight was mine, and I would save the galaxy. I hadn’t played anything like it at the time, and even now, I struggle to think of moments that compare. Its missions and story beats are so ingrained in my mind that you’d think I actually lived them. Such is the wonder of a video game, the freedom to explore and affect the world you’re playing in.View image in fullscreenMass Effect’s unlikely fan favourite, Garrus.Photograph: EA/BioWareMass Effect’s story wouldn’t have hit as hard if it weren’t for its characters: a motley crew of the galaxy’s toughest and cleverest, drawn to your cause for their own, complex reasons. It questioned whether AI had a soul, the sins of the father, and the heaviness of duty. BioWare wrote missions personalised to your squadmates’ causes, asking you to make agonising decisions that could benefit or harm them, and then forcing you to deal with the results. The writers went one further, allowing you to date some of these characters, slowly building from nervous flirting to ratings-friendly romance scenes. Saying goodbye to your squad, who’d been with you through hell, before the third game’s devastating final act brought me to tears over a decade ago. It still does.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s been over a decade since Shepard’s story concluded, and the trilogy is still lauded as among the greatest ever made. I play dozens of games a year, and few have stuck with me as Mass Effect has. Its influence is impossible to shake. It set the standard for action-RPGs for years to come, and despite a furore at its original ending (since changeddue to public outcry), is still beloved and widely referenced in gaming culture.BioWare’s ending feels so final, so abrupt. Despite missteps and mismanagement in recent years, most publicly in the form offailed sci-fi shooter Anthem, getting a glimpse at what the new Mass Effect might have been has left fans bereft. The foundation of the universe was so strong, and in the right hands it could have been another genre-defining story. The loss of BioWare is an enormous one for gaming, a bastion of western role playing games brought down. Its influence will continue to be felt throughout the gaming galaxy.Lucy James is founder and curator oflookingfor.gameand co-host of the Friends Per Second gaming podcast.Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamescommentShareReuse this content

title: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game | Games | The Guardian
description: From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: From parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the game
Content: Gung-ho Hollywood fantasy … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 screenshot.Photograph: ActivisionView image in fullscreenGung-ho Hollywood fantasy … Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 screenshot.Photograph: ActivisionGamesReviewCall of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a gameActivision; PC, PS5, Switch 2, XboxFrom parkour over Manhattan rooftops and car chases in Paris to the climactic battle at a North Korean air base, the developers have thrown absolutely everything at the gameKeith StuartFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd so we return perhaps one final time to Call of Duty’s Modern Warfare strand, with stories, “ripped from the newspaper headlines”, featuring shady terror organisations, nefarious rogue states and the brutally capable, monosyllabic war fighters who stand between us and Armageddon. Last year’s Black Ops 7 instalment was asales disappointmentfor Activision, and that has no doubt put extra pressure on Infinity Ward, the studio leading Modern Warfare 4 development. Fortunately, this developer – like series heroes Price, Gaz and Ghost – seems to thrive on pressure.As you may haveread, this year’s campaign is based around a fictitious North Korean ruling family that has seized an opportunity to invade its southern neighbour. Amid the chaos, a small group of Korean and American marines must help lead the fightback, while in the shadows, SAS hard man John Price makes an unlikely new comrade in his own morally ambiguous quest to put the world to rights. Mads Mikkelsen pops up as evil mastermind The Archer, but like Kiernan Shipka in Black Ops 7 he’s rather wasted, with very little screen time.View image in fullscreenStories ‘ripped from the newspaper headlines’ … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionNevertheless, it’s a bombastic, thrilling airport novel of a game, crammed with classic CoD set pieces, including but not limited to parkour over Manhattan rooftops, a car chase in Paris and a shootout in a train yard that somehow feels like a cross between Frogger and Time Crisis. A climactic battle at a North Korean airbase throws absolutely everything at you from sniper firefights to helicopter gunship attacks.There are also moments where you’re forced into stark unethical actions, faintly recalling the notorious “No Russian” mission from 2009’s Modern Warfare 2. Elsewhere, a whole open-world section lets you explore a snowy landscape, carrying out story missions and side quests to improve your armoury. It’s a nice break from corridor shooting, and somehow it doesn’t stall the game’s momentum. Throughout the six-hour campaign, bullets fly and buildings collapse, friends become enemies, enemies become friends, and a breathless story of geopolitical skullduggery emerges. It’s a shame, though, that the Capt Price arc gets a little overlooked toward the end and his denouement lacks the intended emotional clout, but it’s fun and at least a little bit emotional while it lasts.View image in fullscreenBullets fly and buildings collapse … Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 screenshotPhotograph: ActivisionThe multiplayer mode is a refinement of the turbo-paced, ultra-lethal experience of Black Ops 7. Players are still extremely agile, able to vault over obstacles and skid around corners, blasting their guns like John Wick on a recently polished vinyl floor. But movement is a touch more naturalistic here, and weapons have a heft to them that makes you feel deadly, even if you’re getting shot in the face every five seconds.Alongside all the classic modes there are decent newcomers, such as the epic, up-to-64-player, Combat Outpost, and Collateral, a round-based shootout where you buy new weapons and items at the start of each bout (the better you do, the more cash you get to spend on goodies). The highlight though is Kill Block, which takes place in a modular training centre where three landscape types are randomly selected from dozens of possibilities, then slotted in to a play space at the start of the round so you’re never sure how everything will fit together. You might have to move from a train yard to a storage depot to a trench network, and weapons are randomised too, so you could all be fighting with pistols or sniper rifles, adding to the unpredictable challenge.The last part of the package is a reconstructed take on Call of Duty’s extraction shooter mode, DMZ. Taking place in and around Hajin City, abandoned during the events of the campaign, you parachute in with up to two teammates, then carry out various PvE missions to earn cash and gear, before calling in for air rescue – all while avoiding or attacking other players on the same map. New to this version is the Forward Operating Base, a safe house you return to after each expedition where you can upgrade your weapons, 3D print new gear and get info on the current roster of boss characters. There’s also a three-branch skill tree for your character, which you populate by earning in-game XP. This gives you a range of new abilities and improvements including taking more loot from downed enemies, faster revives and reducing damage from explosives.DMZ, then, is a huge mode with lots to do, set in a dynamic world with a real-time weather system. So far, we’ve only been able to play an early access version, but exploring the world and gambling on just one final side quest before extraction promises to offer the sort of tension and excitement this genre thrives on. However, its success will depend on how many players Activision can attract and retain, and to survive it’ll surely have to tempt people over from established rivals such as Arc Raiders and Escape from Tarkov. That could be the toughest mission of all.Infinity Ward and its co-developers have thrown everything they have at this game, and it shows. The campaign is short but polished, the multiplayer still grabs you by the neck and DMZ is richly detailed and exhaustive. It’s all rendered in incredible audiovisual detail, delivering the spectacle we expect from the series. I’m not sure it’ll bring in a vast new audience, especially with GTA 6 on the way – Call of Duty remains a gung-ho Hollywood fantasy of armed conflict that glorifies the military-industrial complex. But if it’s a glossy, bombastic thrill ride you’re after, there is plenty here to keep you locked and loaded for months to come.Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is out nowExplore more on these topicsGamesCall of DutyPlayStationPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XPCNintendo Switch 2reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: An electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, too
Content: French students protesting over school conditions at the beginning of October.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAView image in fullscreenFrench students protesting over school conditions at the beginning of October.Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPAOpinionParisThe Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutionsEditorialAn electoral supercycle over the next year may redefine the continent’s future. But what’s happening on the streets is shaping it, tooFri 23 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareFrance sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and thenspread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence inMilan,BrusselsandTiranaas well as in French cities.French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minorityhijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macronutterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, withGreek protestersechoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal,housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possiblereintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron.Photograph: Teresa Suárez/EPAUnderlying all these is thebreakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.This unrest also echoes thewave of gen Z protestsseen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, areseeking to capitaliseon the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections,threatening a radical rightwards shiftthat could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’sinternal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Mamdani loves Arsenal. He should challenge them to cut ties with the UAE over Sudan | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: The New York mayor’s passion for the Gunners and human rights presents an opportunity to push back on the club’s lucrative UAE sponsorship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The New York mayor’s passion for the Gunners and human rights presents an opportunity to push back on the club’s lucrative UAE sponsorship
Content: New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is a lifelong Arsenal supporter who has publicly celebrated the club’s success.Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew York mayor Zohran Mamdani is a lifelong Arsenal supporter who has publicly celebrated the club’s success.Photograph: Selcuk Acar/Anadolu/Getty ImagesArsenalMamdani loves Arsenal. He should challenge them to cut ties with the UAE over SudanSasha Lezhnev and John PrendergastThe New York mayor’s passion for the Gunners and human rights presents an opportunity to push back on the club’s lucrative UAE sponsorshipFri 23 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTShareLike him or not, there is no doubt that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s passion for certain issues is electric, and that passion played a large part in him getting elected. But today, two of his biggest passions are on a collision course.On one hand, Mamdani is now arguably the US’s most high-profile supporter of English Premier League champions Arsenal. A superfansince he was a child, he has put the Gunners into the American spotlight more than anyone since becoming mayor. The Empire State Buildinggleamed in Arsenal’s red and whitewhen they won the Premier League title. He wrote anessayabout what Arsenal’s championship means to him, talks about Arsenal atpress conferencesandinterviewsand inauguratedThierry Henry Waynear Times Square in honor of the Arsenal legend.The US love of football is reaching new levels. Just look at Arsenal super-fan Zohran Mamdani | Bryan Armen GrahamRead moreBut another of Mamdani’s passions –standing upagainst genocide and for human rights – is now presenting a problem for the mayor’s Arsenal fandom. One prominent part of Arsenal’s current image is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mamdani.Arsenal’s chief sponsor is Emirates Airlines,ownedby the Emirates Group, a state-owned Dubai-based holding company. Emirates is on the front of every jersey, and the team plays at Emirates Stadium in London.
