The United Arab Emirates hasspentmore than$1bnsponsoring the team, including expanding its contract through 2033 to more than $100m per season. Arsenal is the UAE’s second biggest sports investment globally.The trouble is the UAE is also sponsoring a genocidal militia in Sudan, where war has created the world’s largest displacement crisis, with14 million people, or a quarter of the country’s population, forced to flee their homes, and21 million peoplefacing acute hunger. The UAE has provided the militia, known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), withweaponsand killerdrones, according to numerousinvestigations. In fact, the UAE is the RSF’s biggest supplier of weapons and drones.And therein lies the rub. The UAE is engaging in one of the world’s largest sportswashing campaigns in an attempt to clean up its image, including with Mamdani’s beloved Arsenal. The UAE’s sportswashing isn’t limited to the Gunners. We calculated that the UAE government has spent more than$5.2bnon sponsoring sports teams and leagues around the world, including Manchester City, the NBA championNew York Knicks(a team Mamdani alsocheersfor), theEmirates NBA CupandFormula One. There aremultiple otherfootball, basketball, cycling, rugby, cricket and UAE-sponsored teams as well.The good news is that Arsenal’s ownership isn’t blind to abusive sportswashing relationships. Last year, the clubannouncedit was cutting its sleeve sponsor, Visit Rwanda, after the country’s invasion of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the humanitarian catastrophe that ensued as a result. More than8 millionpeople have been displaced from their homes, as Rwanda has invaded the DRC andcommandedthe deadly M23 militia that hastortured victims, engaged inextensive sexual violenceand enlistedchild soldiers. The Arsenal Supporters’ Trust weighed in on the issue, followingcampaigninitiatives such as Gunners for Peace, and the owners changed course.double quotation markOne prominent part of Arsenal’s current face is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mayor MamdaniNow it’s time for Arsenal to tackle their bigger sportswashing sponsor, and Mamdani can play a key role. As one of the world’s most visible Arsenal fans, his voice would have an important impact on the club’s decision makers. The club’s owners are American, Josh and Stan Kroenke, and they have stood up in the past for human rights – for instance,callingfor a lifetime ban on former Los Angeles Clippers owner Don Sterling for making racist remarks.Mamdani could make the Kroenkes and the rest of the Arsenal board aware of the UAE’s sportswashing and call on them either publicly or privately to move on to another sponsor because of the genocidal militia the UAE is sponsoring in Sudan. The club is, after all, awash in cash after winning the league and reaching the final of the Champions League, earning$411min total, a record for Arsenal. It is now reportedly themost profitablefootball clubin England. So they don’t need the Emirati money.Importantly, the UAE is not the only game in town for football sponsors – there are viable alternatives. Snapdragon, a Qualcomm tech company, pays approximately the same amount for sponsoring Manchester United as the Emirates paysArsenal, and automaker Jeep and telecom company T-Mobile pay Juventus and Bayern Munich just a hair under.Arsenal canceling the deal would also have a meaningful impact on the UAE and on the genocide unfolding inSudan. The UAE is very sensitive to public image, and a cancelled Arsenal deal would be a major public relations blow. Mamdani’s intervention could have major human rights implications.Mamdani is passionate about human rights, combating genocide and supporting his favorite team. Urging the club’s leadership to change its sponsor from the UAE would combine all three passions into one and potentially have a positive impact on the world’s deadliest humanitarian crisis. New Yorkers and Arsenal fans alike should encourage Mamdani to weigh in with the club on this important issue.Sasha Lezhnev is Senior Policy Advisor atThe Sentry, where John Prendergast is Co-Founder.Explore more on these topicsArsenalZohran MamdaniUnited Arab EmiratesSudanFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obvious | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: Republicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney general
Content: ‘If there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one.’Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘If there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one.’Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obviousMoira DoneganRepublicans are resorting to childish taunts to defend an uncommonly dishonorable state attorney generalFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.48 EDTShareIt’s a bit like Lucy with the football. Every few years,Democratsconvince themselves that a Texas Senate seat might finally switch from red to blue. On paper, it makes sense. Texas is a large and urbanizing state with an increasingly educated – and increasingly non-white – population.Other one-time Republican strongholds that have undergone similar demographic shifts have turned purple or even blueish – think Georgia, for example. The border counties along the Rio Grande valley, with their deep poverty and big Latino populations, were long thought to be fertile ground to nurture a kind of anti-Trump populism that could be converted into pro-Democratic sentiment. The state Democratic party is anemic there, but a few talented candidates have emerged.Who else remembers Beto O’Rourke, the formerTexasDemocratic congressman and onetime presidential hopeful, who appeared on a 2019 cover of Vanity Fair, photographed in muted Annie Leibovitz tones along a desert dirt road, promising to deliver his home state, and a crucial Senate vote, from the clutches of Republican control?Donald Trump’s Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa MahdawiRead moreDoes that hope seem naive now? Even almost childish? Given what we know of O’Rourke’s subsequent success – or of the voting trends in the Rio Grande valley – does the past hope of a blue Texas begin to seem at all arrogant?Forgive me, then, for harboring doubts about whether Texas will vote, as some pollsters and many hopeful Democrats now say it will, for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, over his Republican opponent, the odious state attorney general,Ken Paxton.The excitement of Democrats in the TexasUS Senaterace this year carries with it the aftertaste of past disappointments. Lucy swears that this time, she’ll let Charlie Brown kick, and Charlie Brown – a slave to his own optimism – draws back his leg.But if there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one. Polls have put Talarico, a former seminarian, at a steady, though narrowing, lead. And there is reason for his appeal: Talarico speaks in eloquently religious terms that are well-tailored to his Bible belt audience; at 37, his relative youth will probably appeal to voters fatigued by gerontocracy.But the real deciding factor in the election may well be his opponent: Paxton is an uncommonly dishonorable man, even by the very low standards of a Republican Senate candidate. He’s been indicted on various fraud charges by Texas grand juries (he denied wrongdoing and eventually paid $300,000 in restitution).He was sued over similar fraud claims, subjected to multiple whistleblower complaints, nearly disbarred, and impeached in his capacity as attorney general by members of his own Texas Republican party. (He was later acquitted.)He is also going through a messy, public divorce after his wife of several decades, Angela, finally began proceedings against himafter an alleged extramarital affair.He subjects women to systematic mistreatment in public life, too: as Texas AG, he has presided over one of the most maximalist and sadistic abortion ban regimes, leading to one of the highest maternal and infant mortality rates in the country. He is unlikable, and unliked. Republican Texans who would have come out to vote for another candidate are more likely to stay home rather than vote for him.If winning a Texas Senate seat has long been a pipe dream for Democrats, the possibility that they might do so seems to be frighteningRepublicans.A loss in Texas would not just be a strategic defeat for the GOP, but a psychic one – a failure to hang on to unified power in a state that is supposed to be both the geographical center and the cultural linchpin of conservatism. It presents a risk to the emotions and morale of the Republican party much more than other potential losses in states such as, say, Maine, Michigan or Alaska.In a word, it would be emasculating. And in characteristic fashion, Republican power players have sought to assert masculinity as their central line of attack in the race.Over and over, Republicans have sought to keep Texas by insinuating that Talarico is gay, a woman or a pedophile – sometimes all three – and persistently linking him to the issue of gender transition treatment for minors. They have implied that he’s weak, that he’s either asexual or sexually threatening, depending on the occasion, and, weirdly, that he’s vegan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJD Vance, who has used the midterm cycle to informally launch his 2028 bid for the Republican presidential nomination, has seemingly decided to imitate Trump in vulgarity even where he lags him in charisma and humor. Like many, he’s been trying to get a 2016-style nickname for the Democrat to stick: “Talafreako.” It doesn’t quite roll off the tongue.But Vance has also suggested that Talarico is gay – and that he would somehow be disqualified from the Senate if he was. At a rally inTyler, Texas, Vance told a male audience member that he loved him. “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico.” He paused and waited for the crowd to laugh.Before that, he hadinsinuatedthat Talarico was a pedophile. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’sweb browser history,” Vance said.Elon Musk – nominally a resident of Texas, though billionaires don’t really “reside” anywhere – has looked to rescue Paxton’s candidacy with a massive infusion of cash,dumping $158minto the race late last month on the Republican’s behalf. On his social media platform, X, he has taken on a similar tone to Vance in attacking Talarico, alternating between casting vaguely sexual aspersions about Talarico’s character – Musk has repeatedly called him “creepy” – and making specific, incendiary and false claims about the Texas Democrat. “Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them,”Musk wrote.“Not just in Texas, but nationwide. Pure evil.”These kinds of low-brow, sexualized smears are the kind of thing Republicans do to make themselves look tough. The name-calling is supposed to evoke the power of the schoolyard bully in the form of a man in a suit, to conjure the image of someone so powerful that rules, and decorum, don’t apply to him.But I think that really, these kinds of juvenile taunts are a sign of the party’s weakness. Republicans have no answer to mainstream Americans’ economic pain; all they can offer are titillating little libidinal gratifications for their base.They are betting that the grim satisfaction of dominance, of cruelty, will be more important to voters than $5 gasoline. They’re leaning into being mean, in short, because they don’t have anything else.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionTexasKen PaxtonUS politicsUS SenateDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out Ukraine | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approval
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approval
Content: ‘His perceived political need and irreducible pathological neediness dovetail with his longtime admiration of Putin.’Photograph: Jae C Hong/APView image in fullscreen‘His perceived political need and irreducible pathological neediness dovetail with his longtime admiration of Putin.’Photograph: Jae C Hong/APOpinionDonald TrumpThe Trump-Putin love story’s next chapter: selling out UkraineSidney BlumenthalThe US president is portraying Zelenskyy as the villain as he strives for Russia’s approvalFri 23 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTShareIf Donald Trump could, he would fly to Munich to sign away Ukraine toVladimir Putin, and return to wave the document as “peace in our time”, hoping to claim at least the second Fifa peace prize.Whatever the complicated motives of Neville Chamberlain, his well-grounded fear after the carnage of a world war of another apocalypse and his wishful thinking that Hitler would be satiated after carving up Czechoslovakia, Chamberlain had not sent his son-in-law and former golf partner and real estate partner in advance to cut back-end deals with the Nazis to profit for his family and cronies.Though Chamberlain is judged as grievously misguided in history, Winston Churchill eulogized his “perfect sincerity according to his lights” and declared his mistaken gesture as rooted in the “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.Putin has proposed a meeting with Trump and Xi Jinping to settle the Ukraine war on Russian terms without the presence of the troublesome Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Wall Street Journaldescribedsuch a meeting as “unprecedented”.As a historical matter, that would be untrue. The Czechs were not present at Munich when their country was delivered to Hitler.Part of Trump’s urgent reason for selling outUkraineis to cast blame before the midterm elections for the inflation wrought by his tariffs and Iran war. Panicked by plunging polls, he has ramped up his rhetoric against Zelenskyy as the alleged source of the crisis that Trump himself has created.Portraying Zelenskyy as the villain, Trump projects himself, as usual, as the victim. His perceived political need and irreducible pathological neediness dovetail with his longtime admiration of Putin as the unconstrained strongman he has always wished to be.Since Trump’s first visit to Moscow in 1987, he has dreamed of the bonanza of Russian deals to be lavished on him from Putin. Upon his return, he paid for full-pageadsin major newspapers calling for the US tostop fundingthe defense of countries capable of defending themselves and to cease defending the flow of oil through the Gulf. “The world is laughing at America’s politicians as we protect ships we don’t own, carrying oil we don’t need, destined for allies who won’t help,” the ad said.From the start, the ideology has been a token of his greed, decades before he hawked his “America First Collection” ofdigital tokens. Putin has been the unwavering object of his aspiration, one of the few people he has not betrayed or sought to humiliate, but to whom he bends his knee.“Together,”tweetedKirill Dmitriev, Putin’s head of the Russian sovereign wealth fund, over a graphic showing the Russian bear and the American eagle on the same side poised to fight against the British lion and a shattered European Union flag. He was celebrating on 16 October what he conceived as the new axis against the western allies the same day that Trump waived sanctions against Russia under the Lindsey Graham Act.Graham, who died in Washington just hours upon returning from a visit of support to Ukraine, was hailed as Trump’s closest friend in the Congress, which passed the bill overwhelmingly, Democrats and Republicans in rare unity.Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, whom Trump imposed on the South Carolina governor to be appointed as the martyr’s replacement, was prominently made the marquee sponsor, lending the novice senator a credential. In a Republican primary debate, shesaid: “National security is not my thing.”When Trump tossed aside the Graham Act without bothering to consult her, she was left to sputter an ineffectual objection, leaving her vulnerable in an unexpectedly close race. Her prospect and dignity were shards of Trump’s collateral damage.Trump vehementlyblamedZelenskyy for supposedly prolonging the war,called him“not a good guy for us to deal with”, and said that the Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries were a “disgrace” and had “better damn well stop”, and that Ukraine needed a “new leader who can make a deal”.After an hour-and-a-half phone call with Putin on his 74th birthday, so friendly that neither wanted to hang up the phone first,according to Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s aide, Trump announced his sweetheart dealfor 300,000 metric tons of diesel from Russia, followed in November by 500,000 and an additional million. For this, Trump waived sanctions.The stunt gives Putin hard cash to continue operating his war machine, while the diesel will be statistically insignificant to thepricein the US market. The US consumes 300,000 tons within 14 hours. Zelenskyycalledthis a “happy birthday gift to Putin”. The effect of Trump’s transaction could not help struggling American consumers, but is a practical help to sustain Putin’s aggression.Trump’s giveaway was followed by thesudden restrictionof Ukrainian access to the Starshield network, managed by Elon Musk for the Pentagon, that is indispensable to Ukraine’s defense. For a week, in an Abbott and Costello routine of “who’s on first”, Musk blamed the Pentagon, while Trump claimed to be out of the loop. “It wasn’t me and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said.Ukraine’s frontline communications were immediately degraded. The outage directly preceded barrages of Russian missile strikes that knocked out energy infrastructure and left 600,000 Ukrainians without power. Slowly, after outraged reaction from the Europeans and Congress,connectivitywas mostly but not completely restored.Musk, whose businesses are dependent on federal contracts, is thelargest donorto the Republican campaigns in the midterm elections, spending $366m so far, exceeding the $276m he spent to elect Trump in 2024.The diesel deal was a successful ploy as part of Putin’s larger scheme to leverage Russian energy assets as bait to Trump in order to end US support for Ukraine. In early September,Putin pitchedTrump’s self-interested envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, on the vast international assets of Lukoil, Russia’s second-largest oil company, requiring a treasury department waiver, thereby opening the door for a host of shadow agreements.The Abu Dhabi royal family and the Qatari Al-Khayyat brothers would hold a large part of the equity, theNew York Timesreported. The Qatari investors are simultaneously partnered with Kushner on his luxury real estate project in Albania, which has provoked a popular uprising called “the Flamingo revolution”.Another partner in the Lukoil consortium, Todd Boehly, CEO of Eldridge Industries, a holding company, and co-owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers and Lakers, has donated $2m to Trump’s political action committee, Maga Inc.The negotiator on the Russian side, Kirill Dmitriev, is the one who enthusiastically tweeted: “Together.” But the Lukoil deal is hardly the only one apparently in the pipeline; Trump laid the groundwork for an array of post-sanctions opportunities. “A classified report produced by a European intelligence agency states that Trump and people around him have discussed several potential contracts in Russia,” Dexter Filkinsreportedin the New Yorker. The document detailed 10 ventures after a “peace deal” – that is, after forcing a Ukrainian surrender on Russian terms.Against this background of the Russian strategy, large and small movements of Trump and his family become clarified, from the Kushner-Witkoff-Dmitriev negotiations to Don Jr’s wedding party in the Bahamas paid for in part by a Putin thug, Umar Kremlev, head of the Olympic-banned International Boxing Association.A “large” contingent of Russians was present at the intimate wedding party, according toProPublica, but their identities remain unknown. Kushner was also present at the celebration.Fiona Hill, who served as Trump’s director for Russian affairs on the national security council in his first term, has described Trump as awestruck in his relationship with Putin. Trump envied him as the “ultimate badass”. She observed how Trump’s pathetic need to be seen as a peer to the autocrat allowed him to beplayed like a fiddle.At the 2018 Helsinki summit, she was horrified when Trump dismissed the findings of the US intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the presidential election of 2016 on his behalf, deferring to Putinby saying: “President Putin says it’s not Russia. I don’t see any reason why it would be.”Hill thought she might stage a fake medical emergency or pull a fire alarm to stop Trump from humiliating himself and the US.But that was during the first term, before Trump grasped how to use the presidency, with official immunity granted by the supreme court, to forge his own kleptocratic state to achieve his highest aspiration: attaining the exalted law-free status of Putin. Trump’s effort to become the full partner with Russia makes his pay-for-play ballroom seem a mere bauble by comparison.Among Trump’s infinite abuses is his suborning of the Department of Justice to pursue his retribution snark hunt of a “grand conspiracy” of his alleged enemies of the “deep state” for perpetrating the “Russia hoax”, those national security officials who asserted the factual truth that Russia interfered in the 2016 election to benefit him.Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered | Sidney BlumenthalRead moreIn early October, however, the key man appointed to run this operation, the veteran Washington attorney deep into rightwing causes, Joe diGenova, resigned, “saying top department officials were pressuring the team to bring criminal cases before they were ready”, according to theWall Street Journal.Nobody now observing Trump’s relations with Putin is accusing him of “collusion”. There is no secrecy. Trump brazenly proclaims his aspiration to partner with Russia and to become the equal of Putin. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” hesaid.After Russia released an American schoolteacher imprisoned for four years on what the state department called false charges, a human chip to personify Putin’s gratitude to Trump, Witkoff praised Putin: “You are a humanitarian.”ZelenskyytoldNBC’s Meet the Press that if Trump “will take the side of Russia”, it would be a “a historic mistake and big tragedy”. DmitrievtweetedTrump’s remark: “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given us nothing.” Dmitriev added his comment: “Clarity.”Nobody in retrospect will eulogize Trump for “noble and benevolent instincts of the human heart”.Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of theCourt of History podcastExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionVladimir PutinVolodymyr ZelenskyyTrump administrationUS politicsRussiaUkrainecommentShareReuse this content

title: America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity
Content: ‘Part of the project of ridding ourselves of Trump, therefore, must be to rekindle our understanding of the common good.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Part of the project of ridding ourselves of Trump, therefore, must be to rekindle our understanding of the common good.’Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpAmerica must reverse Trump’s moral squalorRobert ReichThe president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanityFri 23 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTShareThe Democrats’ focus on affordability seems to be a winning strategy (we’ll know for sure in a little over two weeks). But we mustn’t lose sight of the moral squalor at the core of the Trump regime and the necessity of ending it.It’s that moral squalor – the utter disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation and, for that matter, of humanity – that uniquely marks Trump and the reprobates he has attracted to Washington. It has also poisoned much of the Republican party, including the billionaires and tech bros who finance it.To put this despicable era behind us, we’ll need to renounce and reverse this squalor.What are loosely described as Trump’s “conflicts of interest”, for example, extend way beyond enriching himself from his presidency. He has violated the norms of presidential decency.Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes appeaser Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon TisdallRead moreHe recently decided to host the Group of 20 annual summit of world leaders at hisprivate golf club in Miamiin December. When he sought to do this during his first term, it was viewed as a blatant violation of the emoluments clause of the constitution. Now, after America’s moral sensibilities have been numbed by Trump’s appetite for foreign gifts – such as Qatar’s “donation” of a $400m jumbo jet – it barely merits a mention.Trump’s social media platform Truth Social couldreportedly chargeup to $100,000 a month for access to “Truth API”, a service that gives subscribers access to potentially market-moving posts by high-profile users such as Trump “in milliseconds”. The service, in other words, enables subscribers to make lucrative stock market trades off market-moving information coming from the president.A company linked to his family files atrademark application for “Trump TV”to control the name of a streaming service that the White House uses for official presidential communications, thereby pocketing the benefits from taxpayer funds used to create and run the channel.His family-backed crypto firm introduces a stablecoin just months before he signs legislation promotingthat type of cryptocurrency. His wife ispaid tens of millionsfor a self-promotional film by Jeff Bezos’s Amazon, a federal contractor and major retailer subject to a myriad of regulations. His son has aRussian oligarch, close to Putin, pick up the tab for part of his wedding afterparty in the Bahamas.He arranges for the justice department togrant him and his family immunityfor any back taxes and penalties they might owe.And so on. Trump has tossed away all constraints on making money off his presidency “because I got no credit in the first term” and “I found out that nobody cared”.Credit?Someone who is entrusted with the highest office in the land must receive “credit” for doing what’s right, in order to continue doing what’s right?Nobody cares?A president can embrace corruption if the public doesn’t mind?It’s not just the blatant self-dealing. His moral squalor extends to every aspect of governing.He lies incessantly – a gushing firehose of deception.His foreign policies make Henry Kissinger’srealpolitikseem principled by comparison. He orders the abduction of the president of another nation, installs a new president of his choosing, and announces he’s taking that nation’s oil – and doesn’t even account for what he does with the oil money.He attacks Iran without consulting America’s traditional allies or even Congress.He turns his back on Ukraine and sides with Putin, the aggressor in that conflict. He pursuesdiesel oil from Putinin violation of US sanctions on Russia andblames the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for high oil prices rather than Trump’s war on Iran. He says Ukraine should get a new president.The moral squalor extends to usurping the authority of Congress to decide on tariffs, wars and whether and how to spend taxpayer money.It extends to his cynical defiance of supreme court orders. When the court invalidates his tariffs, hereimposes themunder a different statute. When the court rules that he doesn’t have grounds to remove a member of the Fed board of governors, heconcocts a meansto do so anyway. When the court says he has to remove his name from the Kennedy Center, he closes the center andthreatens to demolish it.It extends to his using the justice department and the FBI to prosecute people who have stood up to him, including courageous officials.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow We WinBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt extends to his claims that Mexicans are “bringing drugs and crime”; calling Somali-Americans “garbage” anddenouncing“what they’ve done to Minnesota, these people from Somalia”; and taunting Muslims, including by calling Dr Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, “Mohammed”.It extends to giving a gigantic tax cut to America’s wealthiest people, financed by cutting nutrition assistance and healthcare to America’s most vulnerable people.The moral squalor has turned much of America into a police state – terrorizing large numbers of people residing here, including many here legally.Deploying ICE agents at schools, courthouses and hospitals. Forcibly taking parents away from their children. Allowing masked gunmen without identification to grab suspected undocumented immigrants off our streets, from their cars, and out of their homes – giving them no opportunity to defend themselves in front of third parties before putting them into often overcrowded and unhealthy prisons or sending them to other countries where they’re imprisoned. Killing people.When asked if there are limits to his authority, Trumpreplies: “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”“My own” morality is no morality at all. Morality reflects collective judgments about right and wrong, shared values about what we owe one another as citizens of the same society. Morality refers to the ideals we seek to achieve together.Trump is not guided by any sense of right and wrong. He is guided only by what enriches him or gives him more power and glory – a nihilistic might-makes-right in which the strong do whatever they want and the weak suffer what they must.To be sure, Trump’s moral squalor could not have permeated America – he could not have been elected a second time – had our shared norms and ideals not already been compromised.Vast inequalities of income and wealth, coupled with a growing sense that the social contract at the heart of the American system was coming undone and that those at the top have rigged the game, were already fueling anger and distrust. Trump ignited that fuel.Without shared ideals or common moral values, there is nothing pushing back against this despicable president and regime – no countervailing moral force against the ongoing squalor.Part of the project of ridding ourselves of Trump, therefore, must be to rekindle our understanding of the common good and appreciation of what we owe one another as members of the same society.Of course we must make life more affordable; Democrats are wise to emphasize this in the midterms. But we also must demand common decency.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Trump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?  | Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow | The Guardian
description: No one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minors, say students Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: No one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minors, say students Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionChild protectionWe’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us?Rose, Mae, Aylin and WillowNo one should have to feel nervous about walking to school in clothes designed for children. It’s time for UK law to end the disgusting sexualisation of minorsFri 23 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTShareIn the Little Feminist Book Club, we don’t read a lot of books. The group, set up by former students at our school, is more about reading poems and articles, analysing song lyrics, discussing the issues that matter to us and, most importantly, campaigning.Ourcurrent campaign– the one you might have heard of – is to ban school uniform from pornographic content. Simply put, we want to end the depiction of school uniform in pornography to ensure that minors are not viewed as anything other than what they are: children. We were shocked when we realised that this content is currently legal – most of the adults we’ve spoken to agree that it is wrong. But apparently it falls to us – students aged 14 and 15 – to take action.Anew law, due to come into force on 6 November, will ban pornography that shows sexual activity involving anyone pretending to be under 16. But it won’t outlaw the depiction of adults dressed as older schoolchildren. We want to remove this grey area in order to stop normalising the sexualisation of school uniforms. We believe children and children’s clothing should not be associated with sexual acts. Therefore, we believe that school uniform should not be shown as something “sexy”, regardless of the actual age of the person wearing it.Previous members of the Little Feminist Book Club, working withTools for Change, successfully campaigned for better access to period products in our school. We then heard about another school feminist groupwho had campaignedto get school uniforms banned from sex shops. We were appalled that they were being sold in that context, yet somehow not surprised. From an early age, some of us had noticed that school uniforms are depicted in ways that sexualise women wearing them. Mae recalls: “For me it started when I was 12, watching TV with my mother. A female character put on a school uniform to turn on a man and I thought, ‘I’m going to have to wear a uniform like that tomorrow.’”No 12-year-old should feel uncomfortable about going to school in a uniform that is designed to promote unity and community and safety. Yet we did. It made us question how we would be perceived when we left the house in our uniforms. These were women dressing up in school uniform specifically to turn on a man. The only people who should be wearing school uniform are children.This issue has affected us personally. Members of our group feel too uncomfortable to wear their uniform out of school. One no longer wears skirts at all. When we were asked to speak at a Tools for Change event in parliament in July we unanimously agreed not to wear our uniform. In a world of AI, we were well aware of the dangers of being photographed in uniform while being associated with this campaign. Before we sent our first letters to MPs and charities, we discussed what it might mean if anyone actually paid attention to what we were saying. Would we be prepared to take this on, given all that it might mean? We were, and so we did.Since starting this campaign, we have been flooded with support. Sadly, this has included other women and girls sharing their experiences of the same issue – dating back generations. Surveys show thatone in three girlshas been sexually harassed while wearing school uniform, and we have seen comments from many of them. Older women said that they have never been catcalled more than when they wore school uniform as children; others have shared with us their feelings of disgust and horror. One recalled being assaulted by a group of men in the 2000s “explicitly because of my school uniform”. A teenager said that the number of older men who sexually harass her almost every day is “uncountable”.Getting to hear people’s own personal experiences fuels our passion and drives us forward. The overwhelmingly positive response truly gives us hope that we can make a difference. We want to protect children now and in the future.As the campaign continues to gain attention, we have received support from important figures including our local MP and an MSP. One has agreed to directly passour handwritten letterto the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and to table an early day motion. We now also have a meeting scheduled with Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims, and another with Jess Asato MP and the peer Gabby Bertin, who was instrumental in the amendments to the crime and policing bill. Our MP is helping us turn our campaign into a law. He suggested that, instead of creating an entirely new law banning school uniform in pornography, it would be quicker and easier to amend existing legislation – meaning that it would take less time for children to be taken out of this harmful and dangerous position that perverted people have placed us in. But these are not decisions we can make. Everyone has a responsibility to end this cycle of sexualisation and objectification of children. We can’t do that as a few kids in the middle of our GCSEs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe have made a start by launching this petition. Now, we need the adults who vowed to protect us to get behind it. We need the politicians whopledged to halve violence against women and girlsto change the law. It’s all well and good to read this article by a group of kids explaining how we’re trying to keep ourselves safe and think this is a fantastic campaign. But that’s not enough. Things will only change when adults take responsibility for ending the disgusting practice of sexualising clothes made for children. Then perhaps one day young people can go to school knowing the only thing our uniforms signify is that it’s time to learn.Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow are students aged 14 and 15Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsChild protectionOpinionChildrenPornographySexual harassmentSchoolsSocial careWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: Modern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidote | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: Everything has become so frictionless and optimised, that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality – even if it has no explicit market value
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: Everything has become so frictionless and optimised, that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality – even if it has no explicit market value
Content: ‘Looking around – with everyone wearing the same athleisure, staring into the same screens, drinking the same coffee, pouring it into the same-looking plastic faces – you wonder when did all this happen?’Illustration: Spectral-Design/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Looking around – with everyone wearing the same athleisure, staring into the same screens, drinking the same coffee, pouring it into the same-looking plastic faces – you wonder when did all this happen?’Illustration: Spectral-Design/Getty Images/iStockphotoPhilosophyModern life is stuck in a sea of sameness. The pursuit of beauty is a necessary antidoteBrigid DelaneyEverything has become so frictionless and optimised, that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality – even if it has no explicit market valueFri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTShareBy the time it’s 5pm on a Friday, the headache and dry eyes have well and truly settled in. Maybe it’s a long day in front of your four screens while funnelling white noise through a large pair of headphones to cancel out the calls of your co-workers. Or maybe it’s the almost chemical wash of white fluorescent lights that shine from the low ceiling in your open-plan office, or the feeling of enclosure as you look out the window on to the reflective walls of other towers.To lift your spirits, you decide to treat yourself to a weekend at a beachside Airbnb.But the town is not how you remember it as a kid. The farmland has been turned into identical housing estates broken up by highway-hugging shopping centres with the same Guzman, Woolies, Chemist Warehouse, Dan Murphy’s and Priceline as all the other shopping centres.They’re not the only things that are samey. The cars in the car park are mostly white or grey, and stepping out of them, people are in near-identical athleisure or shorts and T-shirts.Our lives and identities have moved online – and it’s driving us insane | Brigid DelaneyRead moreThe Airbnb is how it was depicted in the pictures (minimalist, fancy handwash in the bathroom, Anko soft furnishings) but there is something dispiriting about it. Just like the cars, the interior is grey and white, and it smells of surface cleaner. It’s a house devoid of colour, personality and character.The beach itself is still beautiful, but coming out of the ocean you can’t remember where you left your towel. Every inch of sand is taken up with the same stripy Cool Cabana tents, rendering the visual landscape hectic and disorientating, as if you’d hit your head and were seeing double.At the cafe (minimalist, blond wood, pot plants, $7 flat whites) you run into some people from school who you haven’t seen for ages. You can’t quite put your finger on it but they look different, weird almost. There’s something uncanny about their faces, with their foreheads smooth as a screen, their lips and cheeks plumped.Looking around – with everyone wearing the same athleisure, staring into the same screens, drinking the same coffee, pouring it into the same-looking plastic faces – you wonder when did all this happen? Where did all the beauty go?It’s difficult to believe we are lucky enough to be born on a blue, watery planet that is covered in flowers. And that on this planet everyone is a completely unique individual, all 8.3 billion of us, with our own specific way of expressing ourselves, our unique faces and bodies, our idiosyncrasies, desires, aversions and tastes.Because right now we are stuck in a sea of sameness. Whether it’s the design of our offices, the interior of our houses (major paint brands like Dulux and Sherwin-Williams say grey is a top-searched and frequently used colour, with theFinancial Timesreporting that grey is chosen because it may result in better resale value) or the cars we drive. Modern life is becoming drabber, uglier, more uniform and a lot less pleasing to look at.But there are signs of a resistance – with one of the most fascinating beingdiscussions aroundthe need for beauty.The left are reawakening to the fact that fighting for better material conditions for all people extends to what was previously thought of as a frivolous or optional extra. But beauty – and the elevation of beauty – is central to the project of flourishing.This is an ancient ideal, and its suppression by the powerful is equally old.double quotation markBeauty is not slavishly following trends but working out what you like, what makes you happy – and going with thatThe Greeks had a concept that bound beauty, goodness and truth together askalos kagathos, literally “beautiful and good”. In The Symposium, Socrates describes beauty as the thing that draws the soul upward towards truth, justice and the divine. Ugliness, in this framework, was not merely unpleasant, it was a form of moral disorder.Throughout history, there have been times when beauty has been elevated (the Renaissance) and suppressed (the factory districts in the Industrial Revolution). And in times of suppression, movements have emerged such as the Arts and Crafts movement in the 1860s, aimed at restoring dignity to working people through the elevation of beautiful objects in their homes such as wallpaper, textiles and furniture.We are living in a time where originality and beauty have been suppressed, where everything has become so frictionless and optimised (such as the grey homes optimised for resale, not for living in) that concerted efforts must be made to turn back towards beauty and individuality, even if it has no explicit market value.The tipping point for me is the very devaluation of the role of human-made art, writing, music and design by the rise of machine-made art in the form of AI slop.I can live (I guess … ) with the grey houses and the bland homewares, but not with removing humans from the creation of writing, art and beauty in favour of AI.Suffragists, unionists and workers have long fought under the banner of bread and roses – that is, having basic biological needs met while also having access to the things that elevate the spirit and please the eye.View image in fullscreenA campaign poster for Zohran Mamdani in New York in June 2025.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APNow the project has some new energy. You see it in Zohran Mamdani’s New York (he used the campaign slogan of “Roti and Roses”) where there was bread in the form of a promise of freezing rents, but roses too.Everything from the way his campaign posters, font and videos were designed – with an eye for pleasing human-made (in contrast with the Truth Social slop, such as Trump as Jesus ) – to policy decisions such as releasing70,000 free Metropolitan Opera tickets, has at its core the importance of flourishing on all levels.Critical thinking is one of the most important aspects of being human, according to Stoicism. So why are we handing it over to a machine? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreBeauty can be something we vote for, but it is also something that right now we must fight for – whether we advocate for the natural world, or better-planned communities and housing.It is also something we co-create with the world. Beauty is not slavishly following trends but working out what you like, what makes you happy – and going with that.It could mean a maximalist apartment where the walls are pink. Or it could be wearing colour when everyone else is in black. Or it could be nurturing pot plants in your office or helping with a community garden. Or maybe it’s creating your own art, or employing an artist or writer, rather than using AI.Beauty made by humans (and in the case of nature, protected and nurtured by humans) is not just pleasing to the eye and the spirit, but it is a form of protest. A pushback against dehumanisation of our current age.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsPhilosophyAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: London’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River Thames, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: London’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River Thames, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Hammersmith Bridge in west London, which has been closed to traffic for seven years, in April 2019.Photograph: Johnny Armstead/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHammersmith Bridge in west London, which has been closed to traffic for seven years, in April 2019.Photograph: Johnny Armstead/REX/ShutterstockOpinionLondonHammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’tSimon JenkinsLondon’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River ThamesFri 23 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.41 EDTShareLondon’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge alsonow closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be5,107 homes a year, up from a previoustarget of 1,381.The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion isofficially ratedthe worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation ofcomputer-assisted“smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just27 seconds offindividual bus journeys. A Guardian investigationlast monthtimed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circuswas under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word inLondon.In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter ofsparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with thetotal for 2024at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.Is this Prince Harry or David Brent in The Office? Either way, we’re watching a masterclass in awkwardness | Emma BrockesRead moreHammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but ithas decidedit “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent£54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’sSadiq Khanappears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, theCity of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn.The foundationcurrently spends lavishly oncauses that havenothing to do with bridges.This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLondonOpinionSadiq KhanArchitectureMotoringcommentShareReuse this content

title: This man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the same  | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s future, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s future, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andrew Boff, chair of the London Assembly, at City Hall, London, January 2025.Photograph: See Li/Picture Capital/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAndrew Boff, chair of the London Assembly, at City Hall, London, January 2025.Photograph: See Li/Picture Capital/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionConservativesThis man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the samePolly ToynbeeThe London Assembly’s Andrew Boff is one of many who reject Kemi Badenoch’s authoritarian position. They are the only chance for the party’s futureFri 23 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTShareThe chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports theEuropean convention on human rights(ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch thatothers would follow himover the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent.In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She alsobars anyone supporting net zero.When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race.In a statementhe pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me,the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.The time may come, he warned, when extremists win an election on an even smaller vote sharethan Labour’s 34% in 2024– and overturn all human rights legislation without the protections the ECHR affords. “That’s what authoritarian governments do,” Boff said. But he insisted that the committee, which vets Conservative candidates, didn’t listen. “They just repeated the same tropes, that activist judges are using the ECHR against parliament.”Now he is free of the party straitjacket, Boff is planning to stand for London mayor as an independent, allowing him to say what he thinks about Badenoch.He complains to me that the energy and resources that should promote the party “all go to promoting Kemi, Kemi, Kemi”. Thinking well of her in 2015, he says he had encouraged her to stand for the London assembly, where she served until 2017 before being elected to parliament. He says he found her “lazy and combative”.Few will be surprised by Boff’s departure. But many will be wondering what took him so long.He was ejected from the Tory conference in 2023for quietly heckling the then home secretary Suella Braverman’s speech, accusing her of homophobia and transphobia. “It is a signal to people who don’t like people who are LGBT+,” Boff, who is gay, said at the time as he condemned her speech as “trash”. Boff said that Braverman “was basically vilifying gay people and trans people by this attack on LGBT ideology”.View image in fullscreenAndrew Boff being escorted out of a speech by Suella Braverman at the Conservative party conference in Manchester, 2023.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesHe was not alone in voicing criticism over the party’s direction. The former Tory MP Robert Buckland, fellow one-nationer and director of the Tory Reform Group, hurried out to defend Boff after his ejection from the conference, saying heckling was “part of the democratic debate” and that his treatment by security staff was “heavy-handed”.Buckland was among the many one-nationers who lost their seat at the 2024 general election. But that traditional strand of Conservatism has not vanished – nor have those who used to vote for the Tories but now turn to the Liberal Democrats or simply boycott the ballot box.Boff’s views represent a growing centre-right moderate strand that has been expelled or silenced under Badenoch’s leadership. Facing this hostile climate, one nation Tories have gone to ground in parliament; but outside the Commons, Prosper UK, a centrist Tory grouping led by the former mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson quietly gains strength.Its mission statement is to win back moderate voters who snubbed the Conservatives at the last general election, and this message seems to have struck a chord, with the group attractingnearly 30,000 supporterssince its launch in January.It is worth examining Boff’s views, as many Conservatives who have signed up to Prosper UK are likely to share them. He calls himself a Thatcherite, strongly opposing Labour’s renationalisation plans, backing low taxes and a small state. He voted for Brexit, believing the words of the likes of Daniel Hannan,who claimed“absolutely nobody is talking about threatening our place in the single market”. But instead the Tories delivered a hard Brexit after what he calls an “atrocious” campaign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTimes have changed; as the political analyst Peter Kellnerpointed out this week, Britain’s pro-Brexit majority has literally died out. Any so-called betrayal of the referendum is only betraying the dreadful legacy of the departed.If the Conservative party has any future as a government, it won’t be under its present leader. A small bounce for improved performance in parliament will never overcome Badenoch’s growing distance from voters, including those who should be natural Tories.Boff may be a throwback to an irretrievable, more moderate Conservative brand, like that of the Macmillan era – a voice from the good old days when traditional party allegiances were clearly defined. Or possibly he and Prosper UK are the vanguard of a reconstituted centre-right able to attract new voters as well as those who have deserted the Tories.That won’t be easy: already there are gloating Spectator-aligned Tories who say thatthe party is better offwithout the likes of Boff, or any real concession to centrism. But we should have a care. The success of a respectable right matters to all in the left bloc of progressive parties, too. A centre right is needed to fight off the dark forces of the hard right and worse, here and across Europe. That Overton window framing politics needs a firm shunt towards a more rational debate on our future in Europe – and on saving the planet.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservativesOpinionKemi BadenochEuropean court of human rightsHuman Rights ActcommentShareReuse this content

title: Imagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigration | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration, says the Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration, says the Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionImmigration and asylumImagine if, for once, Labour decided to tell the truth about immigrationGaby HinsliffOur economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integrationFri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.42 EDTShareMy mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.Under the latest attempt by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to ratchet immigration numbers ever further down, “low-skilled” foreign workers will now have towait up to 15 yearsfor the right to become permanent residents. The new rules would be backdated to 2021 to catchwhat the right dubbedthe “Boriswave”, that unexpected surge of workers who came to Britain in the Boris Johnson years – many on health and care visas – and would under the old five-year rule have started qualifying for settlement in 2027. What has unsettled some of Mahmood’s own cabinet colleagues is the sense of the state reneging on what was understood to be the deal when those workers came here. Having to be continuously employed for 15 years instead of five without a break means in practice that some will have to leave, while others will live in mortal fear of losing a job. A growing cabinet revolt against Mahmood’s reforms is now becoming the first real challenge to Andy Burnham’s authority as prime minister, but also more broadly a test of where he really stands on immigration.This month’s budget throws a problem that governments have been trying to ignore for a decade into sharp relief: kneejerk hostility to foreign workers is costing Britain dear, and not just because public services would fall apart without them. Last month, theInstitute for Fiscal Studies warnedthat falling immigration would inevitably mean falling tax revenues, shrinking John Healey’s headroom at the budget by about £4bn. So much for the rightwing myth that migrants are a drain on their host country: if anything, they’ve been bailing Britain out.It’s not just taxes, either. Immigrants pay a surcharge on top for the right to use the NHS if needed while they’re here, which is now raising£2.5bn a year, according to new research from the Nuffield Trust. It seems all those pesky liberals who argued that migrants are generally healthier than the average Briton – and therefore less likely to need a GP – were right after all: the trust estimates that migrants are on average paying in 60% more in surcharge per year than they take out in healthcare services, a handy little revenue stream that for some reason we never talk about. But immigration crackdowns threaten that income too. The trust notes that falling immigration can lead to “a sharp drop in income” for the NHS, much as slashing foreign student visas has hurt universities that were reliant on their fees.As the Office for Budget Responsibilityspelled out in 2024– when it calculated that the surge of immigration under Johnson that so offended Tory voters at the time would help knock more than £7bn off projected government borrowing by 2028-29 – economically speaking, immigration is basically good news. If the country really wants it to fall, then something else – higher taxes, lower spending or more borrowing – is going to have to plug the resulting hole in the finances. Yet for years now, successive governments, fearful of confronting leave voters, have tried manfully to pretend that that choice does not exist.Mahmood’s plan is essentially yet another attempt to square the same old circle, gearing the system around letting in as few people as possible – in keeping with what a furious public has for the last decade seemed to want – while trying to cherrypick those most likely to make an outsize economic contribution. Under her reforms, the highest paid workers (who are likely to pay lots of tax over their lifetimes) would befast-tracked to settlement, while those judged more likely to be an economic burden on the state overall would be pushed away. What she doesn’t seem to have bargained for, aside from the fact that the rest of the world is in hot competition for high-skilled migrants, is the sense of deep disquiet that engenders. As the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, has pointed out, endlessly prolonging settlement risks undermining social cohesion. A country that makes very clear its foreign workers are here at best on sufferance, even if they do hold lives in their hands at work every day, does nothing to encourage them to integrate and put down roots.The logic of Burnham’s announcement that a future Labour government might considerrejoining the EU, meanwhile, leaves Mahmood’s reforms looking strangely like the relics of a bygone era. If rejoining the single market or customs union would inevitably mean accepting freedom of movement again, what’s the point?The truth is that grimly ratcheting immigration down to next to nothing has come at extraordinary fiscal and social cost, and if the aim was to destroy Reform’s raison d’etre then it hasn’t worked. The mainstream right has switched seamlessly from the pre-Brexit days of complaining that Polish plumbers were taking Britons’ jobs, to a much darker post-Brexit stage of painting migrants as rapists and criminals. The far right, meanwhile, has simply moved on from cheerleading for deportations to insisting that even people who were born here aren’t English unless they’re white.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLegal migrant numbers are at a historic low and small boat crossingshave halved, yet that didn’t stop anger at asylum seekers spilling on to the streets again this summer. There is no level of migration low enough to satisfy some people. There is, however, very much a level of migration low enough to make us all even poorer, and the angry somehow even angrier. And right now, we’re living with it.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumOpinionAndy BurnhamShabana MahmoodSocial careNHSLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Giorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down?  | Riccardo Alcaro | The Guardian
description: With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister, says Riccardo Alcaro, head of research at Istituto Affari Internazionali
Author: Riccardo Alcaro
Headline: With elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime minister, says Riccardo Alcaro, head of research at Istituto Affari Internazionali
Content: ‘Roberto Vannacci’s extreme positions and abrasive style quickly made him a regular media presence.’Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Roberto Vannacci’s extreme positions and abrasive style quickly made him a regular media presence.’Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockOpinionItalyGiorgia Meloni is Italy’s great political survivor. Could one man be about to bring her down?Riccardo AlcaroWith elections looming in 2027, Roberto Vannacci’s new far-right movement could fatally outflank the prime ministerFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTShareGiorgia Meloni’s government became thelongest servingin Italy’s republican history last month. This unusual political longevity, a moderate foreign policy, a certain personal charisma and even a recentspat with Donald Trumphave combined to sharpen Meloni’s profile as the go-to leader on the European right.Meloni’spersonal approval rating– at about 41% – is one of the highest among west European leaders. Her far-right Brothers of Italy party has retained most of its support – a striking feat in our anti-incumbent era and by Italian standards, an achievement.Yet all this may not suffice for her ruling coalition to be returned to power at Italy’s next election, in 2027.Even before this week’s riots in Milan, Meloni’s greatest challenge was emerging from her far right, in the form of a new movement led by the former army general, Roberto Vannacci. The firebrand demagogue will, like Marine Le Pen in France, certainly seek to exploit the unrest to promote his party’s law-and-order credentials. If he succeeds, it could come at the expense of Meloni’s ruling coalition.Vannacciwas a high-ranking officer of almost 40 years’ service when in 2023 he self-publishedIl mondo al contrario(The World Turned Upside Down). Filled with hyper-conservative misgivings about such supposed western ills as cosmopolitanism, multiculturalism and feminism, Vannacci’s book became a sensation and the general was suspended from the armed forces.But Vannacci’s extreme positions and abrasive style quickly made him a regular media presence, and with public attention came political interest. Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League and a junior partner in Meloni’s coalition, calculated that pulling the general into his ranks could boost his dwindling ratings. Salvini’s instincts were not wrong: in 2024 Vannacci was elected to the European parliament. However, he soon quit the League and this year founded a new far-right party, National Future, to which,polls suggest, the League has beenlosing support, imperilling Meloni’s coalition’s chances of re-election.Electoral logic and a common ideological background would point to a Meloni-Vannacci alliance, but Vannacci’s ideological extremism makes that difficult.Vannacci has made the “remigration” of foreign nationals – an idea promoted by such radical forces as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) – a central plank of his programme. While opposition to migration is one of the defining features of Meloni’s government, it has never gone that far.Vannacci’s emphasis on the traditional family is so uncompromising that he proposes giving parents additional votes in elections and an advantage in public recruitment. Hisprogrammeinsists that abortion “is not a right” while it promotes the so-called “Mediterranean patriarchy”, and advocates abolishing thespecific crime of femicide. These positions sit uneasily with Meloni’s politics, which combine conservative values with her own self-image of female empowerment.The sharpest divide relates to foreign policy. Vannacci aims at easing the burden of eurozone fiscal discipline and opposes plans for greater defence integration. Tellingly, he has joined the AfD-ledEurope of Sovereign Nationsgrouping in the European parliament, a group shunned even by Salvini’s League, the most nativist member of the Meloni government. On Russia and Ukraine, the gap is wider still. Echoing the AfD, Vannacci hasarguedthat Russia is not an imminent threat to Europe and has called forthe reopeningof trade and diplomatic channels with Moscow, including by buying Russian gas. Vannacci also opposes support for Ukraine. For Meloni, by contrast, backing Ukraine is a pillar of her international positioning, most recently attested by heropen criticismof Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports, ahead of a hard winter for Ukraine.View image in fullscreenUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Giorgia Meloni at Palazzo Chigi in RomePhotograph: Riccardo Antimiani/EPAMeloni’s reluctance to enter an alliance with Vannacci is understandable. Forza Italia, her centre-right coalition partner, fears it would drive away the moderate conservative vote. The League is so shaken that some of its members want to disavow Salvini’s nativist ideology and go back to the party’s roots, representing the interests of business and local communities in Italy’snorthern regions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the time being, Meloni has responded to the far-right challenge by doubling down on migration. Vannacci’s presence in the electoral wings explains some of the background to hersuspensionof the Schengen free-movement rules for air and sea passengers from Spain after the Ceuta tragedy. The same applies to the recent decision to put a30% ceilingon students of foreign origin in schools. But it is far from certain this strategy can work, and pressure to strike a deal with Vannacci may build, not least to prevent the former military man from claiming to be the only politician promising a hardline law and order response to vandalism and looting in Milan. Meloni’sdispatch of 500 troopsto the city ahead of further planned cost-of-living demonstrations was aimed partly at taking the wind out of Vannacci’s sails.While an alliance could increase Meloni’s chances of re-election Vannacci would be a restive and unreliable coalition partner.The alternative is to delegitimise Vannacci as a nationalist force, pointing to his extremism and proximity to Russia. Meloni would hardly regain the most extreme nativist voters lost to Vannacci but could convince a section of the moderate electorate to choose her coalition over centrist parties.This strategy entails a real risk that Meloni will lose the next election. Still, the onus is on her now to articulate why Vannacci’s mix of anti-EU nativism, homophobia and misogyny is incompatible with both her own brand of national conservatism and Italy’s place inEurope. Doing so would send a powerful message that the commitment to the EU’s democratic principles – and European cohesion – is a moral red line. It is also one that can be imposed by conservative nationalists like Meloni on fringe forces to their right. As the now-seasoned leader figures out how to juggle her political ambition against the challenge posed by Vannacci, she should consider how high the stakes are, not just for Italy, but for all of Europe.Riccardo Alcaro is head of research at IAI, Istituto Affari Internazionali, in RomeExplore more on these topicsItalyOpinionEuropeGiorgia MelonicommentShareReuse this content

title: In allowing coal expansion in the Hunter, Chris Minns is pouring fuel on the climate fire. His decision will come back to hurt us all | Jack Egan | The Guardian
description: The high court found NSW is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. What message does it send when the government can step in and bypass the law?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The high court found NSW is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. What message does it send when the government can step in and bypass the law?
