Content: Despite a landmark high court decision, NSW premier Chris Minns has announced plans to introduce special legislation that will allow MACH Energy to increase production at its Mount Pleasant coalmine by nearly a third.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDespite a landmark high court decision, NSW premier Chris Minns has announced plans to introduce special legislation that will allow MACH Energy to increase production at its Mount Pleasant coalmine by nearly a third.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianOpinionEnergyIn allowing coal expansion in the Hunter, Chris Minns is pouring fuel on the climate fire. His decision will come back to hurt us allJack EganThe high court found NSW is responsible for emissions from burning exported coal. What message does it send when the government can step in and bypass the law?Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereThu 22 Oct 2026 21.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 22.14 EDTShareAs someone who lost their home in the black summer bushfires, I was buoyed by the high court finding in favour of a small community group in theHunter Valleyearlier this month.Led by two retired science teachers, Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Grouptook on a massive coal corporation and won. As a fellow schoolteacher, I felt a particular sense of pride seeing these ordinary Australians act on their care for their community and future generations.In their four-year fight against MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine in Muswellbrook,they argued it is no longer OK for big mining corporations to dig up coal and bank piles of cash while pretending the climate pollution from burning that coal is someone else’s problem.The high court agreed that conditions aimed at reducing the climate pollution from burning Australian coal overseas had not been properly considered when the rosily named “Mount Pleasant Optimisation Project” receivedNew South Walesapproval.‘A real-life moment from The Castle’: the retired Australian couple who took on a coal giant and wonRead moreMining interests quickly responded to the high court’s decision, saying it was a threat to investment. Well, of course it is. But only to the wrong kind of investment – the kind that brings us all more frequent, worse and very costly climate-driven disasters.Now, less than two weeks later, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, has announced plans to introduce special legislation that will allow the very same coal company to increase production at Mount Pleasant by nearly a third, bypassing the state’s usual planning approval process and scrutiny by the courts.Minns says this is necessary to protect 400 jobs. But the mine already has approval to operate until 2032. What message does it send when ordinary Australians fight for years to uphold the law, win in the highest court in the land and then watch our government step in to change the rules?The premier tells us he has agonised over the environment versus jobs dilemma. Both, he says, are important. I strongly agree. A just transition for workers into new, good, climate-positive jobs is a core principle of thorough climate action.Two brave, retired science teachers have shown what ordinary Australians can achieve when they act on the science and stand up. The Minns government must look beyond the next election and the demands of powerful fossil fuel lobbyists, search its own conscience and respect the rule of law. Even the big coal corporations need to play by the same rules as the rest of us.View image in fullscreenTony Lonergan (left) and Wendy Wales (middle) speak to media following their win in the high court of Australia on 7 October.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPOn New Year’s Eve 2019, my partner Cath and I saw our home go up in flames before being separated. The fearful feeling of not knowing if each other had made it out alive is a memory that will never fully leave us. Nor will the widespread devastation we witnessed across our NSW coastal community.I knew then that an awful climate future had crashed right through into our present. It was a huge wake-up call. And yet Australian governments have continued to approve new coal and gas mines, pouring more fuel on to the climate fire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOverseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coalRead moreThe evidence is clear: Australia and the world already have enough coal, gas and oil in the pipeline to see us through the transition to renewable energy and reach global net zero emissions by 2050. No new or expanded coalmines, or oil and gasfields are needed on that pathway. This has been the view of the authoritative International Energy Agency since 2021. That agency, of which Australia is a member, is technology-neutral and was created back in the 1970s to ensure the reliable supply of fossil fuels. That reliability is still a big part of its remit. Somehow Australian governments have been missing the IEA’s emails.For Wales and Lonergan, it was hugely stressful spending years taking on a massive coal corporation. But they stepped up, persevered, and they won.Inspired by people like them, I have joined nine other ordinary Australians in taking our concerns to the United Nations human rights committee. The kernel of ourHard Truthscase is that we are asking the United Nations human rights committee to assess whether Australia is breaching our human rights by continuing to approve and support coal and gas exports that fuel dangerous climate change. These are rights that belong to all of us – the right to life, family and home, and the rights of First Nations peoples to protect their Country and culture.It gives us no joy to complain about our own government. But we have tried everything else and yet continue to see huge coalmine extensions approved and vast new gasfields opened. Their pollution will come back to hurt us all. We need the Australian government to come to their senses and act.Jack Egan is a teacher, climate advocate, partner, father and grandfather living on the NSW south coast. On New Year’s Eve 2019, Jack and his partner Cath lost their home when the Currowan fire tore through their community during the black summer bushfiresExplore more on these topicsEnergyOpinionHunter ValleyCoalNew South WalesClimate crisisFossil fuelsMiningcommentShareReuse this content

title: I expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final audition | James Bond | The Guardian
description: Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?
Content: Conjuring chemistry … Turner, Callum Turner at the 82nd Venice film festival, 2025.Photograph: Gisela Schober/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConjuring chemistry … Turner, Callum Turner at the 82nd Venice film festival, 2025.Photograph: Gisela Schober/Getty ImagesJames BondI expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final auditionJack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?Stuart HeritageFri 23 Oct 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis weekend, the identity of the nextJames Bondis finally expected to be known – to the insiders, at least. According to reports, a number of youngish British actors – definitely three, possibly five – will have their final screen tests.To say it has been a long time coming is an understatement. It is five years since Daniel Craig was killed in a hail of missiles at the end of No Time to Die, and in that time – even long before it – a swarm of actors have been tipped to replace him, only to age out of the role due to a combination of indecisiveness and cutthroat backstage corporate shenanigans. Whoever is declared to be 007 will be joining the franchise after what is likely to be the longest fallow period in the franchise’s 64-year history.10:14Who will be the next James Bond? - The LatestAs such, this is kind of a big weekend. Let’s run through what we know so far.The candidatesIf three actors are to screen test for Bond this weekend, then they are Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. If there are more – some outlets state that one other actor might be participating, others two – then they won’t include Jack O’Connell orJacob Elordi, who are both out of the race for one reason or another.The identity of the other actors are not yet known. Let’s take an uneducated guess and assume thatone of them is a Beatle(the best fit is Harris Dickinson) and another one is more famous but less suitable (like Tom Cruise).View image in fullscreenI spy … Jack Lowden at the Golden Globe awards, 2025.Photograph: Matt Baron/BEI/REX/ShutterstockThe screen testOutlets are reporting that the screen test will encompass three main elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. These are all equally important for a modern Bond. Remove stunts from the equation and your film will be boring. Remove camera presence and you’re likely to end up with a George Lazenby type, who has the potential to fluff what would otherwise be an all-timer. Remove dialogue and you’re left with Quantum of Solace, and God knows we don’t need another one of those.The chancesYou could argue that Jack Lowden is the frontrunner, if only because the first scene of the first episode ofSlow Horseswas a pretty good Bond audition in itself. It was, you’ll remember, a race against time sprint through an airport and train station, on foot and in a car, complete with hand-to-hand combat and gun play. And it was very good indeed. Working against him is the sense that he’s a bit too much of a teddy bear for a sociopath like Bond. Plus the fact that he has spent every subsequent scene of Slow Horses doing a pretty good Simon Pegg impression.Callum Turner would seem to make a sexier Bond, partly because he was able to conjure chemistry from the very sillysex purge movie One Night Only, and partly because he’s married to Dua Lipa, who would almost certainly get the role of Bond Girl Who Dies First if he were cast.View image in fullscreenLooks good … Josh O’Connor at the premiere of Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, Los Angeles, 2025.Photograph: Image Press Agency/NurPhoto/ShutterstockI still think Josh O’Connor would be the best fit, though. He looks good in a tux, as anyone who has seen The Crown will testify. He is very good at convincingly delivering absolute nonsense, as anyone who has seenDisclosure Daywill testify. However, his best-known stunt work must be the long scene inThe Mastermindin which he slowly climbs up and down a ladder several times in a row.What’s missing?Now, this is all well and good for a traditional Bond film. But we’re talking about an Amazon Bond film, directed byDenis Villeneuve. This means that more will be asked of whoever gets the role, and the screen tests are the perfect way to see if they can pull it off.For example, which of the finalists will best be able to carry their voice in such a way that it isn’t drowned out by all the seat-rumbling full-volume honking noises that Villeneuve will almost certainly use instead of a traditional soundtrack? Which of the actors will most convincingly be able to interact with a side character created with the express purpose of carrying their own spin-off series, to better sustain cross-media IP synergy? Which of them will least overtly die on the inside during the scene in which an Amazon drone delivers them a gun? That is the stuff that will really make or break James Bond going forward.Explore more on these topicsJames BondJacob ElordiJack O'ConnellJosh O'ConnorJack LowdenDenis VilleneuveSlow HorsesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV show | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Celia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owl
Content: In the hood … Claudia Winkleman, host of The Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/Euan CherryView image in fullscreenIn the hood … Claudia Winkleman, host of The Traitors.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Cody Burridge/Euan CherryThe Traitors‘I always think my head will fall off when Traitors turn on each other’: the inside story of the world’s biggest TV showCelia’s guffs, Richard’s gaffes, Claudia’s glorious knitwear – The Traitors has become the most successful show on the planet. The creators and the queen of the castle herself talk exploding pirate ships, becoming evil and Barry the owlMichael HoganFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt all began on a Dutch trading ship in 1628. No, really. When the Batavia set sail from Amsterdam, it crashed and the shipwrecked survivors were left stranded on a tiny island off the coast of Western Australia. As mutineers eyed the Batavia’s stash of silver, shipmates, friends and families turned on each other. About 100 people were brutally murdered, making it one of the most violent chapters in maritime history.Nearly 400 years later, in 2015, creative entrepreneur Marc Pos had a lightbulb moment while reading about this “adult Lord of the Flies” atrocity. It gave him the idea for a reality TV show – the game of trust and treachery we now know asThe Traitors. It was originally envisaged to take place on a boat, with banished players jumping overboard into the sea.Co-creator Jasper Hoogendoorn joined Pos to develop the idea, The Mutineers. After 20 rejections, they fine-tuned the game further. Filming it on a boat was too limiting, so they shifted the action on to dry land – and looked for more aesthetic inspiration. Pos was once a choirboy in a 14th-century cathedral, gazing up at its spooky gothic architecture. This became the template for the show’s setting: cue cloak-clad figures walking silently down torch-lit corridors to a secret tower. The Traitors was finally born in 2021, now known as De Verraders.UK production company Studio Lambert – maker of superior reality TV from Gogglebox to Race Across the World – soon clocked this new Dutch show. “We watched it in the office and couldn’t stop talking about it,” says creative director Mike Cotton. “Reality TV goes in cycles. At the time, it was in a phase of dating shows. This felt totally different. It wasn’t about love, it was about trust.” He and executive producer Sarah Fay visited the Netherlands to witness the phenomenon first-hand. “We went straight to the set,” says Cotton. “All these people in a castle were discussing how someone had been murdered and taking it very seriously. Even unedited, it was fascinating to watch.”Snapping up the UK and US rights, Studio Lambert began adapting it. “The Dutch version was smaller, so we supersized it,” says Cotton. “We tweaked the format. Changed the endgame. We decided to film the British and American shows at the same castle in the Scottish Highlands.” Each episode is estimated to cost £1m, almost double a normal reality show, enabling it to splash out on cinematic flourishes such as exploding pirate ships and creepy cabins.Now all it needed was a worthy host. Enter Claudia Winkleman, clad in covetable knitwear. “[BBC One controller] Kate Phillips said she had a show for me,” recalls Winkleman. “It was in Scotland for four weeks. But I don’t leave the kids or my bed, so I said no thanks and forgot all about it. Then Kate said: ‘You should rethink. I’m going to send you the original series they made in Holland.’ I watched two episodes and called back to say I was booking my train to Inverness.”View image in fullscreenCaped crusaders … Maya Jama and Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry/PA“Once we had Ardross Castle and Claudia, everything fell into place,” says Cotton. “The UK version quickly became its own thing.” Launching in 2022, it pulled in ratings of about 4 million. As buzz spread and punters caught up on iPlayer, audience figures grew exponentially. The second series leapt to 7 million, the third to 9 million, the fourth to 11.5 million. The inaugural celebrity edition last autumn peaked at 14.9 million, making it the year’s most-watched show.Did Winkleman ever imagine such stratospheric numbers? “Not a chance,” she laughs. “But I don’t like knowing about ratings. My BBC boss Ed [Havard, director of entertainment] called me a couple of weeks ago to say ‘10 million’. I told him it was a clerical error and never to call me again.”Fay believes Winkleman is key to the show’s success. “As much as possible, we wanted The Traitors to feel like a drama,” she says. “That was our approach in every department, be it set design, music or Claudia’s wardrobe. It needed to feel like a premium show. Claudia’s integral to that. It’s not your usual reality host role, where they’re slightly removed from the action. She’s embedded as queen of the castle and obsessed with the game. Right from the start, she begged to have screens in her dressing room so she could watch the footage.”Ever modest, Winkleman plays down her importance. “I disagree with that quite viciously,” she says. “At first, I couldn’t bear being mean or cold. I loathed not smiling and telling everyone they were amazing. But under Sarah’s guidance, I learned to trust that I could be a bit strict. It’s hard because I feel protective and maternal – is that weird? – towards all our players. I want them to know they’re smashing it. Then again, I’m dressed like Chewbacca and throwing portraits on the floor, so I’m hard to take seriously.”Now airing in more than 40 countries, The Traitors has officially become the most successful TV show on the planet. It has won Baftas and Emmys, while spawning board games, stage shows, escape rooms, even a Prom. Did TV insiders expect the show to strike global gold?“Nobody saw it coming,” says Deadline’s TV expert Jake Kanter. “Viewing figures growing steadily is always a good sign because it means word of mouth is strong. The best definition of a hit is that you don’t need to tell anyone how well it’s performing, they just know. Your friends, family and colleagues are talking about it.”When Pos and Hoogendoorn shopped the show around, they resisted pressure to compromise and dug their heels in over certain core principles. One was that gameplay should take place in a self-contained bubble with minimal interference.View image in fullscreenDead end … Claudia Winkleman arrives in style in The Celebrity Traitors.Photograph: Euan Cherry/BBC/Studio Lambert“The Dutch always talked about it as a game, not a TV show,” says Cotton. “This is the game, these are the rules. After that, they’re very hands-off. That’s something we’ve adopted. We set up the game and just let it go. That’s rare nowadays. We never want producers to come up at the round table or be the reason someone’s suspected as a Traitor. If you interfere, they’ll latch on to it. We plan certain elements but have no way of controlling what happens.”Another cardinal rule was that the identity of the Traitors isn’t hidden from the audience. Wouldn’t it be better if viewers played detective, too? “We did dabble with the audience not knowing with the Secret Traitor twist in series four,” says Fay. “But what’s delicious for the viewer is that they’re in on it all. They see the strategies and paranoia on both sides. Imagine if you didn’t know Alan Carr was a Traitor last year. You’d have missed out on the hilarity of him sweating, panicking and going: ‘What am I doing?’”Winkleman finds the psychology of the game endlessly fascinating. “It’s about gut instinct,” she says. “Turns out it doesn’t exist. It’s about what happens when we try and ‘read’ people. It’s about trust, betrayal, friendship, all of it.” It’s no coincidence that The Traitors was conceived during the era of fake news and social media manipulation. In a post-truth world, it offers insights into conspiracy theories, herd mentality and groupthink.“What still wows me is that every series is completely different,” says Fay. “That’s the beauty of a murder mystery. We’re just back from filming the seventh UK series and, again, there are things coming up that you’ve never seen before.”When did the makers realise they had a smash hit on their hands? “For me, it was episode four of the first series,” says Fay. “The Red Breakfast, when Tom stood up and went: ‘Alex isn’t a Traitor, she’s my girlfriend!’ We were watching the rushes with our mouths wide open.”“It’s rare to find a format that’s multi-generational,” says Fay. “Remember when we walked down the street and pubs were showing the series one final on big screens, like a football match?” grins Cotton. “That blew our minds.”What have been Winkleman’s highlights? “There are so many I could bore you for 18 months straight. I often have to stop myself gasping out loud at the round table. When the Faithful catch a Traitor, it’s electric. If Traitors turn on Traitors, I always think my head is going to fall off. And I still get a total buzz from going into the turret. It feels very special to be allowed in there.”For its award-garlanded host, The Traitors has been transformative. “It’s the greatest job I’ve ever been given,” says Winkleman. “It has changed my life and my career, no question. I’ll be there with Barry the owl long after they’ve fired me. I’ve also told the peacock to make room in the shed where he roosts.”View image in fullscreenFlying friend … Claudia Winkleman in The Traitors castle.Photograph: BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryThe Traitors has overtaken Strictly Come Dancing as the BBC’s crown jewel but it’s a mutually beneficial relationship. From Celia Imrie’s guff to Richard E Grant’s gaffe, from Ross Kemp’s twitching paranoia to James Acaster’s trembling terror, the franchise thrives on communal talking points. It wouldn’t work nearly as well being binged on a streamer. “The Traitors demonstrates the power of television to bring people together,” says Kanter. “At a time when there’s lots of existential hand-wringing about the health of the broadcast industry – and the BBC particularly – it’s a reminder that when terrestrial TV is good, it’s something to treasure.”The chaotic second celebrity series reaches its climax this week, with 17 million expected to tune in. What can they reveal about Friday’s final? Fay laughs. “I’m trying to work out what we can tell you without ruining anything.” “It’s stressful and unpredictable,” says Cotton. “Genuinely surprising, even for us,” adds Fay. “With real heart-in-mouth moments.”“I always cry at the endgame, regardless of who wins,” concludes Winkleman. “Whoever is left standing has played the best game. I feel incredibly proud of them. This series is no different. It feels momentous.”The Celebrity Traitors climaxes at 8pm on Thursday 29 October and Friday 30 October on BBC One and iPlayer.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ring | Television | The Guardian
description: Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Human heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation Game
Content: High stakes ones and zeros … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenHigh stakes ones and zeros … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MaxTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Narco Hack review – an epic tale of how detectives’ tech wizardry smashed a billion-euro drugs ringHuman heroism is celebrated in profoundly personal ways in this extraordinary tale of a mind-boggling investigation into massive criminal organisations. It’s part The Wire, part The Imitation GamePhil HarrisonFri 23 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe begin with the audio of a horrifying call made to the French police in 2020. Two men are driving home when their car is attacked. The police ask for the caller’s name as bullets ricochet around the vehicle. “Who cares what we’re called?” the man shouts. “I’m going to die!” Seconds later, his companion is dead. This killing (of a mechanic called Houcine Hakkar) was planned and discussed in detail on an app called Sky ECC. The police were at the tip of an enormous iceberg.Showing modern law enforcement on screen can be a challenge: in the online era, it’s less cops and robbers; more zeros and ones. So it’s a surprise to be confronted with something as thrilling as The Narco Hack. This three-part documentary explores an extraordinary investigation by French, Belgian and Dutch police, during which they undermined several massive criminal organisations via methods at once impressively logical and completely mind-boggling by compromising Sky ECC’s encryption software.Sky ECC was developed by a company called Sky Global, apparently with lawyers and journalists in mind. The app was designed to strip phones of all their normal features, leaving just itself. When the app was shut down, the phones deactivated. Oh, and the phones could be wiped remotely, which was a handy feature. “At Sky, they knew very well that it wasn’t going to be choirboys buying it,” says “Albert”, a drug dealer. “You weren’t going to be talking to your mum on Sky.” Thomas Herdman, who worked for the company, is interviewed and offers an unconvincing defence constructed around the idea that a luxury hotelier wouldn’t ask their guests how they could afford to stay at the hotel.View image in fullscreenEngaging … The Narco Hack.Photograph: HBO MAXAnd so begins an epic tale of brave detective work and tech wizardry. This kind of material is undeniably hard to render visually – but while The Narco Hack does feature an awful lot of scrolling computer text and close-ups of smartphones being turned on, it also hears at length from the cops involved. From shrewd, single-minded prosecutor Johanna Brousse to eccentric cybercrime whiz “Bertillon” (his name is protected and he appears via a series of AI-rendered face-swaps), they’re an engaging bunch.Furthermore, the investigation grips hard, and the stakes are extremely high. As Bertillon walks us through the decryption process (server locations, cryptographic keys: you’re glazing over already, aren’t you?), most viewers almost certainly won’t fully understand. However, what unfolds on the ground is approximately The Wire meets The Imitation Game. The various police jurisdictions involved aren’t singing from the same charge sheet – the Belgians want to stop the drugs and guns moving, while the French want to identify suspects and follow them.Then there’s the issue of how much to reveal to their quarries. As the detectives realise they’re looking over the shoulders of drug kingpins, they also understand that if they act hastily, they’ll only land small fry. How much further could access take them? This dilemma is sharpened by the sheer horror of what is being revealed as indigestible chunks of gibberish text become comprehensible. Sexual torture. Skin flayed with scorching hot skillets. An innocuous-looking pink house in Serbia which turns out to contain meat grinders into which informants are fed. Surely, at some point, the police have to stop intelligence-gathering and start smashing down front doors?Police raids across Europe after encrypted phone network shut downRead moreSoon enough, they do. They uncover billions of euros (mainly laundered via cryptocurrency) and Dubai-resident drug lords calling themselves things like Saddam Hussein, Putin and Hitler. It’s hugely satisfying to witness but feels like a sisyphean task all the same. Underpinning everything is perhaps the crucial conversation of our era. About the thin line between innovation and crime. About who polices tech companies and how. And about where responsibility ultimately lies.This documentary is specific in its field of interest but it’s more widely thought-provoking, prompting consideration of everything from social media companies that enable the creation of child sexual abuse material to AI companies and their laissez-faire attitude to intellectual and creative theft. Sky ECC is what happens when tech finds its ideal users and, for reasons of commercial expediency, simply shrugs its shoulders.Still, there’s a very human heroism being celebrated here. The consequences of the hack were significant in all sorts of smaller, more profoundly personal ways too. In the wake of Houcine Hakkar’s horrible fate, there were mutterings about the unlikeliness of smoke without fire. In revealing the conversations around his killing, the hack unequivocally cleared his name. His murder had been a terrible mistake. The look on his sister’s face as she talks about her brother suggests that’s no small consolation.The Narco Hack is on HBO Max nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewCybercrimeHackingDocumentaryFactual TVOrganised crimeEncryptionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender | Movies | The Guardian
description: The auteur’s new film – a study of class, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says
Author: Rebecca Liu
Headline: The auteur’s new film – a study of class, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he says
Content: Lee Chang-Dong … ‘I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story?’Photograph: Chae Dae-han/NetflixView image in fullscreenLee Chang-Dong … ‘I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story?’Photograph: Chae Dae-han/NetflixMoviesInterview‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contenderRebecca LiuThe auteur’s new film – a study of labour, capital and the fallout of redundancy – won the grand jury prize at Venice. Telling tales of the disenfranchised is ‘our moral responsibility’, he saysFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAquintessential 21st-century horror story: a private equity firm has set its sights on your company. That’s the premise behind director Lee Chang-dong’s new film, Possible Love, and the idea for it first came more than a decade ago, when mass layoffs resulted in a standoff that “fundamentally changed the Korean labour movement”.In 2009, workers at Ssangyong Motors company protested against plans to lay off between 37 and 43% of the workforce, staging a historic 77-day strike and occupation of the factory that was eventually broken up by riot police. “Until that point in time in Korea, labourers’ rights were widely accepted,” Lee says, speaking through an interpreter in a central London hotel; “however, afterwards, the basic rights of labourers changed; to the public, they couldn’t be seen as more important than market profitability or corporate competitiveness.”At the time, Lee shelved the project. “The more I examined the pain of these individuals” – after the violent crackdown on the Ssangyong Motors strike, there were several suicides, and reports of long-term mental health issues – “I constantly asked myself: am I worthy of telling this story? And if I am, how do I tell it? Do I stand close to the workers, or keep my distance?” Later he and his co-writer Oh Jung-mi, wrote “many different” scripts, including one with post-apocalyptic elements, before Oh suggested introducing a character who is a documentary film-maker, thereby finding a way to work in Lee’s ambivalence about his intentions.The result is a sharply observed Russian doll of a film that places a narrative about “labour and its relationship to capital” within a broader story about the ethics of film-making, and the tensions and desires that emerge when a working-class couple collide with an astronomically wealthy one. It has, like many of Lee’s previous films, been received to great acclaim: it recently won the grand jury prize atVenice film festival, and has been hailed by critics as one of the best films of the year.The film’s opening title shows the 10th commandment, “Thou shalt not covet”. You can already guess that it will be swiftly broken. Soon we see the depressed Ho-seok, who has been fired from his job at a metal factory, reprimanding his free-spirited wife Mi-ok for caring about her clothes. They’re on their way to a funeral of Ho-seok’s former colleague, who killed himself after being made redundant, and meet the ambitious film-maker Lee Ye-ji and her financier husband Sang-woo. They radiate the kind of glow afforded by wealth. After a stay at a luxury resort in Qatar made Ye-ji reflect on the nature of hidden labour, she’s making a film about the state of labour in Korea, and believes she’s found her ideal subjects; if only Ho-seok, who refuses to go to therapy let alone talk about his experiences in front of a camera, would agree.Since his first feature in 1997, Lee, now 72, has made luminous yet unsparing films about disempowered people swept up in brutal economic and political circumstances: his protagonists include blue-collar workers, ex-prisoners, people with disabilities. In his previous film Burning, an adaptation of a Haruki Murakami short story, a poor writer battles for a woman’s affections with a wealthier rival. (Possible Love brings together two lead actors from Lee’s most acclaimed films; Secret Sunshine’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu who starred Peppermint Candy and Oasis.) Class tensions bristle throughout his work: now, however, he’s wondering whether we’ve outstripped the usefulness of the term.“It’s difficult to use the word ‘class’ because it is so vast,” he says of the difference between the couples in Possible Love. He describes Sang-woo, who moves about the world with possessive ease, an allure and emptiness, as a “symbol of capital … It’s not even that Sang-woo is a wealthy man. It’s about how he is capable of moving and controlling a huge amount of capital. And that capital creates further wealth. It’s almost as if you can’t really grasp how much wealth it creates. It’s just something of a different dimension.” At the same time, “I didn’t want to show that the two couples belong to completely different worlds, because they do live in the same world.” It is, after all, the abstract financial machinations of people like Sang-woo that materially overturn the lives of people like Ho-seok. Making the characters interact together at restaurants, their homes, and on a charged summer holiday “was going to naturally bring out the tension, the hidden power difference between them. There is a gap that just cannot be crossed.”The film exposes the audience to many different kinds of looking: we are shown Ye-ji’s documentary footage; a CCTV feed; newsreel-style clips of a violent police crackdown on a workers’ strike. Lee wanted to study the “issue of the gaze”; “the ethics of capturing and observing the lives and pain of others”. Ye-ji has a habit of holding her camera up at inappropriate moments, often to the discomfort of Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s young son, Cheol. I wonder if she’s supposed to be a sympathetic character. “Anyone who’s really hardworking, they tend to overdo it,” Lee says. He feels a “closeness” to her, “and cameras by their nature search for drama.” Can there ever be equality between a film-maker and their subject? “It’s very hard to be equal because the person holding the camera without even realising it is given power. And it’s a one-sided relationship.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markI am dependent on capital to get my films made but trying to protect my own voice. It is almost the fate of all film-makersIn his telling, Lee became a film-maker almost by accident. He was a writer in 1980sSouth Korea, then under a military government, feeling called to draw attention to human suffering: “That was our moral responsibility.” As the country moved towards democracy and into the new century, he felt that although the suffering still remained, “that moral responsibility among people in literature began to disappear. Literature that dealt with the close pains of reality were treated as if they were expired goods. I was disappointed with that change.” He took up screenwriting to try something new, before working as an assistant director, “because I almost wanted to punish myself in a way, make myself go through something very tough. I worked so hard at it that people around me were moved, and they said: ‘Oh, you should be a film-maker.’”South Korean films today are known globally for their confronting depictions of capitalism, though unlike, say, Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite (which also features a class divide between two families) or Park Chan-wook’s No Other Choice (also about the misery of corporate layoffs), Lee’s characters are not schemers who attain pyrrhic, depraved victory against the system. We instead are often left to observe how they are marginalised by the world around them; we witness their small disappointments, the cruelties they endure, and how they strain to hold on to their hopes.Yet his films also reveal the small but significant moments of solace and grace these characters find: in nature, other people, or their own willpower. Lee has previously described his films as stories about people taking on impossible fights against large, impenetrable entities. “However, despite that, I think the fight itself has meaning. I think these fights the individuals take on against the world is quite possibly the only way they are able to reclaim dignity. Regardless of your chances of winning, I think the fight itself is significant and meaningful.”Classics of modern South Korean cinema – ranked!Read moreYou could say that his latest film was made after a fight of sorts. Lee struggled to find domestic funding for the film, given the “structural crisis” facing the Korean industry, caused by the economic losses from a strict Covid 19 lockdown, and the rise of streaming services. Netflix stepped in to fund it, granting the film a theatrical release in some countries worldwide. “The character Ye-ji has a wealthy husband. She lives with someone who holds that capital but still tries her best to be independent,” Lee says. (Her husband, Sang-woo, somewhat disparagingly describes an independent film as a “film independent of capital”; “I thought it would be very amusing to have him say that line,” says Lee.) “I feel like she and I are in the same shoes. I am also dependent on capital to get my films made. You could say that I am also someone who is married to capital, but trying to protect my own voice, which I almost think is the fate of all film-makers.”After its victory at Venice, there are already whispers about the Oscars; it is South Korea’s submission for best international feature. I ask what success means to him. “I’ve always made films wanting to connect with audiences. It’s always meaningful for me when my audiences accept the questions that I ask through my films and try to find their own answers. And hopefully that leads to a very small change in their lives.” It’s a fitting answer for a film-maker who has long portrayed the subtle acts of resistance people can mount against a hostile world; who finds in small changes, causes for hope.Possible Love is incinemas now, and on Netflix November 6.Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalSouth KoreainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest films | Movies | The Guardian
description: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
Author: Danny Leigh
Headline: New film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movie
Content: ‘You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria StevensView image in fullscreen‘You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria StevensMoviesInterview‘I struggle to see myself as someone special’: Sandra Hüller on being the star of four - or, possibly, five - of the year’s biggest filmsDanny LeighNew film Fatherland took Sandra Hüller back to a divided Germany. She talks about damaged dreams, Hollywood feelgood and - just maybe - appearing in the new Marvel movieFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSandra Hüller is crying, and it feels very strange. A wildly gifted actor, she can convey every human emotion there is. On screen, though, she is most often asked to embody deep self-possession. Even doing karaoke, Hüller is in control. And in real life, life is good. Her 2026 will end with four high-profile movies this year alone. Two (Fatherland and Rose) are black-and-white arthouse films that centre on her brilliance, and though one of the others (Digger) is already a Hollywood cautionary tale, a second (Project Hail Mary) was a giant $684m hit. (There may also be a fifth movie, bigger still. We will come back to that.)And yet, dressed in film star black, she is in tears. “This is really hard for me,” she says.We are talking about Fatherland. Directed by acclaimed Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski, Hüller plays the German polymath Erika Mann, who in the film drives her novelist fatherThomas Mannthrough newly divided postwar Germany. The Nazi past shadows everything – but the movie is also tied up with the birth of East Germany, where Hüller grew up. (She still lives in what was once the GDR.) I tell her I’ve never before seen a film that acknowledged the utopian dreams of that place and time, however damaged they became. Yes, she replies: German directors don’t know how to approach it.“But Fatherland has a grief that you feel clearer coming from the East.”Toni Erdmann’s Sandra Hüller: ‘Everybody knows the German clichés. Maybe they’re true’Read moreAnd then her voice cracks, and she cries. We reflexively apologise to each other. “I’m just grateful Pawel gave space to this political idea that didn’t survive inGermany, but is one maybe people can still think about. The socialist idea.”Hüller wipes her eyes. Finally, she laughs. “You’re going to say I cried, aren’t you? I can see the headline.”View image in fullscreenIn Fatherland Hüller plays Erika Mann, who drives her father through newly divided postwar Germany.Photograph: Agata GrzybowskaAnd yet she has always been open about the nuance to the East Germany she remembers from childhood – a place defined by more than the Stasi men of cold war thrillers. “What fascinates me is that in East and West were two systems that for a certain time could have learned from each other.” She apologises again; I’m not sure why. “It is this situation we live in now. I feel like I’m on thin ice.”Inevitably, we come to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The subject is doubly unavoidable in light of Fatherland. The Manns originally fled the country in 1933 and they would end up in the US. “It’s no secret there are similarities now,” Hüller says. “Fascism doesn’t arrive overnight. It gets here slowly, in little doses.” Her tone turns businesslike. “The question is what we do about it.”We all contain multitudes, but Hüller more than most. At home in Leipzig, she is a co-founder of the experimental Farn Kollektiv theatre group; a politically engaged woman of 48, she is the single mother to a teenage daughter. She is also deadpan funny. An account of her excellent safety record as a driver is a comic treasure. “Thatshould be your headline. ‘Sandra Hüller – a clean licence.’”She is also a movie actor with snowballing momentum. In 2024, she astonished twice over as the wife of the commandant of Auschwitz in The Zone of Interest and a woman suspected of murdering her husband in Anatomy of a Fall. The latter saw her Oscar-nominated. Now, after Project Hail Mary, Digger and Fatherland, there will also be Rose, a stark 17th century fable in which she plays a war veteran – who is, in fact, a woman passing as a man. Oscar talk is simmering once more. America is freshly excited.“OK, so what is happening is that I made very different movies at different times, but they’re all coming out together. It’s nothing I control.” What is good, she says, is that, with her as the common thread, Hollywood marketing budgets end up spotlighting the likes of Fatherland too. “On the other hand, I struggle with seeing myself as someone special. I still consider myself part of a group. That is actually the highest praise I can give myself.”Curiously, a collective spirit might also apply to the fifth film Hüller is strongly rumoured to be in this year: Marvel relaunch Avengers: Doomsday. Whatever else Marvel movies represent, they have a reputation for an oddly egalitarian vibe on set. I wonder aloud if that’s true. “Me too!” She gives an impish tilt of the head. Ah. For the record, then, Hüller still may or may not be part of the new Avengers.But in theory, a Marvel film might feel unexpectedly non-hierarchical? “I heard that as well! Which would show having a lot of money available doesn’t have to mean abusing your power. And that would be a great thing. In theory.”If the thought of Hüller doing Marvel takes getting used to, it makes more sense after Project Hail Mary. In a deft piece of Hollywood feelgood, she proved the perfect foil for Ryan Gosling’s reluctant spaceman as stone-faced mission controller Eva Stratt. The air of ultra-competence was very Sandra Hüller for Beginners. The film even harked back to her 2016 breakthrough in skewed German comedy Toni Erdmann. Hüller has a glorious singing voice. Then, she karaoked Whitney Houston’s Greatest Love of All. Now, it was Harry Styles’ Sign of the Times.View image in fullscreen‘I love watching people invent’ … Hüller.Photograph: Victoria Stevens“But I think Eva Stratt made some people uncomfortable. It can feel unusual to be governed by a woman.”Still, making Project Hail Mary was another pleasant surprise – her first Hollywood set where the directors – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller – actually lightened the mood. “They made sure we could actually play. Have fun.” She did, though, find it strange being wrangled by runners on the kind of blockbuster where producers want to know where a star is at all times. (Unlike almost every actor on her level, Hüller doesn’t even have an assistant.) “But you can always hide in the bathroom.”Would she spend more time in the US than necessary? “Not right now. No. It’s a workplace.” Anyway, she says, she likes where she lives. “It’s simple. America is just very far away.” And she smiles.She believes audiences embraced Project Hail Mary because the film-makers sought to unite them, inside a cinema at least. “And entertain them without the usual things – death and weapons. So you have a story about a human with a task that lets them be bigger than themselves. That inspired people.”But what about their response to Digger? Directed by Alejandro González Iñárritu, with Tom Cruise as a cartoonish oil tycoon, the movie got poor reviews, then did cataclysmically at the box office. Can we talk about it? “Sure!” she says brightly. “I mean, we expected a strong reaction. It’s a polarising movie. And a political movie, which we weren’t able to say in interviews. For whatever reason.” A beat. “But personally – I was surprised by the harshness of the rejection. People really hated it!”Hüller, though, says she loves it. “Years from now, it will be seen as a document of our times.” But time won’t be able to fix a problem like the thinness of her role as the sister of Cruise’s character. There should have been more of her, I say. “Well, there was.” Naturally, she smiles. Ah. (Again.) More rumours put forward that her role was heavily cut by Iñárritu. “You’d have to talk to Alejandro.” Are they still friendly? “Of course!”At the movie’s royal gala premiere in London, the audience spent hours watching on screen the introductions of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, to the cast and many others. I tell Hüller a cameraman briefly focused on her, waiting in a red carpet frock with a look that suggested a looming medical procedure. The memory clearly tickles her.So what was she thinking? “Well, I thought of the people in the cinema, waiting for us to start the movie, and not being able to leave. Also, my feet really hurt.” But she has a surprise in store. “I mean, I’ve never met any royalty in my life, so I was also fangirling.” Really? Hüller seems an unlikely monarchist. “I don’t find the monarchy interesting. But they are fascinating, remarkable personalities.” So what did she finally talk about with the royal couple? “Oh, I can’t remember. I was in shock!” Would she like to meet them again? “Of course! I want to have tea with them! I want to talk abouteverythingwith them!”‘This is a film to make us unsafe in the cinema. As we should be’: Sandra Hüller and Christian Friedel on The Zone of InterestRead moreHüller is now hooting with laughter.If we do include the Avengers, her fifth film of this most productive year is Rose. Like Fatherland, it is a story of the German past, in black and white. And yet, after fun with royals and Ryan Gosling, Rose now brings her back to modern Germany. It was filmed in Saxony-Anhalt, “where a certain party recently won power”. (This is the German state where the AfD claimed 43.8% of the vote in September.)In preparation to play a character passing as male, Hüller says she watched men more closely than she ever had before. The result was a study of all that goes into being read as male. “Honestly, it left me astonished. I realised that as a woman, I rarely enter a room and think of it as a battleground. But male behaviour is so related to that. Where is the enemy and how can I defeat him?”So do men make bad socialists? “No! Some of the most famous socialists have been men.” Could that be why we don’t have socialism, though? She grins and wags a finger. “You forgot Mamdani?” She also has a related point. “One advantage of being born in the GDR and seeing it fall apart, or reunified, however you want to call it, is you learn no system is for ever. And that is interesting in a time when the things we’ve done so long don’t work any more. So maybe it is good to think of different ways they could work in future.”Hüller is having to rethink the present too. Despite still seeing herself as a theatre actor who sometimes makes films, her German stage career is now on hold – at least in front of the curtain. Fame complicates. “If you are part of an ensemble but people come to see you as if the others matter less, I don’t enjoy that.” But she has a workaround. Farn are now creating two new plays she will instead direct. (“One is about revenge. The other goodbyes.”) So far, she says, the new role has been a pleasure. “I love the discussions. I love watching people invent. And we will see how long this wave continues.”She tells me she is also curious how my piece will turn out. In Germany, she says, interview subjects give notes on a draft before anything goes to print. We don’t do that in the UK, I say. “I know. But as the interviewed person, it gives you a feeling of being respected. Not that I don’t feel respected here. Anyway, I never change much.” She smiles. “Sometimes just a comma.” So will she read this? “No, because I have no say.”And yes, she agrees, laughing, that means I can write whatever I want.Fatherland is out in the UK and US on 23 October, and in Australia on 17 November. Rose is out on 11 December in the US, and 5 February in the UKExplore more on these topicsFilmGermanyPeriod and historical filmsThomas MannEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas | Movies | The Guardian
description: When thousands of dead crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: When thousands of dead crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverups
Content: ‘We just knew that there was something wrong’ … fisherman Stan Rennie in his boat in Hartlepool.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘We just knew that there was something wrong’ … fisherman Stan Rennie in his boat in Hartlepool.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverMovies‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seasWhen thousands of dying crabs washed up on a Yorkshire beach in 2021, Stan Rennie’s livelihood was immediately threatened. Five years later, he’s leading the fight back against toxic ocean pollution – and corporate coverupsRobyn VinterFri 23 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 23 Oct 2026 05.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activismRead moreEnvironmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.View image in fullscreenRelentless campaigner … Stan in All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.Photograph: Courtesy of Andy MartinIn All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like theHorizon Post Office scandal, it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.They includeSeahorse (2019), following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.View image in fullscreenJeanie FinlayPhotograph: Phil  SharpBut it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.Another key figure, snippets of whom we see interspersed throughout, is the Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchen, now the Conservative Lord Houchen. He led the concerningly fast demolition of the old steelworks – featuring the largest UK explosion in 75 years – and rapid construction of the Teesside Freeport project in its place.His denials, as evidence grows that this work may be what caused the die-offs, are a constant frustration for Rennie and the gang. Many of them believe he was involved in corruption and a cover-up, while Houchen denies this, labelling the fishers “activists” and refusing contact with them.“You can say it’s done,” says Finlay. “It’s not done for Stan. It’s not done for Sue. It’s not done for the scientists … or for Simon Gibbon, the chemist who’s trying to get the dredge licence put on hold.”That is something the viewers have understood better than the authorities, as money has poured into an NEFC £100,000 fundraiser for the next round of scientific testing. “Someone in Glasgow donated £1,000 during the Q&A on the night, and people have been putting £5 in the pot, it’s pretty amazing.”Rennie says audience members have been angry on their behalf, and some have cried. “For strangers who aren’t from the area to have that same reaction, it blows your mind.”Finlay says: “People are becoming infuriated by elected officials who use their enormous platform, their enormous loudhailer, to tell you stories that are greatly at odds with lived experience. Our lives are dominated by tech bros and platforms and conglomerates and people that shout very loudly. And that can often feel disconnected from real life.”On top of that, Finlay says, people are simply disgusted by the state of the UK’s waterways. “You can sell off all the utilities in the country, and now we’re living with the consequences of that. You can make as many promises as you like, you can promise as many jobs as you like. But the reality is, the trains aren’t working and there’s poo in the river and everyone’s pissed off with that.”All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in cinemas from 23 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Snowman gets a hi-tech rebuild – with help from Raging Bull and a ‘Hot Santa’ | Christmas shows | The Guardian
description: More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint Nick
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint Nick
Content: In from the cold … Andrew Ashton (The Snowman) and Tate Masuku (The Boy) at Birmingham Rep, with production design by Anna Fleischle.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenIn from the cold … Andrew Ashton (The Snowman) and Tate Masuku (The Boy) at Birmingham Rep, with production design by Anna Fleischle.Photograph: Johan PerssonChristmas showsThe Snowman gets a hi-tech rebuild – with help from Raging Bull and a ‘Hot Santa’More than 30 years after Raymond Briggs’ story became a stage show, director Will Tuckett and Paddington designer Tahra Zafar have refreshed it and added a hunky Saint NickLyndsey WinshipFri 23 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 14.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Top of the show!” says Will Tuckett. On the grand piano, musical director Andy Massey strikes up an arpeggio that could melt the most frozen of hearts: “We’re walking in the air …” It is The Snowman, of course. Raymond Briggs’ 1978 picture book was animated for the screen in 1982 with a score by Howard Blake and became a hit stage show in 1993, an annual outing for Birmingham Rep ever since. Now it’s getting a reboot, directed by Tuckett, former Royal Ballet dancer turned choreographer and director of everything from the National Ballet of Japan’s Nutcracker to a stage adaptation of In the Night Garden.We’re in a studio in Birmingham. As the overture plays, a large wooden box in the centre of the room opens like the cover of a book, to become a house. There’s a kitchen, a couple at the table with a pot of tea and an endearing puppet cat winding round their legs. Upstairs, a boy wakes up, looking forward toChristmas.View image in fullscreenTaking flight … The Snowman at Birmingham Rep.Photograph: Johan PerssonThe Snowman is a perennially popular show but “it needed a bit of a refresh,” says Tuckett. “Theatre’s changed a lot in 30 years – expectations have changed.” Audiences are so used to the latest effects that the scenes where the Snowman takes the boy flying, for example, were starting to lack the wow factor. The old show used a one-point harness to lift the actors, and if you drifted in the wrong direction “you had to swim back,” says Tuckett, miming the breaststroke in mid-air. Now they have a fancy automated system that lets them dance through the air against a backdrop by video designer Nina Dunn. “I was blown away,” says Tuckett. “She made all the snow feel 3D, the landscape 3D.” The effect will be much more filmic and immersive.Puppetry is also much more sophisticated and ubiquitous than it was in 1993, from the trailblazing War Horse to the Paddington musical whose designer Tahra Zafar has created a Snowman costume, which can blink and smile as well as dance. Daisy Beattie has designed a menagerie of puppets, which the dancers manipulate: the curious cat, two pheasants on wheels, a lone fox and some sweet rabbits. Other things you can’t change too much. “The score is the score,” says Tuckett, although there are always tweaks. The original used lots of synth-y samples on keyboards, but the quality of sound you can generate electronically now is completely different.View image in fullscreenPerennially popular … The Snowman at Peacock theatre, London, in 2013.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMost important, though, is the story. “And it’s a story told through dance, it’s not a ballet with a story,” Tuckett clarifies. We might think of The Snowman as a bit saccharine, but “it’s a book about loneliness, and ultimately, it’s a book about loss”. He’s rejigged scenes to show that there’s lots of love, too. The simplicity of this story is the antidote to the fast-cut craziness of modern kids’ entertainment where “there’s a glitter shower – and then all the pyros go off,” he says. “This is very simple, very honest. It’s really about human relationships and family, but none of it is too heavy.” His job is “to slow things down, but keep things moving”.Tuckett and the team had multiple visits to pore over Briggs’ original artworks. “It’s really emotional seeing it, because I was given the book as a kid at Christmas,” says Tuckett. “Going back and seeing his original marks and little notes on it, and the original cover – he used Tippex for some of the snow – it was just amazing.”Tuckett opens his laptop and brings up an illustration of the boy and the Snowman flying. “It’s really hard to look at it and not well up and remember when you were small and when your kids were small.” He zooms in on the details. “I don’t want [the show] to look like a panto – it should feel like the drawings.” He and Zafar had been discussing how the simplest things are often the hardest. “Have you seen Raging Bull?” he asks, a reference I was not expecting. He describes how in Martin Scorsese’s film, all the boxing rings were different sizes and shapes, to give different visual effects, even though it’s ostensibly the same setting. The video projections will do some similar changing of perspective, but there are painted sets too. In the workshop, I find a giant snowy tree taking up the whole room.View image in fullscreenLoss and loneliness … The Snowman, 1982.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyThe book is only around 30 pages long, the film was 26 minutes, and the stage show will be around an hour, so Tuckett’s job is to expand on the material, yet stay true to it, while making it all a bit less gendered. “Like, could the dad not just sit in his chair smoking a pipe and falling asleep while his wife does the washing up and the ironing?” says Tuckett. The biggest change will be more proper dancing. There are some new characters “who are really zoomy” and a Father Christmas who is “a beautiful classical dancer,” says Tuckett. “His jacket is a bit like one of those huge North Face ones, and when he takes it off, he looks like Hot Santa,” Tuckett laughs. “And it means then he can properly dance.”In the previous show, they cast actors in the role of the young boy, but Tuckett has brought in dancers. Four of them, aged 11-14, will rotate the role. “We tried the flying the other day and it was really fun,” says one dancer, Tristan, while Tate, another, adds: “We get all those features from the film and the book and make them come to life.” Jake says: “It’s really cool being part of a new production and seeing how it’s made.” He watches the Snowman film every Christmas with his mum.Tuckett felt that the show, as it was, had become increasingly something for little kids. “I felt there was a bit of a disconnect with the adults in the audience.” The book, he says, is “so well observed, and the humour in it works if you’re a kid, but as an adult, it’s really clever”. Briggs’ illustration of the melted snowman still brings a lump to the throat. Is it going to be a Toy Story vibe, I ask: the kids will be laughing, the parents crying? “It’s totally that,” smiles Tuckett.The Snowman is atBirmingham Repuntil 1 November, thenPeacock theatre, London, 21 November-3 January 2027Explore more on these topicsChristmas showsTheatreDanceBirmingham RepRaymond BriggsSadler's WellsChildren's theatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing? | Music | The Guardian
description: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
Author: Oliver Keens
Headline: Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should be
Content: Rave on … the dancefloor at The Hacienda in  Manchester, 1989.Photograph: Peter J Walsh/PYMCA/Avalon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRave on … the dancefloor at The Hacienda in  Manchester, 1989.Photograph: Peter J Walsh/PYMCA/Avalon/Getty ImagesMusicMurder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?Viral pleas for punters to stop yapping have divided clubland. With ketamine and social media also altering behaviour, DJs and dancers weigh in on how sacred a space the club should beOliver KeensFri 23 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTowards the end of summer, a debate began raging in clubland, kick-started by an Instagram post from the esteemed DJ Jane Fitz. Ahead of the Houghton festival, where she is a regular fixture, she posted a request asking people to stop chatting so much during DJ sets.“What I wrote was super respectful,” she tells me. “A bit of talking is obviously OK. But why would you stand completely still, where the sound is super loud, just to ask your mate about a new boyfriend or what they had for lunch? It’s called a dancefloor for a reason.”View image in fullscreenJane Fitz at Rural in 2025.Photograph: ToshimuraFitz’s plea exploded. It chimed with many, while others were up in arms, claiming that paying an entry fee allowed them to do whatever they wanted. “People were accusing me of being the fun police,” she says. “I’m not trying to stop your fun, mate. I’m trying to give you a better night out.”“I think the dancefloor is dead,” Charli xcx sang on her tongue-in-cheek comeback single Rock Music this spring. Was she right? Many DJs and clubbers are worried it goes further than the yappers Fitz complained about, citing the rise of certain drugs – insular ketamine, chew-your-ear-off cocaine – and TikTok-boosted star DJs bringing in passive fans used to consuming dance music through a screen, who end up standing still filming the DJ and their visuals. Then there is the rising cost of clubbing, prohibiting younger, potentially bouncier dancers from attending raves.As fewer purpose-made clubs have been built in recent years, clubbers have got used to squeezing into one-room raves often in converted arches, warehouses and garages. Josh Aitman, an organiser of the sober-friendly London queer party Good As You, complains that “some parties can be so packed in that I get looks just for dancing”. Separate bar areas are scarce and the 90s concept of a dedicated chill-out room is long gone, so thesmoking areais often the only safe – if smelly – bet for a chat away from the music.View image in fullscreenPaul M’s “The dancefloor is for dancing” card and reasons for it on the reverse.While the audiophilia boom has improved sound quality in many clubs, stricter council licensing demands often result in quieter dancefloors, making chat more liable to cut through and annoy other punters. One diehard group of clubbers detailed the science on cards they handed out this summer on dancefloors including at Houghton. One side read: “The Dance Floor Is For Dancing” with “Please take your conversation to the back” written underneath. The flipside featured a diagram of EQ curves. “Dance music is very bassy, meaning there’s loads of room on the top end of the EQ spectrum for vocals to punctuate,” says Paul M, one of the instigators of the cards.“The sadistic side of me wishes I could just turn the music off for 10 minutes and give these people a lecture on all this so they understand,” says Paul. “The cards were a jokey way of doing that – but it’s no joke. I was watching a DJ I’d wanted to see for ages and two men next to me were having a 20-minute discussion about mortgage rates.” Astonishingly, this group of dancefloor activists wasn’t alone – someone else at Houghton gave out cards that just said: “Stop Talking.”Not everyone in clubland wants the dancefloor to be treated as a sacred space. James Ronald, who plays as Hot Cross Fun and is a resident DJ for the nomadic party Disco Disco, posted a heartfelt rebuttal to Fitz’s post titled: “Please Talk on the Dancefloor.” It garnered a similarly huge reaction. “I get that you should be respectful,” says Ronald. “But she talked about treating it like a church, cinema or a theatre – places where you just observe and nobody communicates.”View image in fullscreenA sign at Gaffe in London tells clubbers to keep chat off the dancefloor.Ronald tapped into an important reason why club culture is such a powerful force: the dancefloor is a place for people to connect. “Community is a really big part of clubbing,” he says. He defends the right for clubbers to get deep. “There’s been instances with a particular friend, for example, who only really opens up when he’s a bit wasted. We’ve had important chats about family and personal issues, chats we wouldn’t have had anywhere else.”It’s a fairly new discussion and, apparently, an intractable one. Dan Beaumont, a DJ who is writing a history of London’s queer club culture, sees it like this: “Gossip is the glue that holds clubbing together. You need an equilibrium of yappers and dancers.Clubbingdoesn’t work when it’s one and not the other.”One possible way forward is for venues to set more direction for what they expect from punters. At Gaffe, a DIY space in north east London, a sign shows two arrows pointing in different directions. One says “Dancing”, the other “Yapping”.View image in fullscreenMichael Peacock having fun on the dancefloor.Photograph: Warehouse Project“The sign is a bit tongue in cheek,” says founder Luca Marchal. “But the arrows point in different directions for a reason. We’re asking people to take the longer chats off the dancefloor. Having a proper catch up is a massive part of going out, so we want that to happen somewhere good.”Until more venues spell it out quite so clearly with signs, interpersonal skills have become more important than ever in this delicate standoff, a challenge for conflict-averse Britons. Compare that with Berlin, where there is far less social stigma around asking someone to take their chat outside. “There’s a certain etiquette that leads to more satisfying and transformative experiences on the dancefloor,” says the British DJ Pandora, who is based in Berlin. “You’re more able to get into a flow state without the distraction of nearby conversations.”British clubs have started to follow Berlin’s lead in banning phones on the dancefloor, a change that many have credited with restoring a bit of life. Michael Peacock, an almost ambassadorial figure for British clubbing, is one of those leading the charge. The 68-year-old likes to arrive at clubs barefoot, often wearing little, and proceeds to have the most fun in the room; he says his peak this summer was dancing for 30 straight hours.In 2022, a video of Peacock going for it at Fabric in London was shared online by a punter with mocking intent. There was a huge outcry: not only are people not dancing because they are filming the DJ (or each other) but they may be worried about someone else filmingthem. “A lot of the debate on social media is about how phones destroy the vibe for the DJ,” says Peacock. “But there’s still scant regard for ravers who are filmed without their consent.”Peacock now campaigns for less phone use in clubs. He praises Amber’s in Manchester which goes further than most “no-phones” clubs with a strictly enforced zero tolerance policy. “There are still times when I have to remonstrate with people,” he says with a sigh.Sheffield DIY venue Plot 22 staff place a sticker over your phone camera on the way in, and will have a word if they catch you breaking the rules. “Our space is small and intimate,” says the venue’s manager, Mike Thompson. “Even just one person filming with a flash would really disrupt the vibe”. Co-owner Adam Seymour agrees: “People say they feel free to enjoy the dancefloor when you take away the ability to use their phone.”If clubbing’s heyday was defined by ecstasy, today’s most popular drugs can pull the dancefloor in disparate and equally destructive directions. Many feel that the rise in ketamine use – a drug that creates a profound sense of dissociation – has made dancefloors markedly less buoyant in recent years.View image in fullscreenLuke Una … ‘For me, music has to be about connection. A night club should be about transcending and escaping together.’Photograph: Sophie FarrellManchester DJ Luke Una stresses that he doesn’t want to be judgmental about drug use, but calls ketamine a “very solo” drug. “It breaks any sense of communal togetherness. For me, music has to be about connection. A nightclub should be about bringing people together and transcending and escaping together.
