The one time I had it, I’ll be honest with you, I thought I was listening to Underground Resistance for 12 hours until I came round and realised that I was listening to the air conditioning unit.”‘Nobody’s going out!’ Why is Britain’s nightlife in such decline – and can anything save it?Read moreThen there’s cocaine, the cost of which has plummeted in recent years and is now as omnipresent as ecstasy used to be. Clubbers have “gone from a drug that makes the music sound amazing, to a drug that makes you think you’re amazing and people need to listen to you instead,” says the DJ Wes Baggaley, a resident on NTS Radio, a London music station.But Luke Una is keen to point out how a revival of a different drug is having the opposite effect. “In the last 12 months, there’s been a lot more unity, love, warmth and smiling – down to people taking mushrooms again. I played a party in Belfast and said to the person running it, ‘Why is everyone so fucking happy?” And he said, ‘Luke, they’re all on mushrooms.’ I’m not advocating using them – but you can see the difference.”Now Jane Fitz feels optimistic: “We started a debate, which was a great first step. I have seen differences, I think people have realised there should be some kind of etiquette. During the breakdowns in songs, the dancefloor has been feeling quiet with people listening again.”When a party pops off, Luke Una also sees optimism: “I believe something is going on which feels like a reaction to what has become a brutal, toxic world out there. It feels like people are coming back to life in 3D again, showing a need to be together and – without being cringe about it – to kind of transcend together too.”This article was amended on 23 October 2026 because an earlier version located the nightclub Gaffe in south London rather than north-east London.Explore more on these topicsMusicMusic festivalsFestivalsClubbingClub culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Which is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debate | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest dates from 1400s
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Historic England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest dates from 1400s
Content: Dr James Wright declared The George Inn in Somerset, which has been serving ale continuously since the early 1430s, to be the oldest pub in England.Photograph: Jane Tregelles/AlamyView image in fullscreenDr James Wright declared The George Inn in Somerset, which has been serving ale continuously since the early 1430s, to be the oldest pub in England.Photograph: Jane Tregelles/AlamyHeritageWhich is really England’s oldest pub? Tree-ring dating helps settle debateHistoric England archaeologist says some inns’ claims to date back 1,000 years are inaccurate and oldest is from 1430Helena HortonFri 23 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 16.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith their low ceilings, timber beams and roaring fires, many of England’s inns lay claim to being the oldest in the land and to have been visited by Vikings and Saxons.But an archaeologist who worked on behalf of Historic England says not one of the more than two dozen pubs that make this claim is being accurate.While many claim origins dating back 1,000 years, Dr James Wright, a buildings archaeologist, said it was difficult to verify whether any pubs were built and used as inns or ale houses and kept in continuous use prior to the 1400s.After painstaking investigation, including tree-ring dating on the wooden beams of pubs – a process known as dendrochronology – Wright named the George Inn, of Norton St Philip, Somerset, as the oldest pub in England. It has fabrics dating from the late 14th century.View image in fullscreenInside the George, set up in the 14th century by the monks of Hinton Priory.Photograph: PRHe told the Guardian: “Not one of the claimants to be the oldest pub (and there are over two dozen of them) are even vaguely close to being so in reality.”I stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all? | Simon JenkinsRead moreOf the George, he said: “The architectural history of the George Inn’s stone and timber suggests that this building has been in continuous service for over 600 years.” He said the pub was set up in the 14th century by the monks of nearby Hinton Priory.Tree-ring dating had helped “to understand scientifically exactly how old the timbers are,” he said. “Because we know medieval carpenters didn’t muck around at all and they would fell the timber when it was green and build almost immediately afterwards, the actual date of felling gives us the near date of construction.”Ye Olde Fighting Cocks in St Albans, Hertfordshire, claims to have been established around AD800, and the Bingley Arms in Bardsey, West Yorkshire, declares on its site: “It’s the original English pub – officially the oldest in Britain – dating back over 1,000 years to a time when Vikings were conquering parts of the country.” Similarly, the Royal Standard in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, boasts that it was a favoured watering hole of King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in around AD880.View image in fullscreenThe Royal Standard in Beaconsfield claims to have been frequented by King Alfred the Great’s West Saxons in the ninth century.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyWright said most of these claims seemed to be “modern marketing strategies”. “The Fighting Cocks is often said to date to AD793. This date was probably not arrived at until 1926 when it appeared on a postcard. Prior to that, it was speculated to date to 1030, 770 and 672,” he said. “There does not seem to be a basis in reality for any of those claims. Instead, the building started as a monastic dovecote, built around 1400. The earliest date when we can say for sure it was active as a public house is the first decade of the 19th century.”Many of the pubs claiming to be the oldest say they were mentioned in the Domesday Book, but the historian said: “There are no pubs mentioned – at all – in the Domesday Book, so any pub claiming to be in it is having you on.”Wright added: “The claims are likely to originate less in folklore and more in canny marketing strategies by landlords, tenants, breweries and pub companies. The claims potentially rely upon the public not being aware of how to accurately date historic buildings.”View image in fullscreenThe King’s Head in Shrewsbury is a serious contender for the title of one of England’s oldest pubs.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamyHe provided the Guardian with a list of the pubs he believes to be the oldest in the country. His methodology was to determine that it was purpose-built as a public house, that it had been in continuous service and that there was archaeological, archival or dendrochronological evidence for the existence of significant primary fabric remaining from the original construction.Pubs, bars and hotels report ‘Burnham bounce’ in optimism but call for further tax reliefRead more“I did consider buildings which had been converted and others which had periodically changed in land use,” he said. “Even with those taken into consideration, there are only about 12 to 16 genuine contenders which have been doing trade since the medieval period. Of these, the oldest date to the 14th and 15th centuries.”Revealed: Wright’s list of oldest pubsGeorge Inn, Norton St Philip, Somerset: late 14th century and 1430-32.Bull Hotel, Ludlow, Shropshire: 14th and 15th centuries.King’s Head, Shrewsbury, Shropshire: 1426, 1430-31.New Inn, Gloucester, Gloucestershire: 1432.White Hart Inn, Hook, Hampshire: 1419-51.George Hotel, Dorchester-on-Thames, Oxfordshire: mid 15th century.Angel Inn, Andover, Hampshire: 1445-55.Kings Head, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire: 1445-55.Angel, Grantham, Lincolnshire: circa 1450.George and Pilgrims Inn, Glastonbury, Somerset: 1461-83.Saracen’s Head, Southwell, Nottinghamshire: 1460s.George Hotel, Odiham, Hampshire: 1486-87.This article was amended on 23 October 2026. A previous version said the Saracens’s Head is in Lincolnshire; it is in Nottinghamshire.Explore more on these topicsHeritagePubsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ryu Murakami, cult Japanese author, dies aged 74 | Books | The Guardian
description: The bestselling writer, known as Japan’s enfant terrible, explored the dark underbelly of Japanese society in more than 40 works of subversive fiction including Audition, later made into a landmark indie horror movie
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The bestselling writer, known as Japan’s enfant terrible, explored the dark underbelly of Japanese society in more than 40 works of subversive fiction including Audition, later made into a landmark indie horror movie
Content: ‘Shone light on the darkest corners of society’ … Ryu Murakami in April 2005.Photograph: Jiji Press/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Shone light on the darkest corners of society’ … Ryu Murakami in April 2005.Photograph: Jiji Press/AFP/Getty ImagesBooksRyu Murakami, cult Japanese author, dies aged 74The bestselling writer, known as Japan’s enfant terrible, explored the dark underbelly of Japanese society in more than 40 works of subversive fiction including Audition, later made into a landmark indie horror movieElla CreamerFri 23 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyu Murakami, the cult Japanese author and film-maker whose subversive, blackly comic novels found millions of readers, has died aged 74. He died on 17 October at home, according to his Japanese publisher Gentosha.Described as the enfant terribleof contemporary Japanese literature, Murakami incorporated violence, explicit drug use and sex into stories that offered a sharp-eyed critique of Japanese and American culture.“It has been a huge privilege to bring many of Ryu Murakami’s strange, original and cinematic novels to an English-speaking audience,” said Adam Freudenheim, publisher and managing director at Pushkin Press, which, along with Bloomsbury, publishes Murakami’s works in translation in the UK.Murakami was the son of two teachers, born in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, in 1952. During high school, he joined a rock band as a drummer, and after participating in a rooftop protest was placed under a three-month house arrest. He published his first novel, Almost Transparent Blue, in 1976. The book, written while he was still a student, is narrated by a character called Ryū, and depicts the hedonistic lifestyle of a group of disillusioned, nihilistic young people. It won the Gunzo prize for new writers along with the Akutagawa prize, Japan’s most prestigious literary award.Murakami was not related to his better-known namesake, Haruki. Ryu Murakami’s books are “edgier and angrier” wrote the journalist David Pilling in 2013. “If Haruki is the Beatles of Japanese literature, Ryu is its Rolling Stones”.View image in fullscreen‘Edgier and angrier’ … Ryu Murakami at a press conference for the Akutagawa prize on 5 July 1976 in Tokyo.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesMurakami went on to write more than 40 novels and short story collections, including Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup, Audition, Piercing and Popular Hits of the Showa Era. Most of his books have not yet been translated into English.Many of his works have been adapted for screen, either by himself or other film-makers. The best-known is Audition, a1999 feature filmdirected by Takashi Miike. The story follows a widower holding fake movie auditions in order to find a new girlfriend. Writing about the novelin the Guardianin 2009, Irvine Welsh described its prose as “elegiac and affecting, but it has the sharp, visceral feel of the butcher’s knife or surgeon’s scalpel”.Murakami’s third novel, Coin Locker Babies, about children abandoned in storage lockers, won the Noma literary new face prize. The novel is “a surreal coming-of-age horror story that runs wildly through the heights of love and superstardom, and the lows of insanity and murder”, wrote Russell Thomasin the Guardianin 2020, selecting the novel as one of the best books set in Japan. “Murakami’s stories never shy away from shining a light on the darkest corners of society,” he added.“All at Pushkin Press are saddened to hear of his death and extend our sympathies to his many readers around the world,” said Freudenheim.Explore more on these topicsBooksJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: Nobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ comments | US television | The Guardian
description: After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye
Content: Adam Brody in season three of Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marchinowski/NetflixView image in fullscreenAdam Brody in season three of Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Katrina Marchinowski/NetflixUS televisionNobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ commentsAfter Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eyeOwen MyersFri 23 Oct 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has responded to star Adam Brody’s recent support of Palestine amid theIsrael-Gaza war.“Everyone is entitled to a different opinion,” Erin Foster said in aninterviewwith the Not Skinny Not Fat podcast when asked about Brodycalling fora free Palestine.Nobody Wants This review – prepare to fall in love again … with a different coupleRead more“You know, it’s complicated,” said Foster, who also has an acting role in the new season. “I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing.“While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s OK.”Nobody Wants This, which returns for its third season this week, chronicles the unexpected love story between agnostic podcast host Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) and rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody).The story was inspired by Foster’s own real-life love story after she converted toJudaismafter meeting her husband.“As the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” Foster said. “The show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person.View image in fullscreenAdam Brody and Erin Foster in Nobody Wants This.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix“Sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”Last month, Brody opened up about his political views for the first time. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he toldGQ. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”Nobody Wants This’s third season sees Joanne and Noah move in together while their siblings continue to look for love. In a four-starreview, the Guardian’s Jack Seale said the new episodes will make fans of the show “fall in love with it all over again”.Foster has often posted about theIsrael-Gaza waron social media.“Nothing that is happening in Israel/Palestine is acceptable or comfortable to look at,” shewrotein 2021. “Innocent lives lost as casualties of war, as well as the atrocious lack of human rights that exist under a Hamas run government.“There is a chance for peace here, and it involves a two state resolution where both exist next to each other, respecting each other’s beliefs, and sharing the holy land that all three major religions call sacred. Palestinians deserve to live in peace without fear. So do Jews.”An independent UNinquiryin June found that Israel continues to commit genocide by targeting children in Gaza.The Guardian has reached out to representatives for Foster,Netflixand Brody for comment.Explore more on these topicsUS televisionTelevisionIsrael-Gaza warJudaismNetflixPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Robson Green stars in a rural culture-clash cosy crime drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Northumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch today
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Northumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch today
Content: Familiar faces … Robson Green (right) as Joe Ruby in The Northumbria Mysteries, with Simon Callow as Father David Rutherford.Photograph: Alex Telfer/BBC/Lonesome Pine ProductionsView image in fullscreenFamiliar faces … Robson Green (right) as Joe Ruby in The Northumbria Mysteries, with Simon Callow as Father David Rutherford.Photograph: Alex Telfer/BBC/Lonesome Pine ProductionsTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Robson Green stars in a rural culture-clash cosy crime dramaNorthumberland is the stunning setting for BBC One’s new daytime mystery series. Plus: The Walking Dead plays what-if. Here’s what to watch todayHollie Richardson,Alexi Duggins,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesFri 23 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Northumbria Mysteries2pm, BBC OneIf you enjoyedSally Phillips’s recent Hairdresser Mysteries, here’s another daytime cosy (if slightly less camp) crime drama with a familiar face. Robson Green plays ex-con and gambler Joe Ruby, who finds himself solving crimes on the Northumberland coast with Liz White’s Oxford-educated DI Rose O’Connell. First up, the body of a monk is found in a priory.Hollie RichardsonOur Great Yorkshire Life7pm, Channel 5More northern countryside goodness, this time with ex-Emmerdale actors Matt Wolfenden and Roxy Shahidi exploring Nidd Valley without any gadgets. Elsewhere, chef Matt Healy is catching lobsters in Flamborough Head and conservators restore Wentworth Woodhouse.HRGardeners’ World9pm, BBC TwoAfter this instalment of the horticultural show, there are only two more episodes before the end of the series. With Monty Don having confirmed his departure, it’s worth soaking up every moment of his tips, centred on Don’s luscious Longmeadow garden.Alexi DugginsWar9pm, Sky AtlanticThe big divorce seems to be heading for a settlement but, in this cheerfully vicious drama, nothing is ever straightforward. A taut episode centres on St John (a frozen-blooded Pip Torrens) trying to bully opposing lawyer Nick (James McArdle) into submission. With his weak spot hit and hundreds of millions on the table, Nick starts to disintegrate.Jack SealeThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneIf the apocalypse had never happened, could farm girl Maggie and drawling killer Negan have been friends, or more? That’s the premise of this alternate-universe episode of the horror drama, which gives the characters (and long-serving actors) a fascinating meet-cute in contemporary, non-zombified New York.Graeme VirtueThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneOne of the nation’s favourite celebrities du jour, Hannah Waddingham, makes her debut on the red sofa. She’ll be sitting next to Cate Blanchett, fresh from her London theatre run, and Steve Irwin’s son Robert. Jorja Smith provides the live music.HRFilm choiceHow to Make a Killing ( John Patton Ford, 2026)9.05am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereEven attempting to remake 1949 black comedy Kind Hearts and Coronets, that undisputed British classic in which Alec Guinness has a virtuosic turn as all eight members of the doomed D’Ascoyne family, is an audacious act of American cockiness. But then “audacious American cockiness” is exactly the vibe that star Glen Powell specialises in. He plays Becket Redfellow, the orphaned son of an estranged heiress, who believes himself entitled to the family fortune and will stop at nothing to secure it – not even serial killing in a succession of silly wigs.Ellen E JonesParalyzedBy Hope: The Maria Bamford Story (Judd Apatow and Neil Berkeley, 2026),NetflixIf you’ve ever wondered how Maria Bamford got that way, here’s the answer: a documentary about the life of this true one-off – your favourite standup’s favourite standup – featuring interviews with Conan O’Brien, Tig Notaro and Stephen Colbert. Bamford also appears, of course, in an intimate interview recorded in her California home, and her singular voice guides us through archive footage, from home movies of her Minnesota childhood through to the basement comedy venues of her early career.EEJLive sportPremiershiprugby: Gloucester v Bath,7pm, TNT Sports 1At Kingsholm Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: A sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and more
Content: Dogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle.Photograph: John DevolleView image in fullscreenDogs, Dogs, Dogs by John Devolle.Photograph: John DevolleChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersReviewChildren’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novelsA sumptuous collection of fairytales; a dreamy Minotaur retelling; the explosive finale of the YA Torch Trilogy and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 23 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDogs, Dogs, Dogsby John Devolle, Pushkin, £12.99“Old dogs, young dogs, dogs on wheels, dogs that want to eat your meals” – this “very silly book about dogs” is a polychromatic picture-book treat for little canine fans, full of bold graphic artwork and audacious rhymes.More!by Ged Adamson, Moon and Bird, £12.99Best friends Squirrel and Mouse are on a blissful walk together, but Squirrel keeps wanting more – a hat, a tie, a boingy stick! – until he realises it’s all pointless without Mouse to share it. A slyly hilarious anti-consumerist picture book that encourages small readers to pore over its delightful background details.The Tale That Time Sewsby Sita Brahmachari, illustrated byJane Ray, Templar, £12.99A little girl waits for her new sibling to be born while Nana stitches together family stories in a quilt that will wrap them both in this 5+ picture book; a lyrical, beautiful account of displacement, migration and learning to flourish in new places while remembering your roots.Little Minotaurby Gaia Alessi, Walker, £14.99In ancient Crete, a boy with a bull head is cherished by his sister Ariadne and mother Pasiphaë. Though he struggles to form words, he rejoices in the natural world. But when fearful rumours rise up, he must find his place – and a better ending to his story – in this dreamy, beguiling picturebook Minotaur retelling for 5+.Pomona: Stories of the Cat Witchby Tor Freeman, Guppy, £14.99Pomona the cat witch lives in the forest, surrounded by pals including Ratso, Elfis and Prince Frog. It’s here that she discovers empathy while dusting her house, finds a friend for a lonely caterpillar and helps Ratso break an annoying curse. These daft, whimsical, highly illustrated stories are perfect for 5+ readers with a taste for thoughtful silliness.View image in fullscreenA Year of Fairy Talesby Sophie Anderson, illustrated by Elisa Paganelli, Usborne, £25This sumptuous hardback collection – one story for every month – features retellings of classic fairytales like Jack and the Beanstalk as well as original tales rooted in world folklore. Anderson’s lively, adventurous writing marries with Paganelli’s swirling, soaring artwork to create a treasure trove for 7+ readers to share at bedtime or explore solo.Lumi and the Wolfby Lottie Saahko, Hachette, £14.99Sent to stay with relatives in Lapland, autistic Lumi struggles to adapt, and her family warns her that a dangerous white wolf is lurking. When she befriends the wolf, Lumi and local boy Oskár set out on a perilous journey to the national park where Wolf can be safe – though she will have to use all her sharp senses and stored knowledge to get him there. Atmospheric and fast-paced, with intricately drawn illustrations, this tense, heartfelt 9+ animal adventure deals both with the impact of climate change on traditional Sami ways of life, and the deep human need to find where you belong.View image in fullscreenThe Rambler’s Curseby Mikey Please, HarperCollins, £14.99Things are going well for the magical Café at the Edge of the Woods until a terrifying customer arrives: a human. His appearance sets off a chaotic chain reaction, involving a temperamental wizard’s staff, a red motorbike, a stolen gold hoard and a blanket of carnivorous moss. Can chef Rene and waiter Glumfoot defend the Woods from catastrophe in this laugh-out-loud, shaggy-dog spiral of purposes mistook? Developing the world and characters of Please’s Waterstones prize-winning picture book, this is the first in a trilogy for 8+.Girl With a Sabretooth Tigerby Jasbinder Bilan, Chicken House, £7.99In prehistoric England, 11-year-old Swallow, afraid her baby sister will die, undertakes a dangerous quest: to fetch a piece of green jadeite from the heart of a mountain god. Ishi, a village boy, insists on coming too – but it’s the spirit of the great tiger whose tooth she wears that will guide and protect her in this poetic, powerful, pared-back 9+ story of love, determination, courage and shared resource.View image in fullscreenAnger Is Only a Shadowby Elizabeth Acevedo, Hot Key, £8.99Lil is on probation. She needs to be New Lil – staying head down and out of trouble until her next court hearing – but Old Lil, barely contained, is desperate to make bad, impulsive decisions. Then her brother Aldwin, hundreds of miles away at college, starts talking about hearing voices, and Lil realises she’s the only one who can help. But can she get to him without sacrificing her freedom? A poignant, complex, thought-provoking YA novel by a Carnegie-winning author.Nightcurseby Emma Hinds, Usborne, £9.99Revenant Emrys Swift has been 17 for 157 years, living a cloistered life in a secret magical library and trying to remember his own death. When three important books go missing, he must collaborate with his nemesis, charismatic shapeshifter Aubrey Vale, to figure out where and why, but as spectral warnings rise around them, and the secrets of Emrys’s death and Aubrey’s life are laid bare, could their antipathy be changing to attraction? A gorgeously readable queer enemies-to-lovers romantasy, set in a richly realised magical world.Flarestormby Moira Buffini, Faber, £9.99In a world where telepaths called Torches are either oppressed or exalted, an uprising is under way, seeking equality for all. The rebels are marching on the Capital, but Torches Elsa and Kaira are struggling to break out of their underground prison, while Rye, in captivity, is being forced to track powerful Torch Petra as she flies into the unknown. And where will conniving Zara Swan decide her ultimate loyalty lies? Messy, explosive, bloody and brutal, the concluding volume of the bestselling YA Torch Trilogy resolves multiple storylines and perspectives in a blaze of pain, fear, loss and glory.Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersChildren's book roundupChildren's books: 8-12 yearsChildren's books: 7 and underFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I wrote my first novel at 12 – it has not yet found a publisher’ | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May Alcott
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May Alcott
Content: ‘The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides is extraordinary’ … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Christopher L Proctor/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides is extraordinary’ … Bonnie Garmus.Photograph: Christopher L Proctor/The GuardianThe books of my lifeFictionLessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I wrote my first novel at 12 – it has not yet found a publisher’The author of the global sensation on being inspired by Harper Lee, the craft of Joan Didion, and the joys of rereading Louisa May AlcottBonnie GarmusFri 23 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryI have a very clear memory of reading Fun With Dick and Jane. I was four years old, and my dad wrote each word on a chalkboard. I memorised them, then opened the book and read them back to him. I couldn’t believe it. It felt like magic! When I was older, I stumbled across the book and was surprised to find Dick and Jane didn’t really have all that much fun.My favourite book growing upHarriet the Spy by Louise Fitzhugh. Eleven-year-old Harriet Welch wants to be a writer, and her nanny encourages her to keepa notebook so she can practise writing every day. But when the other kids at school find her book (which is filled with her meanest, most vulnerable thoughts), she quickly becomes the school pariah. I must have read this story a hundred times. Harriet Welch was the reason I started writing stuff down. She was also the reason I understood that no matter how hard it feels, it is imperative to own and apologise for your mistakes.The book that changed me as a teenagerTo Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee. Scout’s voice grabbed me from the start. It was a deep dive into racism, poverty, hatred and social justice, and it had a direct impact on how I saw the world.The writer who changed my mindHenry David Thoreau. “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately,” he wrote in Walden, “to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.” I was 18, loved the outdoors, craved adventure, and desperately wanted to see what I was made of. But it’s hard to get work from a mountaintop, so I settled for living deliberately in my tiny, overpriced, noisy, too-hot apartment. Survival comes in many forms.The book that made me want to be a writerFun With Dick and Jane! Seriously. I was in love with reading from the very beginning, and writing a story seemed like the obvious next step. At age five I wrote my first book. It was a page long and included an illustration. It has not yet been picked up by a publisher. I also wrote an entire novel by 12. For some reason, that, too, remains unsigned. All offers considered.The book I came back toLittle Women by Louisa May Alcott. I was supposed to love it (I was nine; I fitted the demographic), but it didn’t speak to me. Fast forward 15 years. I was trekking in Nepal’s Annapurna range and found it on a hikers’ bookshelf. I reread it in my tent by candlelight. I couldn’t believe how great it was. Jo is amazing!The book I rereadThe Virgin Suicides by Jeffrey Eugenides. The writing is extraordinary, and the point of view is one of a kind. There isn’t a wasted word in the entire book. I also love to read essays and often return to The White Album by Joan Didion to study the way she crafts sentences. She has an amazing ability to capture the energy of an age, a movement, a fad, just as it begins to slide.The book I could never read againThe Gormenghast Trilogy by Mervyn Peake. I loved this when I was a teenager and maybe I would love it again, but I don’t want to run the risk of spoiling my good memories.The book I discovered later in lifeSo Long, See You Tomorrow by William Maxwell. It’s told from the point of view of a man in his 60s looking back on a childhood upended by murder and the loss of his mother. It’s a brilliant study of how impossible it is to make sense of our memories, because they have a bad habit of rewriting themselves.The book I am currently readingMay We Feed the Kingby Rebecca Perry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy comfort readGrimms’ Fairy Tales.Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus is published by Manilla. title: Taika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movie | Movies | The Guardian
description: Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Waititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feet
Content: ‘Put on ice’ … Taika Waititi at a screening of his new film, Klara and the Sun.Photograph: Steven/AFF-USA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Put on ice’ … Taika Waititi at a screening of his new film, Klara and the Sun.Photograph: Steven/AFF-USA/ShutterstockWeek in geekMoviesTaika Waititi’s Star Wars film is the latest to hit the buffers. At some point Lucasfilm is going to have to actually make a movieBen ChildWaititi joins a long list of movie-makers who were expected to bring a new direction to the franchise, before the studio appeared to get cold feetFri 23 Oct 2026 06.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTShareMovie-making these days is a very expensive endeavour. In 1977, George Lucas’s Star Wars cost $11m to make, which would be approximately $60m in today’s money, and has since amassed $775m at the global box office, including rereleases. Fast forward to 2026 and the most recent film in the long-running space saga,The Mandalorian and Grogu, cost a reported $165m and brought in $346m worldwide. If there was ever a Hollywood gold rush, the mines ran dry long ago.Perhaps this is one of the reasons why Disney-owned Lucasfilm seems to be so terrified of making newStar Warsmovies. Since 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, only one Star Wars film, the aforementioned Mando and Grogu movie, has actually made it into cinemas. But that has not stopped the studio announcing a small armada of other projects – sometimes via press release, more often at various high-profile celebrations, conferences or other corporate jamborees – that have so far failed to reach multiplexes.This week, Taika Waititi revealed inan interview with Inversethat his proposed Star Wars film,announced six years ago, has been “put on ice”. No clear explanation was offered, but frankly nobody should be surprised. It now joins mooted projects from Patty Jenkins, Kevin Feige and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and DB Weiss on the list of Star Wars movies that we were once told we were definitely (probably) getting, but that we never actually did. Some, such as Rian Johnson’s proposed trilogy, have spent years receding into the distance, while others – Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy’s film about Rey’s new Jedi order, anyone? – have never been officially cancelled.The failure of Waititi’s project may be the most damaging of the lot. Why hire a film-maker with such distinctive, punky sensibilities, only to leave them announcing to the world that their movie is now frozen in carbonite? Surely Lucasfilm teed up this film in the first place because it thought it might be an idea to shift away from dynastic daddy issues and planet-sized weapons with inexplicable design flaws, towards something whose plot couldn’t be guessed halfway through the opening crawl?View image in fullscreenNot exactly the Outer Rim … Ryan Gosling and Flynn Gray in the forthcoming Star Wars: Starfighter.Photograph: Shawn Levy via InstagramThere is every chance that Waititi’s movie would have focused on an annoyingly genial Kiwi stormtrooper who insists on interrupting vital lightsaber duels to ask whether anyone fancies a sandwich. Johnson might have delivered 500 minutes of space opera in which the Jedi council are eventually forced to admit that the feeling of a disturbance in the Force is usually just trapped wind. But at least nobody watching the opening crawl would have known what kind of Star Wars movie they were about to witness – and that alone would have been worth the price of entry.This isn’t the film you are looking for: the Star Wars franchise is hamstrung by a massive identity crisisRead moreAt some point, Lucasfilm has to let somebody make one of these films that might go wrong. Familiar faces and established audiences did not guarantee Mando and Grogu the kind of triumphant return we all wanted to see, and bringing back the saga’s big bad, Emperor Palpatine, more than three decades after he fell down an Imperial reactor shaft, was very far from a smart move. The forthcomingStar Wars: Starfighter, starring Ryan Gosling, may yet surprise us, but any film that already has Star Wars in its title and still needs one of Hollywood’s most famous faces to get us through the door isn’t exactly venturing into the Outer Rim.Surely somewhere out there in a galaxy far, far away is a film-maker who can bring something fresh to this venerable old saga. Disney needs to find them, commission them to make a movie, and then actually let them get on and do it.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekStar WarsTaika WaititiRian JohnsonStar Wars: The Mandalorian and GroguFilm industryScience fiction and fantasy filmscommentShareReuse this content

title: Junk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstep | Drama films | The Guardian
description: The Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused tone
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused tone
Content: David Schwimmer in Junk.Photograph: MUBIView image in fullscreenDavid Schwimmer in Junk.Photograph: MUBIDrama filmsReviewJunk review – David Schwimmer is lost in Mubi’s frustrating LA-set misstepThe Friends alum makes up half of a messy and pretentious comedy drama that boasts some visual panache but is dragged down by a confused toneAdrian HortonFri 23 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou could be forgiven, upon watching the first scene of Junk, for believing that this debut feature will boldly, perhaps ill-advisedly, dare to satirize the industry it’s purporting to join. At a swanky restaurant in LA, four people aglow with self-importance embark on the time-honored ritual of discussing the screenplays they’re working on – specifically, the screenplay Martin (David Schwimmer), is “working on”. It’s classic industry navel-gazing, underscored by a tight focus on Martin’s clammy face as he sputters poorly through a confidence game.Clayface review – flesh-stretching DC body horror is very gory but not very goodRead moreSchwimmer, of course, is still best known for playing a perpetually and comedically exasperated sitcom character; it’s hard to square that extremely familiar voice with Martin’s dark bluster on how “drug-addled gen Zers” have “no respect for the communal aspect of the cinema”, an off-putting rant that is also a tad intriguing – who is more pretentious here, the sweaty character or the picture starkly sending him up?But Junk, directed by Jack Begert from a script co-written with Dani Goffstein, swerves quickly and, for too long, inexplicably to a different stratum of Hollywood. Somewhere else in the city, two burnouts, played by Dominic Fike and Talia Ryder, find themselves without their car, pills or plans once a house robbery goes awry. The sharp pivot is confusing, though not unwelcome; Begert, a prolific director of surrealist music videos for artists such asOlivia Rodrigo,Doja Catand Kendrick Lamar, has an eye for LA’s seedy beauty, the way a night can unwind like the city’s endless roads. You could, like the chihuahua nicked from the house and hot potatoed while the thieves flee to the scene to the modest synths of Caroline Polachek’s So Hot You’re Hurting My Feelings, just be along for the ride.Alas, it’s a bumpy and unsatisfying one. Junk is molded from another feature by a different name, Little Death, that premiered at the Sundance film festival back in 2024. According to press notes, that earlier movie was “a different shape entirely” from the new picture released byMubi, though “at heart it’s the same movie.” I unfortunately missed Little Death on its festival run, where it picked up a Sundance innovator award, so I cannot speak to what, exactly, has changed, though the new shape is an odd one: two loosely connected stories of addiction and desperation in LA, one far more compelling and visually stimulating than the other, and only one deserving the film’s billing as a “slacker odyssey” across the city.That section, as AJ (Fike) and Karla (Ryder) struggle to score and strive in nearly equal measure, beguilingly conveys, for a too brief stretch, the feeling of an unplanned evening in LA, hazy and sprawling and peopled by unpredictable characters who are at once assertive and stoned. There’s something appealing, if derivative, to lurking with two kids as they hurdle roadblock after roadblock of their own making. The appearance of Euphoria alum Fike, as another optimistic addict endearing even as he’s lying through his teeth, recalls the audacity of that now-cursed show – an impression unfortunately underscored by a visit to an antiseptic, sinister apartment owned by a drug dealer with “school shooter vibes” (an off-putting Karl Glusman) that undercuts the film’s woozy naturalism.Unfortunate, too, that the 110-minute film’s middle section returns to Schwimmer’s screenwriter, sweatily withdrawing into fantasy with a molten core of self-loathing. The title card, presented 35 minutes in, presents an art exhibit that teases Junk as “a search for meaning in the post-post-modern dilemma” – a line surely meant as a joke, though it more or less describes the film’s grating meta ambitions, as Martin maybe or maybe not writes the other half of the story. It is, I assume, supposed to be ironic that Martin, stymied by a male protagonist deemed too “unlikable” by broadly drawn film executives, resorts to increasingly repellant behavior and flights of fancy. But whatever the intentions (and impressive flourishes of surrealist animation), it is certainly a slog to witness. The fact that, in taking the exec’s notes that he switch his protagonist to a woman in order to get made, Martin is played, for a time, by Gaby Hoffman, scans as unduly cynical. (And the less that is said about a recurring fantasy sequence involving a beautiful woman, played by Angela Sarafyan, in a barn described by his therapist as his “mother’s womb”, the better.) That Jena Malone, as Martin’s beleaguered fiancee, gets a well-earned tirade puncturing his absorption is only fair, though of little comfort.If this sounds like the review of two entirely different movies – well, though connections between the two are eventually revealed, Junk never coheres into one picture. There’s admirable ambition here, and plenty of sumptuous visuals to spare, but the clash between one section’s biting cynicism and another’s ragged heart proves too discordant to overcome. Which is a shame; as a whole, the film may be a mess, but there are little treasures within this Junk to perhaps be reimagined down the road.Junk is now available globally on Mubi nowExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsDavid SchwimmerMubiComedy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stranger things turn an English village upside down in Max Porter’s rural noir Lanny | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emerges
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: A family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emerges
Content: Broken and furious … Hanora Kamen as Jolie in Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenBroken and furious … Hanora Kamen as Jolie in Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewStranger things turn an English village upside down in Max Porter’s rural noir LannyBristol Old VicA family are just getting used to their new home in this haunting drama when a parallel world emergesArifa AkbarFri 23 Oct 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOverheard in the auditorium during the interval: it’s like Tales of the Unexpected meets Jackanory. But if those references are dated by several decades, they go some way to summing up the strange mix of elements in this drama about a boy who goes missing from a village, and the ancient myth of a “green man” who might have something to do with it.But then,Max Porter’s novel, on which it is based, weaves so many seemingly incongruent parts together to create its own beautiful brand of rural noir. It might be better described as The Missing meets This Country meets Stranger Things, except the Upside Down here is English countryside.The story follows townie couple Robert (Raj Bajaj) and Jolie (Hanora Kamen), who move to the sticks and are just settling in when their otherworldly son, Lanny (Lucian Thomas on press night), goes missing. A local artist (Richard Cant), dubbed “Mad Pete” – for his bohemianism or, as a gay man in these parts, for his sexuality? – had formed a friendship with Lanny and is now considered prime suspect. The myth of a pagan figure, Dead Papa Toothwort, looms over the human drama as the police procedural unfolds.It is a lot to transpose to the stage, alongside Porter’s multi-voiced portrait of a village and satirical social observations of country life. Bea Roberts does a deft job of adapting the mixer-blend of reality, imagination and hallucinatory bucolic lore. The production is full of pace and creepiness when it could so easily slide into the ridiculous.View image in fullscreenHaunted set design … Lanny at Bristol Old Vic.Photograph: Helen MurrayIt is much helped by Rebecca Jane Wood’s haunted set design, incorporating the village and its woodland. Screens show scratchy images of bare branched trees and antler-figured silhouettes, reminiscent of a Brothers Grimm storybook. Together with Zeynep Kepekli’s contrasting of warm/cold lighting design, the optics capture the chilling magic of Dead Papa Toothwort’s parallel world.It is smartly directed by Nancy Medina too. Horror and humour squat at close quarters although the story is heavy on green man mythology at first and it does not give enough space to domestic realism. But there is an accomplished bridging of the dark and scary with the satirical and light. The book lends itself to dialogue and the many voices of the village and the babble of modern life criss-cross in disembodied audio, sometimes accompanied by floating sentences written across the set.Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Read moreThis seems, ultimately to be a story about the pain, responsibility and sometimes the emotional disconnect in parenthood. As Robert reflects, “who can have children and not go completely mad?” In this production he is not an emotionally numbed dad but seems a little generic. Jolie is excellently played by Kamen as a mother left broken and furious by her loss, while Thomas does a great job of bringing Lanny to life.Village homophobia is made more emphatic and there is an added racial element: Lanny is a brown boy, we are told, but this does not feel fully developed. Some of the underlying anxieties of the book are lost among the many strands: the sense of dislocation for these urban folk in a village environment and its spikier, more judgmental neighbours; the question of who belongs here, and whom the land itself belongs to, ultimately. Some of these inquires are subsumed by the fever and gothicism of the plot.It swings into the surreally hallucinatory in its final scene. The happy ending might be a story, a song or a miracle – a pagan god showing mercy to the humans that occupy his land.AtBristol Old Vicuntil 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBristol Old VicMax PorterFairytalesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Basma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season | Music | The Guardian
description: Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
Author: Safi Bugel
Headline: Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tension
Content: Swampy sounds … Basma (centre) and Temir Alcy.Photograph: ChloesassiView image in fullscreenSwampy sounds … Basma (centre) and Temir Alcy.Photograph: ChloesassiExperimental album of the monthMusicReviewBasma and Temir Alcy: NAD review – skulking, sultry French-Moroccan crew evoke this shifting season(Stroom)Vocalist Basma and group Temir Alcy offer a dark and disorienting listen that contemplates loss and new beginnings, stoking a captivating sense of tensionSafi BugelFri 23 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe new album from French-Moroccan vocalist Basma and Paris-based group Temir Alcy comes just in time for the changing of the clocks. It’s a dark and disorientating listen, exploring themes of loss and new beginnings over swampy, downtempo rhythms. The 11 tracks here linger somewhere between folk, shoegaze and ambient, with skulking percussion, droning passages and plucked strings soaked in reverb. Opening track Belati sets the tone with its spacious, shapeshifting composition, where ghostly drones and Basma’s layered calls give way to a sluggish beat. Most of the tracks follow a similar non-structure: amorphous but with an intermittent, sultry groove, like the winding bass on Khti Sarah, or the slow, swinging rhythm on Aji M3aya.View image in fullscreenBasma and Temir Alcy: NAD album cover.Basma’s performance is always captivating. Singing in a mixture of Darija (vernacular Arabic) and French, she delivers poetic snapshotsin sensory terms that chime with the shifting seasons: “shy light”, blowing wind and bonfires. On Rised, breathy fragments are looped and reversed into a dreamy haze, while her lilting chants on La Tourne have a hypnotic effect. On standout Al Atlal, which lumbers along like a haunted lullaby, she drifts between soft wails and stoic spoken word.Accentuating the murky atmosphere are the textural elements which lurk between Basma’s vocals and the sub-bass, often so subtle they are barely perceptible. On Belati, traces of oscillating electronics emerge; Khti Sarah features muted flecks of oud. Disembodied field recordings shimmer and glitch like static on Aji M3aya. Cha3ouka is immediately thrown off-kilter by the percussive krakeb, offering dissonant clatter over dubbed-out whorls. On Ana Jaya, where the experimentalism peaks, the line between instruments and vocals blurs as the sound dissipates. The effect is bodily: tension you can feel, but can’t quite pin down. It’s a brilliant, heady formula.Also out this monthDalga(Zel Zele) is an exciting compilation of wonky pop productions made in 1980s Turkey, most of which have never been reissued before. Across these nine tracks, traditional Anatolian psych and pop sensibilities combine with robotic samples, hi-NRG drum programming and delirious, glitching synths.Hysterical Love Projectare part of an ever-expanding pool of artists making atmospheric, trip-hop-inflected pop. The Melbourne duo’s second LP, February’s Album (Motion Ward), is a gorgeous meditation on love and longing, channelled through mumbling vocals and warm, reverb-heavy instrumentals. The quietly pulsing Thinking Woman’s Lament is a highlight. The second album from experimental dubwise groupHoly Tongueis an invigorating listen, propelled by Valentina Magaletti’s ritualistic drums and scattered with haunting samples and effects(AD 93). Ecstatic, echoing guest vocals from Dali de Saint Paul add to the whirlwind on two of the tracks, but it’s the rolling instrumentals that stand out most.Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental album of the monthExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft  | Games | The Guardian
description: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series
Content: Strong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareView image in fullscreenStrong foundations … Mass Effect 3.Photograph: EA/BioWareGamesEA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereftLucy JamesThe closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi seriesFri 23 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTShareEarlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today.It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to aleaked trailer, was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release.The three games that comprise original space-faring Mass Effect trilogy count as my favourites of all time. I first played in 2010, shortly after buying my Xbox 360 and being reassured by my friends that the game was a worthy investment, and have replayed them countless times since. Depending on the day, the top spot fluctuates; more often than not it’s the character-driven sequel Mass Effect 2, which ends with one of the most iconic missions in gaming, that takes the top spot.Released over a five-year period from 2007-12, the trilogy follows the adventures of Commander Shepard: a lawless Spectre special agent who is empowered by the galactic Citadel Council to use any means necessary to protect its interests and get the job done. Shepard’s appointment as the first human Spectre in a galaxy where humans are the new kids on the block aligns with the arrival of the Reapers, an ancient synthetic race that raze all organic life every 50,000 years. Shepard must convince the galaxy that the threat is real and gather its top soldiers, scientists and scoundrels to defeat it.View image in fullscreenComing together to save the galaxy ... Mass Effect 2Photograph: EA/BioWareWhen I played Mass Effect for the first time, I didn’t get it. Its controls felt janky and awkward, and I was thrown headlong into a galaxy full of history and politics that I didn’t understand: the game didn’t spell things out, throwing out names and jargon and expecting me to follow. After one exceedingly frustrating encounter with the Mako, the game’s infamously awkward land buggy, I quit entirely. Some months later, something drew me back: the feeling of a job left half done. The galaxy was in peril, and I had to save it.The second time I tried, something clicked. I focused less on the gameplay quirks and went all-in on its story and characters: the naive archaeologist, Dr Liara T’Soni; the browbeaten Citadel security guard Garrus Vakarian; and Kaidan Alenko, a human enhanced by the military, and suffering because of it. Mass Effect’s story was simple – save the galaxy from a tormenting synthetic race with guns and space powers – but you got to determine how it played out. Players were given the opportunity to make meaningful choices that hugely affected how the story unfolded, and that stuck with me (and millions of others).Throughout the course of the game, you can shape not only Shepard’s gender and what they look like, but how they react to situations. Would they be friendly, and use some inter-species cooperation to defeat the Reapers? Or take the renegade route, tersely shutting down dissenters, sometimes resulting in hilariously out-of-pocket responses? (My apologies to the intrepid space reporter Khalistah al-Jilani.) Regardless of how you played, it was thrilling to have such agency over how Shepard moved and was perceived in the world. But the real fun was in making decisions that altered the story not only in Mass Effect, but its sequels.I agonised over every choice, large or small. Across three games and the far flung reaches of the galaxy, my influence was felt. Races lived and died at my whim, and the consequences of my actions showed up in the most unexpected ways. It made my playthrough feel truly mine, guided by the stern hand of its development team, but shaped by me, and me alone. Shepard’s plight was mine, and I would save the galaxy. I hadn’t played anything like it at the time, and even now, I struggle to think of moments that compare. Its missions and story beats are so ingrained in my mind that you’d think I actually lived them. Such is the wonder of a video game, the freedom to explore and affect the world you’re playing in.View image in fullscreenMass Effect’s unlikely fan favourite, Garrus.Photograph: EA/BioWareMass Effect’s story wouldn’t have hit as hard if it weren’t for its characters: a motley crew of the galaxy’s toughest and cleverest, drawn to your cause for their own, complex reasons. It questioned whether AI had a soul, the sins of the father, and the heaviness of duty. BioWare wrote missions personalised to your squadmates’ causes, asking you to make agonising decisions that could benefit or harm them, and then forcing you to deal with the results. The writers went one further, allowing you to date some of these characters, slowly building from nervous flirting to ratings-friendly romance scenes. Saying goodbye to your squad, who’d been with you through hell, before the third game’s devastating final act brought me to tears over a decade ago. It still does.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s been over a decade since Shepard’s story concluded, and the trilogy is still lauded as among the greatest ever made. I play dozens of games a year, and few have stuck with me as Mass Effect has. Its influence is impossible to shake. It set the standard for action-RPGs for years to come, and despite a furore at its original ending (since changeddue to public outcry), is still beloved and widely referenced in gaming culture.BioWare’s ending feels so final, so abrupt. Despite missteps and mismanagement in recent years, most publicly in the form offailed sci-fi shooter Anthem, getting a glimpse at what the new Mass Effect might have been has left fans bereft. The foundation of the universe was so strong, and in the right hands it could have been another genre-defining story. The loss of BioWare is an enormous one for gaming, a bastion of western role playing games brought down. Its influence will continue to be felt throughout the gaming galaxy.Lucy James is founder and curator oflookingfor.gameand co-host of the Friends Per Second gaming podcast.Explore more on these topicsGamesRole playing gamescommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in Europe | Ski resorts | The Guardian
description: From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowds
Content: Bad Gastein in Austria.Photograph: Guenter Graefenhain/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBad Gastein in Austria.Photograph: Guenter Graefenhain/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsSki resorts‘The run ends in the centre of this beautiful village’: readers’ favourite small ski resorts in EuropeFrom cosy Alpine villages to queue-free skiing, you tell us where to head to avoid the crowdsTell us about a conservation tourism experience– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 23 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 23 Oct 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFree travel to a Salzberg gemBad Gastein is a relatively unknown gem. The Austrian state it sits in, Salzburg, offers free local transport (theguest mobility ticket) if you are staying in the state, so you can travel to the resort via train for nothing. The slopes are directly next to the station, too.Rob OwenFamily fun in the French AlpsView image in fullscreenPuy-Saint-Vincent.Photograph: Santiago Urquijo/Getty ImagesPuy-Saint-Vincentin France is a wonderful, small, child-friendly resort. Our grandchildren learned to ski each morning with great instructors on the gentle slopes under amazing azure skies. Three generations then made memories of a lifetime, skiing the wide quiet slopes together each afternoon. We enjoyed dog sleds and cosy hot chocolate in the slopeside cafes. A wonderful trip.BarbaraProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A historic railway and superb skiing in NorwayView image in fullscreenA ski lift in Gausta.Photograph: Alf Jacob Nilsen/AlamyGausta, Norway, is such fun. Stay at Gaustablikk,thehotel built by Kirk Douglas’s stuntman, a wonderfully quirky piece of local history. Explore Vemork, the historic heavy-water plant where British and Norwegian resistance fighters carried out their daring sabotage during the second world war. For families, the on-piste skiing is friendly and accessible; while the cross-country trails are simply stunning. Then there’s the real adventure: an old US military trainclimbs Gaustatoppen, opening up spectacular off-piste skiing with views and terrain that rival much of mainland Europe. It’s a brilliant mix of history, skiing, scenery and adventure, and somehow remains a wonderfully under-the-radar destination.FionaMarkets and glühwein in the Austrian TirolView image in fullscreenSt Johann in Tirol, Austria.Photograph: Animaflora/Getty ImagesAs a family of four, we lovedSt Johann in Tirol. It’s a comfortable Austrian village with Christmas markets, picturesque churches and gorgeous frozen valley walks – with little marmosets and weasels to look out for along the river. Wherever you stay, you can walk to a gondola. It’s really near to Salzburg airport, too. In Austria, kids get all-day lessons, which is a big bonus. Parents can just kick back or wander around and have aglühweinor two. Prices were very reasonable in the Christmas holidays.NickA locals’ favourite on the Italian borderView image in fullscreenMonte Lussari village.Photograph: Jacques Decro/Getty ImagesTarvisio-Monte Lussarion the Italian-Slovenian border covers 24km (15 miles) of skiable terrain interconnected across two main sectors: the historic and stunning Monte Lussari pilgrimage peak and the Priesnig area. Used by local people and those in the know, it offers sufficient ski runs and good value ski passes and restaurants, and is much cheaper than neighbouring resorts in Austria.NeilMagic in the air at La Rosière, FranceView image in fullscreenFamily-friendly La Rosière.Photograph: Real Image/AlamyStay in the attractive resort ofLa Rosièrein France, in the foothills of the Mont Blanc region. Enjoy the short forest walk to the village, with wind chimes and magic in the air, for an après-ski drink and a cheese fondue in a local tavern with the kids.Oliverskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOff-piste heaven in the Norwegian AlpsView image in fullscreenStrandafjellet.Photograph: Glenn Pettersen/Getty ImagesAbout 50km (30 miles) from Ålesund,Strandafjellethas excellent pistes, but also some of the best off-piste skiing in Norway. Strap on a pair ofrandonnéeskis and you can use the lifts to access spectacular backcountry skiing in the Sunnmøre Alps. The views down to the fjord make this truly special. Pistes are illuminated for evening skiing.GrahamA charming village in Les Trois ValléesView image in fullscreenSaint-Martin-de-Bellevile in the French Alps.Photograph: Delpixart/Getty ImagesSaint-Martin-de-Belleville, in the French Alps (Les Trois Vallées), is low at about 1,500 metres, so go mid-season. The single run ends smack in the centre of the village, which has retained its historical features along with small, friendly bars and places to eat. Plus, it gives access to the whole of the Trois Vallées ski area – absolutely amazing from one small but beautiful village. There are plenty of choices for accommodation, both expensive and cheap.Russell WalkerQueue-free skiing for all in Italy’s DolomitesView image in fullscreenChristmas time in Brunico.Photograph: Nicola Simeoni/AlamyBrunicois tucked away in the Dolomites, just a 90-minute transfer from Innsbruck. I had a great week at the beginning of March. Unlike bigger resorts, queues were nonexistent here. There are runs for beginners through to experts. Great snow and plenty of opportunities to use it.Ian BWinning tip: Bavarian charm and quiet slopesView image in fullscreenA restaurant in Oberstdorf, Germany.Photograph: Harry Laub/Getty ImagesOberstdorfin Germany continues to be my go-to for a quiet and restorative ski week away. There are 130km (80 miles) of pistes for all levels, stacks of Bavarian restaurants, a wide variety of mountain huts, plenty of hotels for all budgets and family sizes, and the novelty of skiing into and out of Austria daily.Neuschwanstein Castleis a short hop away for a day off. Unbeatable value.Daniel StephensView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsSki resortsReaders' travel tipsSkiing holidaysWinter sports holidaysSnowboardingEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Kokum’s spiced tamarind and apple sour – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter

Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Kokum’s spiced tamarind and apple sour – recipeA lively tequila sour shaken up with an injection of tamarind and star aniseDhononjoy Roy DipFri 23 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRich tamarind chutney gives this vibrant tequila sour a sweet-sour depth that pairs brilliantly with crisp apple juice.Spiced tamarind and apple sourServes145ml blanco tequila– we useOlmeca Altos Plata25ml apple juice25ml fresh lime juice20ml sugar syrup½ tsp tamarind chutney–any decent brand will do1 egg white, or 3 drops cocktail foamer1 star anise, to garnishPut everything bar the star anise in a shaker and shake vigorously without ice to set the egg white and build a smooth foam.
