title: Something crunchy, something sharp, something sweet: Sam and Sam Clark’s autumn meze recipes | Autumn food and drink | The Guardian
description: A plate of seasonal flavours and colours – tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A plate of seasonal flavours and colours – tabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms
Content: Sam and Sam Clark's autumn meze (clockwise from top): tabbouleh; oyster mushrooms with garlic and dill; beetroot, apple and mint; Syrian lentils; roast squash, tahini and chickpeas; and fried aubergines, chilli, yoghurt and mint in the middle.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark's autumn meze (clockwise from top): tabbouleh; oyster mushrooms with garlic and dill; beetroot, apple and mint; Syrian lentils; roast squash, tahini and chickpeas; and fried aubergines, chilli, yoghurt and mint in the middle.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.Autumn food and drinkSomething crunchy, something sharp, something sweet: Sam and Sam Clark’s autumn meze recipesTabbouleh, apple, beetroot, minty yoghurt, oyster mushrooms … a riot of colour and autumnal flavours with every forkfulSam and Sam ClarkFri 23 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAutumn is a time of year when our meze plate becomes more comforting and generous, with earthy beetroot, sweet squash and woody mushrooms. The cooking is simple, but the flavours and textures are layered and kept lively with sharp vinegars and citrus. Each one of today’s dishes is considered individually, but also in the context of the plate as a whole, and how each element relates to the others to achieve balance and harmony. And, of course, always serve with pitta or flatbread to scoop up every last morsel.Served together, this meze selection should feed four generously.Beetroot, apple and mintView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s beetroot, apple and mint.Raw beetroot has an earthy sweetness and plenty of crunch that works particularly well with the acidic sharpness of a granny smith. Mint lifts and toasted walnuts bring richness. A good, sweet-sharp vinegar and olive oil are really all the dressing this needs. Serve at room temperature.Prep15 min1½ tbspsweet aged red-wine vinegar(we useForum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar), or good red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilSalt and black pepper250g raw beetroot, peeled and coarsely grated1 large granny smith apple, unpeeled, quartered, cored and cut into very thin matchsticks2 tbsp thinly shredded mint leaves50g lightly toasted walnuts, slicedIn a small bowl, whisk the vinegar and olive oil, season to taste and set aside.Mix the beetroot and apple in a large bowl with half the shredded mint and half the walnuts, pour on the dressing and toss gently. Check for seasoning, then serve with the remaining mint and walnuts scattered on top.Autumn tabboulehView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s autumn tabbouleh.We tend to think of tabbouleh as a summer dish (cucumbers, tomatoes, lemon, parsley, mint), as something fresh and light for when the weather is warm. But the idea of tabbouleh lends itself well to the changing seasons. What matters most is the balance of herbs, grain, fruit or vegetables, something crunchy and something sharp, and all those things can change to suit whatever’s around. This is a celebration of autumn in one dish. Serve at room temperature.Prep15 minSoak10-15 min40g medium bulgur wheat100g white muscat or sultana grapes, halved2 fresh figs, peeled and cut into thin wedges75g lightly toasted almonds, roughly chopped2 spring onions, cut into thin rounds1 small bunchflat-leaf parsley, finely shredded1 small bunchmint, finely shreddedSalt and black pepperFor the dressing½ small garlic clove, crushed to a paste with a little salt1 pinch ground cinnamon1 tbsp orange juice1 tbsp lemon juice3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilPut the bulgur in a bowl, add cold water just to cover and leave to sit for 10-15 minutes. Meanwhile, put all the dressing ingredients in a jar, season and shake well.When the bulgur has absorbed all the water and is soft (if it’s still al dente, stir in another tablespoon of water and leave for a couple of minutes), gently rub it between your palms to fluff it up. Put all the remaining ingredients in a large bowl, then pour the dressing on top. Add the bulgur to the bowl, toss to mix, check the seasoning and serve.Oyster mushrooms, garlic and dillView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s oyster mushrooms, garlic and dill.The seared and nicely caramelised mushrooms give this dish a great complexity of flavour and texture. Serve at room temperature.Prep5 minCook20 min8 large oyster mushrooms, thicker ends of stalks cut off and discarded3 tbsp olive oilSalt and black pepper2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped2tbsp roughly chopped dillPut a large, heavy-based frying pan on a medium to high heat. Toss the mushrooms with a tablespoon of the oil and season. When the pan is hot, lay in the mushrooms gill side down and leave to fry until caramelised and a rich golden colour. Turn over, cook for 30 seconds, then spread out on a platter. Evenly scatter over the raw garlic and dill, drizzle over the remaining two tablespoons of oil, check the seasoning and serve.Fried aubergine, chilli, yoghurt and mintView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s fried aubergine, chilli, yoghurt and mint.A classic Moro recipe that’s also great with salted anchovies. Serve at room temperature.Prep10 minDrain20 minCook30 min1 large aubergine, cut into 1½cm-thick roundsSalt and black pepper100ml olive oil, plus 1 tbsp extra for frying the garlic100ml sunflower oil1 large garlic clove,peeled and cut into thin matchsticks4tsp sweet aged red-wine vinegar(we useForum’s cabernet sauvignon vinegar), or a good aged red-wine vinegar sweetened with a pinch of sugar1 heaped tbsp finely shredded mint, plus extra to serve1 long green chilli, cut in half lengthways, deseeded and finely chopped4dsspGreek yoghurt1 pinchblack onion seeds, to finishPut the aubergine slices in a colander, toss with half a teaspoon of fine salt, then leave for 20 minutes to drain off any excess water and to get rid of any bitterness. Dry the slices on kitchen paper.Heat both oils in a wide frying pan until hot but not smoking. Lay in the aubergine slices in a single layer (if need be, cook them in batches) and fry, turning as required, until deep golden brown and crisp on both sides. Transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to absorb any excess oil. Meanwhile, fry the garlic matchsticks in the extra tablespoon of olive oil, until golden, then drain.Put the drained aubergine slices on a platter, sprinkle over the fried garlic, vinegar and mint, then leave to sit for five minutes.Stir the chopped chilli into the yoghurt and season with a little salt.Spoon a small dollop of the yoghurt on top of each aubergine slice, scatter over a little extra shredded mint and the black onion seeds, season and serve.Syrian lentilsView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s Syrian lentils.The keys to this dish are to toast the cumin, to fry the garlic to the darkened side of golden, and to use the coriander stalks as well as the leaves. Serve warm or at room temperature.Prep10 minCook40 min+4 tbsp olive oil2-3 garlic cloves, peeled and finely chopped1 roundedtsp cumin seeds, roughly ground250g cooked small brown or puy lentils(from a tin or pouch)1 small bunchcoriander, stalks and leaves separated and roughly chopped50g caramelised crispy onions(shop-bought or homemade)Salt and black pepperPut three tablespoons of the oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. When it’s hot but not smoking, add the garlic and cumin, and fry until light brown. Stir in the lentils, chopped coriander stalks, half the crispy onions and enough water to loosen the mix to the consistency of a thick soup. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for five minutes, until the lentils are soft. Take off the heat, stir in the chopped coriander leaves, then season. Scatter the rest of the crispy onions on top and serve.Roast squash, tahini and chickpeasView image in fullscreenSam and Sam Clark’s roast squash, tahini and chickpeas.Kaboucha squash has an excellent sweetness and dense texture, although its knobbly skin is tougher than other squashes and therefore harder to peel. Make this dish last, because it’s the only one here that needs to be served warm.Prep10 minCook30 min1 small-medium kabocha squash(about 450g), or butternut squash, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm chunks3 tbsp olive oil½ tsp ground cinnamon½ garlic clove, crushed to a paste with a pinch of saltSalt and black pepper4tbsptinned chickpeas, drained1 tsp finely chopped red chilli¼ tsp nigella seedsFor the tahini sauce1 small garlic clove, peeled and crushed1½ tbsp tahini1 good squeeze of lemon1½ tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Put the squash in a roasting tray, add the oil, cinnamon and garlic, season generously, then toss to coat. Spread out into an even layer, then roast for 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is soft and caramelised.Scatter over the chickpeas and bake for another five minutes, until they’re slightly crisp.Meanwhile, make the sauce. Mix the garlic, tahini and lemon juice in a small bowl, whisk in two and a half tablespoons of water, then whisk in the oil. Check the seasoning.Transfer the pumpkin mix to a platter, drizzle over the sauce and finish with the chilli and nigella seeds.Sam and Sam Clark are chefs/owners ofMoroandMoritoin London EC1Explore more on these topicsAutumn food and drinkMiddle Eastern food and drinkFoodVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkHerbs and spicesSnacksrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns | Food | The Guardian
description: I like to get pumpkin into everything – including dessert – at this time of year
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: I like to get pumpkin into everything – including dessert – at this time of year
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s chocolate and pumpkin spice choux buns.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for chocolate and pumpkin spice choux bunsWhip winter squash puree into a creamy filling and pipe direct into the heart of a cracking seasonal puddingBenjamina EbuehiFri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this time of year, I aim to get as much pumpkin as I can into my meals, including desserts. If I’ve been organised, I’ll roast and puree some from scratch, but I seem always to have at least one tin of pumpkin puree to hand, which I can use quickly in anything from pumpkin pies to cookies and muffins. Here, it’s whipped into cream with some spices, then piped into crackly puffs of choux for a chic, autumnal dessert.Chocolate and pumpkin spice choux bunsPrep10 minCook1 hr 15 min, plus coolingMakes12For the chocolate craquelin60g unsalted butter65g light brown sugar10g cocoa powder65g plain flourFor the choux50ml milk45g unsalted butter60g plain flour1 tsp sugar1 pinch salt1-2 large eggsFor the filling150g pumpkin puree1 tsp ground cinnamon¼ tsp ground cloves1 tsp vanilla bean paste90g cream cheese75g icing sugar150ml double cream20g pecans, roughly choppedBriefly mix the butter and sugar for the craquelin in a small bowl, until smooth and well combined, then work in the flour and cocoa powder to make a thick paste. Spread this evenly over a sheet of baking paper, top with a second sheet, then roll out to about 2-3mm thick and pop it in the freezer to firm up.Meanwhile, make the choux. Put the milk, butter and 50ml water in a saucepan and heat until steaming and the butter has melted. Off the heat, add the flour,sugarand salt, and stir quickly to bring the dough together. Return to the heat, cook, stirring, for one or two minutes, then transfer to a clean bowl and leave to cool for a few minutes.Meanwhile, whisk the eggs in a jug, then bit by bit work some into the dough, mixing until it’s all incorporated before adding more. The dough will look lumpy at first, but it will come together. Continue mixing in the eggs (you may not need all of them) until the mixture is glossy, falls easily, and leaves a V shape hanging when lifted with a spoon. Transfer to a piping bag, snip off 2½cm from the end and pipe 12 blobs of the choux dough on to a lined tray.Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Take the chilled craquelin out of the freezer and, working quickly, use a round cutter roughly the same width as the piped choux to cut out 12 discs. Gently place a disc on each choux, then bake for 15 minutes. Turn down the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 and bake for another 10-12 minutes, until the buns are puffy and firm to the touch. Remove and leave to cool completely.Meanwhile, whisk the pumpkin puree, spices, vanilla and cream cheese in a bowl until smooth, then mix in the sugar. In a second bowl, whip the cream to very soft peaks, then fold into the pumpkin mix.Use a sharp, serrated knife to trim the top off each choux bun just above halfway. Spoon the cream into a piping bag with an open-star nozzle, then pipe swirls into each bun. Sprinkle chopped pecans on top, then gently top with the choux “hats”. Serve at once.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotBakingPastryPumpkinChocolateDessertEggsrecipesShareReuse this content
